artigo.texto: O Conselho Diretor da Anatel aprovou nesta quarta-feira, 4, a destinação de R$ 375 milhões para a implantação de um data center voltado ao processamento de dados e aplicações de inteligência artificial (IA) do governo federal. A infraestrutura será construída pela Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz (EAF), com recursos remanescentes do leilão do 5G (e posteriormente transferida à União). A Telebras será a responsável pela operação e manutenção. A proposta já havia sido aprovada pelo Gaispi em 27 de outubro. Com o aval do Conselho Diretor, a implementação deverá seguir condições técnicas, jurídicas e financeiras estabelecidas na análise da conselheira substituta Suzana Rodrigues. Entre elas está a exigência de um acordo formal envolvendo o Ministério das Comunicações (MCom) e a Telebras, antes de qualquer contratação. O objetivo seria definir as responsabilidades pela infraestrutura e utilização. Vale notar que os custos permanentes do data center (como conta de energia elétrica, manutenções e equipamentos de segurança, por exemplo) não poderão ser pagos pela EAF nem com recursos do edital do 5G. "Um data center de alta densidade sem fonte de custeio assegurada converte-se, em prazo curto, em passivo operacional", destacou a análise. A estatal também deverá observar requisitos de segurança cibernética e proteção de dados, considerando que a infraestrutura será utilizada para armazenar informações sensíveis e hospedar serviços governamentais. Especificações Em termos técnicos, o projeto prevê dois módulos: um dedicado à IA, com 20 racks, e outro destinado a serviços tradicionais de tecnologia da informação, com dez racks. A configuração de referência contempla 48 GPUs, capacidade elétrica inicial de 2 MW e dois enlaces externos de 100 Gbps cada, além de sistemas redundantes de energia e refrigeração líquida para os equipamentos de IA. Há possibilidade de expansão para 10 MW em dois a três anos, mas qualquer ampliação além da configuração aprovada dependerá de nova autorização da Anatel. De acordo com a agência, a implantação será realizada por etapas, condicionadas à confirmação do terreno, à disponibilidade de energia, à aprovação dos projetos de engenharia e à realização de testes de segurança e desempenho. O prazo previsto de 12 meses é considerado uma meta de planejamento, e não uma garantia de conclusão. Outra condição é que a EAF ficará restrita à implantação e à transferência da infraestrutura, sem autorização para operar o empreendimento, explorar comercialmente seus serviços ou ceder capacidade a empresas privadas. A hospedagem de equipamentos no módulo tradicional será limitada a órgãos e entidades da administração pública federal. A Anatel também determinou a preservação integral dos recursos necessários para concluir as obrigações originais do leilão do 5G, acrescidos de uma margem de segurança de 10%, com atualização trimestral das estimativas financeiras.

artigo.texto: Artigos Quem vai pagar pelas baterias do Brasil? Hoje a regra é clara. A Lei 15.269/2025 atribui o custo do armazenamento aos geradores, como um encargo de uso e de responsabilidade pela variabilidade que eles mesmos inserem no sistema. Na contramão, o PL 3.716/2026, de autoria do deputado federal Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) e relatado pelo deputado federal Danilo Forte (PP-CE), tramita em regime de urgência na Câmara e propõe mudar a lógica e ratear esse custo com todos os consumidores finais, via tarifa de energia. Não é um detalhe jurídico. É uma mudança de filosofia: de um modelo de “causador-pagador” para um modelo de socialização de custos. Os números ajudam a entender o tamanho da discussão. Um estudo da própria Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), feito em parceria com a consultoria Volt Robotics, traz a dimensão do benefício: cerca de 11% a menos de variabilidade intradiária no PLD, trazendo mais previsibilidade para o mercado livre e regulado; cerca de R$ 629 milhões por ano em encargos evitados, com menos despacho térmico fora da ordem de mérito; e de R$ 3,9 bilhões a R$ 6 bilhões por ano em benefícios econômicos totais, considerando redução de encargos, arbitragem de energia, menor acionamento de térmicas, aproveitamento de energia hoje perdida em vertimentos e cortes de geração renovável e um custo efetivo das baterias entre 37% e 57% menor que o de uma referência baseada no último LRCAP. O mesmo estudo estima que, desse total, até R$ 5,5 bilhões por ano poderiam chegar aos consumidores, e cerca de R$ 550 milhões por ano seriam capturados diretamente pelos geradores, sobretudo por hidrelétricas no mercado livre e por renováveis que deixam de ser cortadas. É justamente esse número que os defensores do PL usam. Mas há uma diferença essencial: para o consumidor, o custo seria certo e entraria na tarifa por 15 anos, enquanto o benefício é uma projeção do setor interessado, que depende do volume contratado e da operação real. E o próprio estudo defende que o custeio considere causalidade e benefício. Quem insere a variabilidade no sistema e quem captura o ganho direto precisa estar no centro dessa conta. Principalmente quando lembramos que o consumidor brasileiro já paga uma das energias mais caras do mundo. Segundo o CLP 2026, nossa tarifa é mais cara que a de 77 de 138 países quando ajustada pelo poder de compra. Há dois alertas que precisam ser feitos com transparência nesse debate. Primeiro, falta a conta oficial. Os números que usamos até agora são do setor interessado. Ainda não temos a quantificação oficial e independente de EPE e ONS sobre o custo-benefício sistêmico do BESS no longo prazo. Sem isso, legislar no afogadilho é arriscado. Segundo, o risco regulatório e a insegurança jurídica. O diretor-geral da Aneel, Sandoval Feitosa, já afirmou publicamente que, se a lei mudar às vésperas do leilão, a agência será obrigada a republicar os editais e remarcar as datas. Isso pode adiar em meses a contratação, encurtando o prazo de construção de projetos cujos contratos começam em 1º de agosto de 2028. Trocar a regra no meio do jogo afasta investidor e encarece o capital. As experiências internacionais ajudam a separar fato de discurso. No Reino Unido, as baterias competem no Mercado de Capacidade, e o custo desse mercado é repassado ao consumidor por meio de um encargo cobrado das comercializadoras, mas com regras estáveis, definidas antes de cada leilão. Na Califórnia, o consumidor também paga, mas a lógica é outra: desde 2010, a lei AB 2514 obrigou as próprias concessionárias a contratar armazenamento, com metas que somaram 1.325 MW para as três maiores. Em 2016, a lei AB 2868 foi além e determinou que os custos dos programas de armazenamento das concessionárias fossem recuperados nas parcelas de geração, transmissão e distribuição da tarifa, na proporção dos benefícios que cada uma recebe. Ou seja: lá, quem investe e responde pela solução é a concessionária, e a conta é dividida conforme quem ganha. Aqui, o PL 3.716/2026 propõe o caminho mais curto: tirar o custo de quem gera e colocar no consumidor. E há uma questão de responsabilidade que não pode ficar de fora. Geradoras, transmissoras e distribuidoras operam sob concessões públicas, com a obrigação de garantir qualidade e continuidade do serviço. Em outubro, um temporal em Minas Gerais deixou mais de 636 mil clientes sem luz, e quase 5 mil ainda esperavam três dias depois, no que a Cemig chamou de o evento de maior impacto em sua rede em 74 anos. A fragilidade da nossa infraestrutura mostra que o investimento em resiliência ficou aquém do necessário. Enquanto isso, o consumidor já pagou R$ 4,7 bilhões em encargos entre 2024 e julho de 2026, segundo o próprio estudo da Absae. Pedir que ele pague também pela modernização é cobrar duas vezes de quem já paga a conta mais pesada. Ninguém é contra a modernização do setor, pelo contrário. O armazenamento é essencial para viabilizar a transição energética brasileira e destravar o potencial do Centro-Oeste e do Nordeste. Mas a minha posição é clara: essa conta não é do consumidor final de energia. Se o custo precisar ser dividido, que seja entre geração, transmissão e distribuição, na proporção do benefício que cada segmento captura, como fez a Califórnia, e com base em uma avaliação oficial e independente de EPE e ONS. Socializar o custo na tarifa antes mesmo de operar o primeiro sistema é inverter a lógica e premiar quem deixou de investir. O armazenamento é essencial. E a conta precisa ser de quem ganha com ele, não de quem já paga caro demais. artigo.texto: A part of Watch Medier Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, has bought a 10% stake in battery storage company Aypa Power, it said in a press release. Grid-scale batteries store power from wind and solar farms so it can be used when generation drops, and investors are paying more attention to them as renewables make up a growing share of electricity supply. NBIM is investing as a co-investor alongside Canadian asset manager Brookfield. The stake adds to NBIM’s existing indirect investment in Aypa Power through Brookfield’s Global Transition Fund (BGTF) strategy. The deal was signed and completed on Oct. 28, 2026, and NBIM paid USD 300m for its stake. “This is our first dedicated investment in battery storage. Storage is becoming an essential part of the energy system as the share of renewable generation grows, and it complements our existing wind and solar portfolio. We are pleased to expand our partnership with Brookfield,” NBIM Global Head of Energy and Infrastructure Harald von Heyden says in the press release. Brookfield agreed in July 2026 to buy Aypa Power from funds managed by Blackstone Energy Transition Partners, according to the release. The company also has a development pipeline of more than 20GW, which gives it room to grow as the energy storage market expands. (This article is provided by EnergyWatch’s sister media in Norway, EnergiWatch) English edit by Daniel Frank Christensen

artigo.texto: On a spring evening in Stockton, California, Chase Ott-Wick was strolling into a bar when a stranger stopped him. The man had heard that Chase was the guy building a new data center in town—and he wanted to say: Please don’t. “He had a beautiful home that he paid for and had been living in for years, and was concerned that his view would be disrupted,” Chase told me. But as the conversation went on, he said, it became increasingly clear that what the man really feared was something bigger. “When you turn that thing on,” Chase remembers him saying, “our lives are going to change.” The people of Stockton, which is 40 miles northeast of Silicon Valley as the crow flies, worried the harsh growl of the data center would drown out the lapping sounds of the San Joaquin River; they feared the rampant water use would turn their rolling green golf courses into a sickly bed of beige; they suspected their precious populations of migratory birds and Chinook salmon would be wiped out by pollution. They had heard rumors the data center would soon be operational, and were steeling themselves to fight back.

artigo.texto: The former Hungarian government pledged extensive financial incentives, housing support, expedited immigration procedures and infrastructure development to Chinese battery giant CATL as part of its plans for a major factory in Debrecen. Newly disclosed details of a 2022 investment declaration have shed further light on the scale of commitments made by the Orbán administration. Thousands of foreign workers and rental homes Zsolt Tárkányi, State Secretary at the Ministry of Transport and Investment and a Tisza Party MP representing Debrecen, published further excerpts from the document on Facebook, highlighting promises that could have significantly expanded the Chinese company’s operations in Hungary. According to the declaration, CATL provided the government with annual estimates of its non-EU workforce requirements between June 2022 and December 2029. The figures reportedly started at 42 workers, approached 2,000 by the summer of 2023 and exceeded 6,000 by the end of 2024. The company expected to require between 4,000 and 5,000 non-EU employees in 2025. Following the completion of construction, the projected permanent workforce was expected to stabilise at between 1,000 and 2,000 from 2027 onwards. The Orbán government pledged to prioritise visa and work permit applications, with dedicated officials helping Chinese and other third-country nationals navigate immigration procedures. The local municipality also committed to working with the state to develop thousands of rental homes for CATL employees. Tárkányi criticised the proposal, arguing that the previous government had not shown comparable willingness to introduce housing programmes for Hungarian public sector workers. Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need. Public money for training and infrastructure The investment declaration outlined substantial financial support. Previously disclosed provisions included non-refundable grants covering up to 25 per cent of innovation project costs, energy efficiency tax incentives worth up to EUR 15 million over six years, and training subsidies covering half of eligible costs, capped at EUR 2 million. The government also considered reducing local business taxes and providing municipal support of up to EUR 200,000. Training subsidies could additionally reach EUR 5,000 per employee. Infrastructure commitments were another key element. The government agreed to examine railway modernisation and electrification, while road and rail developments connected to the investment were expected to be financed by Hungarian taxpayers. Stay up-to-date: Hungary’s Foreign Ministry abruptly sacks foreign policy institute chief over links to previous government Potential expansion beyond Debrecen The declaration also envisaged identifying suitable plots of land exceeding 100 hectares within a 50-kilometre radius of Debrecen for possible additional CATL factories. The municipality was expected to acquire land from private owners, prepare and consolidate the plots at its own expense, and subsequently sell them to CATL. The company would not be required to pay any additional fees or costs beyond the purchase price of the land. However, the declaration was non-binding. Individual projects and subsidies would have required further agreements and, where applicable, approval from the Hungarian government, CATL or the European Commission. CATL announced its Debrecen investment in 2022. The first production unit, part of a planned three-phase development, has since received environmental and operational permits, with trial production reportedly beginning in September. The full project, however, remains unfinished.

artigo.texto: The 2026 midterm election blue wave, which shifted the balance of power in Congress and across state races toward Democrats, can be seen as a repudiation of AI and the controversial data centers that provide its computing power. Data center proponents have heavily backed President Donald Trump and Republican candidates, underscored by xAI CEO Elon Musk investing hundreds of millions of dollars into Texas midterm campaigns to support the industry. But in many parts of the country, voters didn’t need to make their voices on data centers heard through candidates. They had direct initiatives on the ballot this week that would decide whether data center projects would move ahead in their districts. In line with a growing backlash against data centers and AI, voters supported about 40 election-day measures that would restrict the construction of new data centers, with only one result — in Harwood, North Dakota — favoring data center expansion. More from CNET (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) As broken down by the website Data Centers on the Ballot, Ohio had the most number of voting measures: 21, all of which were in favor of restrictions. Maine, Illinois, Kansas, New Jersey, California, Florida, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin were the other states with data center voting. Six elections were held earlier in 2026 in California, Michigan, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, with all of them finding voters opposed to allowing data center builds to continue without new restrictions. Not all the proposed restrictions were the same. In some elections, voters decided whether to impose a megawatt cap on data center energy use, while other measures addressed specific zoning issues or whether data center projects should require voter approval. Some proposed an outright ban on new data centers, and six of those were successful. Polls by groups including Pew Research have found Americans have soured on data centers due to high electricity bills, water use and environmental concerns, among other reasons. It’s also hard to separate concerns about data centers from concerns about AI affecting jobs. AI has also become a divisive enough issue to affect midterm voting. More bad news for data centers and their supporters The election results were so bad for the industry that Politico declared data centers to be “the midterms’ other big loser” next to Republicans. Not only did voters enact additional restrictions on builds across the country, but data centers were mentioned in Democratic victory speeches. “I do not work for data centers. I do not work for Wall Street. I work for you, I work for Ohio,” Senator-elect Sherrod Brown said in his victory speech Tuesday night. USA Today reported that two mayors, one in Oklahoma and one in Ohio, were recalled after public backlash over proposed data centers. What’s next for data centers The midterms might have longer-term effects for tech companies and data center firms. It’s likely that with Democratic control of Congress, there’ll be more scrutiny. “Public policy is going to reflect public opinion, and there’s been a very substantial change in public opinion just over the last year,” Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Politico. Political headwinds from the midterms could lead local officials across the country to gain public favor by delaying or canceling data center projects or putting pressure on the companies behind them to offer more attractive deals to communities. The days of huge tax breaks and incentives for data centers could be coming to a close. “Now, (communities) are pushing data centers to pay taxes, create their own power plants, pay for their use of electricity and water and contribute to local community resources like education funds,” The New York Times reported.

artigo.texto: New Congress Set to Intensify Scrutiny of AI Infrastructure, Private Credit and Digital Assets With Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress and securing victories in key gubernatorial races in the U.S. midterm elections, the pro-business, deregulatory approach pursued over the past two years is expected to face changes. Sectors where calls for tighter oversight have grown — including data centers, the core infrastructure of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, as well as private credit and digital assets — are expected to face increased scrutiny and investigations after the new Congress convenes in January 2027. The AI data center construction sector is expected to face some of the most immediate effects. According to reports by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) on Nov. 4, the election of Democratic gubernatorial candidates in major data center hubs such as Texas, Ohio and Georgia has heightened the prospect of permitting delays and tighter regulations. In particular, the election of Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa in Texas — a state expected to account for approximately 30% of the data center capacity projected to come online in the United States by 2028 — sent shockwaves through the market. Bloomberg reported that nearly half of planned AI data center projects across the United States could face temporary construction moratoriums, local restrictions or community opposition when the victories of Democratic gubernatorial candidates in Georgia, Ohio and Pennsylvania are also taken into account. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa pledged to immediately suspend approvals for new data centers until legislation addressing their impact on local communities is passed. The pledge follows criticism that data centers are depleting local drinking water supplies and driving up electricity bills. Hinojosa outlined several proposed measures, including requiring operators to hire union workers, guaranteeing water supplies for local communities, freezing residential electricity rates, eliminating tax incentives and banning nondisclosure agreements. However, regulatory efforts targeting data centers were already underway before the election. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas began auditing data centers’ impacts on water, electricity and land use in August and suspended the issuance of environmental permits in September. Research firm SemiAnalysis warned that even a delay of several months in Texas could disrupt data center expansion plans across the United States. Reflecting growing NIMBY (Not In My Backyard) sentiment, measures restricting data center construction passed in 44 of the 45 local ballot votes held alongside the election. Brad Long, chief investment officer at Wealthspire, said, “The market now needs to consider not whether data centers will be built, but where they will be built and how long it will take.” Andrew Tyler, head of global markets intelligence at JPMorgan Chase, outlined two possible scenarios: existing data center construction and permitting could continue while new projects are halted or relocated to other states, or a slower overall buildout could lead to a reduction in total capital expenditures (CapEx). Markets reacted sharply to regulatory concerns, with CoreWeave plunging 9.9% and SK Hynix’s American depositary receipts (ADRs) falling 5.1%. However, Wall Street analysts do not expect the election results to derail AI development itself. Mabrouk Chetouane, head of global market strategy at Natixis Investment Managers, said that given the intense technological competition between the United States and China, Democrats are unlikely to fundamentally challenge existing measures aimed at strengthening U.S. AI competitiveness. Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, also said that the election of several governors and a change in congressional control alone would not be enough to bring the momentum behind AI industry growth to a complete halt. Some observers believe the regulatory push could slow the race among Big Tech companies to ramp up large-scale capital expenditures (CapEx). Charlie McElligott, a strategist at Nomura Holdings, said a more gradual pace of data center construction could ease concerns about an endless cycle of “prisoner’s dilemma”-style investment among hyperscalers. This could, in turn, ease fears that companies’ free cash flow will be rapidly depleted. However, delays to some projects appear inevitable, potentially pushing back both capital investment and the realization of AI’s economic benefits. Democrats’ increased scrutiny and investigations are also expected to extend beyond technology stocks to the broader financial sector. Key issues include stronger stress testing of the rapidly growing private credit market and a halt to efforts to ease capital requirements for large banks. Democrats have expressed concern about redemption restrictions imposed by private credit funds and the growing flow of retirement savings, including money in 401(k) plans, into the private credit market. They have also criticized the Trump administration’s efforts to ease capital buffer requirements for large banks, arguing that such changes could increase instability in the financial system. Sen. Elizabeth Warren has called for a criminal investigation into Bank of America executives in connection with violations of anti-money laundering laws, pressing for greater scrutiny of the banking sector. Democratic staff on the Senate Finance Committee have also announced plans to investigate the impact of private equity on living costs, including health care and housing expenses. Regulatory debates over digital assets and prediction markets are also expected to intensify. Sherrod Brown’s return to the Senate, given his critical stance toward the crypto industry, has made passage of the Clarity Act, a legislative proposal supported by the digital asset industry, even more uncertain. artigo.texto: South Korea's Mercedes-Benz Korea Ordered to Pay approximately $2,800 per Owner for Concealing Chinese Battery Origin South Korea's Consumer Dispute Mediation Committee has issued a collective dispute mediation decision ordering Mercedes-Benz Korea to pay 4 million won (approximately $2,800) per vehicle owner for failing to properly inform consumers about the manufacturer of its electric vehicle batteries. The committee under the Korea Consumer Agency said on the 4th that it found Mercedes-Benz Korea liable for damages after the company equipped five EQE and EQS models with Chinese-made Farasis battery cells but omitted this from sales guidelines distributed to dealers, presenting the vehicles as being equipped only with CATL batteries. The mediation covers 142 consumers who purchased the EQE 500 4MATIC SUV, EQE 53 4MATIC+, EQE 350+, EQE 350 4MATIC and EQS 350. They filed for collective dispute mediation in May after belatedly learning that Farasis batteries were installed. The compensation amounts to about 4% of the vehicle price, with total payouts estimated at about 560 million won (approximately $420,000). The committee pointed out that Mercedes-Benz Korea produced and distributed sales guidelines containing incorrect information to dealers. It also took issue with the company actively encouraging employees to use those guidelines in sales through staff training. Consumers were deprived of the opportunity to make a rational choice when they purchased vehicles based on explanations from dealer staff, the committee said. In calculating the compensation, the committee considered that batteries are a core component determining vehicle performance and safety. It also reflected differences in market share, brand recognition and technical capability between CATL and Farasis. The possibility that the resale value of Farasis-equipped vehicles declined amid growing negative sentiment toward Farasis batteries after the 2024 electric vehicle fire in Incheon's Cheongna International City was also factored into the calculation. Mercedes-Benz Korea must notify whether it accepts the decision within 15 days of receiving the written decision. Acceptance carries the same effect as a court settlement. If it does not accept, no compensation obligation arises, and consumers may file individual civil lawsuits. The committee plans to proceed with follow-up procedures so that victims who did not participate in the mediation can receive the same compensation. Committee Chairman Han Yong-ho said he hopes Mercedes-Benz Korea will actively engage in resolving the dispute and restore South Korean consumers' trust in German imported cars. The decision dovetails with sanctions previously imposed by the Korea Fair Trade Commission, which investigated Mercedes-Benz's disclosure of battery manufacturer information. In March, the antitrust regulator concluded that Mercedes-Benz had deceived consumers by falsely promoting battery manufacturer information and imposed a corrective order along with a fine of 11.239 billion won (approximately $8.4 million). The consumer committee's mediation is a follow-up decision in a case for which collective dispute mediation proceedings began in July of last year. At the time, 53 applicants sought compensation, alleging that Mercedes-Benz Korea sold EQE vehicles from June 2023 while presenting them as equipped with CATL batteries even though they carried Farasis battery cells. The committee determined that the case met the requirements for initiating collective dispute mediation, as there were more than 50 affected consumers and the core issues of fact and law were common to the case. The controversy began with a Mercedes-Benz electric vehicle fire in the underground parking garage of an apartment complex in Incheon's Cheongna International City in August 2024. After the accident, safety concerns about vehicle batteries came to the fore, and the controversy spread as it became known that the vehicle was equipped with a Farasis product and that the battery had a recall history. With this decision, Mercedes-Benz Korea now faces consumer compensation liability on top of the Fair Trade Commission fine over battery information disclosure. Once the mediation decision is finalized, compensation will be paid to the 142 consumers, and observers say it could influence practices among other imported car brands regarding disclosure of component information. However, it remains undecided whether Mercedes-Benz Korea will accept the mediation, and the possibility remains that the matter could lead to individual lawsuits if it does not.

artigo.texto: South Korea's Big 3 Battery Makers Escape Chasm via ESS, but CATL's 73% Share Keeps Volume Gap Wide South Korea's three major rechargeable battery makers are emerging from the "chasm" of temporary demand stagnation, posting clear earnings improvements in the third quarter on top of gains in the second, driven by surging demand for energy storage systems (ESS). But Chinese competitors are absorbing the market at a faster pace, and the market-share gap is actually widening — prompting South Korean companies to prepare a counterattack on two fronts: the U.S. ESS market and next-generation batteries. According to industry sources on the 3rd, LG Energy Solution posted third-quarter consolidated revenue of 9.6434 trillion won (approximately $7.2 billion) and operating profit of 756 billion won (approximately $562.5 million). Revenue rose 59.0% from a year earlier and operating profit 25.7%, while operating profit jumped 567.3% from the previous quarter. Even excluding 416.9 billion won (approximately $310.2 million) in U.S. government subsidies for North American production, the company still booked a profit of 339.1 billion won (approximately $252.3 million). Samsung SDI, which had remained in the red through the first quarter, completely reversed course with operating profits of 203.8 billion won (approximately $151.6 million) in the second quarter and 407.8 billion won (approximately $303.4 million) in the third. Third-quarter revenue came to 4.6856 trillion won (approximately $3.5 billion), up 52.6% from a year earlier. SK On posted a third-quarter operating loss of 80.5 billion won (approximately $59.9 million), but cut the deficit by 44.3 billion won (approximately $33.0 million) from a year earlier, entering a phase of narrowing losses. Excluding the second quarter, when customer compensation payments were reflected, results are on a gradual improving trend. ESS is at the center of the rebound. LG Energy Solution's ESS shipments rose more than 60% from the previous quarter, and ESS as a share of total revenue climbed from 22.7% in the fourth quarter of last year to the low 30% range in this year's third quarter. Improved utilization at its Polish plant and higher cylindrical battery sales also supported the recovery in profitability. At Samsung SDI, expanded sales of ESS and battery backup units (BBU) for data centers drove the swing to profit. Order backlogs are also building quickly. LG Energy Solution had secured a global ESS order backlog of about 160GWh by the end of the third quarter, and in North America it has locked in most of the volume planned for production through 2028. It recently signed its first direct battery energy storage system (BESS) supply contract with a Big Tech company and was also selected as an "DSX Ready BESS partner" for Nvidia. Samsung SDI has signed supply contracts totaling more than 60GWh from January to October, mainly in the U.S., and plans to raise this year's contract volume to more than 120GWh through additional orders by year-end. SK On has won more than about 10GWh in orders and is negotiating additional contracts with multiple U.S. customers, targeting 20GWh a year. Note: LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI on a consolidated basis; SK On on confirmed third-quarter results The structural growth in ESS demand itself is another tailwind. According to market research firm SNE Research, global lithium-ion ESS battery shipments in the first half of this year totaled 461.3GWh, up 71% from a year earlier. Demand sources are diversifying as investment in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers and power grids expands. "ESS demand is outpacing available production capacity," an LG Energy Solution official said on a conference call. "Supply discussions now cover not only traditional grid and utility customers but also demand from AI data centers and direct purchases by hyperscalers." The problem is China. The global market share of Chinese battery makers led by CATL has climbed to around 73%, and the gap with South Korean companies is widening. Analysts say that while the South Korean Big 3 are climbing out of the chasm, Chinese companies are recovering earnings faster and cementing their market dominance. In response, South Korean companies are using U.S. restrictions on China as a breakthrough. Washington, citing national security, is limiting the use of Chinese batteries in major ESS facilities. Targeting that opening, all three companies have moved to expand North American ESS sales. "South Korean-made batteries are being considered as an alternative in terms of supply-chain diversification, quality reliability and North American market responsiveness," an industry official said. "Companies that previously used Chinese batteries keep inquiring about product specifications, available volumes, pricing terms and the possibility of long-term contracts." Kim Young-kwang, head of SK On's financial management office, said, "Since the Trump administration's tightening of restrictions on China and the push to reorganize supply chains, interest in non-Chinese products has been rising." Capacity expansion is proceeding in parallel. LG Energy Solution plans to raise its North American ESS production capacity from more than 50GWh at the end of this year to 70GWh by the end of next year. "We will strengthen our selection-and-focus strategy to maximize operational efficiency with limited resources," said Lee Chang-sil, chief financial officer of LG Energy Solution. artigo.texto: China's solid-state battery stocks buck market slump with wave of limit-ups; analysts see 2027 as mass-production breakthrough year On Nov. 3, China's A-share solid-state battery sector bucked a weakening broader market. The Shanghai Composite Index widened its afternoon loss to 1.57%, closing at 3,580.79 points, with 717 gainers and 1,577 decliners in Shanghai. The battery index, by contrast, closed up 2.16% at 503.12 points for the full session, outperforming the Shanghai Composite by 3.73 percentage points, with sector turnover reaching 46.858 billion yuan (approximately $7.0 billion). At the stock level, Shangshui Intelligent and Mengguli sealed 20% limit-ups with turnover rates of 27.56% and 11.97%, respectively, both first-board moves. Yema Battery, Fengyuan, Shengyang Power, Shidai Wanheng, Longpan Technology, Baoming Technology and Zhongxin Fluorine Materials all hit their ceilings, Zizhu Gaoke posted a second straight limit-up, and Liwang Shares rose as much as 16.20% intraday. Heavyweight CATL (300750.SZ) gained 4.16% in early trading, logging a fourth consecutive daily advance, and still closed up more than 3%. What is supporting sector sentiment is an increasingly clear timeline for solid-state battery mass production. Southwest Securities believes 2026-2027 will be a period of intensive pilot-line construction, with 2027 likely bringing a window for small-batch production and vehicle validation, before gradual entry into large-scale commercialization in 2028-2030. Guotai Haitong directly defines 2027 as the inaugural year of solid-state battery mass production. Industry progress is confirming that cadence. CATL's Yibin all-solid-state pilot line came online in August this year, with sample energy density exceeding 500Wh/kg, and the company plans small-batch production in 2027. BYD's (002594.SZ) 2GWh automotive-grade sulfide all-solid-state pilot line went into operation in February this year, and the first 20GWh mass-production line in Bishan, Chongqing, is scheduled to break ground in the third quarter of 2026. Gotion High-tech's (002074.SZ) first 0.2GWh pilot line was completed in 2025, and products have already undergone on-vehicle road testing. In addition, Dongfeng's next-generation solid-state battery is nearing the vehicle-installation stage, while Chery has set 2027 as its target for completing validation. Policy backing is equally explicit. The 15th Five-Year Plan for New Battery Industry Development, jointly issued by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and six other departments, proposes that all-solid-state batteries achieve initial large-scale application by 2030, with long-life lithium batteries required to reach 15,000 charge cycles. China's Ministry of Finance and two other departments specified that solid-state batteries will be exempt from consumption tax from Sept. 1, 2026, through Dec. 31, 2028. Shanxi Securities noted that this is a rare case in the battery industry's history of using tax measures to support a frontier technology route in a targeted way; the plan also implements capacity-warning controls and regulates price competition — effectively a battery-sector version of "anti-involution" — providing a five-year institutional lever for industry consolidation. Demand-side data also offer support. Combined power and energy-storage battery output reached 237.8GWh in September, up 57.3% year on year; energy-storage battery sales alone were 73.5GWh for the month, up 104.4% year on year, more than double the growth rate of power batteries. Global energy-storage battery shipments totaled 839.3GWh in the first three quarters, up 96.3% year on year, with Chinese manufacturers accounting for 96.6% of the total. October production schedules for sample battery companies rose 3.8% month on month, with all five core segments hitting year-to-date highs. Several institutions have offered quantitative forecasts for the long-term solid-state battery opportunity. Southwest Securities estimates global all-solid-state battery shipments will rise from 1.87GWh in 2026 to 94.77GWh in 2030 — roughly a 50-fold increase over five years — driven by penetration in high-end new energy vehicles rising from 0.5% to 13%. Precedence Research forecasts the global solid-state battery market will grow from $1.63 billion in 2025 to $7.6 billion in 2030 and further to $31.71 billion in 2035, a compound annual growth rate of 34.56% from 2025 to 2035. Note: Data sources are the public research views and industry forecasts of the institutions above. The sector's deep prior correction also provides elasticity for this rebound. The battery index touched an intraday high of 614.80 points on Oct. 12 and pulled back to 466.93 points on Oct. 23, a maximum drawdown of 24.05% over ten trading days. Meanwhile, CATL disclosed buyback progress on Nov. 2: as of end-October it had repurchased 19.6059 million shares, or 0.4447% of total share capital, for 5.36 billion yuan (approximately $804.8 million), part of a previously proposed 20 billion to 40 billion yuan cancellation-style buyback plan. On valuation, CATL currently trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 13.38 times, with a dividend yield of 3.42%, corresponding to earnings per share of 14.13 yuan. Sell-side institutions have recently turned more positive: Soochow Securities assigned a 20x PE for 2027 and a target price of 431 yuan, while Huayuan Securities initiated coverage with a buy rating on Nov. 2. Sinolink Securities said the lithium battery sector's profitability, valuation and institutional positioning are all at low levels in their historical ranges, and it remains firmly bullish on fourth-quarter performance, believing strong third-quarter results could serve as a catalyst for a rebound. From a fund-flow perspective, some solid-state battery concept stocks, though volatile and weaker recently, have still drawn contrarian leveraged buying. artigo.texto: A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) tem R$ 30,76 milhões em notas fiscais pendentes do contrato de aquisição de seu próprio data center, em Brasília. A agência pediu ao governo Lula (PT) o desbloqueio de recursos e alertou para o risco de ficar sem dinheiro para pagar despesas básicas. A informação é do UOL. Na semana passada, o presidente da Anatel, Carlos Baigorri, solicitou ao Ministério do Planejamento o desbloqueio de R$ 30 milhões. O pedido ocorreu após tentativas de antecipação de recursos negadas pela Secretaria do Tesouro Nacional (STN), vinculada ao Ministério da Fazenda. As informações foram obtidas pela Folha de S.Paulo. Em dezembro de 2025, a agência assinou um contrato de R$ 44,95 milhões para aquisição de equipamentos e serviços de tecnologia. O acordo inclui programas de gerenciamento, conectividade, implantação, migração, suporte, manutenção e garantia. A vigência vai até dezembro de 2030. O data center sustenta serviços digitais oferecidos a cidadãos e empresas de telecomunicações, além de sistemas utilizados pela agência para fiscalizar as operadoras reguladas pelo órgão. Os R$ 30,76 milhões em notas fiscais pendentes estão classificados como “restos a pagar”, categoria que reúne despesas de anos anteriores ainda não quitadas. Em comunicação ao governo, Baigorri alertou para o risco de a agência não conseguir honrar os compromissos financeiros. “As projeções apontam risco de insuficiência de limite financeiro para o pagamento integral dos compromissos previstos, especialmente no último trimestre de 2026”, afirma o presidente da agência, Carlos Baigorri, de acordo com o UOL. A Anatel atribui a falta de recursos ao bloqueio de R$ 51,83 milhões determinado pelo governo em maio. Com a restrição, o orçamento discricionário da agência, destinado a custeio e investimentos, caiu de R$ 275,37 milhões para R$ 223,54 milhões, redução de 19%. Para reduzir os impactos do corte, a agência revisou contratos, projetos e despesas. Também adotou medidas para evitar a cobrança de “multas, juros e outros encargos contratuais”. A Anatel tenta obter recursos adicionais desde agosto. Naquele mês, solicitou a antecipação de R$ 23,3 milhões que estavam previstos para dezembro. Em resposta à Folha, a agência declarou que “até o momento, as medidas adotadas têm buscado mitigar os impactos decorrentes da restrição orçamentária imposta à agência”. “Contudo, a persistência das restrições orçamentárias e financeiras poderá exigir novas medidas de reprogramação de despesas”, afirmou. O Ministério da Fazenda justificou os bloqueios pela necessidade de contingenciamento das despesas do governo federal. Segundo a pasta, “as restrições orçamentárias e financeiras dos órgãos do Poder Executivo decorrem da necessidade de contingenciamento e bloqueio indicados nos Relatórios de Avaliação de Receitas e Despesas Primárias e nos Decretos de Programação Orçamentária e Financeira”. A pasta informou que a manutenção dos cortes “é reavaliada bimestralmente, por ocasião da elaboração dos referidos Relatórios e Decretos, estando a próxima avaliação prevista para 24 de novembro”. Na data, a Junta de Execução Orçamentária vai analisar o espaço fiscal disponível para uma eventual redução dos bloqueios. Sobre os pedidos de antecipação de recursos, a Fazenda afirmou: “Nesse contexto, quanto aos pedidos de antecipação, a Secretaria do Tesouro Nacional analisa os pleitos levando em consideração a preservação da capacidade de pagamento mensal futura de cada órgão, de modo a evitar que o este comprometa sua execução ao longo do ano”, disse a pasta. Sua opinião sobre esta matéria importa.

artigo.texto: Equinix says its smaller data centers could be less exposed to potential U.S. construction restrictions as regulators scrutinize the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. The company's facilities typically range from 30 to 60 megawatts, compared with the roughly 100-megawatt threshold that Cyrus Adaggra, Equinix's Asia-Pacific president, said is generally targeted by U.S. proposals. "We will invest in markets where we see customer demand, and because we have a footprint that is typically less than 100 megawatts, we tend not to fall and be caught by the legislation or the regulation, which is typically at about 100 megawatts in the U.S.," Adaggra told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia." His comments come as the U.S. midterm election results have heightened concerns that new restrictions on data center development could delay projects and raise construction costs. About 53% of projected growth in the U.S. hyperscaler development pipeline is concentrated in states where newly elected governors could impose restrictions on data center construction, according to a Wednesday report from BMI, a Fitch Solutions company. The firm said any impact would likely become more apparent from 2028, as most projects planned for 2027 are already committed. Demand fuels expansion Equinix has increased capital spending from about $2 billion a few years ago to $7 billion, driven by growing customer demand, Adaggra said. "The number one determinant of our capex spend and build is customer demand," he said. Annualized gross bookings exceeded $500 million for the first time in the third quarter, up 35% from a year earlier. Adaggra said growth was driven by demand from large enterprises, including Fortune 500 companies, as businesses invest in hybrid and multi-cloud infrastructure, network connectivity and access to digital infrastructure. Equinix serves about 60% of Fortune 500 companies, he added. Potential restrictions on data center development could also raise costs across the AI infrastructure supply chain, according to Russell Investments. The investment firm also flagged that slower U.S. data center construction could weigh on demand for semiconductors and other infrastructure equipment, including from suppliers across Asia. Asia gains momentum Asia is also emerging as a major destination for data center investment. "After the U.S., we expect actually most data center investments and activity to happen in Asia," Sjoerd Leenart, CEO of JPMorgan's banking business in Asia Pacific, said in a podcast released Friday. Global hyperscalers are seeking Asian markets with sufficient land, electricity and grid capacity, Leenart said. Some of that investment could be spread across several markets, according to a Thursday report from Mirae Asset Securities. The brokerage said South Korea could emerge as a key market for additional capacity in Asia, with operators that secure power, land and long-term customer contracts better positioned to expand. However, Asia faces its own constraints. Power availability, grid connectivity and equipment delays remain as key challenges for data center development, according to a Thursday report from risk advisory and insurance brokerage WTW. Leenart also pointed to regulatory pushback in Thailand and Australia, where he said authorities had paused some projects to assess the impact of data center energy demand on other industries and consumers.

artigo.texto: The New Zealand company Lightyears it obtained NZ$174 million in financing to expand its portfolio of solar energy projects and battery energy storage systems (BESS). The resources will allow progress in the development of more than 300 MW of energy infrastructure over the next five years. The deal combines Japanese investment and Australian financing. Obayashi Corporation will contribute NZD 74 million through an equity investment, while Infradebt will provide a NZD 100 million credit facility to support the company’s growth. Based in Auckland, Lightyears seeks to strengthen its capacity to develop and execute several energy projects simultaneously, expanding its presence in different regions of New Zealand. Obayashi and Infradebt back Lightyears expansion The agreement incorporates Obayashi Corporation, a Japanese group with operations in construction and infrastructure, as a strategic partner of Lightyears. For the Japanese company, New Zealand represents a priority market for expanding its investments in renewable energy. As part of the transaction, Lightyears will establish a new company called LYOC1, which will retain the rights to the solar projects included in the agreement. Obayashi will hold a 90% stake in this entity. The investment will be made progressively, as the facilities complete the various stages of development, this mechanism will allow capital outlays to be adjusted to the progress of each project. For its part, Infradebt, an Australian entity specializing in infrastructure financing, will provide a NZD 100 million credit line. The two companies have maintained a financial relationship since 2025. Matt Shanks, managing director and co-founder of Lightyears, noted that the backing of both partners will allow them to develop more projects simultaneously and accelerate the implementation of new energy facilities in the country. Lightyears has a portfolio of 338 MW in solar energy Currently, Lightyears has 65 MW of installed or under-development solar capacity, in addition to a portfolio of 28 projects totaling 338 MW, a base that supports its expansion plans for the next five years. The funding will enable the company to move forward with commercial-scale solar power plants and battery energy storage systems. Both technologies are part of the company’s strategy to expand its presence in the New Zealand electricity market. The combination of photovoltaic generation and BESS storage it will also allow for more flexible electricity management. The batteries store energy during generation periods and supply it later, although Lightyears has not yet detailed the power or energy capacity of the planned systems. Kuratau and Reefton are focusing on solar projects under development Among the company’s facilities, Te Aho o te Rā Solar Farm stands out, a 15 MW photovoltaic park located near Kuratau on the North Island. Its construction began in October 2026 through a collaboration with eight local entities linked to Māori land and investment. The facility will have an estimated annual production of 23.5 GWh, enough to supply approximately 3,300 homes. Its completion is scheduled for July 2027. Another important development is the 14 MW solar park in Reefton, located on the west coast of the South Island. The project is nearing completion and will contribute to the region’s electricity supply. Lightyears is also preparing a 6 MW photovoltaic installation connected to the local Electricity Ashburton grid, with which it will expand its activity in the South Island. The funding opens a new chapter for renewable energy in New Zealand The backing from Obayashi and Infradebt provides Lightyears with financial resources to advance its project portfolio and arrange for the construction of new solar facilities over the next few years. Founded by Matt Shanks and Sean Tobin, the company has been involved in the development of commercial-scale photovoltaic plants in New Zealand. Its new financial structure combines equity investment and specialized financing to support the growth of its operations. With the planned development of more than 300 MW of solar infrastructure and battery storage, Lightyears seeks to expand its stake in the New Zealand renewable energy sector. Achieving this goal will depend on the technical, financial, and construction progress of each facility. Source: Renewables Now Photo: Shutterstock

artigo.texto: O Ministério Público Federal (MPF) ajuizou uma ação civil pública contra a empresa BR Arbo Gestão Florestal e a certificadora internacional Verra, solicitando a suspensão do Projeto Mejuruá, iniciativa de créditos de carbono desenvolvida no município de Carauari, no interior do Amazonas. A ação aponta possíveis violações aos direitos territoriais de povos indígenas e comunidades tradicionais que vivem na região. Entre os problemas apresentados pelo órgão estão a sobreposição do empreendimento com áreas de ocupação histórica dessas populações, a ausência de consulta prévia e relatos de pressão sobre moradores para obter apoio ao projeto. O MPF também pede que as duas empresas sejam condenadas ao pagamento de R$ 6 milhões por danos morais coletivos, com recursos destinados às comunidades atingidas. O Projeto Mejuruá é uma iniciativa privada de manejo florestal e geração de créditos de carbono, na modalidade REDD+. O empreendimento abrange uma área declarada de aproximadamente 678 mil hectares, localizada nas bacias dos rios Juruá, Riozinho e Ipixuna. De acordo com levantamentos técnicos do setor de geoprocessamento do MPF, mais de 50% da área indicada pelo projeto apresenta sobreposição com territórios indígenas e de comunidades tradicionais. Desse total, 179.149 hectares, equivalentes a 26,38% da área, coincidem com o território das comunidades do Riozinho, representadas pela Associação de Moradores Agroextrativistas do Baixo Riozinho (Asmobri). Outros 38.856 hectares, ou 5,72%, correspondem a áreas tradicionais de comunidades do rio Juruá, representadas pela Associação de Moradores Agroextrativistas do Alto Juruá (Amab). A área restante identificada nos levantamentos apresenta sobreposição com territórios de ocupação tradicional do povo indígena Katukina, na região do rio Ipixuna. Segundo o MPF, a existência de registros de propriedade privada não elimina os direitos territoriais das populações tradicionais, que possuem proteção prevista na legislação brasileira e em tratados internacionais. Projeto teria avançado sem consulta às comunidades Outro ponto questionado na ação é a falta de consulta prévia, livre e informada às populações afetadas pelo empreendimento, conforme estabelece a Convenção nº 169 da Organização Internacional do Trabalho (OIT). O Ministério Público afirma que a BR Arbo negou formalmente o direito de consulta às comunidades ribeirinhas e não comunicou à Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai) a sobreposição do projeto com áreas de ocupação tradicional do povo Katukina. A ação também apresenta relatos de moradores sobre possíveis pressões para conseguir apoio ao empreendimento. Entre as situações mencionadas estão a oferta de benefícios materiais, como caixas d’água, kits de energia solar e antenas de internet via satélite. O MPF relata ainda a circulação de informações falsas sobre a regularização coletiva das terras, incluindo afirmações de que as famílias poderiam perder suas roças e áreas individuais. O documento também menciona áudios com ameaças de desapropriação e medidas judiciais contra moradores que se recusassem a assinar acordos de apoio ao projeto. De acordo com o órgão, os episódios contribuíram para ampliar os conflitos internos nas comunidades e dificultar a mobilização coletiva em defesa dos territórios. Verra também responde à ação A certificadora internacional Verra foi incluída no processo por manter os procedimentos de auditoria e validação do Projeto Mejuruá, mesmo após receber notificações das associações comunitárias e do MPF sobre as irregularidades apontadas. LEIA TAMBÉM: Professor que estuprava enteada desde os oito anos é preso em Parintins O Ministério Público também sustenta que o empreendimento não atende às exigências da Lei nº 15.042/2024, que instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa, e da Resolução nº 19/2025 da Comissão Nacional para REDD+ (Conaredd+). As normas estabelecem que projetos privados de créditos de carbono com sobreposição a territórios comunitários devem destinar pelo menos 70% dos benefícios financeiros diretamente às populações atingidas. Também estão previstas medidas de acompanhamento pelos órgãos competentes e a oferta de assessoria técnica e jurídica independente às comunidades. Na avaliação apresentada à Justiça, o MPF afirma que essas exigências não foram cumpridas pelo Projeto Mejuruá. MPF pede cancelamento de certificações Além da suspensão integral do empreendimento, o Ministério Público solicita que sejam interrompidas todas as atividades nas áreas de sobreposição com os territórios do povo Katukina e das comunidades tradicionais do Riozinho e do rio Juruá. O órgão também pede que os benefícios materiais já entregues aos moradores sejam mantidos, evitando possíveis retaliações e novos conflitos. Outro pedido é o cancelamento dos registros, auditorias e certificações relacionados ao projeto nas áreas indígenas e comunitárias. A ação ainda questiona uma decisão do Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público (CNMP), que suspendeu e posteriormente invalidou, no fim de 2025, uma recomendação extrajudicial do MPF sobre o caso. O órgão argumenta que a decisão desconsiderou dados técnicos sobre a sobreposição territorial e não ouviu as comunidades atingidas. Em fevereiro de 2026, a Corregedoria do MPF arquivou uma representação disciplinar contra o procurador responsável pela atuação no caso.

artigo.texto: AMD posted a massive Q3 2026. Revenue hit $13.377 billion, up 45% year over year and 16% sequentially. Data Center revenue reached $8.546 billion, up 97% year over year. Embedded Revenue was up big, and client revenue fared better than Intel in many respects. AMD Has Record Quarter Driven By Data Center Here is AMD’s Q3 2026 summary slide. This is an enormous quarter. Embedded revenue was up 29% year over year, and yet that almost feels like a footnote. AMD delivered GAAP operating income of $2.832 billion on revenue of $13.377 billion, with net income of $2.428 billion and diluted earnings per share of $1.46. On a non-GAAP basis, which excludes stock-based compensation, amortization of acquisition-related intangibles and other items, operating income was $3.923 billion, net income was $3.471 billion and EPS came in at $2.09. Even the quarterly numbers were up a lot, with 16% growth on the GAAP side. AMD’s Data Center Is Big Time The Data Center segment generated $8.546 billion in revenue, up 97% year over year and 27% sequentially. AMD attributes this Data Center surge to strong EPYC demand and the launch of Instinct MI450 GPUs. The company says major clients, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, are running workloads on Helios rack-scale solutions powered by these chips. The comparison to Intel’s data center results from last week saw its quarterly revenue of $7.3 billion, up 78% year-over-year. AMD’s Data Center segment at $8.546 billion grew faster at 97%. Both companies are clearly seeing surging demand for AI infrastructure and server processors, but AMD seems to be accelerating. Venice is coming, and we expect AMD to have clear x86 performance leadership, as Intel’s PCIe Gen6 Diamond Rapids platform, we expect, will be later in 2027. On technical merits, we expect AMD to be in a great place, and it seems like AMD is better managing its supply to get chips out. AMD Client and Gaming Segment The combined Client and Gaming segment saw revenue down 8% year-over-year, at $3.722 billion. Client notched up a bit, while gaming went down. Memory and NAND prices are keeping a lid on this market. Of note, AMD said its Ryzen AI Halo Platform with the Ryzen AI Max Pro 400 series is not available, so that means Gorgon Halo? We will have our first Gorgon Halo review soon, as that machine is running benchmarks now. Somewhat notable on the slide is that AMD has three AI-related products highlighted, while Intel’s three summary bullets on its CCPG segment were focused on shortages, demand for future products, and a generic AI PC nod. AMD, with the Strix Halo platform, at least has something it can use to run reasonably large models locally, and you have to wonder if that is a driver here. AMD’s Embedded Grows The Embedded segment delivered $1.109 billion in revenue, up 29% year-over-year. AMD says growth came from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications and industrial end markets. Just as a frame of reference, Xilinx’s annual revenue was something like $3.1-3.2B when AMD completed its acquisition of Xilinx. In most markets, if you grow 29% year over year and see a huge margin increase, it is time to throw a party. This seems to simply offset client’s (gaming) weakness. AMD Q4 Guidance Points To Acceleration AMD expects fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of approximately $17 billion plus or minus 3%. At the midpoint, that represents year-over-year growth of about 66% and sequential growth of roughly 27%. If this quarter seems big, then next quarter seems like it will be significantly bigger. Final Words AMD has its Helios rack-scale infrastructure rolling out, and Venice. Ryan recently went into the Venice architecture. If AMD was ahead in many metrics with its Turin generation, then adding more cores, updated cores, and higher memory bandwidth should be a recipe for clear x86 socket leadership, at least until Intel is able to field Diamond Rapids. It will be interesting to see how much of a price premium AMD can extract for a generational advantage and first-mover status. Socket refresh generations are less exciting than the Turin-to-Venice transition, which is a major platform update (DDR5 channel count and PCIe Gen6). That also means PCIe Gen6 development, like PCIe Gen4, will likely happen more often on AMD than on Intel. Gluing chips together seems to be working out reasonably well.

artigo.texto: - U.S. voters pushed back on data center development in the 2026 election - Ohio data center projects faced major setbacks - Elon Musk quipped that his proposed space-based data centers look like a good idea right about now It wasn’t just candidates that were on the ballot in the latest U.S. election. Dozens of localities also had a total of 41 data center measures on the agenda, and voters from Florida to Maine, New Jersey to Illinois resoundingly rejected new facilities looking to come to town. In Edgewater, Florida, voters approved a measure (Amendment #4) to codify in the city charter a data center ban that was passed by city leaders in September. Meanwhile, citizens in four towns in Maine passed restrictions on data center development, with three of those short-term moratoriums. Ohio Ohio proved a hotbed of data center-related election activity, with ballot questions in at more than a dozen municipalities. In Wilmington, voters shot down four zoning ordinances that would have cleared the way for 545 acres to be rezoned for data center use. An effort in Piqua to recall three commissioners who had approved a Meta data center succeeded, as did an amendment restricting data center development in the city. Illinois Illinois voters in Joliet, Granite City, Nameoki, Venice and Chouteau voted against measures which would advise local officials to approve new data center permits, while residents in Bloomington and Morgan approved new restrictions on new data center construction. Kansas In Kansas, citizens in El Dorado and Emporia similarly voted to block the construction of large data centers. Wisconsin Meanwhile, Janesville, Wisconsin approved a measure that would require voter approval before the city can greenlight redevelopment of a former General Motors manufacturing site which was being eyed for a data center. Notable rejections The rejections in Ohio are notable given the state has emerged as a focal point for new data center construction in recent years. Likewise, the results in Midwestern states like Illinois and Kansas follow an uptick data center activity in those areas as developers chase available power. The results flew in the face of an October poll from the American Infrastructure Alliance, which claimed 64% of voters across party lines were in favor of allowing data center construction provided operators commit to energy and environmental protections. The AIA counts CoreWeave, Digital Realty, Open AI, QTS, Blackstone and SoftBank among its members. As the counts rolled in, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX is one of several to propose putting data centers in orbit, couldn’t resist weighing in. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he wrote on X. It wasn’t all bad news, though. Voters in Harwood, North Dakota rejected a measure that would have required the city to seek additional review before approving industrial developments, including data centers. artigo.texto: Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading. Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter: - Earnings per share: $2.09 adjusted vs. $1.95 expected - Revenue: $13.38 billion vs. $13.09 billion expected Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement. Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results. CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth. "We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call. AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand. The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago. After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October. "Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts. PC market struggles AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI. AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm-based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research. AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago. For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount. AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering. AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering. During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung. In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications. artigo.texto: Midterm Voters Sent Data Centers a Message The backlash is about the concentration of power, not AI itself, panelists said on Broadband Breakfast Live Online Broadband Breakfast WASHINGTON, Nov. 4, 2026 – In four of the biggest data center states, voters chose candidates who ran against the industry's buildout, a power-market expert said on Broadband Breakfast Live Online. on Wednesday, a day after the Midterm Elections. Watch Full Video for Free: The results arrive before the Senate's first vote, scheduled for Nov. 9, on a permitting bill that would make data centers pay for the grid upgrades they require. That Monday vote, on a motion to proceed, needs 60 votes just to open debate. Republicans hold 53 seats until January. AI and data centers ranked last of five issues in the NBC News exit poll, behind government corruption at 90% and cost of living at 89%. Still, 56% of voters called the issue a crucial or major factor in their House vote, and 23% called it crucial. Four states, one message Texas, Ohio, Georgia and Arizona all elected candidates who promised to pause, limit or put conditions on data center growth, said Rob Gramlich, founder and president of Grid Strategies, a Washington consulting firm that studies transmission and power markets. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governorship after pledging to halt data center approvals until the Legislature passes protections. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown unseated Sen. Jon Husted by framing him as "the face of data centers," Gramlich said. Amy Acton, who opposed data center development, won the governor's race. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms, who backed a statewide moratorium, was elected governor. Texas faces a practical problem. Large-load requests there total roughly 200 gigawatts, Gramlich said, more than double the grid's record peak of about 85.5 gigawatts. "There's literally no way to meet 200 gigawatts of new demand in Texas, for example. It's just not going to happen," he said. Power in a few hands Voters are not deciding whether they are for or against AI, said Alex Roark, founder and CEO of the American Innovation Policy Forum and former chief of the Federal Communications Commission's Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. "It's really about how Americans feel about the concentration of power and influence over our lives into the hands of a few people," he said. Data centers make that abstraction physical, Roark said, and many arrived "behind non-disclosure agreements with zero community input." Broadband Breakfast's "Broadband and AI in the Next Congress" takes place Tuesday, Dec. 1, at the National Press Club in Washington, with keynotes from Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., and Rep. Buddy Carter, R-Ga. Utah offered an early warning. In June, Senate President Stuart Adams lost his Republican primary to Stephanie Hollist, 43% to 34%, after championing Stratos, a proposed AI campus of up to 9 gigawatts in Box Elder County, north of the Great Salt Lake. Backed by "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary, the project would rank among the world's largest AI data centers. Residents feared it would drain scarce water and strain the grid. As chair of the Military Installation Development Authority, a state body that approved early plans and can override county zoning, Adams became the face of the project. The longest-serving Senate president in Utah history, he had won past races in the deep-red state with ease. He became the first sitting Senate president to lose a primary in modern Utah history. Two Box Elder County commissioners who backed the project also lost. Ohio hosted 21 of the 41 local data center measures on Tuesday's ballots. At least 14 municipalities passed bans or restrictions. In Trenton, a small Butler County city between Cincinnati and Dayton, 80% of voters approved a charter amendment banning data centers that draw more than 25 megawatts. Neighbors gathered the signatures after plans for a data center surfaced last year. In Oregon, Ohio, opponents of data center limits spent more than $300,000 without turning the tide, Roark said. Who pays for the grid Data centers are "one of 20 things" raising utility bills, Gramlich said, alongside replacing grid equipment roughly 70 years old. "But they're kind of getting blamed right now," he said. Electric vehicles, heat pumps that warm homes and offices, and electrified factories are also adding demand. States are already shifting costs. Large-load tariffs, rate schedules that make the biggest customers carry the costs they add, were pending or in place in 36 states as of March, according to the Smart Electric Power Alliance. After AEP Ohio's tariff took effect, the utility cut its large-load forecast from 30 gigawatts to 13. Developers could go further, said Steve Haro, founder of the government affairs firm Haro Solutions. He proposed an Alaska-style dividend for neighbors. "Everyone in this catchment area, we're going to send you 300 bucks a year to go towards your utility bills," he said. The model is Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend, which since 1982 has sent residents a yearly check from the state's oil wealth. Applied to data centers, neighbors would get a direct share of the buildout, not just a promise of future tax revenue. The benefits are real but uneven. Developers argue AI campuses like Utah's bring jobs and millions in local taxes. Gramlich agreed that community benefits matter but said they are hard to standardize, because about half of data center developers are first-timers, many backed by private equity. A narrow window The Senate bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, would make new data centers of 20 megawatts or more pay the full added cost of the power and wires built to serve them. It would also give opponents 150 days to sue over a federal permit under the main environmental laws, down from the six years most challenges get under current law. The bill puts federal reviews on a clock: Two years for a full environmental impact statemen

artigo.texto: Shares of Elon Musk's SpaceX and Tesla fell in premarket trading Wednesday as the Democrats won a significant victory in the midterm elections. SpaceX was last trading down 3.8% and Tesla dropped 3.5% amid big losses for Republican candidates Musk had backed. Artificial intelligence stocks came under pressure overnight as Democrats — seen as proponents of data center moratoriums — won big in midterm elections in key data center hubs. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk, where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats. SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet. Mixed moves for AI stocks The more direct plays were slightly down. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 2.6% and 2.8%, respectively. Peer Nebius Group was relatively flat and Oracle shed 1.3%. Tech giants Nvidia, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft were all up around 1-2%. AMD shares rose 6.8% after announcing earnings on Tuesday. Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 were flat. The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) was up 0.7%. Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow. Democrat Gina Hinojosa is the projected winner over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, according to the Associated Press. "The one thing that could really end up moving stuff though would be if Abbott were to lose Texas," said Scott Ladner, chief investment officer of Horizon Investments, earlier Tuesday as results rolled in. "Because there is a legitimate question about where do you build these data centers?" "Texas is a fertile ground for that. And if he were to lose, I think that fertile ground is largely barren. So, that's going to be a challenge," Ladner added. Hinojosa has been outspoken in her support of a moratorium on AI data centers. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State. 'Left-tail event' The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing. "We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week. Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo. Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end. "Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."
