artigo.texto: Home> Events> Webinar: Energy Storage for a Power-Hungry Future Webinar: Energy Storage for a Power-Hungry Future CEIC EMIS ISI Upcoming Esme del Olmo Garcia 05.11.2026 1 min read As electricity demand accelerates, driven by AI, data centres, electric vehicles, and the broader electrification of the global economy, energy storage is becoming a critical component of future power systems. Join ISI’s researchers for a discussion on how the global electricity landscape is evolving and why energy storage is emerging as essential infrastructure for reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy. In this 30-minute webinar, Ahmet Kaya, Head of Macro Research at ISI Markets, will open with a macroeconomic overview of global energy and electricity trends. He will be followed by Natalia Yanakieva, Head of Industry Research at ISI Markets, who will provide an in-depth analysis of the energy storage market and its strategic importance for the future of power systems. We will explore: – Macroeconomic overview of global energy markets – The changing electricity landscape – Energy storage technologies, markets and applications – Infrastructure, economics and strategic competition The session will finalise with a live Q&A, where you can ask questions submitted during registration or engage directly with our experts. Date: Thursday 26th November Time: 9:00am UK | Poland 10:00 am | India 2:30pm | Singapore 5:00pm | Hong Kong 5:00pm Secure your place to hear from our research experts and explore the forces reshaping global electricity markets and energy storage Speakers: Ahmet Kaya leads the macro research team at ISI Markets, behind its global macro outlook, thematic reports and data stories. He holds a PhD from Hacettepe University and an MSc from the University of Groningen. Over his career, he has held senior economist and advisory roles at NIESR, the UK Foreign Office and the Turkish Treasury, as well as positions at leading international research institutes. His work focuses on global macroeconomics, trade and finance, capital flows, geopolitics and productivity. Natalia Yanakieva is Head of Industry Research at ISI Markets, where she leads the production of proprietary industry research and analysis covering emerging markets across EMEA, Asia and Latin America. With over 19 years of experience in business journalism, economic and industry research, and editorial management, she specialises in identifying key market trends and providing insights relevant to business decision-makers. Her areas of research include renewable energy, transportation, telecommunications, construction and other key sectors shaping emerging market economies. Natalia holds a MA degree in International Economics and Management from the University of National and World Economy and a MSc degree in Environmental Protection from the Forestry University. artigo.texto: People across America rejected data centers during last night’s midterm election. Proposals related to data centers were explicitly on the ballot in more than 40 races across 13 states. People voted against data centers in 38 of them and counting. Six cities voted to ban data centers outright and 12 put limits on the amount of megawatts such buildings could draw. In addition to specific ballot measures, candidates who supported data centers lost across the country. One of the most striking repudiations of pro data center politicians was in Texas, where Gregg Abbott lost a bid for a fourth term as governor. Abbott had made Texas a data center friendly place. The state has more than 300 working data centers and there are plans to double that number. “Texas is the epicenter of AI development,” Abbott said in 2025 at a press conference with Google CEO Sundar Pichai. “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.” He went on to accept more than $9 million from data center-related donors. When public sentiment turned against data centers, Abbott attempted to ride shifting political winds by issuing a “pause” on new projects. The pause wasn’t real. Texas regulators continued to approve data center projects after Abbott’s announcement and only shut down the state’s permitting web portal when 404 Media reported it. Gina Hinojosa, Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, made Abbott’s stance on data centers a central part of her campaign. Abbott’s words about making Texas a data center-friendly AI state played on TVs and the internet over and over again. He lost by more than 700,000 votes. Anti-data center candidates overwhelmingly won statewide races across the country. In Burgin, Kentucky, mayoral candidate George Hensley lost his bid after voting to approve a hyperscale project—to a write-in candidate. Hensley was the only name on the ballot, and he lost to Joe MonroeTK, who ran an anti-data center write-in campaign. Emporia, Kansas — where police arrested a school teacher for clapping during a data center related city meeting — passed a ban on high impact data centers. In Yukon, Oklahoma the mayor lost a recall election after he supported a hyperscale data center project. "These midterms sent a clear message — people don't want to see data centers in their backyards,” Michael Whitesides, the deputy communications director for Local Progress, told 404 Media. “Across the country, people do not see the promised benefit of these data centers, and the AI they power, playing out in their daily lives. They're seeing basic goods and services get more expensive while these billionaire backed monstrosities take up space in their community, poison their air, and drive up their utility bills.” Local Progress is a network of local elected officials. Over the past year, its members have become increasingly focused on data centers as a top political issue. “Last night, we saw local, state, and federal officials who backed data center deals lose their seats,” Whitesides said. He noted that Kim Rooney in Asheville, North Carolina and Amanda Rodrigues in San Marcos, Texas (both members of Local Progress) were elected mayors in their cities after running anti-data center campaigns. “Big Tech will continue its typical playbook of trying to buy and bully local officials into complying with their demands for more data center development, but our hope is that last night's results are a clear signal to local leaders that they can resist and their community will back them up,” Whitesides said. American voters in the communities where they’re being built hate data centers. They run up power bills, burn through water, and power Silicon Valley’s AI apparatus. America rejected data centers last night as both symbols of the big tech oligarchy and a physical manifestation of the future it wants to build. It’s a future Americans seem willing to fight. Elon Musk, one of the night’s big losers, took a break from a weeks-long posting spree on X as the election results rolled in. Musk spent half a billion dollars on the midterms, $224 of it in Texas, the state where he lives and does a lot of business. The world’s richest man wanted to cover the state in data centers. Those plans aren’t looking good now that Abbott is out and Hinojoa is in. Musk broke his election day posting silence a little after 1 am. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he said on X. Chased off the land by its people, the billionaire looks to the sky.

artigo.texto: Aracruz entrou na rota de negociações para receber data centers ligados à inteligência artificial e a outros serviços digitais. A Imetame e a Nova ES, agência de atração de investimentos do Espírito Santo, estão articulando contatos com empresas interessadas na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) do município. O assunto foi apresentado durante um encontro empresarial realizado em Vitória na quarta-feira, 4 de novembro de 2026. A possibilidade é relevante para a economia capixaba, mas existe uma diferença entre negociação e investimento confirmado. Até esta quinta-feira (5), não havia anúncio público, nas fontes consultadas, de empresa contratada, valor fechado ou data de início da construção de um data center na ZPE. A novidade é a aproximação de potenciais investidores, e não a instalação já garantida de uma nova estrutura de inteligência artificial. Data centers em Aracruz: o que foi anunciado Segundo reportagem de Gustavo Andrade publicada em A Tribuna, em 5 de novembro de 2026, Marcelo Robers, assessor comercial da Imetame, relatou contatos com investidores da área de tecnologia e inteligência artificial. A informação foi apresentada no 5º Encontro Empresarial do Centro Capixaba de Desenvolvimento Metalmecânico (CDMEC). A articulação envolve duas frentes: a Imetame pode apresentar oportunidades ligadas à área da ZPE, enquanto a Nova ES atua na interlocução com potenciais investidores e na exposição dos benefícios do Estado. A ideia é aproveitar o ambiente industrial e logístico já planejado para atrair também negócios voltados a serviços digitais e processamento de dados. Nenhuma dessas conversas significa, por si só, licenciamento concluído, capacidade elétrica reservada ou data center em operação. Para que o cenário avance, serão necessários projetos, contratos, definições de infraestrutura e autorizações pertinentes. O que a ZPE de Aracruz oferece aos investidores A página institucional da Imetame informa que a ZPE Aracruz é a primeira zona privada do tipo autorizada no Brasil e tem administração prevista pelo grupo. Uma ZPE é uma área com regime específico para empresas voltadas a operações com o mercado externo, sujeitas às regras da legislação aplicável. O empreendimento informa aproximadamente 508 mil metros quadrados destinados à infraestrutura e a negócios interessados. Também destaca a relação com o complexo portuário do grupo, a malha rodoviária, a proximidade ferroviária e a disponibilidade de serviços logísticos. Tais condições ajudam a explicar o interesse em reunir atividades diferentes na mesma região, mas não bastam para viabilizar automaticamente uma operação intensiva em tecnologia. O leitor pode conhecer mais sobre o contexto econômico do litoral norte em nossa reportagem sobre o Portocel, em Aracruz e no guia dos principais portos do Espírito Santo. São empreendimentos e temas relacionados ao ambiente logístico, mas não devem ser confundidos com o futuro projeto de data center. Energia e conectividade são os principais desafios Data centers são instalações que abrigam servidores, sistemas de armazenamento e equipamentos de rede. Dependendo do porte, demandam fornecimento elétrico contínuo, refrigeração, redundância operacional e conectividade de alta capacidade. A expansão de serviços de inteligência artificial torna esses requisitos ainda mais relevantes na escolha de um endereço. Durante o encontro empresarial, representantes do projeto destacaram a matriz elétrica brasileira e o regime tributário como fatores competitivos. Também foram citados desafios relacionados à disponibilidade de energia e à necessidade de fortalecer a conexão com redes de dados internacionais. A capacidade exigida não é idêntica para todos os data centers e depende do projeto; por isso, não se deve assumir um consumo único para qualquer instalação eventual em Aracruz. O que pode mudar para a economia do Espírito Santo Se as negociações resultarem em projetos efetivos, Aracruz poderá ampliar sua participação na cadeia de serviços digitais, adicionando demanda por manutenção especializada, equipamentos, redes, engenharia e serviços operacionais. No entanto, uma estimativa de vagas ou retorno econômico precisaria considerar o tamanho e a configuração do empreendimento, dados que ainda não foram divulgados. O movimento se conecta à discussão sobre diversificação da economia capixaba. Nosso guia de startups e polos de tecnologia no Espírito Santo mostra outras iniciativas do setor. A diferença é que o projeto citado nesta notícia depende de investimentos privados ainda em fase de prospecção. Perguntas frequentes Aracruz já tem data center de inteligência artificial confirmado? Não. A notícia de 5 de novembro informa negociações e contatos com potenciais investidores, sem contrato ou cronograma confirmado nas fontes consultadas. Onde os empreendimentos podem ficar? As conversas mencionam a Zona de Processamento de Exportação de Aracruz, administrada pela Imetame e associada ao desenvolvimento logístico da região. Por que a energia importa tanto? Servidores e refrigeração precisam de eletricidade contínua. O fornecimento disponível e a conectividade são parte essencial da avaliação de qualquer projeto desse porte.

artigo.texto: The Mecklenburg County Board of Supervisors voted 6-1 Monday to approve a siting agreement with TerraForm Power for a 100-megawatt battery energy storage facility near Chase City, the company’s first battery storage project in Virginia. The vote, which was carried over from the October meeting of the board, was taken without comment from any member of the public or official with the company, though Kathy Keel, who lives in Chase City submitted a packet of information expressing her objections to the project and sharing information about problems and hazards that have arisen at other battery storage facilities. The agreement commits Charlottesville-based TerraForm Power to making $2.75 million in capital payments to the county on top of the annual energy revenue share and real estate taxes it will owe. County Administrator Alex Gottschalk said the county anticipates about $4 million in tax revenue from the project over 20 years. Approval of the siting agreement does not clear the project to be built. TerraForm must still win a special exception permit from the board, and the agreement is void if the board declines to grant one. No hearing on that permit has been scheduled. The project would be TerraForm’s first battery storage facility in Virginia. The company operates similar projects in other regions. One supervisor votes no over electric rates Supervisor Kirk Gravitt cast the lone vote against the agreement at the board’s meeting in Boydton. Supervisors Andy Hargrove and Dennis Spence were absent from the meeting. Gravitt said before the vote that he wanted to discuss the charges being pushed down onto county residents and businesses. He shared a recent utility bill he received from his electricity provider, Dominion Energy. Gravitt said the bill placed a one-month value of $900 for the power he used, but riders and fees brought his total bill for that month to $4,496. “So that’s a huge significant difference in the amount of kilowatts I use versus what I have to pay based upon all the riders and fees,” Gravitt said. Gravitt said he understood why the additional costs are charged but suggested the TerraForm project would do nothing to lower what local customers pay, and he said he was concerned the cost of building the facility would be passed on to them. He asked whether county residents could be guaranteed an exemption from any future charges approved by the State Corporation Commission. “But all this stuff is passed down to all of us,” he said. The project is a 170-acre site near Fort Mitchell and Lenhart roads outside Chase City. Between 10 and 15 acres would hold the battery storage equipment itself. TerraForm Power is a subsidiary of Brookfield Renewable and operates battery storage projects in other regions. What the county gets The siting agreement sets the capital payments at $27,500 per megawatt, paid to the county in five installments as the project passes milestones. TerraForm will owe $100,000 within 60 days of the board approving a special exception permit, $300,000 within 60 days of signing its PJM interconnection agreement, $300,000 within 30 days of the county issuing a zoning permit, $300,000 within 30 days of a land disturbance permit and $1.75 million within 30 days of the date the facility begins storing energy. Gottschalk said the payments track the project’s anticipated nameplate capacity at the time each one comes due. If the project shrinks during development, he said, the total would adjust before the next scheduled payment. The payments are separate from the county’s energy revenue share, which the board assesses at $1,540 a year per megawatt and which rises 10 percent every five years, and from real estate taxes on the property. Gottschalk said the county anticipates about $4 million in tax revenue over 20 years. The agreement also requires a payment of $150,000 to an energy assistance fund for the benefit of county residents, due within 30 days of the land disturbance permit. Gottschalk said the county does not expect to run such a program itself and that an existing provider would receive the money and distribute the assistance. He did not name the provider. If the capital payments are made during or after fiscal year 2029-30, the agreement allows the county to put them toward new apparatus for county fire departments. Gottschalk said the apparatus replacement program is an approved county program that will go forward whether or not the project is built, and that the project would change only the funding source in the year of payment. TerraForm must also permanently protect an equal amount of county land to whatever the facility disturbs. The company chose to meet that requirement by designating a 31- acre residue parcel as Agricultural Conservation. Gottschalk said the company represented at its October presentation that 29 acres would be disturbed. Separately, the company must post a decommissioning bond that cannot be reduced for salvage value, and the agreement bars the county from accepting a parent company guaranty from Brookfield Renewables in its place. TerraForm must also deposit $100,000 in escrow before submitting a final site plan to cover the county’s third-party review and inspection costs, replenishing it in $25,000 increments. Fire response and the fence line The Chase City Volunteer Fire Department would have first response obligation due to the site, Gottschalk said. As part of the negotiation for the siting agreement, Gottschalk said the battery company presented its project and its fire safety components to the Mecklenburg County Fire Chiefs’ Association in June. Gottschalk did not say if there were any concerns or issues raised by the fire chiefs at that presentation. The agreement additionally requires TerraForm to submit an emergency response plan with its final site plan, including fire suppression methods that can be deployed during construction and operation and “a program of education and training” for county emergency responders

artigo.texto: After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers. In a post on X, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers. Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear. "National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future." In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!" According to the CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress. Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%. Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers. South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline." In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C." Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown, who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers." Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said. Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign. "When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight."

artigo.texto: Scarborough Town Council unanimously approves ban on data centers The council voted to lift a 180-day moratorium on data centers after approving zoning changes prohibiting them in all districts Scarborough Town Council unanimously approves ban on data centers The council voted to lift a 180-day moratorium on data centers after approving zoning changes prohibiting them in all districts The Scarborough Town Council voted unanimously Wednesday night to ban data centers across town. The council also unanimously voted to lift a temporary moratorium on data center development following its approval of the ordinance. They approved changes to the town's zoning ordinance that prohibits data centers in all zoning districts. The vote comes five months after the town enacted a 180-day emergency moratorium on data centers over concerns about electricity consumption, noise, water usage and impacts on surrounding properties. According to town documents, Scarborough's Sustainability Committee determined that the potential drawbacks of data centers outweigh their benefits. The committee cited concerns about increased electricity costs, strain on the electrical grid, water consumption, air pollution and limited long-term employment opportunities. The council also voted to repeal the temporary moratorium, which town officials said would no longer be necessary following the zoning changes. The new ordinance establishes a definition for data centers but excludes smaller server rooms and similar spaces used by businesses, schools and other institutions.

artigo.texto: OpenAI quer chamar “campus de IA” aos data centers A OpenAI estará a preparar uma campanha para mudar a forma como os americanos veem a inteligência artificial e até o nome dos seus data centers poderá ser alterado. Neste artigo encontras: A empresa estará a ponderar a expressão “AI Compute Campuses”, ou “campus de computação para IA”, numa altura em que cresce a oposição local às enormes instalações necessárias para alimentar os seus modelos. OpenAI quer mudar a imagem dos data centers A proposta, divulgada pelo Axios, faz parte de uma estratégia de comunicação mais ampla. A OpenAI pretende destacar os benefícios económicos dos projetos e responder às críticas relacionadas com o consumo de energia, a utilização de água e o impacto nas comunidades. Segundo a empresa, a nova designação descreve melhor infraestruturas que combinam capacidade de computação, energia e criação de emprego especializado. Na prática, porém, a mudança de nome não altera a dimensão nem o funcionamento dos data centers. Por que motivo existe resistência? Os centros de dados dedicados à inteligência artificial exigem grandes quantidades de eletricidade e água. As comunidades próximas também têm levantado preocupações sobre ruído, poluição, aumento das faturas de energia e falta de transparência nos processos de aprovação. Um inquérito citado pela publicação Redfin indicou que 47% dos americanos questionados se opõem à construção de um novo data center nas suas comunidades. Negociações realizadas através de acordos de confidencialidade têm aumentado ainda mais as dúvidas dos residentes. A oposição já teve consequências concretas. De acordo com o mesmo relatório, pelo menos 19 municípios do Michigan avançaram com restrições a novos projetos. No norte da Virgínia, a Amazon terá abandonado planos para quatro data centers após contestação local. O impacto político da inteligência artificial Chris Lehane, responsável global pelos assuntos públicos da OpenAI, considera que as eleições intercalares norte-americanas serão uma espécie de antevisão do debate presidencial de 2028. A inteligência artificial deverá estar no centro da discussão devido ao seu possível impacto no emprego, na economia e no ambiente. A empresa também quer promover medidas de proteção para sistemas avançados, comparando-as a “limites de velocidade” aplicados à tecnologia. Microsoft e outras empresas seguem caminho semelhante A OpenAI não é a única tecnológica a tentar melhorar a relação com as comunidades onde instala a sua infraestrutura. A Microsoft anunciou uma abordagem centrada nas comunidades, incluindo a promessa de compensar aumentos nos custos de eletricidade associados aos seus data centers e investir em infraestruturas locais. Outras empresas estão igualmente a apostar numa nova linguagem para descrever a corrida à inteligência artificial. Jensen Huang, da Nvidia, já usou a expressão “fábricas de superinteligência” para falar de data centers, enquanto a Meta criou uma unidade dedicada à superinteligência. Um novo nome chega para resolver o problema? A mudança para “campus de IA” poderá tornar a comunicação da OpenAI mais positiva, mas dificilmente eliminará as preocupações das populações. Os residentes continuam a exigir respostas sobre o consumo de recursos, os benefícios locais e os riscos ambientais. Para conquistar apoio, a empresa terá de ir além da publicidade: acordos públicos, dados verificáveis e compromissos claros poderão ser decisivos. Como reconheceu Lehane, as comunidades devem responsabilizar as empresas e garantir que estes projetos trazem benefícios reais. Fonte: Tom's Hardware

artigo.texto: Technology giant Google will build its first data center in southeast Wyoming, and potentially invest $17 billion in computing centers here. The company confirmed its Equality State data center plans Thursday afternoon, “designed to deliver lasting benefits for Laramie County families and businesses.” “We’re committed to partnering with communities to build data centers the right way,” the company said in a prepared statement. “We will pay for 100% of the power we use, and when we build data centers, we’ll cover the infrastructure needs directly driven by our growth.” It was unclear as of press time Google’s timeframe for building the first facility and how long it might take to complete its $17 billion buildout near Terry Ranch Road in Laramie County. The news comes amid a whirlwind of data center speculation throughout much of the state, including in the Cheyenne area, where the industry is already established, with 10 in operation and more than a dozen on the planning books. The bevy of data centers has provoked a backlash in Wyoming and elsewhere. Prominent politicians, including Secretary of State and soon-to-be Congressman Chuck Gray, have come out in opposition to new AI data centers in Wyoming. A University of Wyoming poll published last week found only 30% of residents here supported allowing the construction of more large data centers for AI technology. Google says it is partnering with natural gas pipeline company Tallgrass Energy, electric utility Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and data center developer Related Digital for the “long-term” investment plan. The first step is a 702-megawatt facility, powered by fuel-cell technology — converting natural gas into electricity — and a plan to permanently sequester electrical generation emissions deep underground, the company said. Tallgrass is already developing a carbon dioxide sequestration hub in Wyoming, it noted. Regarding water consumption — a major concern among Wyomingites — Google said, “our Wyoming data center will be air-cooled to minimize strain on local water resources.” “This is not speculative. This is happening,” Cheyenne Mayor Patrick Collins told WyoFile. “I’ve been talking to Google, for at least a year now, about looking at Cheyenne to see if we’re a good fit for them and they’re a good fit for us, and I think they have determined we’re a great fit for them.” Tallgrass is already prepping a one-square-mile area for the first phase of the project, he said. “They have spent millions of dollars already, and Google will break ground here soon.” Prior to Thursday’s announcement, Google officials met with “more than 200 residents in Laramie County” to gather feedback to tailor its plans, the company said. Cheyenne City Councilman Larry Wolfe said Google’s announcement feels like a confirmation. “You know, we’re not easily dazzled anymore,” Wolfe told WyoFile. “I will tell you that it’s $10 billion here, $20 billion there. What it’s done is it has made us really cynical about projects that aren’t of that magnitude.”

artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil: país vira válvula de escape dos EUA Com comunidades em todos os Estados Unidos rejeitando data centers, cresce a pressão política para limitar sua construção. Mas, a milhares de quilômetros de distância, o maior país da América do Sul já é um dos principais mercados de IA e está facilitando a chegada de grandes projetos. O Brasil tem sido cortejado pelas gigantes do setor para a construção de grandes projetos de data centers, e pode se tornar uma válvula de escape para a demanda reprimida nos EUA. Por que data centers são importantes? Os data centers são a espinha dorsal da economia digital, abrigando servidores que processam desde transações bancárias até modelos de inteligência artificial. No entanto, essas estruturas consomem enormes quantidades de energia e água, gerando controvérsias em regiões onde a infraestrutura elétrica já está sobrecarregada. Nos EUA, a resistência local tem levado a restrições e atrasos em projetos, o que abre espaço para outros mercados. O Brasil, com sua matriz energética majoritariamente renovável e território vasto, desponta como destino natural para esses investimentos. A fonte não detalhou os números exatos de consumo, mas especialistas apontam que a disponibilidade de energia limpa é um diferencial competitivo. Brasil já é potência em IA Os brasileiros enviam 215 milhões de mensagens ao ChatGPT por dia, segundo a OpenAI, o que torna o país o terceiro maior mercado do criador do chatbot em número de usuários semanais, atrás dos Estados Unidos e da Índia. Esse volume massivo de interações demonstra a familiaridade da população com ferramentas de IA e a demanda crescente por infraestrutura local. O Google disse que planeja dobrar sua infraestrutura de nuvem no país até 2030 em resposta à crescente demanda, e chegou a assinar um acordo de patrocínio com a Confederação Brasileira de Futebol em março para integrar o Gemini às seleções nacionais masculinas, femininas e de base. A iniciativa reforça o interesse estratégico da big tech no mercado brasileiro. Incentivos fiscais impulsionam o setor Uma lei sancionada pelo presidente Lula reduziu impostos de equipamentos para data centers, tornando o ambiente de negócios mais atrativo para investidores estrangeiros. A medida busca equiparar o Brasil a outros países da região que já oferecem condições tributárias mais favoráveis. Com uma população de quase 215 milhões de pessoas distribuídas por uma área maior do que a dos 48 Estados contíguos dos Estados Unidos, o Brasil faz sentido como um país a ser cortejado pelas empresas de hiperescala. A combinação de mercado consumidor robusto e incentivos governamentais cria um cenário promissor. Demanda local versus transferência de operações A demanda local, e não a transferência de operações de empresas americanas para o exterior, impulsionou grande parte do crescimento dos data centers na América Latina. Mas Carlos Barrera, CEO da Atlas Renewable Energy, acredita que isso pode mudar. “De fato, vemos a região como uma válvula de escape atraente para algumas das restrições de capacidade que vocês estão vendo agora nos Estados Unidos”, disse. Essa visão é compartilhada por outros analistas. “A reação negativa nos Estados Unidos não está tanto expulsando as empresas de hiperescala do país, mas direcionando-as para onde a energia estiver disponível primeiro”, disse à Fortune James Mercer, diretor da Metro Colo Advisory, empresa de consultoria em data centers. Ou seja, o Brasil pode captar projetos que seriam inviáveis em solo americano devido à escassez de energia ou à oposição comunitária. Desafios: energia e impostos Mas a eletricidade barata do Brasil também pode ficar mais cara. Barrera disse que o Brasil precisará de mais linhas de transmissão para conectar grandes data centers à rede elétrica, e que autoridades do governo estão divididas sobre a possibilidade de as contas de luz aumentarem ou não. A expansão da infraestrutura de transmissão é um gargalo crítico para viabilizar novos empreendimentos. Outro obstáculo ao crescimento da IA no Brasil é o sistema tributário. Os altos impostos federais de importação tornavam mais caro construir grandes data centers no País em comparação com outros países da região. Embora a recente desoneração de equipamentos represente um avanço, a carga tributária sobre outros insumos e serviços ainda preocupa investidores. Para empresários e comerciantes do noroeste paulista, o desenvolvimento de data centers pode gerar oportunidades indiretas, como demanda por serviços de construção, manutenção, segurança e alimentação. A instalação de grandes estruturas em cidades médias do interior poderia aquecer a economia local, criando empregos formais e movimentando o comércio regional. Perguntas Frequentes Por que o Brasil pode se tornar uma alternativa aos EUA para a construção de data centers? O Brasil é visto como uma válvula de escape para as restrições de capacidade nos EUA, onde comunidades estão rejeitando data centers, e o país já é o terceiro maior mercado do ChatGPT, com 215 milhões de mensagens diárias. Quais empresas de tecnologia estão investindo em data centers no Brasil? O Google planeja dobrar sua infraestrutura de nuvem no país até 2030 e assinou acordo com a CBF para integrar o Gemini às seleções; outras gigantes do setor também têm cortejado o Brasil para grandes projetos. Quais são os principais desafios para a expansão de data centers no Brasil? O Brasil precisa de mais linhas de transmissão para conectar data centers à rede elétrica, e os altos impostos federais de importação encarecem a construção em comparação com outros países da região.

artigo.texto: Eleição de Gina Hinojosa como governadora do Texas ameaça frear megaprojetos de data centers de IA no estado Democrata eleita quer suspender novas instalações no estado até que empresas assumam custos de energia e revelem o consumo de água, ampliando a incerteza sobre projetos de OpenAI, Google, Microsoft e Anthropic Atualizado A eleição de Gina Hinojosa como governadora do Texas abre uma frente de incerteza para um dos maiores polos de construção de data centers de inteligência artificial dos Estados Unidos. A democrata derrotou Greg Abbott depois de defender uma moratória para novos projetos e regras mais duras sobre consumo de água, uso da rede elétrica, incentivos fiscais e custos repassados à população. Hinojosa será a primeira mulher latina a governar o Texas e a primeira democrata a ocupar o cargo desde Ann Richards, na década de 1990. Segundo a Associated Press, a oposição aos data centers de alto consumo energético tornou-se um dos eixos de sua campanha, ao lado do custo de vida, das escolas públicas e das acusações de favorecimento a grandes empresas. A mudança ocorre no estado que se tornou um dos principais destinos dos investimentos destinados a sustentar o avanço da IA. Um levantamento do Texas Tribune identificou pelo menos 248 data centers planejados no Texas, incluindo complexos que exigiriam sozinhos mais eletricidade do que algumas das maiores cidades americanas. Entre os empreendimentos estão o Stargate, construído em Abilene para a OpenAI e operado com infraestrutura da Oracle, e o Project Matador, complexo da Fermi America nos arredores de Amarillo. Também há projetos de Google, Microsoft, Anthropic e outras empresas em diferentes estágios de desenvolvimento. Água, energia e bilhões em incentivos Durante a campanha, Hinojosa pediu a suspensão de novos data centers até que o Legislativo estadual aprovasse proteções permanentes para as comunidades. Sua proposta prevê permitir que autoridades locais participem da aprovação dos projetos, obrigar empresas a divulgar o consumo de água e eletricidade e impedir que os gastos com novas linhas de transmissão e geração sejam transferidos às contas residenciais. A governadora eleita também quer retirar os incentivos fiscais concedidos ao setor. O Texas oferece isenção temporária do imposto estadual sobre equipamentos e outros itens utilizados por data centers que cumpram requisitos de investimento e criação de empregos. Dependendo do tamanho do projeto, o benefício pode durar até 20 anos, segundo a Controladoria do Texas. O custo desses incentivos aumentou com a corrida pela infraestrutura de IA. O Texas deixará de arrecadar cerca de R$ 17,6 bilhões (US$ 3,2 bilhões) em dois anos por causa da isenção, de acordo com estimativas da Controladoria obtidas pelo Texas Tribune. A pressão sobre a rede elétrica também passou a pautar a disputa. Em agosto, o órgão responsável pelo sistema texano analisava pedidos de conexão de data centers equivalentes a mais de 474 gigawatts, volume superior a cinco vezes o recorde de demanda de todo o estado. Hinojosa acusa as empresas de avançarem sobre comunidades sem transparência suficiente. Sua plataforma determina que contratos de fornecimento de água possam ser revistos quando ameaçarem o abastecimento local e propõe proibir acordos de confidencialidade usados para esconder informações sobre consumo e incentivos. Stargate, Google e um projeto maior que grandes cidades O crescimento dos data centers no Texas ganhou escala com projetos voltados especificamente ao treinamento e à operação de sistemas de IA. Em Abilene, o Stargate pode alcançar uma demanda de 1,2 gigawatt, equivalente a cerca de um terço da eletricidade consumida pelas residências de Houston, segundo o Texas Tribune. A OpenAI afirma que o complexo utiliza um sistema fechado de refrigeração, no qual a água circula continuamente depois do abastecimento inicial. A empresa diz que, quando estiver totalmente construído, o consumo anual do sistema de resfriamento será comparável ao de um prédio comercial de porte médio. Perto de Amarillo, o Project Matador foi projetado pela Fermi America para atingir até 17 gigawatts de capacidade energética. A primeira locação assinada, com a empresa de computação em nuvem TensorWave, prevê uma instalação de 222 megawatts e receita contratada de aproximadamente R$ 35,7 bilhões (US$ 6,5 bilhões) em 15 anos, segundo o comunicado da Fermi. O Google, por sua vez, começou a construir com a Intersect o Meitner Energy Center, nos condados de Gray e Roberts. O projeto combina um data center com nova capacidade de geração e utiliza resfriamento a ar para reduzir o consumo de água, segundo a empresa. Essas diferenças serão importantes na aplicação de eventuais regras. Projetos já em operação, obras iniciadas e instalações ainda à espera de licenças ou conexão à rede não necessariamente receberiam o mesmo tratamento. A extensão de uma moratória dependerá das medidas adotadas pelo governo estadual e das leis aprovadas pelos parlamentares. Abbott já havia determinado em setembro a interrupção de novas licenças ambientais até a conclusão de uma auditoria sobre o impacto dos data centers. Conduzido pelo operador da rede elétrica do Texas, o levantamento reúne informações sobre energia, água, incentivos públicos e efeitos locais dos projetos com demanda igual ou superior a 25 megawatts. O relatório está previsto para 10 de dezembro.

artigo.texto: A battery measuring just 2.77 micrometers thick could offer a route to powering wearable electronics, tiny sensors, and medical devices. Developed by a team at Dongguk University in South Korea, the thin-film platform uses tin and carbon layers to control lithium deposition and reduce lithium loss during charging and discharging. Led by Professor Hyun-Suk Kim of the Department of Energy and Materials Engineering, the researchers combined the coating with an added lithium reserve to improve battery stability. The university announced the findings on November 3. Tackling uneven lithium deposition All-solid-state batteries replace liquid electrolytes with solid materials, offering potential safety and energy-density advantages. However, uneven lithium plating and stripping can destabilize their operation. Anode-less designs address part of the manufacturing challenge by allowing lithium from the cathode to deposit onto a current collector during the first charge, forming the anode in place. This architecture can simplify fabrication and increase volumetric energy density, particularly in thin-film batteries. But lithium can become electrically isolated, forming “dead” lithium, or lose contact with the solid electrolyte during stripping. These processes reduce the lithium available for subsequent cycles and compromise capacity. The Dongguk team investigated whether a coating on the current collector could help control that process. “Our interlayer acts as a seed for Li nucleation, promoting uniform Li plating and reducing Li loss and improving the reversibility of repeated charging and discharging,” Kim said. More from Energy See All Tin and carbon guide lithium growth The researchers screened carbon-only, metal-only, and combined metal/carbon coatings. A tin/carbon bilayer on a copper current collector delivered the best overall performance among the configurations tested, showing favorable lithium deposition and interfacial stability. The two layers perform different roles. Tin lowers the energy barrier for lithium nucleation, helping lithium begin forming at the interface. The carbon overlayer regulates subsequent growth, potentially limiting uneven deposition and stabilizing the region where tin and lithium interact. The team also deposited a thin metallic lithium layer onto the coated collector. This prelithiation step created a reserve to compensate for lithium lost during initial cycling. During the first lithium plating, a three-dimensional textured region containing tin and lithium-tin formed within the interlayer. According to the researchers, this structure could accommodate volume and shape changes during later cycles, helping maintain contact and stability. Ultrathin platform shows storage potential The completed battery combined a lithium vanadium oxide cathode, a lithium phosphorus oxynitride solid electrolyte, and the coated copper current collector. It achieved a volumetric energy density of 235.13 Wh/L at its 100th cycle, measured at a reported rate of 0.01 C. Its overall thickness was 2.77 micrometers. “Our approach shows how interface engineering and lithium-inventory management can improve anode-less thin-film batteries,” Kim said. “This approach could support the development of ultrathin batteries for wearable electronics, IoT sensors, and medical devices, as well as scalable anode-less ASSBs for industrial-scale power,” he added. The findings identify a way to manage both lithium deposition and the lithium supply within an ultrathin battery architecture. The study was published in the journal Advanced Energy Materials.

artigo.texto: After ChatGPT launched in late 2022, tech companies raced to open data centers at unprecedented rates, pouring billions of dollars into AI hubs in states like Texas and Ohio. Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, and others did so even as polling showed the centers were highly unpopular among a large swath of the U.S. population. On Tuesday, the issue came to a decisive tipping point. U.S. voters delivered an overwhelming victory for Democratic candidates throughout the country that will upend the halls of power in Washington and data center hotbeds like Texas. While tech companies have established years-long plans to keep opening the centers, and are regularly plugging more online, they will be met with new state and national political leaders whose mandate is to slow down the unpopular facilities. They also now face a wave of voter rejection on numerous projects across the U.S. Voters sided against data center development in all but one of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts tracked by Redbud Consulting, a Washington, D.C., polling and data science firm, according to preliminary results. That includes Piqua, a 20,000-person city in west central Ohio, where Meta is planning to spend $1 billion to construct a data center with a capacity of up to 1.4 gigawatts. Residents voted to recall the mayor and two city commissioners who supported the project. In Ohio, voters in at least 14 municipalities approved data center bans or other restrictions, showing that the opposition extended well beyond a handful of high-profile projects. And in Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated longtime Republican Gov. Greg Abbott after campaigning on a moratorium on data center development until lawmakers establish additional protections for residents. Texas has more than 400 data center facilities and many more under construction, according to the American Edge Project and Technology Councils of North America. “Most definitely, there will be challenges — two or three steps forward, one step back,” Baron Fung, senior research director at market research firm Dell’Oro Group, told Fortune, speaking about what Big Tech companies now face. “There could be delays … trying to address any kind of guidelines that weren’t really reinforced before regarding data centers.” Fung said overall progress will continue, but companies may shift projects as they deal with pushback, and they will be asked to assume more of the financial and energy burden going forward rather than relying as much on municipalities. Elon Musk, whose SpaceX expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditures in the quarter ending in December, wrote on X Tuesday night that “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” Musk spent more than $200 million supporting Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who lost. The unpopularity of data centers in the U.S. has been a central theme of the AI revolution. Most Americans oppose data centers and are more fearful about AI than hopeful, according to recent Pew Research Center polls. During the second quarter of this year, at least 45 data center projects worth roughly $68 billion were disrupted by local opposition, according to Data Center Watch, a research project run by the company 10a Labs. The hyperscalers opening the centers have themselves warned about disruptions to their plans. In September, Oracle executives noted during an earnings call that the company doesn’t assume every project will arrive on time, that it has backup options, and that it brings large campuses online in phases. The company has developments across the U.S. and internationally, so “all of our eggs are not in a single basket,” Co-CEO Clay Magouyrk said. Oracle, in particular, has stood out for its risk-taking during the AI buildout, having more than $125 billion in debt and other notes payable and fundraising aggressively. Earlier this year, the company said it would need to raise between $45 billion and $50 billion in 2026 alone to fund its infrastructure expansion. Before Tuesday’s election results, Microsoft, Amazon, and other major companies had mounted charm offensives in communities throughout the country in the hopes of winning over weary residents. The strategy has centered on money, utility-bill protections, local jobs, and transparency. In October, Amazon announced “Built Together,” pledging more than $1 billion over five years to U.S. communities hosting its data centers. Amazon also pledged to publish its annual energy and water use, install lower-emission backup generators at new sites, and pay enough for power to avoid increasing other customers’ electricity bills. In January, Microsoft promised to cover the power infrastructure costs associated with its facilities and stop seeking local property-tax breaks. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google also dropped requirements that local officials sign nondisclosure agreements regarding data center projects. That may not be enough in states like Texas. Incoming Gov. Hinojosa has called for repealing data center tax breaks and requiring developers to protect household utility bills and local water supplies, while giving residents more say over new projects. “The impact may ultimately be less about restrictions than extracting more from data center operators for the social license to operate through taxes, power rates, environmental considerations, and community support,” analysts at investment banking firm Macquarie Group Limited wrote in a note Wednesday. AI cloud providers could face higher rents for power-equipped data center buildings needed to fulfill customer contracts, potentially passing those costs on to customers, the analysts wrote. Demand from large cloud companies and AI labs could further tighten the supply of available sites. Big Tech companies may also fall back on upgrading or retrofitting existing data centers, Dell’Oro’s Fung said. artigo.texto: Ohio voters rejected the AI buildout almost everywhere it was on the ballot Tuesday, with at least 14 municipalities passing bans or other restrictions on data centers. The Buckeye State is on its way to becoming the prototype for how American voters respond in the face of mass AI infrastructure expansion. Ohio residents across 18 municipalities voted on 21 ballot measures on data centers on Tuesday—more than half of the 41 data center-related ballot measures across the country. With more than 200 operational data centers, Ohio ranks No. 5 among U.S. states in number of data center projects. According to state data, companies plan to invest up to $40 billion in AI infrastructure in the state by 2030. Plans for AI infrastructure expansion across the country face strong national opposition—including in the form of 125 local data center moratoriums already in place in Ohio. Ohio voters’ decisive stance against the buildout could foreshadow not just future election results, but how stakeholders in the private sector and government respond. “With over 100 Ohio townships adopting moratoria or restrictions, strong voter turnout against expansion would signal to statehouses nationwide that ratepayer protections, transparency, and grid safeguards should dominate policy agendas,” Keith Durkin, a sociology professor and director of the Ohio Northern University Institute for Civics and Public Policy (ICAPP), told Fortune. How did Ohio vote? In central Ohio, all five communities with data center measures on the ballot voted against data centers. In Sunbury, residents appear to have passed a charter amendment banning data centers that use 25 megawatts or more, with 100% of the unofficial vote counted. The measure was aimed at a possible hyperscale Amazon project, though the project’s fate remains unclear, NBC4 reported. Pataskala voters also approved a charter ban on large data centers. In Trenton, a ban passed 80% to 20%. Organizers hope it will keep an 18-building Amazon Web Services data center out of the city, though it likely won’t affect a four-building AWS campus already under construction nearby, the Journal-News reported. In Perry, more than 87% of voters approved a measure requiring developers seeking tax breaks to offer the village financial guarantees. In Wilmington, around 80% of voters rejected rezoning across four separate referendums meant to accommodate a data center project. Results in Oregon weren’t yet available as of midnight. Ashville residents voted in favor of entirely blocking a data center campus that is already under construction. The bulk of the ballot measures came from 13 municipalities voting on measures to ban or heavily restrict data centers, including “high impact” campuses using more than 25 megawatts of power. Those measures were on the ballot in the municipalities of Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Grove City, Hubbard, Monroeville, Oregon, Pataskala, Piqua, Sunbury, Trenton, Upper Sandusky, and Urbana. Two measures in Monroe and Sprigg townships, respectively, decided whether zoning restrictions on large data center developments should be implemented as a means to preserve agricultural land. Wilmington voters also decided on four separate referendums on whether to uphold the rezoning of four rural residential sites to light industrial sites to accommodate data center construction. Ashville residents voted on a measure to entirely block a campus that is already under construction, and Perry voters decided on a resolution to require data center developers to implement noise limits and make financial commitments to the village before receiving local tax breaks. What do polls say about Ohio’s sentiment toward AI expansion? A Gallup poll published in May found about 70% of Americans opposed the construction of data centers in their local areas, and Ohio appears to largely mirror the national sentiment. ICAPP, in partnership with SurveyUSA, found in a poll of 1,650 Ohio adults published last month, that 55% opposed data center construction in the state compared to 22% in support, while 65% opposed tax breaks for data center developments compared to 15% in support, and 57% said they would vote in favor of a proposed state constitutional amendment banning new large-scale data centers exceeding 25 megawatts in power demands. About 20% of respondents said they’d vote against the amendment, and 21% were undecided. Durkin attributes the negative sentiment toward data centers to a confluence of factors, primarily fear of the environmental and economic risks associated with the AI boom that has emerged as a result of little knowledge about data centers. “I’ve never seen any pro-data center advertising. I’ve never seen any op-eds from the industry,” he said. “Everything we know is that humans don’t like uncertainty from social behavioral science, and there’s uncertainty around data centers.” This skepticism is bipartisan across both Ohio and the country, and it’s allowed Democrats to make data center construction a wedge issue this election, Tatishe Nteta, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, previously told Fortune. Ben Green, assistant professor of public policy at the University of Michigan’s Ford School, similarly argued data centers have become bipartisan because it has struck ideological chords in both parties. Democrats may oppose the campuses because of climate change concerns, but Republicans similarly value environmentalism through the preservation of land. “Democrats and Republicans might talk about that differently, but massive corporations coming in and forcing a community to deal with some type of project and not really giving a community any voice and operating in secrecy—no one’s really a fan of that,” Green told Fortune. Indeed, in Ohio, the environment was the top reason for negative data center sentiment, with quality of life and the economy representing the second and third most common reason for opposition, respectively,

artigo.texto: In Ohio, 14 municipalities restricted data centers — Fortune In the United States, at least 14 municipalities in Ohio on Tuesday approved bans or other restrictions on data centers. They include Sunbury, where the restriction is aimed at a planned Amazon data center. As Fortune reports, rising electricity bills have become one of the main arguments of opponents of the large-scale expansion of infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Electricity and the election campaign Candidates from both parties in Midwestern and Mid-Atlantic states linked the cost-of-living issue to electricity consumption by data centers. Abdul El-Sayed, who NBC News projected to win the Senate election in Michigan, called for not raising rates for households and demanded that data centers pay for their own energy demand. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted while advocating for the repeal of tax breaks for companies building data centers and for those companies to pay for the utilities needed to operate such facilities. Both candidates for Ohio governor — Democrat Amy Acton, who won, and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy — proposed a moratorium on new data centers. In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers supported a one-year moratorium in August, while Republican Byron Donalds, who won the Florida governor's race, proposed restrictions for such facilities. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Rising costs Fortune notes that grid operator PJM Interconnection, which serves 13 states from New Jersey to northern Illinois, recorded a jump in prices for reserve generating capacity: from $28.92 per megawatt-day in 2024–2025 to $329.17 in 2026–2027. Independent market monitor Monitoring Analytics estimated that data centers accounted for 63% of the price increase at the 2025–2026 auction. According to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, this amounted to $9.3 billion, which was recovered from consumers through higher rates. According to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, this adds about $16 per month to the average household bill in Ohio and $18 in western Maryland. Consulting firm ICF forecasts that by 2030, rates for residential consumers in the PJM area could rise by 30–60%. At the same time, the Ohio Manufacturers' Association rejected claims that data centers themselves are causing electricity to become more expensive. Amazon did not say whether the local votes would affect its expansion plans, but stated that its commitments to the communities where it operates remain unchanged.

artigo.texto: Why Don't More Data Centers Use Liquid Nitrogen For Cooling? In our technology-oriented world, data centers keep everything running. From cloud storage and websites to AI, both individual users and businesses rely on these facilities. However, all those computers generate a huge amount of heat. As servers get more powerful and packed much tighter together, overheating becomes a pressing issue. Cooling is among the biggest ongoing expenses due to electricity usage. Some estimates say that cooling can eat up to 40% of a data center's total power use. In one of the more innovative ways to fight this, Amazon is using reclaimed water to keep its data centers cool. One solution that might seem like a no-brainer is liquid nitrogen. At -321 °F (-196 °C), liquid nitrogen can pack a huge amount of cooling power into a small space. Despite that, it's not something data centers use, and one of the main reasons is the cost. Any company looking to add liquid nitrogen to its existing data centers would have to change its whole infrastructure. As for new construction, there's still the specialized training needed to work with cryogenic systems safely. Data centers would need special storage and dispensing gear, and that kind of equipment isn't cheap nor easy to use. Anyone operating liquid nitrogen equipment needs proper hands-on knowledge to keep things running smoothly and avoid accidents. Liquid Nitrogen can serve as a backup Still, that doesn't mean liquid nitrogen can't be useful. One place it could come in handy is as a backup for emergency cooling. Namely, when overheating happens or some systems fail, liquid nitrogen could be pumped straight into heat exchangers to cool things down quickly. Even if the power goes out or the main cooling system stops working, liquid nitrogen cooling can still be applied. As such, it can keep temperatures steady long enough to shut things down properly or get systems back online. While it remains far from widespread use, there have been recent developments. In mid-September, Utah-based company Reflect Scientific, which specializes in cryogenic cooling systems, announced that its liquid nitrogen cooling technology is ready for use in AI data centers. Either way, with the ever-growing reliance on data centers, the cooling technology is bound to move forward, and there have already been talks about data centers using nothing except their own heat for cooling.

artigo.texto: Company withdraws application to build battery storage project in Madison County A company that proposed two battery energy storage facilities in Madison County has withdrawn its application. As IPR’s Thomas Ouellette reports, that’s after it received an unfavorable vote from local officials. Audio Transcript Jupiter Power wanted to build two separate facilities that hold surplus energy from a local power grid. The energy is stored in large lithium batteries until it’s needed in times of peak power use. Before voting unanimously for an unfavorable recommendation, the Madison County Planning Commission raised questions about the safety of the project and any future land sales. The majority of public comment was also firmly against the proposal. Officials from Jupiter Power have not given an exact reason for the withdrawal. In a statement, the company says “Indiana’s need for more power has not changed, and we will continue to evaluate how best to help meet this challenge and support everyone who depends on a reliable grid for their families and businesses.” Jupiter officials had said the completed project would have resulted in a $500 million investment in the county, with no tax abatements requested. The rezoning was proposed in September, but Jupiter Power developers at that meeting requested a continuance to better respond to concerns and questions. At past meetings, Madison County officials, and community members spoke at length about long-term risks of these facilities, including lithium fires that burn hotter and longer than wood fires. Indiana Michigan Power had signed an agreement to purchase one of the finished facilities. Thomas Ouellette is our reporter and producer. Contact him at thomas.ouellette@bsu.edu.

artigo.texto: The ACT's largest battery storage system is now online, located in Williamsdale, south of Tuggeranong. Private company Eku Energy designed, built, and owns the 250-megawatt system, with the ACT government saying it will eventually generate revenue for the territory. The project's timeline blew out by a year after the ACT government and Eku Energy first announced the system was expected to be completed in 2025. The largest battery energy storage system in Canberra's history is online, with the ACT government saying the batteries could power one-third of Canberra's electricity needs for two hours in times of peak demand. The Williamsdale site, south of Tuggeranong, has 136 Tesla Megapack 2 batteries and connects to the electricity grid, absorbing excess energy in times of low demand, before returning it to the grid when demand is high. The project is a partnership between the government and private company Eku Energy, which designed, built and owns the 250-megawatt capacity batteries. The timeline to complete the project blew out twice after its delivery was projected to be in 2025, then later extended to early in 2026, which was also not realised. ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr said as part of the operating agreement, the government would pay Eku Energy a support charge of $368 million in instalments across 15 years. The government is entitled to 50 per cent of the battery's net revenue, which it earns when energy is sold back to the grid. Mr Barr said he expected the project to become revenue-positive. "So, the territory makes a contribution, then receives more in its share of the revenue," he said. "We are building this technology for households, small business, for our hospitals, for our schools, for our universities, for all of the industrial output that occurs in Canberra ... data centres are part of that," Mr Barr said. "That's why this is such a good project for the ACT." How does it work? Eku Energy policy director Rachel Rundle explained that the battery system was connected to Evoenergy's infrastructure. "Essentially they're plugged into the electricity network," she said. "They are always on … [and] because they're always on, they soak up all of the excess energy that is in the network. "Lots of that excess energy comes from the great wind and solar resources that we have in Australia. "It stores and holds onto that energy for a number of hours. "And then when that demand picks up … say, on a hot evening night or when there's a lot of industrial processing, the battery discharges that energy back into the grid, helping meet that peak demand and reducing the strain on the network." Ms Rundle said it could quickly store up to 500-megawatt hours and then discharge that amount each day. Eku Energy chief operating officer Tom Best said there were no promises that the system would put downward pressure on Canberra household electricity bills. "It's an open market, so we can't influence the market outcomes, but by bidding the capacity during those periods of high demand, we may have an impact on pricing, but it's not something we can guarantee,"

artigo.texto: “People really effing hate data centers,” Abdul El-Sayed said at a campaign event in July, E&E News reported. On Tuesday, he won Michigan’s Senate race, NBC News projected. El-Sayed was one of many winners Tuesday who made the AI buildout part of their argument about the cost of living. Voters named the cost of living a top issue in AP exit polls. In much of the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic, the clearest way that issue showed up was the monthly electric bill, and candidates in both parties blamed data centers for it. The bill The link runs through PJM Interconnection, the grid operator serving 13 states from New Jersey to northern Illinois. Capacity prices on PJM’s grid, which pay power plants to guarantee future supply, rose from $28.92 per megawatt-day in 2024-25 to $329.17 for 2026-27. Monitoring Analytics, PJM’s independent market monitor, estimated that data centers were responsible for 63% of the price increase in the 2025-26 auction, or $9.3 billion recovered from customers through higher rates, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. That adds roughly $16 a month to the average residential bill in Ohio and $18 in western Maryland, IEEFA estimated. The increases may not be over. Consulting firm ICF estimated that residential rates across PJM could climb 30% to 60% by 2030. Consumers have already noticed. In an October Consumer Reports survey, 81% of people who had lived in the same home for at least three years said their electricity bills had risen, and 84% said they’d support their utility creating a separate rate category for large users like data centers. The candidates The candidates who won on this issue made the bill the point. El-Sayed’s plan called for “no rate hikes,” arguing data centers should pay for their own energy demand. Two months after OpenAI and Oracle broke ground on a massive data center campus in Saline Township, he held a rally in front of the site. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted after calling him “the face of data centers,” citing the deals Husted worked on as lieutenant governor. Brown campaigned on eliminating tax breaks for data center companies and requiring them to pay for the utilities their campuses use. Logan Phillips, founder of the election forecasting site Race to the White House, told Fortune that Brown focused on the issue “way before anyone else was focused on it,” while Husted had been “basically at every single ribbon cutting for data centers across the state.” “Boy, did that not age well,” Phillips said. By the end of the cycle, Republicans were moving in the same direction. In Michigan, El-Sayed’s opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, said in August he supported a one-year moratorium on new data centers. In Ohio’s governor’s race, both nominees proposed moratoriums: Democrat Amy Acton, who won, and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds, who won the governor’s race, proposed restrictions on data centers. Voters Where voters could decide the question directly, they mostly said no. At least 14 Ohio municipalities passed bans or other restrictions on data centers Tuesday, including Sunbury, where a ban targets a planned Amazon data center. Nationally, voters in 10 states considered 41 data center measures. The polling matched. More than 70% of Americans said they would oppose a data center planned for their area, according to a Heatmap poll published last week, and rising electricity prices were the top reason for opposition. Not everyone accepts the link. The Ohio Manufacturers’ Association has rejected the claim that data centers are driving up energy costs. “Ohio does not have a data center cost crisis,” the group said. Amazon has declined to say whether Tuesday’s ballot measures will change its expansion plans, and said its commitment to the communities where it operates remains unchanged. The industry also made its case on TV. Build American AI, a nonprofit linked to the AI industry’s Leading the Future super PAC network, spent at least $2.54 million on Ohio ads touting data centers’ economic benefits, according to an investigation by DeSmog. The new Congress could take up the issue. Goldman Sachs strategists believe a Democratic Congress could curb data center tax incentives, though they see a nationwide moratorium as unlikely. The buildout is still accelerating: data center capacity under construction is up 48% nationwide, according to Reuters.

artigo.texto: Midterm results could bode poorly for data center projects It’s clear voters from both parties hate data centers. • less than 3 min read The midterms’ biggest loser wasn’t any particular candidate, but instead, the hulking, grey data center. Democratic lawmakers took the House, Senate, and a number of important gubernatorial races with promises to pump the brakes on AI development and data center build-outs, while local communities also voted to restrict future construction projects. Three key states just became less cozy for AI. Analysts warned in the lead-up to the election that governor races could have a huge impact on pending compute projects. And it looks like they were right: - In Texas—where over a fourth of the tech industry is planning to build new data centers—Democratic underdog Gina Hinojosa beat Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott. Hinojosa promised a data center moratorium. - Ohio elected Amy Acton, a Democrat who called for an immediate conditional moratorium. Meta and Amazon Web Services have plans to spend a combined $3 billion on data centers there. - Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, who campaigned on a new construction moratorium, won in Georgia. Since Pennsylvania also kept its governor’s mansion blue, roughly half of proposed data center projects in the US are now in areas with leaders who have promised to halt them. Elon Musk’s very costly loss The world’s richest man set a record for an individual donor in a US election by spending at least $474 million trying to get Republicans elected, especially in states crucial to AI infrastructure build-out. And the party’s losses could set him back even more…His companies Tesla, SpaceX, and X relocated to Texas with promises of tax breaks and unencumbered build-outs. Musk posted on X yesterday, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” It’s clear voters from both parties hate data centers: At least 38 localities across nine states voted to either ban or restrict data center construction. Some communities like Edgewater, FL, included a data center ban in its city’s charter. There was only one local vote on Tuesday that went against restrictions on data centers, in the town of Harwood, ND, per an analysis by Ballotpedia.—MM Morning Brew delivers quick and insightful updates about the business world every day of the week from Wall St. to Silicon Valley. artigo.texto: The City of Emporia acknowledged voters’ approval of restrictions on high-impact data centers and certain battery energy storage systems Wednesday, while emphasizing that a court must still determine whether the petition measures are legal under Kansas law. “The legal process remains ongoing,” the city said in a statement. “The Court must still determine whether the petition measures are legal under Kansas law. The election results do not resolve that question.” The statement followed Tuesday’s election, in which Emporia voters approved both measures. Question 2, prohibiting the construction and operation of high-impact data centers, passed 4,346 to 2,891, receiving about 60% support. Question 3, prohibiting the installation and operation of Tier 2 and Tier 3 battery energy storage systems, passed 4,067 to 3,117, with about 57% support. Those totals are unofficial until canvassed. The city thanked residents for participating in the election and said the results reflected support for the restrictions. “Thank you to everyone who voted and helped shape this community decision—your participation matters, and your voices have been heard,” the statement said. “The ‘yes’ vote reflects voters’ support for the restrictions outlined in the ballot questions.” The measures reached the ballot through petitions supported by Emporia Neighbors United. Their approval establishes the election outcome but leaves the legal questions identified by the city unresolved. The city said it would inform residents about the court’s ruling, explain its implications and outline the city’s next steps. The statement did not provide a timeline for a ruling. “We remain committed to providing clear information, answering questions, and conducting City business transparently,” the statement said. The city’s response follows differing reactions from petition supporters and economic development officials. Jay Vehige of Emporia Neighbors United celebrated the results in a video posted Tuesday night, thanking volunteers who organized petition sites and went door to door. “Each and every one of us made tonight possible and we’re just getting started,” Vehige said. “So, let’s continue to work. Let’s continue to organize.” The Regional Development Association of East Central Kansas said approval of the measures would create challenges for economic development by limiting the community’s ability to evaluate covered projects individually. “We respect the voters’ decision,” RDA interim President Lyle Butler said in a statement. “Beyond restricting data center development, this outcome signals to potential investors that Emporia is narrowing its opportunities for new investment.” The city said Wednesday that it would continue working with residents, community partners and businesses to address local needs and explore future opportunities. “Our responsibility is to serve all of Emporia,” the statement said.
