artigo.texto: Regulation Ohio Voters Back Local Data Center Limits in Unofficial Results Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google Voters in Trenton, Pataskala, Granville, Sunbury, Grove City and Ashville backed local data-center restrictions in Ohio’s November 3, 2026 general election, according to unofficial county results that included Delaware County’s election-night summary. Trenton’s Issue 17 drew 79.68% support. Butler County’s unofficial results gave Trenton 3,541 yes votes to 903 no votes, with all eight precincts reporting. Licking County’s results showed Pataskala’s data-center charter amendment passing 5,418 to 1,941, or 73.62% yes, and Granville’s amendment passing 2,015 to 429, or 82.45% yes. Sunbury’s charter amendment passed 2,809 to 763, or 78.64%, with all six precincts reporting. Grove City’s Community Consent Amendment passed 11,317 to 9,411, or 54.60% yes, with all 30 precincts reporting in Franklin County’s summary. Ashville’s referendum drew 1,469 no votes, or 81.61%, against 331 yes votes in Pickaway County’s unofficial results. The Ohio Secretary of State’s ballot catalog identifies the Ashville question as whether to approve a resolution enacting a development-and-supply agreement term summary with EdgeConneX. The totals remain unofficial. The Ohio Secretary of State says certified results will be published approximately three weeks after the election. Construction Bans and Community Consent Pataskala’s official sample ballot shows a direct prohibition on covered data-center construction within city limits, effective immediately. The measure defines covered facilities as buildings, physical facilities or infrastructure used primarily or exclusively for digital information services, with aggregate monthly demand or peak load greater than 25 megawatts. Sunbury’s proposed charter text also uses the greater-than-25-megawatt threshold and defines construction to include related preparations and modifications on single, contiguous, adjacent or otherwise aggregated parcels. Grove City’s Community Consent Amendment applies to heavy industrial development, including data centers, server farms, power generation and large-scale warehousing or logistics facilities. It requires voter approval before city approvals for developments meeting at least one threshold: 50 or more contiguous acres, more than 20 megawatts of electrical power at peak capacity, or more than 500,000 gallons of water per day. Covered approvals include rezoning, conditional-use permits, planned-unit development approvals, annexations and building permits. Applicants must fund an independent impact study but have no control over the selected firm or its findings. The study must address water use, grid demand, noise, traffic, employment, tax revenue against infrastructure costs and environmental effects, and be posted publicly at least 60 days before the referendum. A failed vote blocks city approval and bars the same or a substantially similar application for 24 months. A successful vote permits the normal zoning process but guarantees no permit. Cumulative increases above 10% in acreage, peak electrical demand or daily water consumption trigger another referendum. Trenton’s Court-Ordered Path to the Ballot Trenton’s vote followed a September 1, 2026 Supreme Court of Ohio opinion holding that the city council had a mandatory constitutional duty to certify residents’ data-center amendment petition. The proposed charter change would prohibit data-center construction. Council members had refused certification after concluding that the petition lacked sufficient valid signatures. Trenton Data Center Campus, L.L.C., an entity constructing a data center in the city, intervened as a respondent. The petition contained 336 valid signatures. The council derived its 820-signature requirement from 8,197 registered voters, while the court held that 128 were required based on the 1,277 ballots cast at the preceding municipal election. The court reasoned that the constitutional signature percentage rests on total votes cast, not total registered voters, and that a municipal charter cannot be interpreted inconsistently with the Ohio Constitution. Its limited writ ordered certification for a special election within the constitutional 60-to-120-day period and denied requests for attorney fees and court costs. Statewide Infrastructure Growth and Polling The local votes intersect with Ohio’s broader data-center expansion. The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel says Ohio has more than 200 data centers, the fifth-highest count among states, with most in Central Ohio, and that companies plan to invest up to $40 billion more by 2030. These facilities support artificial intelligence, cloud storage, streaming and online business operations. A large hyperscale facility can use as much electricity as 100,000 homes, while some data centers use millions of gallons of fresh water daily for cooling. An October 22, 2026 Ohio Northern University release adds statewide polling context. Its Institute for Civics and Public Policy, working with SurveyUSA, surveyed 1,650 Ohio adults between October 8, 2026 and October 14, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. The university reported that 55% of respondents opposed data-center construction in Ohio and 22% supported it; that 57% would vote for a constitutional amendment banning new large-scale data centers with peak demand above 25 megawatts; and that 79% expected higher local water and electricity costs, including 49% anticipating significant increases. For AI infrastructure developers, the practical consequence is a layer of local approval alongside power, water and permitting decisions. Pataskala and Sunbury prohibit covered projects outright, while Grove City requires an independent study and voter approval before city approvals, followed by review of material expansions. Securing land and utility capacity therefore does not settle whether these projects can proceed

A summary of a Goldman Sachs note, posted on X by the Walter Bloomberg account and reported by us, said Texas, Georgia and Michigan “could introduce restrictions on tax breaks, electricity, water and environmental permits”. That covers four of the five; the fifth, state land, surfaced in Texas this week. This explainer maps each lever to who decides it and to the responses builders have made so far, using only our reporting from 3 to 6 November. By our count, seven of the nine named AI builds in that coverage, 78%, sit in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, from OpenAI’s Stargate to Meta and the Tesla-SpaceX Terafab. Business Pill · Who Pays for the Grid A short explainer on who pays for the grid upgrades that data centres need. It teaches the general idea only and does not discuss this story. The key insight: As we read it, the cost of an AI data center in the US is now partly set by five state levers: permits and zoning, grid and power costs, tax incentives, water, and state land. A Goldman summary posted on X named four of them for Texas, Georgia and Michigan, and Texas raised the fifth this week near SpaceX’s Starbase; seven of the nine named builds in our coverage, 78%, sit in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, by our count. Why States Now Set Part of the Price Data center politics in the US runs on three levels: local ballots, statewide races and federal pledges, as we explained on 4 November. At the local level, data center limits led 40 of 41 measures on Ballotpedia’s 3 November list. At the state level, the Wall Street Journal said candidates promising to freeze data-center development won statehouses in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and Michigan, as we reported. Analysts size the exposure in two ways. Texas, Georgia and Ohio account for more than 40% of all planned US data-center capacity, according to Evercore ISI, the Journal reported. Goldman Sachs puts about 45% of planned US capacity in states likely to tighten data-center rules, with Texas alone about a quarter, investingLive reported; that makes Texas about 56% of the capacity Goldman sees at risk, by our arithmetic. The two are different measures from different firms. Lever 1: Permits and Zoning Permits are decided by county boards, local ballots and state agencies. Of the 41 local measures, 21 sought a ban or pause, by our reading of Ballotpedia’s descriptions, and ten of those would bar only data centers above a size or power line, as we reported. Texas already has state-level pauses. Starting in August, Abbott began issuing pauses on data center approvals at the state grid and then at the environmental permitting agency, so information about the facilities could be audited, the Texas Tribune reported; the audit was expected to last until December. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa told CNN the state should go further: “We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections”, Reuters reported, as we covered. Lever 2: Grid and Power Costs In Texas the grid operator, ERCOT, and the Public Utility Commission decide who connects and who pays. ERCOT’s September board materials show about 194 GW of large loads conditionally kept in its Batch Zero study, 2.1 times the grid’s record peak demand of 91,134 MW, by our arithmetic, and its energization of new data centers is already paused pending reports due 10 December, as we reported. Hinojosa’s affordability page says she “will direct the Public Utility Commission to freeze the rates residential customers pay until we have laws to ensure that data centers and other high-load users pay for themselves”. OpenAI’s blueprint makes a similar ask of regulators: “State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid”. Lever 3: Tax Incentives Tax breaks are set by legislatures. Hinojosa’s platform says House Bill 2712, signed in 2015, gave hyperscale data centers “20-year tax breaks”, and ending tax subsidies is among the priorities she set out for lawmakers, the Tribune reported. Locally, only one of the 41 ballot measures, in Perry, Ohio, dealt with tax incentives. Lever 4: Water Water rules sit with localities and states. One of the 41 local measures, in Grove City, Ohio, named a water threshold, and protecting communities’ water supplies is on Hinojosa’s list of priorities for lawmakers, as the Tribune reported it. Lever 5: State Land States also own land. The Texas Tribune had previously reported that a draft agenda for the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission included a discussion about the possible disposition of approximately 1,300 acres of public land near SpaceX’s Starbase, and the item was later removed, as we reported. Hinojosa said she had contacted the department’s executive director and requested that no action be taken during the transition, Click2Houston reported. In a CNN clip, by our own machine transcript, she said: “We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms. These local and state measures are expected to delay, relocate, or raise costs for individual projects rather than materially reduce total U.S. data-center spending. artigo.texto: Phone battery complaints tend to be the norm, and chances are you know them better than most. “It just doesn’t last.” “I can’t get through the day.” We’ve heard it all and try as we might to get away from them, mobile phone owners tend to rely on power banks for obvious reasons. While battery development continues to improve, there’s a good chance that your phone still hasn’t seen many of those benefits come to fruition. Or worse: it did once and now it doesn’t because phone batteries decay over time. Their once impressive battery life starts to lose power the more you use it, resulting in a battery issue that affects how long you have a phone for. Power banks are therefore the obvious solution, but one that can come with an obvious risk. In fact, it’s a risk that has seen disaster at times from how flammable they can be. Now you can’t use power banks on flights for a seriously good reason. That still doesn’t mean using a power bank is necessarily safe all the time, but manufacturers are working to improve the safety because of the risks as they are now. If a standard power bank is dropped badly or pierced in any way, the contents can explode. Those contents are often using a liquid electrolyte to move the electrons that power your devices, and they can catch fire. That’s not a good thing. With the newer approaches, the electrolyte doing the lifting is suspended in a thick gel, reducing the amount of liquid and making it a “semi-solid state”. You can probably imagine what a true solid-state battery is, but that’s something further off down the track. Baby steps for the moment, and semi-solid state now, with the main differences being less flammable liquid, less chance of it leaking, and less chance of it decomposing which can lead to it overheating. “Safety is one of the most important considerations when it comes to portable power, and semi-solid-state battery technology represents an important step forward,” said Chris Lau, Managing Director at Laser. “This technology is designed to make portable power safer by reducing the amount of flammable liquid electrolyte inside the battery,” he said. “Its gel-based composition helps minimise leakage and improve heat stability, addressing some of the key safety considerations associated with traditional lithium-ion batteries.” While Laser wouldn’t be drawn to just how much of the content was gel-based versus liquid, tests show the battery not only can sustain puncture without disastrous consequences. In some instances, it actually keeps working even after being punctured. Laser’s launch in the category covers three models in its ChargeCore Semi-Solid models, ranging from a 10,000mAh battery all the way up to a laptop-focused 27,000mAh, the largest you can really carry with you in most luggage without needing a special permit. However, it’s not the only company going down this way. Journey has previously launched semi-solid state locally, and other power banks are definitely going this way, with less risk and more stability the obvious benefits. “For consumers, it means greater peace of mind when powering their everyday devices on the go,” said Lau.

artigo.texto: Regulation Data Center Policy Fears Hit AI Stocks After Hinojosa’s Texas Win Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google CNBC reported on November 4, 2026, that AI-linked stocks and Nasdaq-100 futures fell in overnight trading after Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s projected victory in the Texas governor’s race intensified investor concern that state restrictions could delay data-center projects. Nasdaq-100 futures were down 0.8% as election results arrived, more than double the decline in Dow Jones Industrial Average futures. The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF was down 2% on Robinhood. Companies with direct exposure to AI infrastructure posted steeper declines. CoreWeave, which uses borrowed money to build data centers, fell 7% on Robinhood. Texas-headquartered SpaceX dropped 6%, while Nebius Group and Oracle each lost 4%. Hinojosa Campaigned on a Data Center Moratorium Hinojosa was projected by the Associated Press to defeat incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott. In victory remarks published by her campaign on November 4, 2026, she said Abbott had called to congratulate her and offer assistance with the transition. She said the transition would begin the following day and that she would take the oath of office in January. Her campaign platform calls for an immediate moratorium on data centers until the legislature can enact protections and give Texans a role in deciding whether and how facilities enter their communities. It urged Abbott to issue an executive order halting new data centers and to call a special session to address the issue. The platform also criticized a 2015 law signed by Abbott, which the campaign described as providing 20-year tax breaks to hyperscale data centers. It demanded an end to what it called tax giveaways and said passing legislation was the only way to protect Texans. Those positions explain the policy concern, but the election itself did not enact a moratorium or change project rules. Texas Exposure Shaped the Market Reaction The state’s share of planned development helps explain why the result resonated with investors. CNBC cited Wells Fargo estimates that Texas accounts for 27% of planned U.S. data-center gigawatts. Georgia accounts for 7%, while Ohio and Pennsylvania each account for 5%; Democrats were projected to win or retain the governorships in Georgia, Ohio and Pennsylvania. Horizon Investments chief investment officer Scott Ladner said an Abbott loss would raise the question of where to build data centers and warned that Texas could cease to be a favorable location for them. Wells Fargo chief equity strategist Ohsung Kwon had described a Democratic victory in Texas as a potential “left-tail event” for the AI trade. The political result reached a market already under pressure. The Nasdaq-100 entered correction territory at the end of October 2026 amid concern that growth in data-center spending by large hyperscalers and private AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing. The overnight moves therefore added a state-policy risk to existing questions about the pace of AI infrastructure spending. For developers and investors, the immediate issue is implementation rather than a restriction already in force. Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium, community participation and legislative protections, while her victory remarks established a transition timeline. How those proposals affect project approvals, tax treatment and construction schedules will determine the practical consequences for Texas’s planned data-center capacity.

artigo.texto: SpaceX hosts community meeting about proposed massive data center in Cochise County Residents express mixed reactions to proposal TUCSON, Ariz. (13 News) - A proposed data center in rural Cochise County is drawing mixed reactions from residents following a community meeting hosted by SpaceX on Wednesday evening. Residents gathered at Cochise Elementary to learn more about the proposed development and raise questions about its potential impact on the surrounding community. Elon Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX, made news earlier this week when he claimed cooling data centers would be easier in space than on Earth. The project, proposed near the Apache Generating Station along U.S. Highway 191, would cover approximately 747 acres and include nine data center buildings used for artificial intelligence operations. According to a special use application filed with Cochise County under Tombstone Resources LLC, the facility would require up to 6,000 megawatts, or six gigawatts, of electricity at full build-out. That would make it one of the largest proposed data center developments in the country by electricity demand. A map of the proposed facility’s footprint can be seen below. The applicant claims the project could create thousands of construction jobs and potentially lower electricity bills for customers. For some residents, the proposed development represents an opportunity for the future. “We need AI centers. It’s the future,” said Herald Satterlee, who attended Wednesday’s meeting. Others expressed concerns about the project and whether enough information has been provided to the community. “We don’t know enough, therefore just say no,” said Michael Gregory, another attendee. During the meeting, residents also raised questions about water usage, wildlife, and noise levels. The application outlines plans to use a dry-cooling system to reduce water consumption, along with other proposed measures intended to address environmental impacts. Jason Bowling, CEO of Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative, acknowledged the different opinions surrounding the project. “There are some that are excited about it and some that are concerned about it. All of that is valid,” Bowling said. “The concerns are valid, and the excitement is valid, and I think we just need to let the facts come out and let folks evaluate it for themselves.” While SpaceX hosted the meeting, the special use application identifies Tombstone Resources LLC as the applicant. The exact relationship between the two companies is unclear. 13 News reached out to SpaceX for an interview during Wednesday’s meeting, but a representative was not available for comment. No decision has been made on the proposed development. The Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission is scheduled to hold a formal public hearing on Dec. 9. artigo.texto: - Google announced a $17 billion investment to construct its first data center in Wyoming, contracted with American Electric Power (AEP) to draw power from a 702 MW solid-oxide fuel cell deployment manufactured by Bloom Energy. - Emissions from the natural gas-powered fuel cell installation and adjacent power infrastructure will be captured and permanently sequestered at Tallgrass Energy’s nearby Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub, expanding Google’s contracted CCUS capacity to nearly 1 GW nationwide. - To preserve regional aquifers, the facility will utilize air cooling instead of water cooling while Google, AEP, Black Hills Energy, and local partners form a Community Council to address public concerns and oversee infrastructure delivery. Tech giant Google has announced a $17 billion long-term commitment to construct its first data center campus in Laramie County, Wyoming. To meet the compute demands of the new facility while upholding its corporate carbon targets, Google entered into a commercial-scale energy agreement with American Electric Power (AEP) to contract power from a 702 MW fuel-cell deployment, marking the largest planned fuel-cell power development for a data center to date. Under the structure, AEP will operate the generation facility using solid-oxide fuel cells manufactured in the US by Bloom Energy. The electrochemical system converts natural gas into electricity without conventional combustion, yielding a concentrated CO2 stream that improves post-combustion separation efficiency. The captured emissions will be piped and permanently sequestered underground at Tallgrass Energy’s Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub, located in the Denver-Julesburg Basin. CCUS Portfolio Expansion and Local Community Commitments The Wyoming deal expands Google’s power purchase strategy for carbon-captured natural gas generation. Building on its October 2025 agreement for the 400 MW Broadwing Energy gas-fired CCS project in Decatur, Illinois, the Wyoming fuel-cell agreement brings Google’s total contracted CCUS capacity to nearly 1 GW. Additionally, Google, Black Hills Energy, and Tallgrass Energy are conducting front-end engineering and design (FEED) studies to evaluate retrofitting carbon capture equipment onto nearby combined-cycle gas turbines. To manage regional resource constraints, and consistent with Google’s corporate water stewardship policy for water-stressed regions, the Wyoming campus will feature an air-cooled architecture. While air cooling consumes roughly 10% more power than wet cooling systems, the choice eliminates operational strain on local municipal and groundwater supplies. Relevant: Wyoming Carbon Storage Hub Gains Federal Approval Google has also committed to paying 100% of the data center’s direct power consumption and grid upgrade expenses, shielding existing regional rate-payers from capacity expansion costs. The project is projected to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in local property tax revenues for Laramie County and School District 1. Following downtown Cheyenne public forums, Google, AEP, Black Hills Energy, Tallgrass, Related Digital, and Bloom Energy are standing up a multi-stakeholder Community Council to address resident concerns over hyperscale expansion while directing target grants toward local K-12 STEM programs, trade apprenticeships, and economic development. Commercial operations for the initial fuel-cell power phase are targeted for late 2028. Read more: Oracle Grants $1M To Study Carbon Capture Potential At Data Center

artigo.texto: Bluebird Solar Private Limited is strengthening its presence in the clean energy sector with the introduction of its Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) portfolio, featuring energy storage solutions based on immersion cooling technology. As battery energy storage adoption expands, thermal management has become an important consideration for system performance, operational reliability, and safety. Maintaining suitable battery temperatures is essential, particularly in installations operating under demanding environmental conditions. Recognising this requirement, Bluebird Solar has introduced two featured energy storage solutions: a 208.99 kWh Immersion Cooling Mobile Energy Storage Vehicle and the ePower T2 Immersion Cooling Containerized Energy Storage System. Immersion cooling is a thermal management approach in which battery components are immersed in a specialised dielectric fluid. The fluid absorbs heat generated during battery operation, helping regulate temperature and support thermal stability. Unlike conventional air-based cooling approaches, immersion cooling brings the cooling medium into direct contact with the battery components. This approach is designed to improve heat transfer and manage thermal conditions within the energy storage system. The company’s new portfolio is intended to address both mobile and stationary energy storage requirements. Its solutions are positioned for applications across commercial and industrial facilities, utility-scale projects, residential energy systems, and telecom infrastructure. This technology-focused expansion forms part of Bluebird Solar 2.0, the company’s broader strategy to move beyond solar module manufacturing and participate in the development of integrated clean energy solutions. With a focus on advanced cooling systems, modular scalability, and operational reliability, Bluebird Solar is expanding its capabilities in India’s growing battery energy storage market.

artigo.texto: Os investimentos do Grupo Schwarz em inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital podem alcançar € 16,6 bilhões em dois projetos de data centers na Alemanha. Controlador das redes Lidl e Kaufland, o conglomerado pretende ampliar a oferta de computação em nuvem e serviços tecnológicos para empresas. A expansão ocorre enquanto sua divisão digital, Schwarz Digits, ainda representa uma pequena parcela do faturamento total. No exercício fiscal de 2025, o grupo registrou € 185,6 bilhões em receitas, crescimento de 5,8%. A Schwarz Digits faturou € 2,2 bilhões, avanço de 15,8%. Com base nesses valores, cálculo do Economic News Brasil aponta participação aproximada de 1,2% da divisão digital na receita agregada do conglomerado. Os números constam dos resultados oficiais, divulgados em junho de 2026. Investimentos do Grupo Schwarz têm prazos e condições diferentes O projeto de Lübbenau prevê € 11 bilhões para ampliar a capacidade de processamento de dados, com a primeira fase programada para 2027. Já o empreendimento de Dummerstorf poderá receber até € 5,6 bilhões até 2033, dependendo de aprovações e decisões futuras. Portanto, o valor agregado reúne iniciativas em estágios distintos. Não representa recursos integralmente desembolsados nem compromissos financeiros com execução definitiva. A infraestrutura integra a estratégia da STACKIT, plataforma de nuvem do conglomerado. O objetivo é atender clientes que procuram alternativas para armazenar e processar informações, especialmente organizações com exigências de segurança e controle de dados. Essa expansão acompanha o aumento dos investimentos em data centers em diferentes mercados, impulsionado pela demanda por capacidade computacional. Cohere amplia a estratégia tecnológica da dona do Lidl Em 29 de outubro de 2026, a canadense Cohere anunciou o fechamento inicial de uma rodada de financiamento liderada por empresas do Grupo Schwarz. A operação pretende captar até 7 bilhões de dólares canadenses, mas o comunicado não informa quanto já foi levantado nem atribui o valor total ao conglomerado alemão. A parceria aproxima a Schwarz Digits de modelos de inteligência artificial destinados ao mercado corporativo. Além disso, pode complementar os serviços da STACKIT e ampliar as oportunidades comerciais fora do varejo. O desafio será converter a capacidade tecnológica em contratos capazes de remunerar o capital aplicado. Embora a receita digital esteja crescendo, o Grupo Schwarz não divulga margem operacional específica da Schwarz Digits nem projeções de retorno dos novos empreendimentos. Sem esses indicadores, a rentabilidade futura da expansão permanece indeterminada.

artigo.texto: Bow residents petition town officials for data center moratorium Bow officials heard from a resident who organized a petition asking to temporarily block any data center applications Thursday night. The select board heard from the group, which said they're worried about any negative environmental and health impacts. They delivered the petition asking for a moratorium with more than 800 signatures to the board on Wednesday. The select board said they're open to hearing people out, but ultimately it's the board that will make the final decision. "That's a step forward because before we were getting blocked at every step. This is a positive step forward, and I'm glad for that," Lynn Lull, a Bow resident, said. Board officials said they will be thorough about any future proposals. "If a data center application comes towards the town, it will be vetted better than any other town in the state," Kip McDaniel, a selectboard representative, said. The temporary freeze proposed by residents aims to give the town time to research the impacts, cost and benefits of a data center. "That's basically what we want to do is find out what is a safe way to do this," Lull said. A moratorium would not just hit the pause button; it would also change the ordinances already in place in case a developer applies to build a data center, according to town officials. "We have already started discussing changes to our ordinances that would begin to address the concerns about large electrical use," McDaniel said. Town officials have not received any formal development application for a data center. In September, filings were made that hinted a company was exploring a project that could use as much power as a data center. No decisions on that have been made. After Thursday night's meeting, the select board agreed to hold another meeting to hear residents' concerns about data centers and whether one should ever be allowed in the town. The planning board isn't expected to vote on this until March.

artigo.texto: The vote to ban data centers in Trenton has passed, according to unofficial election results on Tuesday, Nov. 3. With 100% of precincts reporting, the measure passed by a landslide 80% to 20%. Trenton resident Barry Blankenship, who led efforts in the city to get the ban on the ballot, said seeing the results was emotional. “Everybody’s just so happy right now that a group of citizens came together, stood up for an issue — Democrats, Republicans alike,” he said. “We stood together and we beat a city.” Looking forward, he hopes the ban will keep an 18-building Amazon Web Services data center from developing within the city and could rein in the electric use of a four-building AWS data center already under construction. Council member Marci Butts told Journal-News she was happy the community got to vote on the measure. “It was very telling to me,” she said. “To see that the number was almost 80% for (the ban), really speaks to what the community actually wants. And I think it’s now our responsibility to respond to that in kind and move forward in the best way.” Butts said she did vote on the measure, but declined to say how she voted. Council member Austin Proffitt congratulated Blankenship and the Woodsdale and Trenton Environmental Resistance group, which “fought hard to have their voice heard.” “I am proud to be a part of a community where residents were unhappy with decisions made by their leaders and chose to get involved and do something about it,” Proffitt said. The Journal-News has reached out to the five other council members and did not receive responses from four of them. Mayor Ryan Perry declined to comment. The measure bans data centers requiring more than 25 megawatts of electricity from developing within city limits. Voters decided on the ban following more than a year of controversy over proposed data center developments, including an annexation fight, contentious council meetings, a citizen-led charter amendment, an Ohio Supreme Court case and Perry’s resignation, effective Jan. 1, 2027. (Perry had said his resignation stems from increasing obligations from both his full-time job and mayorship.) Residents began pushing back after plans surfaced in October 2025 for a data center, citing concerns about noise, light pollution, environmental impacts, rising utility demands and transparency. Path to the ballot In September, the Ohio Supreme Court unanimously ordered the charter amendment onto the ballot, ruling residents had collected enough signatures. The measure would likely not affect the four-building AWS data center already under construction on 141 acres in Trenton. However, it could impact a proposed 18-building AWS project tied to 600 acres in Madison and St. Clair townships. A petition to annex that land into Trenton was withdrawn in September but could be refiled. If annexation eventually succeeds, the ballot measure's outcome could determine whether the project moves forward within the city. Elsewhere, Butler County and other Ohio communities have enacted temporary moratoriums on data centers, though Ohio has no statewide ban. New York remains the only state with a statewide moratorium on large-scale data center development.

artigo.texto: DFW’s Fight Between Data Centers and Clean Water DFW’s Fight Between Data Centers and Clean Water Press Release Date 11-05-2026 Local residents grapple with data centers and water pollution FORT WORTH, TX, UNITED STATES, November 5, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- The Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex holds the unofficial title of top data center construction market in the United States. While tech advocates point to the growth potential of local power grids, residents and environmental experts have serious concerns about local water pollution. These fears have driven legislative action by local officials to hear public sentiment about the future of AI-related construction and its effects on water quality. On August 11, 2026, the Fort Worth City Council initiated the process for a 90-day moratorium on data center development and construction. Its first public hearing about that moratorium is scheduled for November 10. While the process allows time for stricter water and power usage regulations to be created, local water quality experts still have concerns. “Between PFAS and blue-green algae, we’re already struggling to get good water into homes,” says Steven Smith, Responsible Master Plumber at DFW’s Mother Modern Plumbing. “If we don’t get the regulations right, data centers will add cooling tower chemicals and salts to the mix.” The debate over data centers and chemical runoff extends beyond Fort Worth. Current and proposed sites stretch from the I-35 corridor in southern Dallas and Ellis County to new extensions in Irving and Garland. Still others exist in Plano and Allen. Current construction in the Metroplex boasts a 760 megawatt capacity- enough electricity to power over 550,000 homes at the same time. Proposed data center sites will use another 3.7 gigawatts of power, nearly five times what currently exists. “That much power needs 3 or 4 commercial nuclear reactors or a bunch of coal-fired power plants,” Smith remarks. “The issue is more than the raw power- all the runoff and coolant has to go somewhere.” While cities like Fort Worth look to enact closed-loop systems in an effort to conserve water, this does little to solve the problem of potential chemical runoff in water. City officials note the treated water will be hauled off to treatment plans across Fort Worth. Still, locals are unclear on exactly how effective the separation between cooling tower water and their incoming water supply will be. “We’re seeing a rise in homeowner interest when it comes to home water filtration systems,” Smith reports. “Not just at the tap. Whole home systems that get installed right on the main water supply line. People want their water treated before it even reaches the house.” Until greater clarity is offered to DFW residents regarding the precise treatment of water from data centers, this trend is likely to continue. artigo.texto: Prime Minister Narendra Modi gestures during a ceremonial reception at the presidential palace Rashtrapati Bhavan in New Delhi on October 27, 2026. (AFP Photo) India has launched a $1.5-billion scheme to develop 92 gigawatt-hours of energy storage capacity as it seeks to accelerate its shift towards renewable energy, the government said. India is the third-biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and remains deeply dependent on polluting coal to meet its soaring energy demand. Energy demand in India, home to more than 1.4 billion people, is expected to continue rising rapidly even as the government pursues its goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2070. The scheme, which runs from 2026-27 to 2030-31, will support 60 gigawatt-hours of pumped hydro storage, 30 GWh of battery storage, and two GWh using emerging technologies, the government said. New Delhi's incentives would support an estimated $10 billion of investment in the next five years, it added, with the planned additions equivalent to 170 percent of India's existing grid-scale energy storage capacity. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the scheme would help deliver "more reliable power, greater renewable energy integration, and stronger energy security." India's cabinet on Nov. 4 also approved a $300 million scheme to support four domestic processing plants for lithium and nickel, critical minerals used in electric vehicle batteries, energy storage systems, and electronics. "At present, India remains substantially dependent on imports," the cabinet said in a statement. "Domestic processing capacity is therefore imperative."

artigo.texto: SpaceXAI to build 2 more AI data centers in Southaven Colossus 2 in Memphis just named most powerful data center on the planet SOUTHAVEN, Miss. — Elon Musk said SpaceXAI is building two more data centers in Southaven adjacent to Colossus 2 right across the state line in Memphis. This will make six SpaceXAI data centers operating in the Memphis metro area. Data centers in Memphis and Southaven SpaceXAI has three data centers in Memphis: Colossus 1 in South Memphis, Colossus 2, nicknamed Macrohardrr, in Whitehaven, and Minihard next door. A fourth, called Macrohardrr, is across the state line in Southaven near the SpaceXAI power plant which is located in the 2800 block of Stanton Road. Musk said two more data centers are under construction nearby on Tulane Road. One, called Gun Range, is at the city’s former training facility. The other, called Spam, is being built at the old Hormel building. The Gun Range data center is expected to come online in November. Spam is expected to be operational in December. Southaven business owner reports a dip Terry Tongumpun, a Southaven business owner, said the data center boom has hurt his business at Game Over Arcade Bar near Stanton Road and U.S. Hwy 51. “We’re hurting really bad,” Tongumpun told Action News 5, “The traffic is nuts and it’s affecting my business. I definitely noticed a dip, and people are not coming out as much. They’re trying to avoid xAI traffic.” The congestion on Stateline Road has increased near the SpaceXAI power plant and the Macrohardrr data center, where the two new data centers are already under construction. Dust billows up. Cars sit at green lights going nowhere because the traffic is so deep. Mayor cites tax revenue Southaven Mayor Darren Musselwhite said growing pains aside, the SpaceXAI development is bringing unprecedented tax revenue. “We knew it would be expanding in a campus-type format,” Musselwhite said, “It nets about $63 million a year to DeSoto County Schools, DeSoto County and the City of Southaven. It’s a good thing for Southaven.” Buyout offer and environmental questions Musselwhite confirmed that SpaceXAI is offering to buy more than 400 nearby homes and businesses if owners are bothered by noise or pollution. In fact, the mayor said he asked Elon Musk’s company to make the gesture. “I think the number one goal,” said Musselwhite, “is for them not to be intrusive or invasive in any way with noise and anything else. That’s been the goal the whole time.” The environmental impact of the data center development and subsequent expansion is not yet known. In Memphis, activists are still waiting for information about water, electricity, and gas usage for the three data centers operating in the city. “We have a pending records request to MLGW that we are now three months in,” said Sarah Houston, executive director of Protect Our Aquifer, “We’ve been waiting for the records on the most recent utility bills from Colossus 1, 2 and Minihard. We don’t have an accurate picture of water use, but we heard from MLGW CEO Doug McGowen that by the end of the year SpaceXAI could be in the top 5 water users.” Back in Southaven, Tongumpun said he worries SpaceXAI’s growth could mean it’s game over for his business. “The complaint is…we just hate what xAI has done," he said, “The roads are too small. There’s not enough parking spots. And it’s just oversaturated. We feel like we’re at FedExForum every night. It’s crazy!” Click here to sign up for our newsletter! artigo.texto: A Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) decidiu não expandir seu contrato de locação de data center com a provedora britânica de infraestrutura de inteligência artificial Nscale, no Texas, de acordo com uma reportagem do Financial Times publicada na quinta-feira, enquanto a Nscale se prepara para uma possível oferta pública inicial (IPO) avaliada em aproximadamente US$ 35 bilhões. A decisão diz respeito a uma opção que teria mais do que duplicado o contrato existente da Microsoft para alugar capacidade computacional nas instalações da Nscale no Condado de Ward. A expansão proposta poderia ter gerado dezenas de bilhões de dólares em receita contratual adicional, de acordo com três pessoas familiarizadas com o assunto citadas pelo jornal. A Nscale agora precisará garantir clientes alternativos para a capacidade disponível, a fim de concretizar a receita potencial associada à expansão. Microsoft recusa aumento na capacidade de computação no Texas A decisão da Microsoft afeta uma opção de expansão vinculada ao seu contrato existente para centro de dados no Condado de Ward, Texas. Em outubro de 2025, a Nscale anunciou um acordo para fornecer à Microsoft aproximadamente 240 megawatts de capacidade computacional em uma instalação adjacente que está sendo desenvolvida pela empresa de mineração de criptomoedas Ionic Digital. O acordo incluía uma opção para uma segunda fase de desenvolvimento, inicialmente descrita como a previsão de fornecimento de 700 megawatts adicionais. No entanto, a Nscale informou ao Financial Times esta semana que a opção abrangia cerca de 500 megawatts e envolvia capacidade adicional em suas próprias instalações. A Microsoft optou por não exercer a opção de expansão, deixando a Nscale em busca de outros clientes para a capacidade. De acordo com os documentos da Ionic Digital junto à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos EUA (SEC), a Nscale ainda não garantiu o fornecimento de energia elétrica para a capacidade restante no data center da Ionic. A Microsoft mantém o direito de preferência sobre essa capacidade. A Nscale busca clientes alternativos para o projeto no Condado de Ward Na sequência da decisão da Microsoft, a Nscale está a procurar novos acordos com empresas interessadas em arrendar infraestruturas computacionais no seu empreendimento no Texas. A empresa assinou um contrato com a empresa de robótica Figure em setembro e também firmou acordos com outros clientes cujas identidades não foram divulgadas. Uma pessoa próxima à Nscale disse ao Financial Times que estavam em andamento negociações com vários outros potenciais clientes para o local no Condado de Ward. A capacidade de garantir novos contratos de leasing é importante para os fornecedores de infraestrutura de IA, pois a receita contratada futura pode sustentar os empréstimos utilizados para financiar a construção de centros de dados. Sem clientes substitutos, a Nscale pode perder bilhões de dólares em receita potencial associada à expansão proposta pela Microsoft. O Financial Times informou que a decisão da Microsoft não afetaria a carteira de contratos da Nscale, que atualmente totaliza US$ 103 bilhões. O financiamento da infraestrutura de IA enfrenta maior escrutínio O desenvolvimento ocorre em meio à crescente atenção às necessidades de financiamento das empresas que constroem infraestrutura computacional para inteligência artificial. Empresas que alugam capacidade de computação de IA, frequentemente descritas como provedoras de neocloud, normalmente precisam de financiamento substancial para desenvolver instalações e adquirir equipamentos antes de receberem receita dos clientes. Empresas como a CoreWeave e a Nebius têm atraído atenção devido ao uso de dívida para financiar investimentos em infraestrutura de grande escala. Novos contratos com clientes podem ajudar esses fornecedores a demonstrar compromissos de receita futura e manter o acesso ao financiamento. A Nscale reportou um prejuízo líquido de US$ 1 bilhão sobre uma receita de US$ 141 milhões durante o primeiro semestre de 2026. Os números destacam a diferença entre a receita operacional atual da empresa e as necessidades de investimento associadas aos seus planos de desenvolvimento. A Microsoft já havia desistido de um acordo para data centers no Reino Unido A decisão do Texas surge na sequência de uma alteração anterior nos acordos da Microsoft com a Nscale no Reino Unido. No início de 2026, a Microsoft desistiu de um acordo proposto de US$ 3 bilhões para alugar capacidade de computação no centro de dados da Nscale em Essex. A decisão mais recente representa mais um exemplo em que a Microsoft optou por não prosseguir com a expansão da capacidade fornecida pelo provedor de infraestrutura britânico. A Nscale continua a desenvolver seu portfólio de data centers e a buscar acordos com outras empresas de tecnologia. Empreendimento na Virgínia Ocidental enfrenta atrasos na construção De acordo com o Financial Times, o principal projeto da Nscale na Virgínia Ocidental também enfrentou atrasos na construção e oposição das comunidades locais. O desenvolvimento constitui uma parte central do acordo de computação de US$ 45 bilhões da empresa com a empresa de inteligência artificial Anthropic. A Nscale está atualmente discutindo uma possível expansão dessa relação, que envolveria o arrendamento de um segundo centro de dados de 460 megawatts em sua localização na Virgínia Ocidental. A instalação adicional proposta aumentaria a capacidade abrangida pelos acordos das empresas, caso um acordo seja alcançado. No entanto, o relatório não indicou que um contrato final para a segunda instalação tivesse sido assinado. Desenvolvimentos regulatórios aumentam a incerteza na expansão de data centers Os desenvolvimentos políticos nos Estados Unidos também podem afetar a construção de instalações adicionais de computação de IA. Os governadores democratas eleitos, incluindo os do Texas, pediram uma moratória imediata no desenvolvimento de centros de dados. Essas propostas podem influenciar

artigo.texto: Data center backlash ousts incumbents in some Minnesota towns Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Quick Read Fervent opposition to large-scale data centers proved to be a motivating political factor in high-profile races from Ohio to Texas in this year’s election. The hot-button issue also played a major role in some local races across Minnesota. In Pine Island, a town of 4,000 just north of Rochester, a political neophyte who opposed the planned Google data center there won two-thirds of the vote against the incumbent interim mayor who supports the project. And in Hermantown, where a second Google data center generated a fierce backlash from local residents, two political newcomers won seats to the city council, outpolling an incumbent who voted to approve the massive project just last week. “The people of this community have spoken up loud,” said Emma Richtman, who won 36 percent of the vote, the most among the four candidates for city council. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. “It’s so validating,” Richtman added. “It feels like a public referendum on the community's feelings about this data center.” Richtman had no political ambitions before she became involved with the grassroots group Stop the Hermatown Data Center, which formed last year after plans for a 1.7 million square foot data center in a rural residential corner of the city near Duluth first became public. “I went from everyday mom to citizen activist,” Richtman said. From there it was an easy step to run for city council, she said. “The people of this community needed to have someone championing them.” An issue bridging the political divide At polling places around Hermantown Tuesday, several voters said the data center was a motivating issue. And it’s one that transcends typical partisan divisions. Both liberal Democrats and conservative Republicans who spoke to MPR News – who don’t agree on much – agreed on their opposition to the data center. "It's just one of those things that's being shoved down our throats,” said Jack Liabraaten, 81, a Republican who cited immigration and preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon as key issues for him. Locally, he said he voted for Richtman and Candi Mock, another candidate who ran on an anti-data center platform. Mock finished second and won a seat with 28 percent of the vote. “They’ve spent hours upon hours just reading through the documents, and they're doing stuff so the rest of us don't necessarily have to read all that fine print,” said Liabraaten. “To me they both have the right ideas, and they both talk about doing things peacefully.” Many voters who were somewhat ambivalent about the data center itself were nonetheless incensed with how city leaders handled its development and approval. Two city officials signed non-disclosure agreements, or NDAs, that prevented them from discussing the issue for over a year, while the groundwork was being laid for the project. "I personally don't know if I'm for or against the data center,” said Leann Fahlsing, a lifelong Hermantown resident. “But what I am against is the lack of transparency, the idea that a lot of this happened underground, before anybody knew anything that was happening.” Mark Lang, the mayor-elect in Pine Island, said voters there feel the same way. Locals accuse city officials of hashing out details for the data center in secret. “A lot of people aren't really against data centers,” Lang said. “What we were really against is how we were left out of the loop.” Lang is also a political newbie. He’s a corporate pilot who was motivated to run by the data center issue. He said in Pine Island it’s also brought people together from across the political spectrum. The project there is on hold following a recent settlement that calls for a more thorough environmental review overseen by the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency. Lang said he hopes to eventually sit down with everyone involved to find areas where Google and new city leaders can find common ground to improve the project as much as possible. “We're going to agree right off the bat not to be disagreeable. We're going to respect each other,” Lang said. Lang will have an ally in Tosca Wohl, another first-time candidate who opposed the data center who ran for one of two seats on the City Council. She received the most votes, with 28 percent of the tally. Mixed message in some communities But the anti-data center sentiment wasn’t universal around the state. Some cities split their votes among candidates who both support and oppose the projects. Two city council candidates in Pine Island who support the Google data center there tied for the second council seat. In Monticello, about 40 miles northwest of Minneapolis, Mayor Lloyd Hilgart retained his seat by a slim 40-vote margin over Monica Primeau, who has voiced opposition to a hyperscale data center proposed for the city. Meanwhile, Derek Armstrong defeated incumbent Tracy Hinz for a seat on the Monticello City Council. Armstrong also has raised concerns about the data center project, as has council member Charlotte Gabler, who was elected to another term. In Hermantown, data center opponents continue to fight the project in court. This week the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy and Stop the Hermantown Data Center filed a lawsuit in St. Louis County court alleging the project’s environmental review doesn’t meet state requirements. The groups argue for a more robust environmental study, similar to what was agreed to recently in Pine Island following a lawsuit there. “Google is pursuing a state-level environmental review in Pine Island. artigo.texto: Elon Musk, owner of X and head of SpaceX and Tesla, posted two jokes within hours of the 2026 US midterm results, and one of them pushed orbital computing back onto the news agenda. The Times of India ran it under a headline saying Musk sent a “let’s go to Space” message to Google, Amazon, Meta and other data-centre builders. The posts themselves named none of those companies. The first post read “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” The second read “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.” Both were reported on November 4, 2026. They tell us about Musk’s mood and his politics, and they tell us very little about any actual hardware program. Google has been talking publicly about space data centers costing up to 100x more than ground sites, which is a far more concrete data point than a late-night joke. This analysis separates what the record confirms from what headlines imply. It covers the election backdrop, the AI power squeeze that gives the joke its edge, the one orbital project with real reporting behind it, and five predictions for the next year. Where a detail is not on the record, we say so plainly. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Elon Musk Actually Posted on X After the Midterms Two posts anchor the story. Both appeared on X, the platform Musk owns, after the 2026 US midterm elections closed. Outlets including The Economic Times, Rediff and Implicator carried them on November 4. The wording matches across those reports, which is why the quotes above can be treated as accurate. The space-lasers line is a sarcastic reference to accusations that Musk’s political spending or his companies tried to tilt elections. The Economic Times described the posts as Musk mocking his own election spending after what it called a Democratic midterm sweep. The paper also suggested the data-center line could reflect worry about how AI infrastructure might be regulated in the coming years. India Today reported that claims tying Starlink to election manipulation lacked support, and that no credible evidence had surfaced of Starlink being used to hack or sway voting systems. That context matters. The “space lasers” phrase is a punchline built on an internet conspiracy theory, not a confession or a product reference. Nothing in the reported posts mentions a SpaceX program, a launch date, a chip, a satellite count or a budget. Any article that tells you Musk “announced” orbital data centers on election night is stretching the record. He said they looked appealing. He did not say what he would build. The Times of India Headline Versus the Verified Record The Times of India headline is the reason this story trended. It says Musk sent a message to Google, Amazon, Meta and other companies building data centres. The reporting we reviewed says the posts did not directly address Google, Amazon or Meta. Those companies were described as firms expanding data-center capacity for artificial intelligence, which is true, but the link to Musk’s posts is the paper’s reading rather than something Musk wrote. That gap is common in fast news cycles. A joke gets framed as a signal, the signal gets framed as a message, and the message gets an addressee. By the third step the original text has disappeared. The table below keeps score. Readers who want the cleanest takeaway should hold onto the first three rows. Everything below them is interpretation, and some of it is good interpretation, but it is not fact. The Midterm Backdrop: A Democratic Sweep and Its AI Stakes NBC Los Angeles ran live updates under a headline stating that Democrats won control of the House and Senate. The Economic Times used the word “sweep.” For a tech billionaire who spent heavily on the other side, that is the context for a self-mocking post about lasers. The AI industry was already watching the vote closely. Our earlier piece on how investors gamed out congressional control and $1.5T of AI capex laid out the logic. A new majority can hold hearings on power use, tax breaks for data centers and chip export rules. None of those hearings has been scheduled in the reporting we reviewed, so treat them as risks, not events. Business reaction was loud. Yahoo Finance UK collected executive responses under the word “blunami” to describe the election-night result. We did not find a verified statement from Google, Amazon or Meta responding to Musk’s posts, and none of the reports we reviewed claimed one. One point deserves care. Reports conflict on how much Musk spent on the cycle, so we are not repeating any total. A number that varies by outlet is a number we cannot defend. Why Data-Center Politics Gave the Joke Its Edge Implicator tied the posts to a headline about Texas threatening the AI buildout, and Axios linked the remarks to Texas politics and local opposition to data centers. The thread connecting them is simple. Data centers need land, water, transmission lines and enormous electricity, and voters notice when their bills rise. We have tracked that friction for months. A Florida poll found 59% of respondents opposed data centers near them, and the issue landed in a governor’s race. Separate coverage looked at power bills, utilities and nine commission seats on the midterm ballot. Local politics, in short, has become a real constraint on where AI compute can sit. Read that way, “data centers in space looking pretty appealing” is a joke with a logic underneath. If ground sites face permitting fights and angry ratepayers, a site with no neighbors starts to sound attractive. The punchline works because the grievance is real. It is still only a punchline. The technology broadens energy storage options, with a focus on long service life, safety and flexibility. Bratislava, Slovakia - November 3, 2026 - Slovak technology innovator INO-HUB Energy unveiled its proprietary commercial prototype of a vanadium redox flow battery (VRFB) to customers, technology partners and potential investors at its first Tech Day event in Bratislava. Designed for long-duration electricity storage, the technology makes a significant contribution to grid stability and the more efficient use of renewable energy sources. The prototype unveiling was the highlight of the event, at which the company presented the results of its research and development activities and outlined their practical applications in industry and the energy sector. The programme also included a technical tour of the battery storage system. "Presenting our proprietary commercial prototype of a vanadium flow battery is an important step for us. Our goal is not to keep technologies at the laboratory research stage, but to turn them into practical solutions for industry and the energy sector. Europe will need ever greater energy storage capacity, alongside technologies that are safe, cost-effective and reliable over the long term. This is precisely where we see significant potential in the technologies we are developing," said Rudolf Sihlovec, Chief Executive Officer of INO-HUB Energy. European technologies for safer energy systems The development of energy storage technologies plays an important role in Europe's energy transition. It helps make better use of renewable energy sources, supports the stability of electricity systems and strengthens energy security. The company's research project has been notified by the European Commission as an Important Project of Common European Interest (IPCEI). "The transition to clean and sustainable energy is one of the European Union's main priorities. However, to fully harness the potential of renewable energy sources, we need innovative solutions that ensure the stability and safety of our energy networks. The INO-HUB Energy project is an excellent example of how European Union investment can support the development of breakthrough technologies right here in Slovakia. Thanks to more than 17 million in European funding, solutions are being developed that could serve as an inspiration for the whole of Europe. Slovakia is demonstrating its potential to become a leader in green technologies and innovation that strengthen our energy security and competitiveness," said Peter Stano, Head of the European Commission Representation in Slovakia. Vanadium technology as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries Vanadium redox flow batteries expand the range of available energy storage solutions, with particular emphasis on safety and long service life. Energy is stored in a water-based electrolyte containing vanadium salts. The technology allows the energy capacity and power output of a storage system to be sized independently, enabling the system to be tailored to the specific needs of each customer. Key advantages include a long service life, which can exceed 25 years under suitable operating conditions, and the ability to undergo repeated charging and discharging cycles without significant capacity loss. Another major benefit of vanadium flow batteries is their high level of safety, as the risks of thermal runaway and explosion are eliminated. "Vanadium batteries offer an attractive combination of long service life, safety and flexibility. From an economic perspective, it is important to assess not only the initial investment but also the total cost of energy storage over the system's lifetime. When the secondary use of the electrolyte is considered, this cost is comparable to that of other electrochemical energy storage technologies," explained Rudolf Sihlovec. The importance of energy storage in Europe is growing alongside the expansion of renewable energy sources. According to a June 2026 report by SolarPower Europe, Europe's total operational battery storage capacity had exceeded 100 GWh by the end of 2025. Under the medium forecast scenario, this capacity could reach 582 GWh by 2030. As the share of renewable energy sources in the energy mix continues to grow, so does the need for technologies capable of storing electricity and supplying it when required. From battery development to intelligent energy management The company's portfolio also includes its proprietary AORTA+ software, which uses artificial intelligence to simulate, optimise and manage energy systems. The software analyses each customer's electricity generation and consumption profiles and uses the resulting data, together with the DigiTwin digital twin tool, to optimise the design of a solution tailored to that customer's specific needs. This helps optimise energy use and operating costs while improving the economic efficiency of the investment. At the event, the company also presented the potential practical applications of its solutions in industrial settings. INO-HUB Energy's strategy for developing comprehensive energy solutions for industrial customers and energy infrastructure operators is built on combining the development of its own battery storage technologies with intelligent software. Arruda O governador Otaviano Pivetta (Republicanos) quer criar uma empresa estatal para estruturar, administrar e comercializar créditos de carbono e outros ativos ambientais de Mato Grosso. O Projeto de Lei nº 1.156/2026 cria a Companhia Matogrossense de Ativos Ambientais S.A. (CMAA), vinculada à Secretaria de Estado de Meio Ambiente (Sema). A proposta foi elaborada em setembro e começou a tramitar na Assembleia Legislativa no dia 7 de outubro, três dias após o primeiro turno das eleições. Nesta quarta-feira (4), terminou de cumprir o prazo de pauta e poderá seguir para análise das comissões temáticas. A CMAA funcionará como um braço empresarial do Governo do Estado no mercado ambiental. Poderá administrar, comprar e vender ativos ambientais, captar investimentos e participar de projetos de redução de emissões, conservação, biodiversidade, recuperação ambiental e mudanças climáticas. Entre as atribuições estão a negociação de créditos de carbono, projetos de REDD+, pagamentos por serviços ambientais, captação de recursos nacionais e internacionais e prestação de serviços ligados à redução ou remoção de gases de efeito estufa. A companhia também poderá criar subsidiárias e entrar como sócia de empresas ou fundos privados, desde que os negócios estejam relacionados às políticas ambientais e climáticas do Estado. O capital inicial será de R$ 2 milhões, e o projeto autoriza o governo a abrir crédito especial de até o mesmo valor para colocar a empresa em funcionamento. Mato Grosso deverá manter a maioria das ações com direito a voto, mas empresas públicas ou privadas, brasileiras ou estrangeiras, poderão ser acionistas. O Estado também poderá vender parte de sua participação, desde que mantenha o controle da companhia. O projeto permite que o Estado entregue à CMAA o direito de estruturar, administrar e comercializar programas e ativos ambientais pertencentes a Mato Grosso, inclusive os gerados em terras e áreas públicas estaduais, sem transferir a propriedade desses bens. Também poderão ser cedidos à empresa créditos de carbono jurisdicionais já gerados, verificados e certificados. Como regra, porém, fica proibida a venda antecipada de créditos ou outros ativos que ainda não tenham sido gerados e certificados. A transferência de imóveis, direitos de grande valor ou ativos considerados estratégicos dependerá de autorização específica da Assembleia Legislativa. O texto ainda prevê a divisão de receitas e benefícios com povos indígenas, comunidades quilombolas e tradicionais, extrativistas, agricultores familiares e assentados quando esses grupos participarem dos projetos. A CMAA ficará vinculada à Sema, mas terá funcionamento empresarial. Os funcionários serão contratados pelo regime da CLT, e a companhia poderá contratar empresas e profissionais para serviços e consultorias dentro das regras aplicáveis às estatais. Na justificativa enviada à Assembleia, Pivetta afirma que a nova companhia permitirá ao Estado participar diretamente do mercado de carbono, captar investimentos privados e internacionais e transformar ações de preservação e redução de emissões em ativos capazes de gerar receita. artigo.texto: Just a little rain falling all around, The grass lifts its head to the heavenly sound, Just a little rain, just a little rain, What have they done to the rain? . . . Just a little boy standing in the rain, . . . And the grass is gone, The boy disappears . . . By Mary O’Brien When Joan Baez sang “What Have They Done to the Rain” in 1962, she gave voice to a song Malvina Reynolds had recently written as a protest against aboveground nuclear testing. The nuclear fallout from the testing contained radioactive Strontium-90, which can enter the food chain through grass eaten by cows that are eaten by humans. Later the song became identified with acid rain, produced by burning high-sulfur or high-nitrogen fossil fuels, whose sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form sulfuric and nitric acids when mixed with rain. And now, 60 years later? We realize we have done the most un-intelligent thing imaginable to rain: Addicted to fossil fuels, we’ve heated our atmospheric blanket, creating long stretches of no rain, punctuated by storms bringing “historic” floods. The rain’s offspring — streams, rivers, springs, sole source aquifers — are smaller. We bake. We know we need to turn to other sources of energy such as the sun and wind. We are asked to not water our lawns after 10 in the morning. But then enters a juggernaut directed by a few unaccountable billionaires: Artificial intelligence (AI). It’s designed to be smarter than people and to be cheaper than either hourly wages or salaries that humans demand. While humans think about almost anything, AI data centers dutifully undertake intelligence tasks that are assigned to them (or occasionally run loose into other systems). Currently, the AI industry is on the honor system to voluntarily regulate (or not) the digital services it develops. One painfully immediate problem with data centers is that they consume vast amount of fossil-fueled power to be artificially intelligent, and they depend on vast amounts of water to cool their heated, silicon-based thinking. Which leads to a data center question that Grand County (the second driest county in Utah) must answer before Jan. 3, when our 180-day moratorium on data centers expires: Do we write no AI data centers into our land use code, or do we lay out the welcome mat for such data centers in Grand County? A Utah State University poll (and most national polls) indicates that about 75% of Utahns (and Americans) don’t want any more data centers. It is legal for Grand County to say “No.” If the county is going to say “Yes” to permitting data centers, then specifications need to be written into the land use code before Jan. 3 by someone: Where would data centers be allowed? How large could they be in terms of fossil fuel consumption and emissions? How much water would be needed to cool the chips that heat up as they process data? What water source(s) would be used and for which type of cooling processes? What would be the limit on noise at the factory boundary? What light pollution would be allowed? What amount of heat would be permitted for release? What bond requirements would be needed to address failures or shutdown? (For the past 48 years, the public has been paying for cleanup of the abandoned uranium mill tailings site of a private, commercial business.) Grand County Commissioner Brian Martinez has proposed that our county’s land use code permit data centers (and other unnamed industries) that require up to 10 MW continuous power or 20,000 gallons of water a day for evaporative cooling. Ten MW would power all houses in Grand County for a year. (And, a mistake on Brian’s part? A 10 MW data center uses 200,000, not 20,000 gallons of water a day for evaporative cooling. And requires even more water to generate electricity if cooling is by closed loop.) Planning Commissioner Bob O’Brien proposes that the land use code exclude AI data centers. Such a land use code exclusion (1) is responsive to the large majority of the public, (2) requires no water or fossil fuels, and (3) by not requiring extensive, technical data center specifications, can easily be written prior to Jan. 3. If the Utah Legislature, against the wishes of most Utahns and Grand County residents eventually mandates that every county must submit to requests for data centers, then Grand County’s land use code could be revised. But while it’s still legal for Grand County to say no to data centers in the land use code, the county shouldn’t obey in advance. Turn up and speak out. Increase the chance rain will keep falling all around. Mary O’Brien writes from Castle Valley, where she lives with Bob O’Brien.

artigo.texto: CATL, Ampace and Octopus Energy have signed a strategic memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore next-generation home energy storage solutions for European households. The partnership aims to combine advanced battery technology with intelligent energy management software, potentially making residential batteries more affordable, efficient and capable of reducing electricity bills. The collaboration brings together three companies with complementary expertise. CATL will provide battery technology and supply chain support, Ampace will focus on battery cell and energy storage system development and manufacturing, while Octopus Energy will contribute its digital platform, smart electricity tariffs and Virtual Power Plant (VPP) capabilities. The initial focus will be on European markets where Octopus Energy operates, with the UK, France and Spain among the priority countries. The partnership aims to move home energy storage beyond conventional battery systems that simply store electricity for later use. Instead, the companies want to develop connected energy solutions that automatically respond to electricity prices, renewable energy availability and grid demand. CATL and Ampace will contribute their research into next-generation battery technologies, including sodium-ion batteries, high-density cell designs and long-life battery systems. These developments could help improve battery safety, extend service life and reduce the cost of residential energy storage. However, the companies have not yet announced specific battery models, capacities, prices or commercial launch dates. Ampace will take responsibility for researching, developing and manufacturing battery cells, battery management systems (BMS) and complete energy storage systems. CATL will provide technological expertise and supply chain support. Octopus Energy will connect the hardware to its smart energy ecosystem, using its dynamic electricity tariffs and energy management software to optimize how household batteries operate. One of the main objectives of the collaboration is to make home batteries work more intelligently. Instead of charging whenever electricity is available, connected systems could automatically identify the cheapest periods to store energy. They could also prioritize electricity generated by rooftop solar panels when conditions allow. During periods of high electricity demand, stored energy could be used inside the home or exported back to the grid, depending on the household’s energy setup and applicable market arrangements. This approach could provide several advantages: – Lower electricity bills: Batteries can charge when electricity prices are low and supply power when prices increase. – Better use of solar energy: Households with rooftop solar installations could store excess generation instead of immediately exporting it to the grid. – Grid flexibility: Connected batteries could help balance electricity supply and demand during peak periods. – Greater energy independence: Households could rely less on electricity purchased during expensive periods. – Improved renewable energy integration: Smart charging and storage could help make better use of electricity generated from renewable sources. A key part of the strategy is Octopus Energy’s Virtual Power Plant technology. By connecting multiple residential batteries into a coordinated network, the company can potentially manage distributed energy resources as a larger, flexible power asset. This could allow individual households to benefit from energy markets while helping improve the stability and resilience of Europe’s electricity grids. The three companies are also exploring opportunities to connect home energy storage with other technologies, including rooftop solar, smart EV charging and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) systems. Vehicle-to-grid technology allows compatible electric vehicles to send electricity back to a home or the wider power grid. Combined with residential batteries and intelligent energy management, it could create a more integrated household energy ecosystem. For example, a home could use solar panels to generate electricity during the day, store excess power in a stationary battery and charge an electric vehicle when electricity prices are lowest. In the future, the same system could coordinate electricity flows between the home, the vehicle and the grid. [source: Octopus Energy]
