artigo.texto: While data centers were taking it on the chin in Tuesday's midterm elections, the people building them were playing pickleball at a conference in Virginia. And they weren't exactly reacting constructively to the news. "Suddenly we have protesters and people saying four-letter words about us," Jeff Wabik, the chief technology officer at DC BLOX, a data center developer based in Atlanta, said of common complaints about the centers, like their noise. "You know, most of that is just straightforward misinformation," he added. "There have been some bad actors." At the conference, held on November 3 and 4 by Data Center Dynamics, a trade publication and the event's organizer, over 3,000 industry professionals gathered to network, strategize, and share positive thoughts, according to its billing materials. "The data center industry is set to build at record pace," the company posted on LinkedIn on Thursday. The timing of the event and its messaging, though, couldn't have contrasted more with the nationwide votes taking place. Data centers took a resolute drubbing the day the conference kicked off. Over 40 ballot propositions around the country during the midterm election supporting the construction of data centers went down in defeat. Only one, in a tiny town in North Dakota, was successful. Democrats, meanwhile, swept into power by an electorate disgruntled with the Iran war and high prices, and have promised to focus their scrutiny on data centers and the people building them when they take power in January. "We need real action on data centers," Sen. Chuck Schumer, the democrat septogenerian from New York poised to become majority leader, said in September. Chip stocks, after soaring on Wednesday, tumbled drastically on Thursday as investors digested the possibility of major AI regulation pushed by democrats. None of this portends good news for data centers (or, as OpenAI now wants you to call them, "compute campuses"). That didn't seem to bother people at the conference, though. "An exciting time to be in the data center industry," Beau Couden, a sales manager at Watts Water Technologies, a cooling company, said in a LinkedIn post on Thursday. Stephen Forgy, an executive at Hyper Solutions, a company that manufactures electrical infrastructure for data centers, said there are "plenty of other variables" that could put a kabash on the data center buildout. "But it's still a great time to be in this industry," he said in an interview with JSA TV, a trade news site. The event holder, Data Center Dynamics, did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday. While the conference itinerary mostly hinged on working groups, panels, and classes for data center builders to learn the nitty-gritty of running the massive AI-powering factories, there were also some lighter events. A pickleball tournament, for one, was offered at 8 a.m. on Tuesday, about an hour after polls opened on the East Coast. At 6:15 p.m. on Tuesday, while the polls were closing and millions were tuning in to national news to watch the tally, data center execs enjoyed an "icebreaker party." Then, at 7 a.m. on Wednesday, while most Americans were waking up to a stunning blue wave, conference attendees were treated to take a relaxing jog to "experience the serenity of Virginia." "Kickstart your day with a 5k networking run or an inspiring 2.5k Walk & Talk," the schedule read.

artigo.texto: AI data center investment keeps expanding, but the companies supplying that capacity face different paths to profit. The International Energy Agency's October 2026 report estimates that hyperscalers will spend more than $700 billion on capital investment this year, mostly on new data centers. The report also points out constrained electricity networks, connection queues, and slow permitting as obstacles. For investors, spending commitments establish an opportunity. On the other hand, access to power and the ability to deliver working infrastructure determine when that opportunity becomes revenue. Our earlier 7 Cheapest AI Data Center Stocks to Buy Now explores the industry's broader investment universe. Leasing figures show why developers keep building. CBRE's first-half 2026 report found that supply across primary North American markets rose 33.7% year over year to 10,903 megawatts, while vacancy fell to 1.4%. Customers had already committed to 80.4% of capacity under construction. Average asking rents for deployments requiring three to ten megawatts rose 8.3% during the first half. Those figures suggest that demand persists to absorb new supply. But preleasing cannot eliminate construction delays or guarantee a project's eventual profitability. The next phase could require substantial financing. In its 2026 Global Data Center Market Outlook, JLL projects roughly 100 gigawatts of additional capacity between 2026 and 2030. It estimates approximately $1.2 trillion in real estate investment and another $1 trillion to $2 trillion in tenant equipment spending. These estimates cover different parts of the buildout. So investors should not add them to unrelated spending forecasts. They still show why investors must weigh financing needs alongside projected demand. More capacity can create sales opportunities. It can also raise interest costs, depreciation and competition. Construction costs add another constraint since JLL forecasts an average shell-and-core construction cost of $11.3 million per megawatt in 2026, up 6% from 2025. That figure excludes the tenant's technology fit-out, which can cost as much as $25 million per megawatt for AI infrastructure. Therefore, the buildout reaches well beyond processors: electrical installation, cooling and site development all influence the cost and timing of new facilities. 7 Best Data Center Engineering and Construction Stocks To Buy examines that part of the supply chain. Meanwhile, the IEA's April 2026 analysis projects that global data center electricity consumption will roughly double from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 terawatt-hours in 2030. It expects AI-focused facilities to grow faster but warns that equipment shortages and grid constraints could limit near-term expansion. That distinction matters when searching for cheap stocks. A low forward price-to-earnings ratio depends on an earnings forecast that may change. Investors should ask whether growth comes from sustainable customer demand, favorable component pricing, acquisitions or unusually strong margins. Our 8 Most Undervalued AI Stocks to Buy According to Hedge Funds offers another perspective on that valuation question. We considered US-listed AI data center companies that operate AI computing infrastructure or supply essential chips, memory, storage, servers, networking, electrical systems, and construction services. We screened for a positive forward P/E below 20 and quarterly revenue growth of at least 15% year over year. Note: All data was sourced on November 2, 2026. Then we ranked all stocks that met our criteria by Insider Monkey's 2026 Q2 billionaire count and broke ties with the lower forward P/E. Why are we interested in the stocks that hedge funds pile into? CATL (HKEX: 3750) has signed a strategic memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Octopus Energy and Ampace, targeting Europe's smart home energy storage market. The 3 parties recently signed the agreement and will prioritize markets including the UK, France, and Spain to explore energy storage solutions for European households, CATL said in a statement on Wednesday. The tie-up extends the scope of cooperation between CATL and Octopus Energy from commercial heavy-duty trucks to household energy. The 2 companies previously announced a partnership in June this year, planning to build a heavy-duty truck battery-swapping network in Europe. Under the latest MoU, CATL will provide technological and supply chain support, while Ampace will be responsible for the research, development, and manufacturing of battery cells, battery management systems (BMS), and energy storage systems. Octopus Energy will provide European user channels and introduce smart dynamic tariff algorithms as well as virtual power plant (VPP) access services, integrating energy storage hardware with home energy management. The 3 parties will also explore synergies across areas including rooftop solar, smart charging, vehicle-to-grid (V2G), and VPPs, enabling household energy storage assets to participate in grid dispatching. The cooperation aims to reduce household electricity costs while improving the flexibility and resilience of European power grids, CATL said. The company and Octopus Energy will also explore launching co-branded home energy solutions. Ampace, a joint venture between ATL and CATL whose business spans energy storage systems as well as batteries for micro-vehicles and smart products, will provide cell and system manufacturing capabilities for the partnership. The signing extends the European cooperation between CATL and Octopus Energy this year. On June 22, the 2 companies announced plans to establish a 50-50 joint venture to introduce Qiji Energy's battery-swapping technology into the European heavy-duty truck market. According to the plan disclosed by the 2 sides at the time, the first batch of demonstration battery-swapping stations is expected to be put into operation in the UK in 2027, prioritizing coverage of main highway trunk lines and core logistics ports.

artigo.texto: SpaceX hosts community meeting about proposed massive data center in Cochise County Residents express mixed reactions to proposal TUCSON, Ariz. (13 News) - A proposed data center in rural Cochise County is drawing mixed reactions from residents following a community meeting hosted by SpaceX on Wednesday evening. Residents gathered at Cochise Elementary to learn more about the proposed development and raise questions about its potential impact on the surrounding community. Elon Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX, made news earlier this week when he claimed cooling data centers would be easier in space than on Earth. The project, proposed near the Apache Generating Station along U.S. Highway 191, would cover approximately 747 acres and include nine data center buildings used for artificial intelligence operations. According to a special use application filed with Cochise County under Tombstone Resources LLC, the facility would require up to 6,000 megawatts, or six gigawatts, of electricity at full build-out. That would make it one of the largest proposed data center developments in the country by electricity demand. A map of the proposed facility’s footprint can be seen below. The applicant claims the project could create thousands of construction jobs and potentially lower electricity bills for customers. For some residents, the proposed development represents an opportunity for the future. “We need AI centers. It’s the future,” said Herald Satterlee, who attended Wednesday’s meeting. Others expressed concerns about the project and whether enough information has been provided to the community. “We don’t know enough, therefore just say no,” said Michael Gregory, another attendee. During the meeting, residents also raised questions about water usage, wildlife, and noise levels. The application outlines plans to use a dry-cooling system to reduce water consumption, along with other proposed measures intended to address environmental impacts. Jason Bowling, CEO of Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative, acknowledged the different opinions surrounding the project. “There are some that are excited about it and some that are concerned about it. All of that is valid,” Bowling said. “The concerns are valid, and the excitement is valid, and I think we just need to let the facts come out and let folks evaluate it for themselves.” While SpaceX hosted the meeting, the special use application identifies Tombstone Resources LLC as the applicant. The exact relationship between the two companies is unclear. 13 News reached out to SpaceX for an interview during Wednesday’s meeting, but a representative was not available for comment. No decision has been made on the proposed development. The Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission is scheduled to hold a formal public hearing on Dec. 9. artigo.texto: On the edge of Nigeria’s commercial capital Lagos, where the city gives way to the Atlantic, behind walls of concrete and steel are rows of machines designed to store, process and move the digital records of the West African nation. Nigeria’s banks, fintech companies and payment processors have spent years building businesses on computing infrastructure that can sit anywhere in the world. Now, beginning January 1, 2027, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) is requiring financial institutions and participants in the country’s payments system to ensure that payment transaction data generated in Nigeria is stored and managed in Nigeria. Dr Ayotunde Coker, CEO of Pan-African data center operator Open Access Data Centres (OADC), says engagement with companies seeking local infrastructure has increased since the directive. “We’ve got what I call a reasonable level of requests in terms of colocation. We’re ready to really onboard a lot as is required,” Coker discloses to FORBES AFRICA. But the country’s other technology executives, engineers and AI specialists describe a reality bordering on shortage of reliable power, high-density cooling, redundant connectivity, cloud services, cybersecurity, disaster recovery, engineering talent and, perhaps most consequentially, control over the technology that processes Nigerian data. Loading... “Data sovereignty is not achieved simply because the server is physically located in Nigeria. Physical location is only the first layer,” explains Kemisola Adalumo. “Data sovereignty is not achieved simply because the server is physically located in Nigeria. Physical location is only the first layer,” explains Kemisola Adalumo, a Nigerian cybersecurity, governance, risk and compliance and AI-governance specialist, to FORBES AFRICA. That distinction is becoming critical as Nigeria moves from an era of data storage into one dominated by AI. Nigeria’s data-center market has changed in a relatively short period. Industry estimates put the country at roughly 26 data-center facilities, with about 18 operating commercially. The figures vary depending on what qualifies as an operational facility and whether private corporate installations are included, but the country’s infrastructure footprint has expanded substantially. Most of the commercial market is concentrated around Lagos. OADC announced plans in 2025 for a $240 million expansion of its Lagos facility to 24MW by 2027. The project was described as part of a broader $500 million African investment program. Coker says the company is now designing for substantially more AI capacity than previously envisaged. He put the eventual figure at roughly 40MW within the same development shell. Rack Centre commissioned its 12-megawatt (MW) LGS2 facility in 2025, describing it as a Tier III, carrier and cloud-neutral facility serving enterprises, cloud providers and financial institutions. MTN Nigeria has also committed more than $240 million to a 9MW Dabengwa data center in Ikeja. Its first phase was designed as a 4.5MW Tier III facility, with cloud infrastructure developed in partnership with Dell Technologies. And then there is Kasi Cloud. The company broke ground in 2022 on what was initially described as a $250 million data-center campus in the Lekki neighborhood of Lagos. Four years later, the first phase has been commissioned. The broader campus is designed to scale toward 100MW and has been positioned as infrastructure for hyperscale cloud and AI workloads. “We’ve got what I call a reasonable level of requests in terms of colocation. We’re ready to really onboard a lot as is required.” – Ayotunde Coker That matters because conventional data-center infrastructure and AI infrastructure are different businesses. A traditional enterprise workload can be distributed across relatively modest server densities. AI workloads, particularly those involving large numbers of graphics-processing units (GPUs), concentrate enormous amounts of computing power into comparatively small spaces. That changes the engineering equation: power, cooling, rack density and network architecture all become more demanding. A February 2026 analysis by TechCabal noted that Nigeria’s then-operational data centers generally had capacities below 20MW, while hyperscale AI campuses target 50MW to 100MW or more. Engineer Adetola Ibironke, General Manager for Systems Engineering and Projects at PPC Limited, argues that Nigeria remains in a “critical build-out phase”. “Announced capacity must not be confused with operational capacity,” he says to FORBES AFRICA, noting that projects exist at different stages of construction, commissioning and customer onboarding. That gap between announced and usable capacity is one of the least visible features of the boom. A building can be finished while its computing equipment is still being installed. A facility can have power infrastructure without having the required IT load. A data center can have racks without the cloud platform, cybersecurity controls or network redundancy a financial institution needs. The data-center industry uses tiers to describe levels of redundancy and availability. Tier IV represents the highest level in the Uptime Institute’s tier classification system. In Nigeria, Galaxy Backbone’s northern Nigeria city Kano facility holds Uptime Institute certification for both Tier IV design documents and the constructed facility. Uptime’s database also lists numerous Nigerian facilities with Tier III certifications. Galaxy Backbone describes its Kano installation as a Tier IV facility and its Abuja facility as Tier III. But Tier classification answers a narrower question than AI operators now need to answer. It addresses resilience and availability characteristics of the facility. It does not tell a bank whether a particular application can be migrated there without redesign. artigo.texto: Democrats won big on Tuesday in the midterm elections, and while the party's opposition to data centers has been spooking Wall Street, it may actually be a good thing for the artificial intelligence trade. It's counterintuitive, but analysts and economists were arguing on Wednesday that political pushback to the data center buildout may help to productively deflate what is widely acknowledged to be a market bubble in tech resulting from AI-related investment. This could make the investment boom more sustainable in the longer term while broadening it to other areas of the economy, even though it may add chop to the trading waters and contribute to a down-turn in the market over the short to medium term. "It is necessary that the investment in AI slow to a more sustainable pace. It is in the interest of the AI trade itself," RSM US chief economist Joseph Brusuelas said in a Wednesday analysis. "In all bubbles there is mal-investment, malfeasance, and failures. This boom will experience its bust and a slow deflation of the bubble is clearly in the interest of a broader and more sustainable AI trade." Markets were breathing a sigh of relief on Wednesday with all the major indices up. The S & P 500 was up 2% as of 12:00 p.m. ET; the Dow was up about 3% and the Nasdaq Composite was ahead 1.5%. Notably, the capital spenders in the AI trade were being rewarded on Wednesday as hurdles to the buildout could improve their sagging financial statements and bolster cash flows at a time when finance capital for the buildout has been growing scarce, as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently observed. Hyperscalers Meta , Google , Amazon and Microsoft were all up more than 4% as of 2 p.m. The iShares Broad USD Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF ( USIG ), a proxy for the high-quality corporate bond market, was up 0.6%, meaning yields were lower and overall financing costs were cheaper on the day. AMZN 5D mountain Amazon 5 day Conversely, recipients of that capital spending — notably power companies — are being hit hard. GE Vernova is down about 10% and Constellation Energy is down 6%. GEV 5D mountain GEV 5 day Like almost all previous market bubbles related to new technologies, over-investment of capital is almost certainly a factor in the AI boom. Economists think the check on data center expansion from Democrats could help to let some air out of the bubble without popping it with a single prick. "A slower buildout isn't entirely a bad thing," Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economics research at Bank of America, said in a Wednesday note. "The AI-related categories of capex have been growing at a 26% annualized pace in real terms since the beginning of last year. Such a front-loaded capex wave is symptomatic of over-investment. It means we face a greater risk of a hard landing down the line." He added that "adding a bit of sand in the gears might actually benefit markets and the economy in the medium term. The jury's still out." Slowing the buildout could also push investment into other areas of the economy in a potentially stabilizing way. Brusuelas said it could "result in a rebalancing and redirection of capital into the real economy." Not all sectors of the AI trade were doing well on Wednesday. The financially fragile, AI-dedicated neoclouds were getting hit hard, with CoreWeave down about 9%, Nebius down 6%, and IREN down 11%. Research firm Gartner predicted in October that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by the end of 2030 due to insufficient AI revenues at the consumer and enterprise level, translating to a dearth of profitable returns for some investments. Starwood Capital's Barry Sternlicht made a similar point on Tuesday, saying that some neoclouds could fail. Credit defaults swaps on CoreWeave – a form of risk insurance on their bonds – widened a bit on Wednesday morning, with the 5-year rising by 3.5%. Companies across the AI trade are still hungry for capital with hyperscalers, equipment providers, and algorithm companies seeking hundreds of billions over the past two weeks, according to Evercore. They want this money quickly and political roadblocks could make it harder to put it to efficient use. "The pace and scale of activity have put the cost of capital and funding capacity in focus," Julian Emanuel at Evercore said in a Wednesday note. "While strong oversubscription suggests capital remains available, rising borrowing costs, dilution concerns, and reliance on structured financing have weighed on the space." Political analysts see compromises on the horizon between Democrats and Republicans that ultimately bolster the buildout in the medium term. "This fall, we saw several state-level policy rollouts, led by governors in both 'red' and 'blue' states, that suggested a compromise is slowly emerging from lawmakers to allow some data centers in exchange for other policy concessions [Meta (META), Microsoft (MSFT), Google (GOOG), Amazon (AMZN), among others]. We think this trend will continue," Rob Rains at Washington Analysis wrote in a Wednesday note. Even as Wall Street analysts and the big stock indices were signaling encouragement on Wednesday, the overall environment for the AI trade remains "challenging," according to 22V Research. This is especially true in Texas, which has 27% of the total U.S. data center gigawattage, according to Wells Fargo, and whose newly elected next governor Gina Hinojosa (D) is expected to be tougher on data centers than her predecessor Greg Abbott (R). "While the macro indicator is multiple states moving towards data center pauses, the size of the buildout in Texas and the likely additional months of delays and uncertainty around the new governor will be a key focus for stocks tied to the state," Dauvin Peterson at 22V said in a Wednesday note. "At a higher level, the AI story will move forward – and from current levels, today's reaction and capability to compartmentalize will be telling."

artigo.texto: EBRD finances major battery energy storage project in Bulgaria - EBRD finances major battery energy storage project in Tenevo, south-eastern Bulgaria - Bank lends €30 million as part of a €60 million financing package with Raiffeisen Bank International AG - Battery energy storage projects strengthen grid stability and support integration of large-scale renewable energy The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is providing a €30 million loan to Tenevo Solar Technologies for the development of a major battery energy storage project in south-eastern Bulgaria. The financing is being complemented by €30 million in parallel funding from Raiffeisen Bank International AG (RBI). The €60 million package will finance the construction and operation of a battery energy storage system (BESS) at Tenevo, one of the largest battery storage projects in Bulgaria. The new facility will have a power capacity of 246 MW and be able to store 512.5 MWh of electricity. The BESS facility will be co-located with an existing 242 MWp solar photovoltaic (PV) plant (also financed by the EBRD and RBI), and a 65 MW battery installation capable of storing 260 MWh of electricity. It will increase energy storage capacity at the site, enhancing grid stability and supporting the integration of additional clean energy into Bulgaria’s power system. Tenevo Solar Technologies is a long-standing client of the EBRD. Previously the Bank provided €50 million to build and operate the fully merchant Tenevo solar PV plant. The project was supported by first loss risk cover deployed under the EBRD’s InvestEU Framework for Sustainable Transition. As Bulgaria accelerates its energy transition and reduces its reliance on fossil fuels, renewable energy generation and battery storage are becoming increasingly important for the decarbonisation of the power sector, improving flexibility and strengthening energy security. The rapid growth of battery storage capacity, which is exceeding 6.2 GW / 19 GWh according to latest estimates, is one of the country’s most significant energy transition achievements, positioning Bulgaria among the regional leaders in terms of renewable energy integration and decarbonisation. From 2023, the EBRD worked with Bulgaria’s Ministry of Energy on the design of grant schemes, competitive allocation and technical verification to support renewable energy and electricity storage projects under the country’s Recovery and Resilience Plan. September 2026 marked the successful completion of these crucial schemes, which have transformed Bulgaria’s renewable energy market. Manuela Naessl, EBRD Head of Bulgaria, said: Bulgaria has made remarkable progress in deploying battery storage, and this project is another important step in that journey. “By increasing the system’s flexibility and helping to integrate more renewable energy, Tenevo will contribute to a more resilient, secure and sustainable power sector. Supporting investments of this kind is central to the EBRD’s commitment to Bulgaria’s green transition.” The EBRD is a leading institutional investor in Bulgaria, having invested almost €5.3 billion in the country through 330 projects to date, with a strong focus on private sector development, competitiveness and the green economy transition. artigo.texto: This Startup Is Turning Used E-Bike Batteries Into Affordable Energy Storage Why throw away old e-bike and e-scooter batteries when they can be repurposed? Best of all, they don't even need to be dismantled. - Used batteries from e-bikes and e-scooters have been integrated into an industrial energy storage system. - German startup EDENenergy used over 100 second-life e-scooter batteries for a 70 kWh ESS. - In the future, the tiny startup's system will be able to accommodate multiple types of batteries in the same enclosure. Millions of e-bike and e-scooter batteries are thrown away every year, even though they might still have life in them. Now, a German startup is trying to reduce battery waste by integrating used batteries from e-mobility vehicles into energy storage systems. EDENenergy, which has just three part-time staff members in addition to its three founders, has shipped its first commercial product, a 70-kilowatt-hour battery system that uses no fewer than 112 second-life e-scooter batteries. EDENenergy's first commercial energy storage system uses 112 repurposed e-scooter batteries.Photo by: EDENenergy All modules were thoroughly tested, and the results were better than expected. The company's founders, who used to be researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, said that they expected the old batteries to have roughly 80% life left in them, but the tests revealed that most retained about 90% of their original capacity. After being abused in their previous life, the e-scooter batteries will have a much easier future in the startup's energy storage systems, where vibrations and large temperature fluctuations are non-existent. What's more, the long-term energy capacity of the system can be easily kept at 70 kWh by simply replacing modules that become unusable down the line. The startup said it remotely monitors each module, and when it's time for a replacement, it can be done without powering down the whole system. That's a big plus, especially for energy-sensitive scenarios where cutting the power would result in massive losses. The keen-eyed among you might have noticed that there's a solar inverter on one side of the battery box. That's because EDENenergy's first product was designed for companies that have solar panels but can't store solar energy yet. "In mid-October, we delivered the first storage system to a customer, which was an important milestone for our young company," said Florian Bierwirth, one of the founders. "With this storage size, we initially aim to target medium-sized companies in the region that have a photovoltaic system but do not yet have a storage solution." For its next step, the startup wants to come up with a way of using different batteries from different manufacturers. "To do this, the connector interfaces, battery management system, and communication protocols must be adapted for each new battery. There's a particularly wide range of options when it comes to e-bikes," said Bierwirth. Currently, the small company relies on large suppliers that can send in large numbers of the same battery type. A larger-capacity battery system of up to 300 kWh is also in the works, putting roughly 500 second-life e-scooter modules to good use instead of sending them to the landfill. The batteries will eventually give up, but when that happens, they'll be sent to a recycling facility where they'll be dismantled, and their contents will be reused, if possible.

artigo.texto: This year’s blue-wave election could have a dramatic impact on data center policy at the national, state, and local levels. New leadership for major congressional committees and a different political environment in many states and localities likely will shift policy debates in ways that are tougher for data center construction and operations. Several dozen cities and counties across the country held referenda on bans or major zoning restrictions, and in many places, those limits were approved by more than three-quarters of the vote. Some of the policy levers available in the new year include tougher permitting reform rules, an expansion of moratoriums, a stronger Ratepayer Protection Act, the construction of data centers on federal lands, limiting by-right development, mandatory disclosure of rogue artificial intelligence (AI), repeal of sales tax exemptions, excise taxes, abolition of nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) for data center deals, strengthened community engagement, and lawsuits or political action. Taken together, these shifts would dramatically alter the future policy environment affecting data center infrastructure as well as the broader tech sector itself. Permitting reform A bipartisan group of senators is supporting a bill promising expedited reviews of energy and infrastructure projects amid a pledge from President Donald Trump that he would reduce his attacks on wind and solar energy. Over the past two years, his administration blocked several offshore projects, cut subsidies for wind and solar, and encouraged oil and gas production. The U.S. House of Representatives is likely to vote on the legislation in November, but it is unclear whether there will be enough votes to speed up environmental reviews and limit opportunities for local community input into data center infrastructure in the aftermath of the elections. Democrats may be inclined to wait until their majority is sworn in and chairs top committees, and some legislators do not trust Trump to deliver on his wind and solar commitments and feel they should drive a harder bargain with the chief executive. Some Republicans also may be reluctant to embrace permitting reform given the defeat of some of their more visibly pro-data center representatives. They may argue it is better to slow down rather than speed up data center construction. Construction moratoriums or pauses With rising public opposition to data centers, some states and localities enacted moratoriums or pauses on construction so leaders could gauge the energy, water, and land use needs of data centers. Local officials want to make sure developers cover the full energy costs of their projects and that there is sufficient water in areas already facing scarcities. While meant as a short-term fix that buys leaders time to figure out their longer-term policies, these bills could become more widely adopted and perhaps even extended. A number of Democrats hammered Republicans for supporting tax breaks for data centers, and with the defeat of many Republicans in 2026, the political environment going forward likely will become tougher for data center developers. Local leaders will need to determine what they want their actual policies to be once moratoriums lapse. Ratepayer Protection Act Trump issued an executive order calling for data center developers to cover the new energy costs of their proposed projects instead of passing them on to consumers. But many of these requirements are voluntary and apply to future projects, not those which already are in operation or have been approved by local authorities. In addition, there are concerns that federal legislation in this area would preempt state prerogatives on energy utilization and land use. Historically, many of those rules have been at the local or state level. The new political landscape after the midterms could shift these rules from voluntary to mandatory. With most Americans expressing concerns about data centers, especially around energy, any new ratepayer protection bills are likely to be tougher on industry than what has been the case over the past year. There could be efforts to get tech firms to pay not only for the added energy costs but for infrastructure improvements and/or electric grid modernization. A step in either of those directions will increase construction and operational costs and affect the models of relevant businesses. Data centers on federal lands Facing growing opposition to data center construction, the Trump administration has proposed building facilities on federally owned land. Administration officials have pushed plans for data center-related development in Arizona, Oregon, Utah, and Nevada. The last proposal includes the Townsite Data Center on 88.5 acres of land owned by the Bureau of Land Management. That possibility became a significant issue in the Nevada gubernatorial election, and similar proposals are likely to become a lightning rod in many Western states since much of the area is under federal control. From the standpoint of the administration, the virtue of this shift is it bypasses the need for local approval and local construction permits. Instead, the projects need approval from agencies like the Bureau of Land Management, which the Trump administration is pushing to speed up construction. However, local communities are likely to perceive these projects as efforts to bypass local control, sparking outage among those who don’t want data centers in their areas. Limiting by-right development Some areas are limiting by-right development that allows large data centers to be built without local approval. For example, Prince William County in Virginia voted in September to end automatic approvals for data centers once a 90-day grace period ends. The rationale was that the county already has a number of data centers, and it wants to make sure the board of supervisors gets a chance to examine and vote on those proposals. artigo.texto: China Baowu Steel Group State-owned conglomerate Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te has announced that the government intends to develop a domestic version of the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism and to introduce an emissions trading system, according to Materiaintel. The initiative is aimed at helping local businesses comply with international climate standards and at converting the pressure of the transition toward net zero emissions by 2050 into longer-term competitiveness. Taiwan already operates an official carbon fee system covering large industrial enterprises and energy companies whose annual emissions exceed 25,000 tonnes of CO2 equivalent. The base rate is NT$300 per tonne, while companies with approved decarbonization plans can qualify for preferential rates of NT$50 or NT$100. The rules took effect in January 2025, and the first payments for 2025 emissions are scheduled for May 2026. A domestic equivalent of the EU mechanism would also place a carbon fee on imported materials, a step expected to have a significant effect on the steel industry. Taiwanese exporters face a separate challenge in their interaction with European rules. According to Taiwan's Climate Change Administration, roughly 2,600 local companies fall under the EU CBAM, with steel products making up the bulk of exports to the EU at approximately 2.8 million tonnes per year. The EU regulation permits carbon payments made in the country of origin to be credited against the number of CBAM certificates a European importer must purchase. This requires clear proof of the amounts actually paid, such as the preferential NT$50 rate rather than the standard NT$300. Where a plant passes costs on to the buyer through the material price, the EU importer pays part of the carbon costs in the supplier's invoice and the remainder through CBAM certificates. GMK Center previously reported that the UK government has published indicative figures for calculating its national CBAM, which takes effect in 2027. An analysis of those figures indicates that the British system will be considerably softer and cheaper for steel importers than the EU's comparable mechanism. artigo.texto: With smartphone sales tanking by around 20 percent compared to 2025, Qualcomm is looking to data centers to help boost its bottom line. During its Q4 2026 earnings call, the company laid out its plans to make a splash in the AI data center business, through partnerships with companies like Amazon and Meta announced earlier this year. The company expects that portion of its business to grow quickly, forecasting around $650 million in data center revenue during the first quarter of 2027. But it anticipates that will reach $5 billion by the end of 2027 and $15 billion by 2029. Qualcomm is betting big on data centers as smartphone sales sink Qualcomm expects data center chips will eventually account for 30% of its business. Considering the company’s total revenue for 2026 was $10.4 billion, that would constitute a significant share of its earnings. It confirmed during the call that it expects data centers to eventually account for around 30 percent of its business. That’s not quite as ambitious as AMD, which says that it expects over 80 percent of its revenue will eventually come from data centers. But it suggests there’s plenty of demand that needs to be filled and enough AI money to go around.

artigo.texto: Restrições nos EUA podem atrair US$ 500 bi em data centers no Brasil A expectativa de um aperto na regulação para construção de data centers nos Estados Unidos deve beneficiar a atração de investimentos para esse setor no Brasil. Segundo Marcos Peigo, CEO da Scala, o país tem potencial para multiplicar por 17 sua capacidade instalada e atrair US$ 500 bilhões em investimentos. A declaração foi dada em um contexto de crescente pressão regulatória nos EUA, que pode redirecionar projetos para mercados emergentes. O executivo aponta que o Brasil ainda precisa ampliar os incentivos fiscais para se tornar um destino competitivo. A fonte não detalhou quais incentivos específicos seriam necessários, mas a sinalização é de que o ambiente tributário atual pode não ser suficiente para capturar todo o potencial de investimento. Restrições nos EUA impulsionam busca por alternativas Nos Estados Unidos, a preocupação da população com escassez de energia devido à instalação de data centers ganhou força política. No Texas, o senador James Talarico venceu disputa contra o republicano Ken Paxton, apoiado por Elon Musk, que planejava desenvolver projetos da Space X e da… A fonte não detalhou o desfecho completo da disputa, mas o resultado reflete um sentimento crescente de cautela em relação a esses empreendimentos. Um levantamento do site The Information revelou que, em 34 dos 36 estados analisados, os candidatos vencedores ou que lideram a apuração defendem algum tipo de restrição ao setor. As medidas incluem proteções aos consumidores de energia, exigências ambientais, revisão de incentivos fiscais e até moratórias para novos empreendimentos. Esse cenário pode levar empresas a buscar locais com menos barreiras regulatórias. Brasil tem potencial de multiplicar capacidade por 17 De acordo com Marcos Peigo, o Brasil pode multiplicar por 17 sua capacidade instalada de data centers. Atualmente, a capacidade potencial do país é pequena, de cerca de 1,5 GW a 2 GW, segundo o executivo. No entanto, ele estima encerrar 2026 com 200 MW de capacidade contratada, com espaço para crescer até 5 GW. “Mas a capacidade potencial do país é pequena de cerca de 1,5 GW a 2 GW, e os americanos não vão querer correr o risco de perder a corrida para a China”, diz o CEO da Scala. A declaração sugere que o Brasil precisa agir rapidamente para se posicionar como alternativa viável no mercado global de data centers. Incentivos fiscais são cruciais para atrair investimentos O Paraguai, por exemplo, lançou incentivos fiscais para importação de equipamentos e incluiu isenção de imposto sobre dividendos e remessas de lucros para o exterior para grandes projetos. No mês passado, anunciou a Iguazú AI City, desenvolvida pela Araico em parceria com a americana Crusoe, com apoio do governo americano, para começar a operar em 2027 com energia de Itaipu. Essas medidas mostram como incentivos podem atrair projetos de grande porte. O Brasil, apesar do potencial, ainda não oferece um pacote fiscal tão agressivo, o que pode limitar sua competitividade frente a vizinhos como o Paraguai. Oportunidade para o comércio e indústria do interior paulista Para empresários e comerciantes de Araçatuba e região noroeste paulista, a expansão de data centers pode gerar demanda por serviços locais, como construção civil, fornecimento de equipamentos e mão de obra especializada. A instalação de grandes estruturas exige infraestrutura de energia, refrigeração e segurança, o que pode movimentar a economia regional. Além disso, a atração de investimentos bilionários pode criar empregos formais e estimular o desenvolvimento de fornecedores locais. A fonte não detalhou projeções específicas para o interior paulista, mas o impacto potencial é significativo para o setor produtivo. Desafios regulatórios e energéticos no Brasil Embora o potencial seja grande, o Brasil enfrenta desafios regulatórios e de infraestrutura energética. A capacidade atual é limitada, e a expansão exigirá investimentos em geração e transmissão de energia. A fonte não detalhou quais políticas públicas seriam necessárias, mas a ampliação de incentivos fiscais é apontada como um passo essencial. O cenário internacional, com restrições nos EUA, pode acelerar a tomada de decisão de investidores. No entanto, o Brasil precisa agir com rapidez para não perder a oportunidade para outros países da América Latina, como o Paraguai, que já saiu na frente com incentivos agressivos. Perguntas Frequentes Quanto o Brasil pode atrair em investimentos para data centers devido às restrições nos EUA? O Brasil tem potencial para atrair US$ 500 bilhões em investimentos e multiplicar por 17 sua capacidade instalada, segundo Marcos Peigo, CEO da Scala. Quais restrições a data centers estão sendo consideradas nos Estados Unidos? Em 34 dos 36 estados analisados, candidatos vencedores ou líderes defendem restrições como proteções aos consumidores de energia, exigências ambientais, revisão de incentivos fiscais e moratórias para novos empreendimentos. Qual é a capacidade atual e projetada de data centers da Scala no Brasil? A Scala estima encerrar 2026 com 200 MW de capacidade contratada, com espaço para crescer até 5 GW.

artigo.texto: NEW DELHI: India has launched a $1.5 billion scheme to develop 92 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage capacity as it seeks to speed up its shift toward renewable energy, the government said on Wednesday. The scheme, running from 2026-27 to 2030-31, will support 60 GWh of pumped hydro storage, 30 GWh of battery storage and 2 GWh using emerging technologies. The government said the incentives would support an estimated $10 billion in investment over the next five years. The planned additions are equal to 170 percent of India’s existing grid-scale storage capacity. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the scheme would help deliver “more reliable power, greater renewable energy integration, and stronger energy security”. India, home to more than 1.4 billion people, is the world’s third-biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and still relies heavily on coal to meet soaring energy demand. Demand is expected to keep rising rapidly even as the government pursues its goal of net-zero emissions by 2070. The cabinet also approved a $300 million scheme on Wednesday to support four domestic processing plants for lithium and nickel, critical minerals used in electric vehicle batteries, energy storage systems and electronics. “At present, India remains substantially dependent on imports,” the cabinet said. “Domestic processing capacity is therefore imperative.” — AFP

artigo.texto: The PJM Interconnection on Thursday filed a revised reliability backstop procurement, or RBP, proposal with federal regulators, with a goal of beginning the process on March 1 — about seven months later than originally planned. The revisions come after the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in late September rejected most of PJM’s initial proposal, which was designed to fill a capacity shortfall driven by data center development. FERC said in its decision that the original plan’s provisions for cost allocation, transmission owner exit rules and load-serving entity, or LSE, collateral requirements may have been unjust and unreasonable. The proposed revisions were “carefully tailored” to address the issues identified by FERC while keeping the RBP’s fundamental structure and policy objectives intact, PJM said in its recent filing. Under the new proposal, “PJM is using more current information on large-load growth to improve cost causation, revising the collateral methodology, and, importantly, recognizing that an RBP obligation and its associated collateral can move with the load-serving obligation when a large customer changes LSEs,” Maria Scheller, vice president of energy and planning at the consulting firm ICF International, said in an email to Utility Dive. The proposal sharply reduces risks for providers of last resort and default service providers — utilities that provide power to customers that don’t buy electricity from power marketers, according to Scheller. “If a large load initially relies on default service, the [provider of last resort] may temporarily carry significant RBP collateral and liquidity requirements,” she said. “The key credit question is whether state rules provide timely, certain recovery and adequate customer security, so the utility remains an administrative intermediary rather than taking meaningful balance-sheet or stranded-cost risk.” As a result, the state role is especially important in the process’ outcome, and some state utility regulators may need to craft new rules, according to Scheller. “Regulators may need to determine customer-specific allocation, establish appropriate security and cost-recovery rules, track changes in suppliers, and decide what happens if the underlying large load shrinks, defaults or disappears,” she said. The proposal reduces the direct risk to residential and other existing customers, but it does not eliminate it, according to Scheller. “Administrative costs, collateral and financing costs, regulatory lag, customer default and stranded-cost risk can still create indirect exposure if the state-level mechanisms do not keep the obligation tightly attached to the large load that caused it,” she said. The planned procurement aims to fill a 6.8-GW capacity shortfall from PJM’s 2028/29 base residual auction. However, the procurement may shrink significantly from the initial target after PJM recalculates how much capacity is needed, according to equity analysts with Jefferies. PJM utilities, such as PPL Electric, FirstEnergy and AES Ohio, recently lowered their overall, near-term large load forecasts by 6.5 GW, the analysts said in an Oct. 28 note, citing recent filings to PJM’s Load Analysis Subcommittee. That reduction could reduce PJM’s 2027 load forecast, which would affect the grid operator’s backstop procurement target, they said. With that reduction, the procurement could be for as little as roughly 630 MW, according to the note. The procurement could also shrink if data center developers enter into bilateral contracts with power suppliers. Even so, analysis by Charles River Associates discussed Monday by the subcommittee found that PJM could face a roughly 11.5-GW shortfall by 2030. PJM hired CRA to provide an independent data center demand forecast. Under the proposal, PJM will close the RBP bid window on March 28, with the final procurement target and supply amounts determined on April 28, the grid operator said Thursday. PJM would post the results on May 10.

(WTOC) - A crowded room of Effingham County residents and local leaders gathered on Election night expecting a vote on OpenAI’s proposed AI data center campus. Instead, commissioners pushed pause. The Effingham County Board of Commissioners voted Tuesday to postpone a decision on the site plan for “Project Camellia”, following sharp exchanges between commissioners and developers over residential protections, earthen berms, and environmental impacts. Before commissioners began their debate, residents lined up at the microphone during the public hearing portion of the meeting, expressing continued frustration over a perceived lack of transparency surrounding the project. “Until y’all start being transparent, until y’all can start answering some questions, I’m going to be up here each and every week,” one person told the board. Revised Site Plans and Project Reductions During the meeting, Rich Modliszewski, a representative for project developer Octans GA LLC, presented an updated site plan. While early conceptual plans showed four large buildings, the formal layout now features six compute buildings across two designated project areas: - Area 3: Four 471,000-square-foot buildings, a 100,000-square-foot warehouse, a 75,000-square-foot operations office, and a 300-foot natural wooded buffer separating the site from northern residential properties. - Area 4: Two 471,000-square-foot buildings, with a 300-foot wooded buffer along Hodgeville Road. Modliszewski outlined several project reductions, stating the overall campus buildout was scaled back from an original 30-million-square-foot proposal to roughly three to four million square feet, with the total number of buildings cut from an initial 30 down to six. He also noted projected water consumption was reduced from 100,000 gallons per day down to 30,000 gallons per day using a closed-loop cooling system, and asserted that 1,500 morning and afternoon daily vehicle trips would be taken off local roads compared to previous industrial estimates. The proposed building heights, however, increased from 35 feet to 42 feet. Modliszewski maintained that the formal engineering plans meet all current standards under Effingham County’s existing I-1 (Industrial) zoning. Commissioners Demand Enforceable Protections Despite those reductions, the presentation sparked intense pushback from commissioners seeking enforceable guarantees. Commissioner Roger Burdette zeroed in on Area 4 along Hodgeville Road, pressing Modliszewski to commit on the record to constructing an additional 20-foot earthen berm inside the buffer zone to shield nearby homes from noise and light. When Modliszewski said he could not commit without consulting the development team, tensions escalated. “That’s currently planned as a variable screening buffer, and we’re going to do whatever is allowed in that space to ensure that—” Modliszewski said. “That’s not what we discussed. You’re not going to say we’re getting a 20-foot berm there?” Burdette asked. “I’m not saying we are or aren’t,” Modliszewski responded. Modliszewski pushed back, stating that developers had followed every legal standard required by the county. “[We] did submit a site plan that is in complete conformance with your codes and—” Modliszewski began. “We’re following precedent. I’m not asking you a question, I’m making a statement,” Burdette interrupted. “I understand your request, but I’m not able to—” Modliszewski said. “You came ill-prepared tonight. I think you guys should have been a lot better prepared,” Burdette said. Burdette, who noted he supports the economic potential of the data center, insisted that protecting surrounding neighborhoods must come first before he could cast an affirmative vote. “I put so much into this. I have to look these people... You might not agree with this, but I have to look everybody in the eyes to say it’s safe at the end of the day. And I am very uncomfortable right now,” Burdette said. Commissioner Beth Helmly raised additional concerns regarding electrical demand, cooling water sources, and wetland mitigation. Helmly questioned the exact acreage of wetlands that would be permanently disrupted after hearing an additional 1.18 acres could be impacted. “I just feel like there’s not enough time to make a decision,” Helmly said. “I don’t have a problem—I’m not sitting here telling everybody sitting in this room that I won’t vote for this one day. But I do not feel comfortable voting for it tonight.” What’s Next Following a brief recess, commissioners voted unanimously to table the site plan approval until their regular meeting on Tuesday, Nov. 17. Commissioners stated the delay will give developers time to return with firm answers regarding wetland impacts and written assurances that the 20-foot berm will be built along Hodgeville Road. Long-duration energy storage systems (LDES) are energy storage technologies designed to retain electricity or energy for extended durations and discharge it when required to maintain a reliable balance between power generation and demand. Unlike conventional short-duration storage systems, LDES technologies can provide sustained energy delivery over several hours and, depending on the technology, for periods extending to multiple days or longer. These systems are increasingly important for integrating variable renewable energy sources, improving grid flexibility, reducing reliance on conventional peaking generation, and strengthening power system resilience. The LDES technology landscape encompasses a diverse range of storage approaches, including mechanical and physical storage technologies such as pumped hydro, compressed air energy storage, liquid air energy storage, and gravity-based systems; electrochemical technologies such as flow batteries, metal-air batteries, and high-temperature or liquid-metal batteries; thermal energy storage; and chemical storage solutions including hydrogen-based power-to-power systems and other Power-to-X technologies. Each technology offers distinct characteristics in terms of storage duration, energy and power capacity, efficiency, response time, geographic requirements, and suitability for different grid and end-use applications. The long-duration energy storage systems Market encompasses the development, manufacturing, system integration, deployment, and commercialization of technologies capable of providing extended-duration energy storage. These systems are utilized for renewable energy integration and firming, grid balancing, ancillary services, energy arbitrage, load shifting, peak demand management, backup power, microgrid resilience, off-grid electricity supply, and industrial decarbonization. Their ability to store surplus electricity and release it during periods of higher demand or reduced renewable generation makes LDES an important component of increasingly flexible and decentralized energy systems. The market ecosystem includes technology developers, equipment and system manufacturers, engineering and infrastructure companies, project developers, utilities, independent power producers, grid operators, and energy service providers. LDES technologies range from established infrastructure-based solutions to emerging storage systems progressing through laboratory development, pilot projects, demonstration facilities, and large-scale commercial deployment. Continued advances in materials, system design, power conversion, thermal management, hydrogen technologies, and energy management systems are broadening the technological landscape and expanding the role of long-duration storage across modern power systems. artigo.texto: Oregon approves data center restriction charter amendment OREGON, Ohio (WTVG) — Voters in Oregon, Ohio approved a charter amendment on the November ballot to restrict data center construction. Issue 25 is a charter amendment question on the ballot that caps data centers at 25 megawatts. It passed with 60% of the vote. The push for the ballot question came after weeks of signature gathering by United Neighbors of Oregon over the proposed Vantage Data Centers project near Wynn and Cordurory roads. Supporters of bringing data centers to Oregon argue the multimillion-dollar developments bring tax relief, funding for schools and high-paying jobs. Concerns over strained power grids, water resources and noise have led residents in multiple communities to demand a final say at the ballot box. Oregon’s mayor said the city was the first jurisdiction in the area to bring forward a citizen-led petition aimed at limiting data center development. Citizen-led ballot initiatives in the area are highlighting a tension between local quality of life and economic investment. In Defiance, voters approved a charter amendment that places limits on the size of data centers in the city. The proposed amendment does not ban data centers outright but prohibits data centers that are over 25 megawatts within city limits. Defiance also has a moratorium on data centers that went into effect in September. It will stay in place for six months. Council said it needed the time to study the impact a facility would have on the community. In Huron County, voters in Monroeville overwhelmingly rejected a data center advisory question. The decision does not prohibit the development of data centers, but it helps village council members gauge public sentiment. artigo.texto: As ações da Drax Group plc (LSE:DRX) subiram 0,9%, para 870,46 pence, durante o pregão de quarta-feira, estendendo a alta do dia anterior, enquanto os investidores continuavam a avaliar o projeto de desenvolvimento de um centro de dados com inteligência artificial proposto pela empresa em parceria com a Brookfield Asset Management e a Radiant. As ações subiram mais de 8% na terça-feira, após o anúncio dos planos para desenvolver um centro de dados com capacidade superior a um gigawatt no complexo da usina elétrica de Drax, no norte da Inglaterra. Parceria com a Brookfield cria nova oportunidade de crescimento O acordo reúne a Drax, a Brookfield Asset Management e a Radiant, plataforma de infraestrutura de IA da Brookfield sediada no Reino Unido, para explorar o desenvolvimento de instalações de computação em larga escala. A primeira fase do projeto deverá fornecer até 100 megawatts de capacidade computacional, apoiada por um investimento inicial de 2,5 bilhões de libras. A previsão é que as operações comerciais comecem no início de 2028, embora o projeto ainda não tenha chegado a uma decisão final de investimento. Esse desenvolvimento pode criar uma nova oportunidade de negócios para a Drax, à medida que a demanda por capacidade computacional aumenta juntamente com o investimento em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. JPMorgan vê potencial de valorização para a Drax Os analistas do JPMorgan reagiram positivamente ao anúncio, sugerindo que a parceria poderia aumentar a avaliação que os investidores atribuem às ambições da Drax no setor de data centers. O banco também destacou a importância potencial do empreendimento para o futuro a longo prazo da Usina Termoelétrica de Drax. Os atuais acordos de subsídio à biomassa da instalação têm previsão de expirar em março de 2031, criando incertezas sobre suas perspectivas comerciais após essa data. O JPMorgan indicou que a parceria para o centro de dados poderia aumentar a confiança na continuidade das operações do local após o término do período de subsídio. Citi destaca incertezas remanescentes do projeto O Citi adotou uma posição mais cautelosa, observando que o projeto proposto ainda está em fase inicial e que a Drax divulgou informações financeiras limitadas. O banco destacou a ausência de uma decisão final de investimento, o que levanta dúvidas sobre os custos finais do projeto, a estrutura de financiamento e o retorno financeiro. Apesar disso, o anúncio continuou a atrair o interesse dos investidores, com as ações da Drax ampliando seus ganhos na sessão de quarta-feira. As condições gerais do mercado favorecem a negociação O índice FTSE 100 também registrou leve alta na quarta-feira, com a queda dos rendimentos dos títulos do governo britânico após os ganhos dos democratas nas eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA. Os investidores avaliaram se o resultado das eleições poderia limitar o escopo para novas políticas fiscais que aumentassem o déficit nos Estados Unidos. No entanto, o sentimento do mercado permaneceu cauteloso antes da decisão do Banco da Inglaterra sobre a taxa de juros na quinta-feira, com as expectativas de um possível aumento da taxa pressionando os setores sensíveis a elas. Os ganhos da Drax foram impulsionados principalmente por desenvolvimentos específicos da empresa, permitindo que as ações tivessem um desempenho superior ao do mercado britânico em geral. Desempenho e perspectivas do preço das ações A 870,46 pence, as ações da Drax permaneceram abaixo da sua máxima de 52 semanas, de 937,5 pence, mas recuperaram significativamente da sua mínima de 52 semanas, de 702 pence. A parceria proposta com a Brookfield introduziu uma oportunidade adicional de crescimento potencial para a empresa, embora sua contribuição financeira a longo prazo permaneça incerta. É provável que os investidores se concentrem em novos anúncios relativos a aprovações de projetos, compromissos de investimento e cronogramas de desenvolvimento, à medida que a Drax avança com seus planos de infraestrutura de IA. Mais sobre Drax A Drax Group plc é uma empresa de energia do Reino Unido com operações focadas na geração de eletricidade e energia de biomassa. Seu principal ativo é a Usina Termelétrica de Drax, em North Yorkshire, onde a empresa está explorando oportunidades para desenvolver infraestrutura de data center de IA em larga escala, em conjunto com suas operações de energia existentes. artigo.texto: Elea avança no Rio, mas energia desafia expansão de data centers Prefeitura discute licenciamento de projeto próximo ao Parque Olímpico; Microsoft e GE Vernova apontam desafios de infraestrutura. O projeto de data center da Elea no Rio de Janeiro já conta com um parceiro para acesso à energia elétrica e está em discussão na prefeitura para licenciamento. A informação foi apresentada pelo secretário municipal de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Osmar Lima, durante o DCD Connect Live Brasil 2026, em painel que reuniu representantes da Microsoft, GE Vernova e BNDES para discutir a expansão da infraestrutura digital na cidade. O empreendimento foi anunciado durante o Web Summit Rio de 2025 e está previsto para uma região próxima ao Parque Olímpico, na Barra da Tijuca. Segundo Osmar, a área dispõe de infraestrutura implantada para os Jogos Olímpicos de 2016, incluindo conectividade e duas subestações de energia elétrica em pontos diferentes. O secretário explicou que a prefeitura identificou na região um terreno de aproximadamente 1 milhão de metros quadrados, originalmente destinado ao desenvolvimento imobiliário. A instalação de data centers passou a integrar a estratégia municipal de aproveitamento dessa infraestrutura, sem ampliar a ocupação urbana na mesma proporção de um empreendimento residencial ou comercial. De acordo com Osmar, a Elea não solicitou incentivos municipais de ISS ou IPTU para desenvolver o projeto. O pedido apresentado à administração foi de apoio institucional para viabilizar sua implantação. “A primeira reação, enfim, todo mundo pode imaginar, a gente falou, bom, beleza, o que vocês querem, vocês querem incentivo de ISS, IPTU, etc., e para a nossa feliz surpresa não era nada disso”, relatou o secretário. A prefeitura considera os data centers parte de sua estratégia de atração de investimentos em tecnologia, associada à disponibilidade de energia, conectividade e áreas próximas aos centros consumidores. GE Vernova aponta necessidade de reforços na transmissão Rodrigo Queiroga, responsável pela área de Grid Systems Integration da GE Vernova na América Latina, afirmou que o Rio de Janeiro reúne condições para receber grandes empreendimentos de processamento de dados, mas precisará de investimentos na infraestrutura de transmissão elétrica. Segundo ele, projetos que demandam blocos de carga de 100 MW, 200 MW ou 300 MW exigem uma avaliação da capacidade de conexão à rede, além da disponibilidade de geração. O executivo mencionou corredores de transmissão de 500 kV e instalações como Grajaú, Terminal Rio, Zona Oeste e Nova Iguaçu, que integram a infraestrutura elétrica relevante para o atendimento dessas demandas. “Essa evolução para que o Rio de Janeiro se posicione nesse cenário vai passar por uma demanda de investimentos estruturantes, na nossa visão, especificamente para reforçar a malha de transmissão”, afirmou. Queiroga destacou que empreendimentos voltados ao processamento de IA podem exigir soluções adicionais para manter a estabilidade do sistema elétrico. Entre as tecnologias mencionadas estão subestações compactas e sistemas de compensação estática. Outro ponto levantado foi a diferença entre os prazos de expansão da rede de transmissão e os cronogramas de implantação dos data centers. Segundo o representante da GE Vernova, a compatibilização desses processos é necessária para dar previsibilidade à conexão dos empreendimentos. Ele também mencionou mudanças nos procedimentos de solicitação de acesso à rede elétrica, com maior utilização de critérios técnicos e exigência de garantias para reduzir pedidos especulativos de conexão. Microsoft defende licenciamento paralelo e previsibilidade tributária Para André Pedral, responsável pela gestão de custos de projetos da Microsoft no Brasil, a previsibilidade de prazos e custos é um dos principais fatores considerados na implantação de data centers. O executivo explicou que os empreendimentos envolvem investimentos elevados e precisam cumprir cronogramas definidos para que a operação comece na data prevista. Entre os pontos que exigem atenção, ele destacou os procedimentos de licenciamento, que atualmente envolvem diferentes etapas e órgãos responsáveis. Na avaliação de Pedral, a realização paralela de processos de autorização poderia contribuir para reduzir os prazos de implantação, em comparação com a tramitação sequencial. A tributação também foi mencionada como fator que interfere no planejamento financeiro. O representante da Microsoft citou a reforma tributária, a definição da alíquota da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS) e as incertezas relacionadas ao Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços (IBS). Segundo ele, a avaliação dos investimentos precisa considerar não apenas a construção, mas os custos de operação ao longo de períodos que podem chegar a 15 ou 20 anos. Pedral também destacou a importância de explicar às comunidades os efeitos da instalação dos data centers, incluindo a formação de cadeias de fornecedores e a atração de outras atividades econômicas. BNDES destaca conectividade e formação de profissionais Marconi Viana, representante do BNDES, afirmou que a expansão dos data centers exige uma combinação de infraestrutura de telecomunicações, energia, demanda por serviços digitais e disponibilidade de profissionais qualificados. Segundo ele, a implantação de um empreendimento não pode ser analisada isoladamente da capacidade de transmitir os dados processados e da existência de mercados consumidores próximos. O representante do banco defendeu a articulação entre os governos municipal, estadual e federal para assegurar condições regulatórias e infraestrutura capazes de sustentar investimentos de longo prazo. Viana também chamou a atenção para a necessidade de comunicar à sociedade os efeitos dos data centers sobre a economia. A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou os editais dos certames, […] 4 de novembro de 2026, às 10:42 O setor elétrico brasileiro se prepara para uma nova etapa de desenvolvimento com os primeiros Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade destinados à contratação de potência de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês). A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou os editais dos certames, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. A iniciativa busca ampliar a disponibilidade de potência no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), contribuindo para a segurança do fornecimento de eletricidade. Os leilões contemplam duas modalidades: uma com exigência de nacionalização dos equipamentos e outra sem esse requisito específico. Os contratos preveem o início do suprimento em agosto de 2028, com duração de 15 anos. A iniciativa também coloca em evidência as condições necessárias para desenvolver uma cadeia de fornecedores e serviços especializados em armazenamento de energia no país. A expansão das fontes renováveis e as mudanças no perfil de consumo de eletricidade aumentam a necessidade de recursos capazes de proporcionar maior flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico. Projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), reunidas no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE), subsidiam o planejamento da oferta e da demanda de energia no país. Nesse contexto, os sistemas de armazenamento podem absorver eletricidade e disponibilizá-la posteriormente, contribuindo para o atendimento da demanda em horários de maior consumo e para a integração de fontes cuja geração varia conforme as condições climáticas. Dados e análises da BloombergNEF (BNEF) também acompanham a evolução das tecnologias de armazenamento e seu papel nos sistemas elétricos. Entre as características das baterias está a capacidade de responder rapidamente a comandos operacionais, permitindo absorver ou fornecer energia conforme as necessidades da rede. A contribuição efetiva desses sistemas depende, entre outros fatores, do dimensionamento dos projetos, das condições de conexão e dos requisitos operacionais estabelecidos. A implantação de empreendimentos BESS envolve mais do que os módulos de bateria. Os projetos também dependem de conversores de potência, sistemas de controle e gerenciamento, proteções elétricas, monitoramento e infraestrutura de conexão. A compatibilidade entre esses componentes e o atendimento aos requisitos técnicos são aspectos importantes para a integração dos sistemas à rede. Nesse processo, as etapas de testes e comissionamento permitem verificar o funcionamento dos equipamentos e das interfaces antes da entrada em operação. Conforme as características de cada empreendimento, os procedimentos podem incluir ensaios de carga e descarga, verificações de desempenho, avaliação dos sistemas de proteção e validação da comunicação entre os diferentes componentes. A infraestrutura elétrica de suporte também pode ser necessária para a realização de ensaios e a verificação das condições operacionais previstas no projeto. A exigência de conteúdo nacional em uma das modalidades dos leilões reforça a discussão sobre o desenvolvimento da cadeia produtiva brasileira. Além da fabricação de equipamentos, a estruturação desse mercado envolve competências em engenharia, integração de sistemas, instalação, testes e suporte técnico, com a participação de diferentes fornecedores e prestadores de serviços. Para Jorge Moreno, diretor de Novos Negócios da Tecnogera, a integração dos componentes é um dos pontos de atenção na implantação dos sistemas de armazenamento. “Os projetos de armazenamento exigem uma visão integrada de engenharia. Além das baterias, é necessário considerar os inversores, os sistemas de controle, as proteções e a infraestrutura elétrica, garantindo que os diferentes componentes funcionem de forma coordenada. Os testes e a validação técnica são etapas importantes para verificar o atendimento aos requisitos de cada projeto”, afirma o executivo. Com os primeiros leilões, o armazenamento em baterias passa a ocupar um espaço mais definido no planejamento da capacidade elétrica brasileira. A implantação dos empreendimentos dependerá dos aspectos contratuais, dos requisitos técnicos e das condições de conexão à rede, além da capacidade de fornecedores e integradores de atenderem às necessidades de cada projeto. artigo.texto: - Microsoft will not extend an existing agreement with Nscale to rent more computing power at a Texas data center, Reuters reported. - The companies struck a deal in 2025 for Nscale to deploy around 200,000 Nvidia AI chips with Microsoft across its data centers in Europe and the U.S. - Retail sentiment for MSFT flipped to 'bearish' from 'bullish.' Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) will not exercise an option to more than double its existing agreement with AI cloud provider Nscale to rent more computing power at a Texas data center, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The companies struck a deal last year for Nscale to deploy around 200,000 Nvidia (NVDA) AI chips with Microsoft across its data centers in Europe and the U.S. The reported development signals more pain for the IPO-bound Nscale. Last month, Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's flagship data center project in Essex, the UK, after power connection delays pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s. Nscale, backed by Nvidia, filed for an IPO in September, although a report last month said it faced opposition from investors over its $130 billion IPO valuation target. Reuters reported that Microsoft's decision to not expand the Texas contract was made several months ago, before Nscale filed for its IPO, and that its existing workflow, as per the original, was not affected. Cloud Industry Faces Pressure The development comes as the cloud industry faces increased scrutiny. In recent weeks, the debt-heavy model of neocloud firms such as CoreWeave has come under the scanner even as concerns prevail over overcapacity. The decisive midterm win by the Democrats, who are seen to be pro-AI regulation, has added concerns that new data centers will be harder and costlier to build. That could stifle the growth in cloud capacity essential to support AI. Meanwhile, the delays in bringing new cloud capacity online are also drawing attention. The Information reported on Wednesday that delays from IREN Ltd (IREN) contributed to Microsoft spending less than it had earmarked in capital expenditures last quarter. Retail View On MSFT On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for MSFT flipped to 'bearish' from 'bullish.' "$MSFT microsoft jumped 6% today on a bet the build slows down. seems like the best ai news left is less ai spending, and a rally for not building tells you where the capex story actually stands," a trader wrote.
