TREX Energy Commissions BESS Manufacturing Facility in Hyderabad PR Newswire 4 min read The new facility features a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line, capable of producing 5 kWh to 5 MWh BESS solutions, with Phase 2 expansion planned in Madhya Pradesh Key pointers: TREX Energy commissions its Hyderabad lithium battery manufacturing facility on 21 September 2026, featuring a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line. The company's product portfolio spans 5 kWh energy storage systems (ESS) to 5 MWh Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), with a focus on Commercial & Industrial (C&I) applications and home inverter batteries. TREX Energy plans to expand its manufacturing footprint through a Phase 2 facility on four acres of land allotted by the Madhya Pradesh Government. HYDERABAD, India, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TREX Energy, an Indian energy storage company, today announced the opening of its lithium battery manufacturing facility at E-City, Raviryal, Maheshwaram, Hyderabad. Equipped with a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line, the line is designed to produce 52S battery packs used in 261 kWh and 5 MWh energy storage systems. Supporting India's Growing Energy Storage Requirements As India expands its renewable energy capacity, the need for reliable energy storage is growing across industries, utilities, and households. Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and other energy storage system (ESS) solutions can help manage fluctuations in power supply, support peak-load management and provide backup power across a range of applications. TREX Energy's Hyderabad facility is intended to support this evolving demand through local manufacturing. The company aims to develop energy storage solutions suited to Indian operating conditions while helping reduce dependence on imports and improve delivery timelines. "We're focused on reducing financing costs to make BESS more affordable and reliable for the Indian market. Energy must be available when it's needed, and BESS is a key solution," said Bharat S. Chhittarka, Director, TREX Energy. Automated Manufacturing for Diverse Applications The Hyderabad facility features a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line, designed to manufacture battery modules at a rate of 12 parts per minute. Automation is intended to support production consistency, manufacturing efficiency and quality control as demand for energy storage solutions grows. The facility will manufacture battery packs for applications including 261kWh BESS configurations and larger energy storage systems. The company's offerings are designed to address the requirements of customers across residential, Commercial & Industrial (C&I) and utility-scale segments. "Our 12 PPM automatic module assembly line marks a significant step forward in TREX Energy's manufacturing capabilities. It enables us to produce battery modules efficiently and consistently, supporting BESS solutions ranging from 5 kWh to 5 MWh. This facility strengthens our ability to meet India's growing energy storage demand with scalable, reliable, and high-quality solutions." — Roshan Shaik, Technical Director, TREX Energy Energy Storage Solutions from Homes to Utility-Scale Projects TREX Energy's product portfolio spans systems ranging from 5 kWh to 5 MWh BESS solutions, enabling the company to address energy storage requirements across different scales. Its offerings include: Commercial & Industrial (C&I) BESS: Energy storage solutions for factories, offices and commercial facilities seeking to manage energy use, support backup power and improve operational resilience. Utility-scale BESS: Battery energy storage solutions for grid-related applications and large renewable energy projects. Residential energy storage systems: Solutions designed to meet household energy storage requirements. Home inverter batteries: Battery solutions for residential inverter applications, supporting household backup power needs. Battery packs and energy storage system (ESS) solutions: Configurations including 52S battery packs designed for 261kWh BESS and 5 MWh systems. By serving both residential customers and larger energy users, TREX Energy aims to address a broad range of energy storage requirements through its expanding product portfolio. Phase 2 Expansion Planned in Madhya Pradesh TREX Energy is also planning the next phase of its manufacturing expansion. The Madhya Pradesh Government has allotted four acres of land to the company for its proposed Phase 2 facility. The planned expansion is expected to increase the company's manufacturing footprint and support its efforts to serve customers across additional markets in India. Further details regarding the facility's capacity, development timeline and commissioning are subject to confirmation. Building for India's Energy Transition The Hyderabad facility represents TREX Energy's commitment to developing local manufacturing capabilities for India's evolving energy storage ecosystem. Through its focus on C&I applications, residential energy storage and utility-scale BESS solutions, the company aims to serve the varied requirements of businesses, households and energy infrastructure providers. As it progresses with its planned expansion, TREX Energy intends to continue investing in manufacturing capabilities, technology and local talent to support the adoption of energy storage solutions in India. artigo.texto: Financiamento XIIlab aprova bônus conversíveis de KRW 10 bilhões para expandir seus negócios de data centers de IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A XIIlab, empresa sul-coreana de infraestrutura de IA, informou em um comunicado regulatório de 6 de novembro de 2026 que seu conselho aprovou a emissão privada de bônus conversíveis no valor de KRW 10 bilhões para seus negócios de data centers de IA. A subscrição e o pagamento em dinheiro estão previstos para 16 de novembro de 2026; portanto, o comunicado registra um financiamento aprovado, não uma captação concluída. O anúncio da XIIlab vincula os recursos ao capital de giro para a construção de clusters de GPUs e a um modelo operacional mais amplo. A empresa planeja aplicar seu software AstraGo à infraestrutura que construir, buscar contratos de operação e gestão e gerar receita recorrente além das atividades de construção. Condições dos bônus e opções de resgate Os bônus da primeira série são ao portador, sem garantia e colocados de forma privada, e o valor total é classificado como recursos para operações. Tanto a taxa de cupom quanto a taxa de juros no vencimento são de 0%; não há pagamento de juros separado antes do vencimento, e o principal será reembolsável em 100% do valor registrado eletronicamente em 16 de novembro de 2031. Portanto, os bônus mantidos até o vencimento continuam sujeitos à obrigação de reembolso integral, apesar da ausência de juros de cupom e de vencimento. O preço de conversão foi fixado em KRW 8.106 por ação e, caso seja exercida integralmente, resultará em 1.233.654 ações ordinárias registradas. Os investidores poderão solicitar a conversão de 16 de novembro de 2027 a 16 de outubro de 2031. Os bônus não incluem cláusula de reajuste do preço de conversão em caso de queda no preço das ações, embora se apliquem ajustes específicos a determinadas operações societárias, incluindo emissão de ações abaixo do preço de mercado, fusões, reduções de capital, desdobramentos e grupamentos de ações. A XIIlab ou seu indicado poderá resgatar até 50% da subscrição original de cada investidor, limitado ao total de KRW 5 bilhões, em datas trimestrais entre 16 de novembro de 2027 e 16 de novembro de 2028. A empresa apresenta essa opção como uma forma de reduzir a possível diluição caso o preço de suas ações suba. Os investidores, por sua vez, têm uma opção de venda: podem solicitar o resgate antecipado por 100% do valor a partir de 16 de maio de 2029 e nas datas trimestrais subsequentes. Em conjunto, essas disposições equilibram a possível diluição acionária com uma opção de compra por parte da empresa e preservam para os credores a possibilidade de solicitar o reembolso em dinheiro antes do vencimento. Fundos de política pública e cronograma de gastos As subscrições previstas incluem KRW 8 bilhões provenientes de subfundos do National Growth Fund administrados por Korea Investment Value Asset Management, DB Asset Management, Susung Asset Management e Orion Asset Management, além de KRW 2 bilhões de outros fundos administrados pela Orion. A XIIlab caracteriza o National Growth Fund como um instrumento de política pública criado para fomentar setores estratégicos avançados, como IA, semicondutores e biotecnologia, e considera que seus negócios de infraestrutura de IA se enquadram nos principais alvos de investimento do fundo. O cronograma de gastos destina KRW 5 bilhões a 2027 e KRW 5 bilhões a 2028 e aos anos seguintes, tudo para negócios relacionados a data centers de IA. A XIIlab afirmou que está assegurando capital de giro para a construção antes da demanda esperada por GPUs mais recentes, incluindo a Vera Rubin, e que pretende ampliar a construção de clusters de GPUs em sua atuação como parceira NVIDIA Elite. O papel da AstraGo na geração de receita recorrente A documentação do produto AstraGo da XIIlab descreve uma plataforma baseada em Kubernetes para alocar recursos de GPU, executar cargas de trabalho de treinamento e inferência e gerenciar recursos e cargas de trabalho em um único ambiente. A plataforma é compatível com servidores de GPU NVIDIA existentes e com os NPUs específicos da Furiosa e da DeepX, clusters com vários servidores e implantações locais ou em redes fechadas. O preço combina uma licença de assinatura anual com uma tarifa de instalação do servidor por nó, conferindo ao plano operacional uma estrutura comercial baseada em assinaturas. A XIIlab lançou o AstraGo 2.1 em 1º de abril de 2026 e afirmou que a versão divide uma GPU física entre cargas de trabalho de inferência isoladas, executa treinamento e inferência no mesmo cluster, prioriza recursos para inferência em tempo real e separa os históricos de alocação e uso por organização ou serviço em uma estrutura multi-inquilino. Essas são as funções operacionais que a XIIlab planeja desenvolver ainda mais à medida que ampliar sua atuação na gestão de data centers. O financiamento conecta a carteira de projetos de construção de clusters de GPUs da XIIlab a um modelo operacional baseado em AstraGo, estruturado em torno de assinaturas anuais e serviços contínuos de gestão. A questão central para a trajetória da empresa no médio prazo é se essa atividade de projetos se converterá em receita recorrente de operações, enquanto a empresa administra as alternativas de diluição e reembolso em dinheiro previstas nos bônus.

artigo.texto: American voters roundly rejected data centers nearly anywhere they were on the ballot Tuesday, a rebuke sure to rattle investors already growing skittish about the AI buildout. Residents in more than 30 localities across nine states voted for moratoriums, outright bans, and other measures, some in direct response to specific projects underway. Edgewater, Fla. overwhelmingly voted to embed a data-center ban in the cityâs charter, and voters in Perry, Ohio passed a measure placing financial and operational constraints on hyperscalers seeking tax breaks. Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, one analysis showed. The pressure pushed some Republican candidates including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, an AI booster just a few months ago, into promises of tougher regulation; he lost anyway. Banks and asset managers financing the buildout have already begun treating local opposition as a credit risk, while hyperscalers are rushing to hire community liaisons. Meanwhile, tech companies bracing for the vibe shift are trying to rebrand the data centers as âcompute campusesâ with mixed results, Semaforâs Ashley Gold reported.

artigo.texto: Ohioans overwhelmingly pass data center bans, restrictions on ballot Ohioans made their opinion on data centers clear on Election Day: No. Voters in Ohio municipalities with data center bans on the ballot overwhelmingly supported more restrictions on the controversial developments. Voters in at least 14 Ohio municipalities passed bans or other restrictions on data centers Nov. 3, including in Trenton. Across Ohio, 18 municipalities voted on data center-related measures, the most of any state. Residents in 11 of these municipalities voted on outright bans, while the other seven weighed measures that added new regulations or oversight. How did they vote? The following 10 municipalities passed bans on data center construction: Hubbard, Sunbury, Pataskala, Urbana, Defiance, Upper Sandusky, Piqua, Granville, Conneaut and Trenton. Voters in Oregon also voted on a ban, but the Lucas County Board of Election was not reporting any results as of midnight Nov. 4. The following cities, townships and villages passed other restrictions: - Ashville: Almost 82% of Ashville voters voted to reverse its village council's agreement and negotiations with EdgeConneX to build two data centers. - Grove City: 55% of voters approved a charter amendment that requires voter approval for future large-scale developments, including data center developments that use more than 20 megawatts of electricity or 500,000 gallons of water. - Perry: Over 87% of voters passed an ordinance that requires developers seeking tax abatements or other financial incentives to offer the village financial guarantees. - Wilmington: Through four separate referendums, around 80% of voters rejected rezoning for parcels of land to accommodate a data center project. Monroe and Sprigg Townships in Adams County and Monroeville also had data center related measures on the ballot, but results are not yet available. In Trenton, 80% of voters support ban Almost 80% of Trenton voters passed Issue 17, which bans data centers that use over 25 megawatts of electricity. Debates over two proposed data centers in or bordering Trenton have consumed the Butler County town of around 14,000 for months. Residents with the Woodsdale and Trenton Environmental Resistance, a group that opposed the data centers, collected signatures to get a ban on the ballot earlier this year. After the Trenton City Council voted not to certify the petition in August, the Ohio Supreme Court intervened. The court found the council "disregarded" the law and ordered it to certify the petition. Lacy Roth, 30, voted to support the ban. She told The Enquirer that she wants her 9-month-old son, who she brought with her to the polls, to grow up in a small town without noise and air pollution. "I think Issue 17 is one of the biggest factors to get voters out today," she said. "Because people don't want to see their community change in such a grand way without them actually getting support for it." 40-year-old Lauren Johnson, who stood outside Edgewood Middle School with signs urging people to vote for the ban, said she wants Trenton to remain "a quality place for kids to grow up." "I think our farmland is very important and our greenspace," Johnson said. "I'd like to see it still around for my grandkids." 'We need the data centers' But other residents worry a ban would hurt Trenton economically. "I think we need the data centers," said Daniel Davis, 76. Davis thinks data centers will bring in more jobs and revenue for the city. Two advocates for the Trenton Community Alliance, who sat in lawn chairs outside Edgewood Middle School with signs encouraging people to vote "no," declined to share their names or be photographed. They alleged they've been harassed and that those who disagree with them have been "nasty." One advocate said that data centers are coming to the area, whether people like it or not. "I believe Trenton should get income from the data center, not someone else," she said. The other advocate said she's not for or against data centers, but she's against the Trenton charter changing in a way that could stifle future business. She's also concerned that residents might next try to recall members of the Trenton City Council. Future of Amazon data center in SW Ohio The vote Nov. 3 creates an uncertain future for an Amazon Web Services data center planned for land located just outside Trenton. The city tried to annex land for the project from its two neighboring rural townships, but withdrew its petition in September. Because the ban only applies to land within city limits, the data center could move forward on the land if it remains part of the rural townships. However, the St. Clair Township Zoning Commission passed a resolution Oct. 13 to ban data centers in the township's zoning. That resolution goes to a Butler County hearing Nov. 10 but indicates the AWS data center could face another hurdle. artigo.texto: Anatel aprova destinação de R$ 1,65 bi do leilão 5G a data center e TV 3.0 Conselho referenda projetos do Gaispi para infraestrutura soberana operada pela Telebras e distribuição de conversores a 910 mil famílias do Bolsa Família. O Conselho Diretor da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) referendou nesta quarta-feira, 4, duas propostas do Grupo de Acompanhamento da Implantação das Soluções para os Problemas de Interferência na faixa de 3,5 GHz (Gaispi) que destinam aproximadamente R$ 1,65 bilhão em recursos remanescentes do leilão do 5G à implantação de um data center soberano voltado à inteligência artificial e à distribuição de conversores de TV 3.0 para famílias de baixa renda. Os projetos contemplam R$ 375 milhões para a infraestrutura computacional, que será operada pela Telebras, e R$ 1,28 bilhão para a aquisição e distribuição de equipamentos destinados a cerca de 910 mil famílias inscritas no Bolsa Família. A soma dos valores previstos alcança R$ 1,655 bilhão, montante que a Anatel também apresenta, de forma arredondada, como R$ 1,7 bilhão. Segundo o conselheiro Edson Holanda, presidente do Gaispi, a destinação dos recursos foi definida sem comprometer os investimentos necessários ao cumprimento das obrigações originalmente estabelecidas no edital do leilão do 5G. “Liberamos cerca de R$ 1,7 bilhão das sobras do leilão do 5G para dois projetos, mantendo a obrigação do edital original. Fizemos isso com uma garantia que considero inegociável: a reserva integral do que falta para concluir os projetos originais, acrescida de margem de segurança. Nenhuma obrigação do Edital é tocada”, afirmou. Data center soberano terá operação da Telebras O projeto de infraestrutura computacional prevê investimento de R$ 375 milhões na implantação de um data center soberano destinado ao processamento de dados e aplicações de inteligência artificial do governo federal. A instalação será construída em um terreno de 5 mil metros quadrados, sob titularidade da União, e terá sua operação a cargo da Telebras. O empreendimento também será integrado à Rede Privativa da Administração Pública Federal, projeto de infraestrutura de telecomunicações voltado ao atendimento de órgãos federais. Entre as características técnicas previstas estão um módulo de processamento de inteligência artificial com refrigeração líquida, servidores de alta capacidade e sistemas redundantes de alimentação elétrica. A refrigeração líquida integra a arquitetura planejada para o módulo de IA, enquanto a redundância de alimentação está prevista para a infraestrutura energética do empreendimento. Durante a reunião do Conselho Diretor, Holanda relacionou a iniciativa à necessidade de ampliar a infraestrutura pública destinada à inteligência artificial e à discussão sobre soberania digital. “Em um momento em que a soberania digital deixou de ser tema de especialistas para se tornar questão de segurança nacional, este projeto coloca a infraestrutura onde ela precisa estar”, declarou o conselheiro. As informações divulgadas não especificam a localização do terreno, a capacidade de processamento dos servidores, a potência elétrica prevista ou o cronograma de entrada em operação. TV 3.0 prevê conversores para 910 mil famílias A maior parcela dos recursos, de R$ 1,28 bilhão, será destinada ao projeto de distribuição de conversores para recepção da TV 3.0. A iniciativa prevê atender aproximadamente 910 mil famílias inscritas no Bolsa Família, localizadas nos estados de São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro e no Distrito Federal. O planejamento contempla um período de 24 meses e inclui tanto os equipamentos quanto a logística necessária para sua distribuição aos beneficiários. Segundo as informações apresentadas pelo Gaispi, o projeto abrangerá conversores baseados no sistema Android ou no Android Open Source Project (AOSP), projeto de código aberto utilizado como base para diferentes implementações do sistema operacional. A distribuição pretende permitir que famílias de baixa renda tenham acesso aos recursos da nova geração de televisão aberta sem depender da aquisição de um televisor compatível com a tecnologia. Holanda afirmou que o projeto busca evitar que a implantação da TV 3.0 restrinja o acesso às novas funcionalidades aos consumidores com capacidade de adquirir equipamentos. “A TV 3.0 é a maior transformação da televisão aberta desde a digitalização. Sem este projeto, a transição tecnológica criaria uma nova exclusão, quem pode comprar o aparelho novo entra na nova era e quem não pode, fica para trás. Este Conselho decidiu que ninguém fica para trás por falta de um conversor”, afirmou. Recursos preservam obrigações originais do 5G A destinação dos recursos remanescentes foi condicionada à preservação dos valores necessários à conclusão dos projetos originalmente previstos no edital do leilão do 5G. Segundo Holanda, a reserva inclui uma margem adicional de segurança financeira, destinada a resguardar o cumprimento dos compromissos existentes. Os dois novos projetos seguirão mecanismos de governança utilizados no acompanhamento das iniciativas vinculadas ao leilão, com execução em etapas, reserva prudencial de recursos e fiscalização permanente pelo Gaispi. O conselheiro também relacionou esse modelo à experiência anterior do Grupo de Acompanhamento da Implantação das Soluções para os Problemas de Interferência (Gired). A aprovação pelo Conselho Diretor autoriza o encaminhamento das iniciativas no âmbito da estrutura de governança responsável pelos recursos remanescentes. As próximas etapas incluem a definição e a execução dos procedimentos necessários à implantação do data center e à aquisição e distribuição dos conversores, conforme os projetos referendados.

artigo.texto: Alliant Energy will receive more than $5 billion in federal loans to help the company modernize and build natural gas and energy storage infrastructure. But environmental groups argue the investment’s emphasis on fossil fuel infrastructure will make it harder to reduce emissions and address climate change. U.S. Department of Energy officials announced the low-interest financing last week at an Alliant Energy natural gas plant in Beloit. Federal officials say the funding will help the utility expand power generation, strengthen electric grid reliability and lower costs in Wisconsin and Iowa. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. The Energy Department said the $5.1 billion loan package will help Alliant add more than 2.6 gigawatts of new or upgraded electricity generation capacity. The agency says those projects could add enough electricity to power almost 2 million homes. It comes as peak energy demand in Wisconsin is projected to increase 40 percent by 2032, driven by data centers. One of the three large data center projects under construction in the state is being built in Beaver Dam, inside Alliant’s service territory, by social media giant Meta. Alliant Energy CEO Lisa Barton said the new loans would help the company lower construction costs, which could save customers $1.2 billion over their lifespan. “We’re going to be using these dollars to support upgrades, to invest in new generation facilities, new technologies and so forth,” Barton said in Beloit. “Every dollar that we invest is going to enhance our reliability, our system resiliency and help to drive affordability and economic development in the areas and the communities that we have to serve.” The projects funded by the loan package could also create more than 1,600 jobs during construction, according to the company. With the federal financing, Alliant says the company can pursue 1.6 gigawatts of new natural gas generation, 240 megawatts of increased capacity at existing facilities, 1 gigawatt of energy storage and 2 billion cubic feet of liquefied natural gas storage. The company did not identify any specific projects in the announcement. Gregory Beard, director of the Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing, said the loan package was “common sense” because it supported new electricity generation, storage and expanded liquefied gas storage. “We’re proud to be here to partner with Alliant,” he said. “We’ll be proud to see the projects that come online with all these $5.1 billion of invested capital.” But Jadine Sonoda, campaign coordinator for the environmental nonprofit Sierra Club’s Wisconsin Chapter, said her organization was disappointed to see such a large investment in fossil fuels, though they were grateful for the support for energy storage. She said the investment represents “a massive amount” of new natural gas generation potentially coming onto the grid. “Continual investment in more fossil fuels means more pollution. It means more health impacts and all of the costs that come with it,” Sonoda said. “We are already seeing so many new gas plant proposals. We absolutely do not need more incentives from the Trump administration to expand these options.” Reuters reports that the loan had been initially proposed by the Biden administration as a $3 billion conditional loan tied to clean energy and batteries. But Sonoda said the funding is a “really blatant example” of the Trump administration’s efforts to prop up the data center and fossil fuel industries. “Our electric sector landscape is heavily fossil fuels already. We really need to correct that and turn in the other direction,” she said. “All of these efforts to subsidize and support big tech and the fossil fuel industry are leading us in the completely wrong direction.” Wisconsin Public Radio, © Copyright 2026, Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin System and Wisconsin Educational Communications Board.

artigo.texto: The election of a new Texas governor could have major ramifications for the construction of massive AI data centers in North Texas, and also for the nation. Analysts say new state rules on how or where data centers can be built appear to be on the way under a new administration, but some believe Texas will still become the largest data center market in the country, with Dallas-Fort Worth at the center of that growth. Watch NBC 5 free wherever you are During her campaign, Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa called for a moratorium on data center construction until the Texas Legislature could meet next year and pass laws giving local communities more control over construction. The question now is whether that could mean a temporary halt to construction next year, how long that pause might last, and whether it might cause some data center companies to see Texas as a short-term risk. "I think that a moratorium or the threat of a moratorium is enough to get the developers to consider other states. They are in a race and they want speed to power and one of the reasons why they like Texas is because they can move quickly here," said Michael Webber, an energy policy researcher who studies the data center market at the University of Texas at Austin. Webber said a short pause in development could help communities, companies and lawmakers find common ground. But he worries a longer halt could hurt the nation's ability to compete with China in the race to develop artificial intelligence, with Texas slated as the top state for future data center construction. Local The latest news from around North Texas. "That's the concern I have. And that's why I think it's important not to just have a moratorium, but instead to have a conversation and a negotiation," Webber said. Webber expects the Texas data center market to slow in the short term as new rules are considered, then accelerate again. "So I think we'll still become number one, we tend to do that. We're number on in wind, we're number in batteries, we're in solar, we'll probably be number one in data centers. These things all go hand in hand," Webber said. Researcher Mohammed Islam, who studies the impact of data centers at UT Arlington told NBC 5 Investigates he believes many data center operators will be eager to collaborate with regulators to develop and comply with new regulations to ensure that projects remain on track. Islam is also an advisor to the City of Fort Worth's Data Center Commission. "I believe if everyone works together, we'll be able to clarify these things, really understand what are the impacts," Islam said. In a statement to NBC 5, the Data Center Coalition, which represents the data center industry, said, "DCC looks forward to working with state leadership along with local officials, stakeholders, and Texas communities to continue building trust and supporting responsible data center growth," said Jess Heck, Texas Director of Government Affairs with the Data Center Coalition. Even before Tuesday's election, Gov. Greg Abbott had paused state permits for new data centers to give state agencies time to audit projects in the pipeline and analyze impacts on the electric grid. But many analysts expected the permitting process could begin moving again once that review was completed in December. Now, with a new governor set to take office a month later, there are new questions about what will happen in January and beyond.

artigo.texto: OpenAI issues new data center policies after midterm elections Many Democrats criticized AI data centers on the campaign trail. OpenAI issued a new set of data center policies on Thursday, just days after a midterm election landslide for Democrats, many of whom voiced concern about potential negative impact from the facilities. The ChatGPT-maker said it would abide by fresh commitments, including a vow to pay for all electricity and infrastructure used at its facilities. It will create a "water plan" for each location as part of an effort to "protect local resources," the artificial intelligence company said. Meanwhile, the practice of establishing non-disclosure agreements with public officials will largely end, OpenAI said, except for a narrow set of exceptions focused on security or trade secrets. Each data center will form a "local compact" with the nearby community to address issues specific in a given area and improve transparency, according to the company. OpenAI also committed to provide "sustainable investments" in support of neighboring communities, such as funding for free school lunches or improved childcare offerings. To help local residents secure jobs generated by its data center projects, OpenAI will work with training providers in the area, the company said. "Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people's hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology," OpenAI said in a blog post. "The communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too." The company also urged policymakers at the state, local and federal level to "establish clear rules for how the industry builds." "New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies," OpenAI added. The announcement came after a Democratic landslide in the midterm elections on Tuesday catapulted the party's Senate and gubernatorial candidates to statewide victories in Republican strongholds like Ohio and Texas, both of which play host to a number of AI data centers. About 6 in 10 House voters nationally said AI is a bad thing for society and about three-quarters oppose the construction of new data centers in their communities, according to the ABC News Voter Poll. A joint data center project between OpenAI and Oracle in Saline, Michigan, for instance, drew backlash from some local residents concerned about impact on the area's power grid and water supply, Reuters reported in July. In a statement about the project in June, OpenAI said: "From the beginning, our goal has been to build infrastructure in a way that does right by the people and communities helping make it possible." Oracle expressed a similar sentiment about the project in September. "We know a project of this scale comes with responsibilities. We are committed to meeting them by protecting local natural resources, paying our own way for the energy infrastructure required to serve the campus, and investing in the community where we will operate for decades," the company said in a statement. Ahead of the midterms, President Donald Trump stressed his strong support for them, saying they could help enrich communities and assist in the United States' effort to defeat China in the global AI race. Many candidates, mostly Democrats, criticized the data centers, citing potential strain on local water systems and high residential utility bills as a result of increased demand, among other concerns. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinajosa, a Democratic state representative, made opposition to data center construction a central part of her race against incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. Hinojosa, who won by 7 percentage points, told ABC News last month she supports a moratorium on new construction, stricter regulations on water and power usage and an end to tax breaks. She has criticized Abbott for signing tax breaks for data centers and promoting the industry's growth. Texas hasn't elected a Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1990. ABC News' Emily Guskin and Diana Paulsen contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: A comprehensive review published in Frontiers in Carbon evaluates the use of olive pomace, an abundant and chemically versatile agro-industrial lignocellulosic residue, as a sustainable feedstock for electrochemical energy-storage materials. The assessment examines how valorizing this agricultural waste can simultaneously address waste management, support resource recovery, and provide sustainable electrodes for advanced energy technologies. Focus is placed on establishing the fundamental relationships connecting feedstock composition and synthesis strategies with resultant structural properties, surface chemistry, and ultimate electrochemical performance. The review analyzes the primary thermal and chemical conversion routes used to process olive pomace into functional carbons, specifically detailing pyrolysis, hydrothermal carbonization, physical activation, and chemical activation. In particular, chemical activation routes employing activating agents such as potassium hydroxide, zinc chloride, phosphoric acid, and potassium carbonate are evaluated for their specific influences on material characteristics. The authors trace how these distinct synthesis pathways govern porosity development, structural ordering, heteroatom functionality, and overall electrical conductivity in the final carbon products. Different electrochemical applications impose distinct material requirements, which the review categorizes across electric double-layer capacitors, pseudocapacitive and hybrid systems, and battery anodes for lithium-ion and sodium-ion devices. The synthesis indicates that chemical activation methods generate highly porous carbons possessing competitive capacitance well-suited for capacitive mechanisms. In contrast, high-temperature carbonization routes favor the development of turbostratic hard-carbon structures, which provide the structural framework required for sodium storage in sodium-ion battery anodes. A key analytical finding of the review is that high specific surface area alone does not serve as a reliable predictor of electrochemical performance. Instead, practical energy storage depends on an interconnected network of factors, including pore accessibility, pore-size distribution, surface chemistry, electrical conductivity, electrolyte composition, and electrode architecture. Furthermore, a comparative benchmarking of reported olive-pomace materials highlighted substantial discrepancies in testing conditions across existing studies, complicating direct performance evaluations. Finally, the authors outline major technical and economic hurdles facing the field, including feedstock variability, process optimization, high chemical and energy consumption, scalability, techno-economic feasibility, and broader life-cycle impacts. To advance beyond material-level optimization, future research must prioritize reproducible synthesis, processing methods that tolerate feedstock variability, green activation strategies, rational heteroatom engineering, and integrated biorefinery approaches. The review concludes that olive pomace offers a promising platform for sustainable energy storage only if its environmental, economic, and electrochemical benefits are demonstrated at realistic device and process scales. artigo.texto: Bow residents are requesting a town-wide vote on an ordinance that would pause data center permitting and construction for at least a year, halting a plan to convert the closed Merrimack Station power plant into a server hub. Protect New Hampshire from Data Centers, a new advocacy group, said that over 800 Bow voters signed a petition in support of the vote, which the organization delivered to the town’s planning board on Thursday. “If we don’t have a moratorium, aren’t we more susceptible to being approached by a data center?” Bow resident Sue Moore said to the planning board. Speakers argued the one-year pause would provide much-needed time for further study, citing potentially adverse health effects on humans and animals, the impacts of noise and damage to the environment. After a discussion between planning board members and public commenters, the board unanimously voted to discuss and refine the ordinance put forward in the petition, and open the measure for a public hearing at the board’s Dec. 3 meeting. Protect New Hampshire’s action comes on the tail-end of residents’ September protests against a potential data center in town. In September, Granite Shore Power, which owns the shuttered Merrimack Station, filed a request with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to discuss connecting a 350-megawatt project to the regional power grid. While no developer has submitted a formal application to the planning board, Bow residents stressed the need to be proactive in shielding their community from possible harm. Kip McDaniel, chair of the Bow Board of Selectmen and planning board member, reasoned that if one town institutes a moratorium and another allows data center development, some might take advantage of the additional tax revenue, while passing off the “negative externalities” to neighboring municipalities. “It should come at the state level, so every town is on the equal playing field, and you’re not pitting town against town trying to entice development,” McDaniel said. Despite the chance of uneven enforcement, residents expressed satisfaction that their petition will move through the town government process. “They were very gracious in listening to us,” Moore said in an interview. “It’s small town Bow. You know, these are our neighbors,” added Barbara Bennett, another Bow resident. “When we were collecting signatures, you would see your neighbors coming up in the voting line, so obviously we’re friends with each other. That makes it a little easier.” The dueling desires to boost the town’s tax base and keep out a certain type of development may prove contentious. “I think they were aware that there’s a lot of tension about the possibility of having that data center,” said Bow resident Joanne Jenks. “People are very unhappy about that.”

artigo.texto: Democrats win Georgia utility board seats after data center backlash ATLANTA - Georgia voters ended a three-decade Republican majority on the state’s Public Service Commission on Tuesday, electing two Democrats who campaigned on capping Georgia Power rate hikes and curbing data center expansion. Georgia power regulatory shift The backstory: Democrats have captured control of the regulatory panel deciding customer electric rates across Georgia for the first time in 30 years. Kristin Phillips, an associate professor and anthropologist at Emory University, noted that the Tuesday election breaks a multi-decade streak. "We have not had a Democratic majority on the Public Service Commission in the last 30 years," Phillips said. Election outcome oversight goals What they're saying: Democratic challengers Peter Hubbard and Sheila Edwards defeated their Republican opponents after campaigning for tighter limits on energy infrastructure. Phillips said the outcome signals "much more regulation and oversight of Georgia powers." Edwards also endorsed a data center construction freeze championed by Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms. "We need to pause," Bottoms said. "We need consumers like you. We need experts in this field to sit around the table." Rising electric bills tension Local perspective: Neighborhood battles over high-voltage facilities have erupted statewide as residents express frustration over climbing electric bills. One resident who spoke out said, "I’ve lived here for 25 years. I love this town." Phillips explained that residents now question the true value of tech developments, adding, "Georgians are beginning to question whether data centers bring the kind of economic growth that they want." Tech oversight energy debate The other side: Advocates for stricter utility rules contend residential customers shoulder an unfair financial burden caused by electricity-hungry facilities. "We're paying higher rates at home because these data centers are gobbling up more and more energy," said Sacha Haworth, founder of The Tech Oversight Project. Haworth added that Thursday's stock market decline caused by artificial intelligence oversight concerns should not deter policy changes. "It is going to correct itself," Haworth said. "I think we have to let those concerns play out." Legislative calendar power transition What's next: Commission structural shifts will take significant time before translating into household billing adjustments. "I do anticipate that we will see some very different, a different style of regulation and decision-making on the commission, but some of those effects won't actually go into place for, for a number of years," Phillips said. The newly elected commissioners take their oaths of office on Jan. 1, 2027, while the Georgia legislative session begins addressing data center policies on Jan. 11, 2027. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from FOX 5 Atlanta reporter Rob DiRienzo, who covered the election results and spoke with an Emory University energy expert and a tech oversight advocate, as well as candidate statements.

artigo.texto: A Anatel alertou o governo federal que pode ficar sem dinheiro até o fim de 2026 para pagar suas próprias contas, incluindo as do data center que mantém em Brasília. A agência reguladora tem R$ 30,76 milhões em faturas pendentes. A Anatel atribui o aperto a um bloqueio orçamentário de R$ 51,83 milhões. A medida foi determinada pelo governo Lula em maio. O presidente da agência, Carlos Baigorri, pediu ao Ministério do Planejamento o desbloqueio de R$ 30 milhões. Sem o desbloqueio, a Anatel corre risco de não fechar as contas do ano. Por que a Anatel ficou sem caixa O aperto nas contas da Anatel vem do contingenciamento geral do Orçamento, usado pelo governo para cumprir a meta fiscal. A agência arca com despesas fixas, como o data center, mesmo com parte do orçamento bloqueada. Em outubro, mesmo sob aperto, a Anatel liberou espectro para a Starlink. O atrito com o governo não é novo: em setembro, a Anatel abriu uma consulta sobre o leilão do 6G sem aval prévio do Planalto. Publicidade A próxima avaliação dos bloqueios está marcada para 24 de novembro. Nessa data, a Junta de Execução Orçamentária deve reexaminar o espaço fiscal para possível redução do contingenciamento. No mesmo dia do alerta sobre o data center, dois deputados apresentaram um projeto para suspender parte da regra da Anatel que torna obrigatória a biometria facial para contratar linha de celular. O PDL 1027/2026 ainda precisa ser votado pela Câmara. O que acontece agora A Anatel aguarda a resposta do Ministério do Planejamento sobre o desbloqueio dos R$ 30 milhões, antes da reavaliação de 24 de novembro.

artigo.texto: As home batteries move from simple wall hardware to fully connected, intelligent energy assets, the partnership will focus on bringing cutting-edge battery innovations directly to everyday households. The partnership brings together two industry heavyweights: CATL and Ampace’s experience in battery chemistry and manufacturing, alongside Octopus Energy’s software platform, smart tariffs, and Virtual Power Plant flexibility capabilities. The collaboration will draw on CATL and Ampace's pioneering research into next-generation battery chemistries – including breakthrough developments in sodium-ion technology, high-density cell designs, and ultra-long lifecycle systems – to build safer, greener, and far more affordable home batteries. Paired with Octopus’s smart tech ecosystem, these systems will automatically charge up when energy is cleanest and cheapest and share power back to the grid during peak times to slash household bills. The collaboration will initially explore opportunities across European markets, where Octopus has retail energy offices. “Combining CATL and Ampace's world-leading battery chemistry with Octopus's smart tech and customer platform will transform home energy storage” said Greg Jackson, Founder and CEO, Octopus Energy Group. “Together, we're building next-generation batteries where hardware and software work in complete harmony to slash energy bills and speed up the green energy transition.” The MoU builds on the relationship between CATL and Octopus, who previously collaborated to roll out 'Swaptopus' battery swapping stations across Europe, demonstrating the strength of their ongoing technical and operational partnership. The partnership improves on Octopus existing suite of offerings in low carbon technology, which currently includes the Octopus Cosy heat pump range, Octopus Charge EV charger range, and Octopus Nook home battery range. Ampace’s battery chemistry technology combined with Octopus’ software will help make existing residential home energy batteries cheaper and better. “The future of energy is not just about generating or storing more power, but about making energy smarter, more connected, and more accessible” added Jason Zhu, President of Energy Storage Systems, Ampace. “We believe the convergence of advanced battery technologies, intelligent energy management, and innovative energy services will fundamentally reshape how energy is delivered and consumed. Through this strategic collaboration with CATL and Octopus Energy, we aim to accelerate this transformation, unlock new possibilities for the global energy ecosystem, and contribute to a more resilient and sustainable energy future.” For additional information:

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The U.S. Department of Energy is launching a new initiative to speed development and deployment of advanced battery technologies, DOE Assistant Secretary Audrey Robertson told Utility Dive. - The Battery Manufacturing Accelerator, or BattMan, aims to strengthen domestic supply chains for battery materials and components, reduce manufacturing costs and shorten commercialization timelines, the department said on Wednesday. - U.S. demand for batteries across transportation and grid management applications is expected to increase from 179 GWh in 2025 to 707 GWh in 2035, according to a June analysis from Bloomberg NEF that DOE cited in a white paper published last month. Dive Insight: A secure, scaled-up domestic battery supply chain is critical for U.S. economic growth and security in the years ahead, DOE said in the white paper, “A National Strategy for American Leadership in Batteries.” For utilities, batteries are increasingly indispensable for improving grid reliability and shifting load, particularly in regions where data center loads threaten to disrupt power flows, DOE said in the paper. Data centers themselves could account for one-quarter of total U.S. battery demand by 2030, according to a Benchmark Mineral Intelligence forecast cited in the paper. The U.S. today is heavily dependent on external trade partners — particularly China — for battery materials and components, which “poses substantial supply chain risks,” DOE said in the paper. Recent investments in U.S. battery cell and pack manufacturing have not been matched by investments in U.S. production of precursor components, creating gaps in the supply chain, DOE said. “We have substantial work to do to secure the materials and manufacturing capabilities [lithium-ion batteries] require,” Robertson said in an email. “China currently controls between 60% and 100% of global production capacity across several critical stages of battery materials and component manufacturing … [which] represents a serious vulnerability for American industry and national security.” China and other Asian countries host nearly all global lithium-ion battery cathode, anode and separator manufacturing and nearly 93% of electrolyte manufacturing, DOE said in 2024. Robertson said the BattMan consortium, which has support from DOE’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, would expand the Trump administration’s efforts to boost domestic sources of battery materials and components. The Pacific Northwest National Laboratory leads the consortium, with participation from Argonne National Laboratory, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the National Laboratory of the Rockies, formerly known as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. BattMan’s research university partners include the University of Alabama, Arizona State University, Binghamton University, the University of Michigan–Dearborn and the University of Washington. DOE says the consortium will advance three strategic objectives: establish a “mine-to-market” domestic supply chain by 2030; develop new battery technologies that are “more affordable, longer lasting, higher performing, and less reliant on critical minerals;” and scale deployment of advanced battery technologies in sectors critical to national security. “We’re excited about technologies that use more abundant domestic materials, reduce dependence on foreign supply chains, and can be manufactured competitively here in the United States,” Robertson said in an email. In August, DOE announced $500 million in funding for seven projects to expand U.S. critical minerals and materials processing, battery manufacturing and recycling projects. Award recipients include a California-based company expanding lithium-ion battery anode manufacturing with U.S.-sourced materials and another firm piloting battery production using ultra‑thin lithium‑metal films and “prelithiated” material. The latter “could enable higher-energy, faster-charging batteries,” Robertson said. According to PNNL, BattMan will work to overcome barriers that have kept promising, U.S.-developed energy storage technologies like these from reaching commercial scale. The consortium will use a “cost-focused” research and development strategy that “[takes] performance, manufacturability and scalability into account up front;” broaden innovation beyond lithium-ion technologies using “platform technologies that are applicable to all energy storage chemistries;” modernize energy storage manufacturing using digital twins and other AI-enabled tools; and develop reliable, data-driven frameworks for validating emerging energy storage technologies, PNNL said.

artigo.texto: SMM, November 4: Entering Q4, the sodium-ion battery industry chain has reached the most critical delivery verification period of the year. SMM data shows that in October, sodium-ion battery cathode material production increased 3% MoM and surged 260% YoY, while hard carbon anode production pulled back slightly by 4% MoM but surged 186% YoY—the high YoY growth confirms the industry is still on a zero-to-one volume ramp-up trajectory, but the mediocre MoM performance reveals another reality: capacity ramp-up pace is generally slower than market expectations, with a clear time lag between order growth and actual delivery. On the price side, cathode NFPP quotes are diverging, precursors are hovering near the cost line, and iron phosphate supply-demand tension remains elevated—the two-way squeeze of cost and order losses is reshaping the industry's competitive landscape. 1. Cathode materials: production up 3% MoM, capacity release below expectations, orders accelerating toward top-tier players 1. Supply side: ramp-up hindered, delivery capacity supplemented by "outsourcing + toll processing" In October, sodium-ion battery cathode material production increased 3% MoM and surged 260% YoY. The overall market operated steadily, but capacity release falling short of expectations was the most prominent contradiction this month. Although 10 kt-scale new lines gradually entered commissioning, compounded by line switchovers and equipment changes, actual output still failed to meet the original ramp-up targets; some enterprises boosted delivery capacity through outsourced processing, and once downstream processes are fully connected after mid-November, monthly capacity is expected to reach the kt level. 2. Demand side: clear divergence, growth concentrated in small power and energy storage The demand side showed significant divergence: in October, some enterprises shipped only a few hundred mt, while November orders have grown to several hundred mt and will be delivered in batches, with growth mainly from small power and some energy storage orders. However, it is worth noting that if lithium carbonate prices continue to weaken, December market conditions may fall short of November—some clients' new orders are already showing loss inversion, and downstream willingness to take orders has clearly declined. From the perspective of enterprise operations, the trend of orders concentrating toward top-tier players is increasingly evident: industry top-tier players already have orders on hand exceeding 1 kt, while their own monthly capacity is only a few hundred mt and cannot fully cover demand, requiring a dual-line approach of "in-house lines + toll processing" to ensure delivery. 3. Price side: NFPP quotes diverging, cost pressure focused on iron phosphate In October, NFPP quotes remained relatively stable, with mainstream transactions concentrated at 24,000-27,000 yuan/mt. In the short term, there is clearly no room for price increases, nor room for cuts—prices have entered a stalemate range. Cost side pressure remains concentrated in the iron phosphate segment. Although phosphoric acid prices have pulled back from 12,000 yuan/mt to around 9,000 yuan/mt, iron phosphate prices remain at around 16,000 yuan/mt due to tight supply-demand conditions, significantly above the reasonable range of 12,000-13,000 yuan/mt. The persistently high raw material costs are driving downstream material enterprises to accelerate the construction of their own iron phosphate production lines or form joint ventures with phosphorus chemical enterprises, advancing industry chain integration. In the precursor segment, mainstream transaction prices are 19,000-20,000 yuan/mt, with large orders as low as 17,000-18,000 yuan/mt, already basically approaching the cost line. Enterprises generally adopt tiered pricing to lock in major clients. 4. Competitive Landscape: Accelerating Tier Differentiation From the competitive landscape perspective, tier differentiation in the industry is accelerating. Top-tier cathode enterprises with planned capacity of 10 kt-level projects are successively coming online, steadily expanding their leading edge. Small and medium-sized startups are under pressure due to tightening financing environments and lagging production line construction, with some enterprises still showing a gap between publicly claimed capacity and actual production. Another noteworthy signal is that NFPP precursor enterprises generally have low willingness to cross over into cathode production, mainly due to concerns about direct competition with downstream clients—this objectively maintains the competitive boundaries of the existing cathode segment. Looking ahead, Q4 cathode shipments may show a "high first, low later" trend, with prices remaining weak under the dual squeeze of cost support and order losses. Top-tier players with scale capacity, integrated costs, and quality client structures will be the first to benefit, with industry consolidation and concentration expected to accelerate. November sodium-ion battery cathode production is expected to increase 9% MoM and surge 162% YoY. II. Hard Carbon Anode: Production Edges Down 4% MoM, Commissioning Window Determines Year-End Output, Stockpiling Willingness Rising 1. Supply Side: Orders at Hundreds of mt Level, Deliveries Yet to Scale Up In October, the hard carbon anode material market operated steadily overall, with production edging down 4% from September and surging 186% YoY. Although most enterprises received orders at the hundreds of mt level in October, actual deliveries have yet to scale up due to capacity constraints—"orders without goods" is the current reality of this segment. 2. Enterprise Operations: October-November Is the Critical Window Before Ramp-Up, Inventory Strategies Diverge From enterprise operations, industry capacity had not yet completed expansion in H1, and new self-owned production lines entered a concentrated commissioning period in H2. artigo.texto: Energy Management Software Can Improve Battery Storage Economics: Interview Kosol Energie expects rapid growth in battery storage adoption in India November 5, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights India’s growing renewable energy capacity is creating opportunities for battery energy storage systems (BESS), particularly as developers and consumers seek to manage intermittent generation, reduce electricity costs, and meet peak-hour demand. However, the economic viability of storage depends on how effectively it integrates with renewable energy systems and how intelligently it is managed through software, according to Kayan Kalthia, Executive Director, Business Development, Kosol Energie. In an interview with Mercom India on the sidelines of the recently concluded Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo 2026, Kalthia said BESS should no longer be viewed merely as a backup power solution. Instead, it should be treated as an energy-management asset that can optimize electricity consumption, enable energy arbitrage, and improve returns on renewable energy investments. What are Kosol Energie’s plans for the Indian battery energy storage market? We have introduced KoBESS, our new vertical dedicated to battery energy storage solutions. While BESS may be relatively new to our Indian operations, we have been working in this segment in the U.S. market since 2015. We entered the Indian BESS market around November 2025. We have worked extensively to develop solutions for residential, commercial and industrial (C&I), and utility-scale applications. We recognized early that battery storage would become increasingly important for India as the country expands its renewable energy capacity. Renewable energy is becoming central to the country’s energy mix. As renewable penetration increases, storage will be essential to manage generation variability, reduce curtailment, and shift electricity to periods of higher demand. How do you assess the commercial viability of BESS for C&I consumers? Consumers should not view BESS merely as a backup power solution. Storage becomes economically attractive when it is integrated into the overall electricity consumption and renewable energy management strategy. For example, a battery can be charged using electricity generated by an on-site solar system or power purchased from the grid when market prices are low. The stored electricity can then be used during periods when electricity prices are higher. This creates opportunities for energy arbitrage and lets consumers optimize electricity procurement costs. Our calculations indicate that properly optimized storage systems can achieve investment payback periods of approximately three to three-and-a-half years. This makes storage attractive not only for C&I consumers but potentially for residential customers as well. How can energy management software improve the economics of battery storage? The decision-making process for electricity consumption and storage should be data-driven, not reliant on manual intervention. Our energy management system acts as the brain of the battery storage installation and the consumer’s overall electricity management system. It evaluates whether to purchase electricity from the market, consume it directly from solar generation, or store it in the battery for later use. For example, if the system anticipates lower solar generation over the next few days because of unfavorable weather conditions, it can prioritize charging the battery when electricity is available at lower prices. Similarly, it can decide whether buying electricity from the market is more economical than using stored energy. If a consumer installs a conventional solar-plus-storage system without intelligent energy management, the investment payback period could extend to six or seven years. However, integrating software that continuously optimizes electricity procurement and storage operations can significantly improve the economics. We also structure our software pricing around customer savings, receiving a small percentage of the savings the system generates. What is your outlook for battery storage adoption in India over the next two to three years? I expect the Indian battery storage market to grow rapidly, similar to the solar industry’s initial expansion. However, the storage industry will also see greater accountability among manufacturers and solution providers. Unlike some other renewable energy equipment, where performance issues may take longer to become apparent, battery performance and reliability problems can emerge within one or two years. As a result, manufacturers offering poor-quality products or inadequate technical support will struggle to sustain their market position. Companies that focus on product quality, reliability, and long-term customer performance will be better positioned to benefit from the industry’s growth. Do you see transmission infrastructure becoming a major challenge for India’s renewable energy expansion? Transmission infrastructure will remain a significant challenge as renewable energy installations continue to increase. The electricity system requires additional substations, greater connectivity, and upgrades to existing infrastructure to accommodate growing generation capacity. Building new substations and upgrading existing grid equipment require substantial investment. While expanding physical infrastructure is necessary, we should also focus on making the existing electricity network more intelligent. Smart grid technologies can manage electricity flows more efficiently, reduce renewable energy curtailment, and better utilize available infrastructure. This can provide a more practical near-term approach to addressing certain grid integration challenges while longer-term transmission expansion continues. artigo.texto: Aramex lança Data Center Logistics para entregas com prazos críticos A Aramex apresentou o Data Center Logistics, serviço voltado à gestão de entregas com prazos críticos para a construção e a operação de data centers, segundo o TradeArabia News Service. A provedora de logística informou que a oferta começa na região do Conselho de Cooperação do Golfo, no Sudeste Asiático, em Taiwan e no Sul dos EUA, abrangendo localidades como Abu Dhabi, Riad, Johor, Texas e Louisiana. A empresa afirmou que a carga destinada a data centers está entre as mais exigentes da logística. Transformadores e chillers podem levar um ano ou mais para ir do pedido ao canteiro e precisam chegar em linha com o cronograma da obra, enquanto cada rack de IA encaixotado pesa cerca de 1,75 tonelada métrica, tem valor de vários milhões de dólares, está sujeito a controles de exportação e pode sofrer danos em trânsito sem deixar marcas visíveis na caixa. A Aramex observou que essas entregas costumam ser divididas entre agentes de carga, despachantes aduaneiros, empresas de transporte pesado e instaladores distintos, sem que uma única parte responda por todo o trajeto. Segundo a empresa, um único embarque atrasado ou danificado pode adiar a data em que um data center entra em operação. O novo serviço foi concebido para assumir a responsabilidade por todo o trajeto. Na construção, abrange transformadores, painéis de manobra, geradores e chillers, incluindo cargas pesadas e fora de medida, acompanhados desde o pedido de compra e entregues em sintonia com o cronograma da obra. Para equipamentos de computação, cuida de racks de IA e equipamentos de rede vindos de fábricas em Taiwan, no Sudeste Asiático, no México, nos EUA e na Europa, por voo fretado ou transporte rodoviário seguro, com conformidade aduaneira e de controles de exportação. Dentro do data center, o serviço inclui manuseio white-glove na doca de carga, desembalagem e posicionamento no salão de dados. O suporte pós-venda cobre peças de reposição, substituições e devoluções depois que a instalação entra em operação. Cada rack de IA é movimentado sob um único processo documentado, com sensores lacrados dentro da caixa que monitoram choque, inclinação, temperatura e umidade desde a fábrica até a entrega assinada no data center. A Aramex afirmou que o serviço se apoia em mais de quatro décadas de experiência em agenciamento de cargas, desembaraço aduaneiro e logística de projetos. No CCG, a Aramex opera o que descreve como a maior rede logística da região, com mais de 7.000 pessoas e estações, armazéns, caminhões e equipes aduaneiras próprios em todos os mercados. Em Taiwan, na Malásia, em Singapura, nos EUA e na Europa, suas equipes trabalham diretamente com as fábricas que produzem os equipamentos, de modo que uma única empresa responde pela carga nas duas pontas do trajeto. O CEO do grupo, Amadou Diallo, disse que um data center é tão rápido quanto sua entrega mais lenta, observando que as empresas que constroem capacidade de IA trabalham com datas fixas e equipamentos fabricados em um continente e instalados em outro. Ele afirmou que transportar esse tipo de carga entre fronteiras no prazo e intacta é a razão de ser da Aramex, acrescentando que o Data Center Logistics aplica essa força a uma expansão exigente e representa um passo importante no crescimento da empresa como provedora de logística global.

artigo.texto: Boulder City voters reject ballot question easing path for data centers LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Boulder City voters overwhelmingly rejected a ballot question that could have made it easier to bring data centers to the city, with about 71 percent voting no and 29 percent voting yes according to the latest data. The question asked: “Should data center facilities be an approved land use within the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area outside of the Multi-species Habitat Conservation Easement?” Residents who opposed the measure said the vote was a major step, but not the end of the fight. “Forget about the environmental effects that we do not want, it just does not fit in a historic town like this,” said Branden Smith, a Boulder City resident. Smith and Brynn Delorimier, also a Boulder City resident, have been involved in efforts to stop two separate data center sites from being used. One site was blocked earlier this year after a City Council decision banning it from use. The second site, at the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area, was defeated by voters. “The revenue that it is supposed to generate is just not worth the return of the environmental effects that they deliver,” Smith said. Delorimier described how opposition to the project grew from grassroots organizing. “This is a small community. We stick together,” Delorimier said. “We started making signs. I made a template that I can use for spray paint, and somebody kindly offered to donate a bunch of blank yard signs. So we just started spray painting yard signs, all the same motif, some different color schemes, 550 of them all over Boulder City,” Delorimier said. Opponents said they are also watching another potential location. An additional site around Boulder City on Bureau of Land Management land could eventually be used for another data center project, and Smith said residents will continue working to block future attempts. “Even still, there are not a lot of people that understand that it is actually three distinctly different areas that are at play here,” Smith said. Delorimier said the group is not interested in negotiating. “Our answer to them, ‘what it would take?’, was a one state buffer. So I would say we are pretty uncompromising on that,” Delorimier said. Tara Bertoli, owner of the Boulder City Co. Store, said she voted against the measure in Tuesday night’s election and argued that data centers would strain local resources. Bertoli runs the Old Boulder City Company Store, which is on the National Register of Historic Places. “We do not need to deplete our energy or our resources to feed people’s pockets,” Bertoli said. “I am glad that our town is sticking together. We are a unique community in Nevada and we want to stay that way,” she said. Political strategist Tal Eslick said data center developers are struggling to make their case in small towns like Boulder City, citing concerns about disruptions to the local economy, health impacts and environmental issues. “If we cannot do it here, then where in the world do you think you are going to be able to do it?” Eslick said. He also criticized how developers have approached the issue. “If I am advising data centers, I am asking first; ‘If AI can help make a time machine because they are need to go back about two years and get to work. It appears that they have done nothing to help their cause. If you were designing a way that you can ensure that a data center never got built, then they are right on plan,’” Eslick said. Bertoli said she would continue opposing data centers if the issue returns to the ballot. “Absolutely. We know too much about the negative effect it would have on our community and on our resources in the state. We are doing fine without it. And we will continue to do just fine without it,” she said.

artigo.texto: The November 3 midterm results gave Democrats full control of Congress, setting the stage for what could be one of the most divided U.S. governments this decade, with Republicans in the White House. Tuesday’s results suggest that anger over data centers, the large facilities that house the computers powering AI, is becoming a political force. With Democrats now in control of Congress, that could lead to new limits on where data centers can be built and how much say local communities have. Data centers became a ballot-box issue in various states. An NBC exit poll showed how concerned voters are about AI: More than half of respondents believe that AI will do more harm than good, while almost 80% are against the building of data centers in their neighborhoods. Almost 60%, meanwhile, said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote. Nadine Smith, president and CEO of the racial justice organization Color of Change, called Tuesday’s election a referendum on “who this economy is built for.” “National security matters,” Smith said, referring to a common argument from data center supporters that the infrastructure is essential for the U.S. to stay ahead in war and in its rivalry with China. “And so do the families in South Memphis breathing exhaust from the gas turbines powering an AI supercomputer.” (She was referring to xAI’s data center in Memphis, Tennessee, which uses gas turbines for power.) Voters in several states pushed back against the AI buildout, even as pro-AI super PACs spent millions hoping to sway them this midterm. The anti-data center backlash was especially felt in states like Ohio, where OpenAI has eyed a $500 billion data center, backed by more than $100 billion in financing from Nvidia. In fact, the Ohio county where Meta had planned a 700,000-square-foot facility just passed a ban on data centers, and local communities across the state overwhelmingly voted against data center buildout measures. Analysts at Morgan Stanley predict that Democratic governor-elect Amy Acton will also pose a major risk to Ohio’s data center buildout. Elsewhere, candidates in Texas, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Georgia, and South Carolina all won seats after taking a stance against the rapid buildout of data centers. “It is clear that money does not buy outcomes,” said Anshi Bhatt, a tech and policy researcher, adding that in modern politics, creating a “local villain” is one way to build campaign momentum. Likely next steps include more construction moratoriums or requiring data centers to pay for their own power grid upgrades instead of passing those costs on to nearby communities. Goldman Sachs, in fact, predicts data center construction delays in states like Georgia and Texas because of Democratic gains. Democratic control of Congress could also improve the odds for bills like the one Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced earlier this year, though any such bill would also face a possible veto. It proposes a nationwide moratorium on new data centers until Congress adds new guardrails and ensures that the buildout does not raise electricity costs, harm the environment, or proceed without community approval. There are also bills like the GRID Savings Act, proposed by New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, which would prevent grid infrastructure costs from being passed on to communities during large AI data center buildouts. The environment is also a major concern, especially at xAI’s data center in Memphis and at the data centers throughout Virginia, known as the world capital of data centers, where gas turbines are used for power. Maia Woluchem, program director at Data & Society, a nonprofit research group, believes that changes to energy regulations, land rights, and other environmental policies could affect the data center buildout, especially as congressional Democrats look further into the Trump administration’s rollback of certain energy protections, as the New York Times reported they might. “Regardless of federal action, I could imagine that we will see additional movement at the state and local level, given the momentum that’s been building from the ground up,” Woluchem continued, citing governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who supports a statewide moratorium on data centers, as an example. Both Hinojosa and Gov. Greg Abbott called for some limits, but Hinojosa centered much of her campaign on opposing data centers, a notable choice in Texas, whose electrical grid has proved vulnerable over the past decade. But the hard part is still to come. Smith, for example, is now expecting a fight, or even more executive orders, to bypass what Congress is now likely to block. “Even among Democrats, a blanket freeze is contested,” she said, referring to some Democrats’ worry that a moratorium could slow AI progress and hurt national security. She also expects AI lobbyists to start calling lawmakers. “Democrats ran on making Big Tech pay,” Smith said. “Our job is to make sure they remember it once the cameras leave.” The backlash runs deeper than the buildings themselves, which aren’t new. One private equity executive told me recently that people don’t necessarily hate data centers, but rather AI, and that data centers have become a stand-in for people’s fears and anxieties about the technology. “It does look like the results are pointing to a real frustration with tech power at minimum,” Woluchem said, noting that this is also a bipartisan issue. For the past month, people have told me they are worried about data centers’ effect on the environment and about their lack of say in whether they’re built. Amazon, for example, built a data center in Gilroy, California, without many residents knowing, by satisfying a 45-year-old zoning law. Vague or outdated zoning laws, along with requirements that local officials sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) barring them from discussing data center projects, have only fueled people’s outrage about the buildout.
