artigo.texto: O mercado de geração distribuída (GD) de energia solar no Brasil começou 2026 em ritmo mais lento, com retração nas novas conexões, queda nas importações de módulos fotovoltaicos e dificuldades para transformar propostas comerciais em vendas. Ao mesmo tempo, sistemas de armazenamento com baterias e infraestrutura de recarga de veículos elétricos ampliam sua participação nos negócios dos integradores, indicando uma diversificação das soluções oferecidas pelo setor. Os dados fazem parte do Estudo Estratégico de Soluções Energéticas Distribuídas (SED), elaborado pela Greener, com resultados referentes ao primeiro semestre de 2026. O levantamento mostra que o Brasil chegou a 53 GW de potência instalada em geração distribuída até junho, com a adição de 3,97 GW no período, volume 23% inferior aos 5,2 GW registrados no primeiro semestre de 2025. A desaceleração foi mais expressiva na minigeração distribuída, com queda de 33,7% na potência adicionada em comparação com o mesmo período do ano anterior. Já a microgeração permaneceu praticamente estável, com retração de 0,8%. Na quantidade de novas conexões, o recuo foi de 16%, passando de 488 mil no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 411 mil nos seis primeiros meses de 2026. O número de novas unidades consumidoras que passaram a receber créditos de energia de forma remota também diminuiu, com queda de 43%, de 951 mil para 541 mil. A distribuição da potência adicionada por classe de consumo também revela mudanças no perfil da geração distribuída brasileira. O segmento residencial passou a concentrar 65% da potência instalada no primeiro semestre de 2026, ante 57% em 2025 e 39% em 2019. Em sentido contrário, a participação comercial caiu de 30% em 2023 para 19% no período mais recente. A expansão da GD continua distribuída pelo território nacional. Os 3,97 GW adicionados no semestre foram registrados em 5.192 municípios. São Paulo liderou a lista de cidades com maior potência adicionada, com 43 MW, seguido por Brasília, com 36 MW, e Cuiabá, com 32 MW. Importação de módulos fotovoltaicos recua 48% O movimento de desaceleração também aparece na cadeia de fornecimento de equipamentos. As importações de módulos fotovoltaicos nacionalizadas no Brasil somaram 5,5 GWp no primeiro semestre de 2026, retração de 48% em relação aos 10,6 GWp do mesmo intervalo de 2025. A maior queda ocorreu na geração centralizada (GC), cujo volume importado diminuiu 82%, passando de 2,3 GWp para 0,43 GWp. Na geração distribuída, a redução foi de 39%, de 8,2 GWp para 5 GWp. Com isso, a GD respondeu por aproximadamente 90% do volume nacionalizado no período. Apesar da retração, os custos de nacionalização continuam representando uma parcela relevante do valor dos equipamentos. Segundo o levantamento, esses custos correspondem a 44% do valor CIF, com o Imposto de Importação, de 25%, como principal componente. Dificuldade de integradores na conversão de proposta O cenário de desaceleração também se reflete na atividade comercial das empresas integradoras de energia solar. A média mensal de orçamentos avançou de 20 no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 25 no mesmo período de 2026, crescimento de 25%. Entretanto, a taxa de conversão das propostas em vendas ficou em apenas 18%. Na prática, aproximadamente oito em cada dez orçamentos não se transformaram em negócios. A média mensal de sistemas vendidos passou de quatro para cinco por empresa, acompanhando a recuperação na quantidade de propostas. O financiamento também perdeu participação nas vendas. No primeiro semestre de 2026, 33% das vendas contaram com crédito, oito pontos percentuais abaixo do registrado em 2025. Os juros elevados e as dificuldades de aprovação bancária continuam entre os principais obstáculos para o fechamento de negócios. A concorrência baseada em preços aparece como a maior pressão sobre os integradores, citada por 63% das empresas entrevistadas. Na sequência estão os juros elevados no financiamento, mencionados por 52%, e as dificuldades de aprovação de crédito, apontadas por 40%. Outro desafio é a inversão de fluxo de potência, que passou a atingir 38% dos integradores, ante 28% no primeiro semestre de 2025. Embora a taxa de resolução dos casos tenha avançado de 39% para 50%, metade das ocorrências ainda não havia sido solucionada, segundo o levantamento. Baterias ampliam participação no mercado solar Em meio à desaceleração dos sistemas fotovoltaicos convencionais, o armazenamento de energia começa a ganhar espaço no portfólio das empresas. O estudo aponta que 86% dos integradores já oferecem sistemas híbridos, percentual 15 pontos percentuais superior ao registrado no primeiro semestre de 2025. A participação dessas soluções nas vendas também aumentou, passando de 2% para 5% em um ano. Além disso, 38% dos integradores realizaram pelo menos uma venda de sistemas com baterias no primeiro semestre de 2026. A principal motivação dos consumidores para procurar soluções de armazenamento é a confiabilidade do fornecimento de energia e a continuidade das atividades, responsável por 51% da demanda identificada. Outros fatores incluem consumidores sem acesso à rede elétrica, interesse em novas tecnologias e redução de custos em horários de ponta. O segmento residencial concentra 65% das vendas de sistemas com baterias, com destaque para residências de alto padrão, que representam 40% do mercado. Já os segmentos comercial e industrial somam 25%, com oportunidades relacionadas à proteção de cargas críticas, ao perfil tarifário e aos impactos financeiros de interrupções no fornecimento. Apesar do avanço, a ampliação das vendas ainda depende da capacitação técnica e comercial dos integradores. O levantamento destaca a necessidade de desenvolver competências para diagnosticar o perfil de consumo dos clientes, dimensionar os equipamentos e avaliar a viabilidade econômica das soluções. Recarga de veículos elétricos abre oportunidades A mobilidade elétrica também aparece como uma frente de diversificação dos negócios. A frota brasi

artigo.texto: Google planeja data center de US$ 17 bilhões nos EUA Projeto será abastecido, em parte, por um empreendimento de células de combustível de 702 megawatts O Google investirá US$ 17 bilhões na construção de seu primeiro data center no estado norte-americano de Wyoming, anunciou a empresa nesta quinta-feira (5). O projeto será abastecido, em parte, por um empreendimento de células de combustível de 702 megawatts, equipado com tecnologia de captura e armazenamento de carbono. As células de combustível serão fornecidas pela Bloom Energy. O Wyoming é um reduto republicano, onde Donald Trump obteve mais de 70% dos votos na eleição presidencial de 2024. O anúncio ocorre em um momento em que os investidores reavaliam o ritmo da construção de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial. As vitórias de candidatos democratas contrários à expansão de data centers em disputas importantes durante as eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA aumentaram preocupações de que a resistência política possa complicar a rápida expansão do setor.

artigo.texto: Technology giant Google announced plans to build its first data center in Wyoming, representing a long-term $17 billion commitment aimed at expanding its digital infrastructure while supporting local energy, economic, and community development. The facility, located in Laramie County near Cheyenne, will feature an innovative energy framework developed in partnership with American Electric Power, Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, Related Digital, and Bloom Energy. At the heart of the project is a commercial-scale, 702-megawatt fuel cell system with carbon capture and storage (CCS). Built by US-based Bloom Energy, the natural gas-powered solid oxide fuel cells generate electricity electrochemically, delivering high efficiency with low emissions and minimal water use. Captured carbon will be permanently sequestered at Tallgrass Energy’s nearby Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub, bringing Google’s contracted CCS capacity to nearly one gigawatt. Additionally, the complex will utilize an air-cooling design rather than water cooling to protect local municipal water supplies. Google stressed its commitment to local integration after gathering feedback from more than 200 Laramie County residents at a recent town hall in Cheyenne. Company representatives confirmed that Google will pay for all of its power use and fund any infrastructure upgrades the project’s expansion requires. The development is projected to deliver hundreds of millions of dollars in property tax revenue to Laramie County and School District 1. Alongside municipal revenues, Google plans to issue targeted grants to support local K-12 science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) programs, entrepreneurial initiatives, and skilled trades training across the state. To address broader local concerns regarding infrastructure pressures, Google and its project partners are establishing a joint Community Council to collaborate directly with Cheyenne residents and municipal leaders on growth strategies.

artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: Interior de um data center do Google: expansão da infraestrutura digital enfrenta restrições locais nos EUA (Google/Reprodução) Editor de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 4 de novembro de 2026 às 11h31. Eleitores americanos aprovaram novas restrições a data centers. As votações ocorreram em uma eleição com 41 propostas locais sobre o setor em dez estados, segundo a Ballotpedia. Eleitores dos Estados Unidos aprovaram restrições à expansão de data centers nas eleições de terça-feira, 3 de novembro. O resultado amplia a pressão política sobre a infraestrutura que sustenta a corrida pela inteligência artificial. O debate chegou às urnas por diferentes caminhos. Um levantamento da Ballotpedia publicado antes da eleição identificou 41 propostas locais em dez estados: 28 buscavam limitar o desenvolvimento desses empreendimentos e 13 poderiam facilitá-lo. Esses números representam medidas submetidas à votação, não o total de restrições aprovadas. Entre as propostas restritivas, havia proibições, pausas temporárias, exigências de aprovação popular e garantias financeiras para comunidades. Ohio concentrou 21 das 41 medidas previstas para o dia 3, o maior número entre os estados. As consultas não tinham todas o mesmo efeito: algumas poderiam mudar regras locais; outras apenas expressavam a opinião dos eleitores. A Ballotpedia contabilizou, por exemplo, perguntas consultivas sem força vinculante, além de referendos sobre zoneamento e acordos específicos. Em análise publicada em agosto, os pesquisadores Nicol Turner Lee e Darrell M. West, da Brookings Institution, apontaram a ligação entre o debate sobre data centers e as preocupações com custo de vida. Consumo de energia e água, uso do solo e empregos passaram a integrar críticas de candidatos dos dois partidos. A escala da demanda ajuda a explicar a atenção ao setor. Um relatório do Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory publicado em junho de 2026 estima que os data centers poderão responder por 11,8% do consumo de eletricidade dos EUA em 2030, no cenário de referência. Os cenários alternativos vão de 9,5% a 15,3%. São projeções, sujeitas a mudanças na instalação e na operação dos equipamentos. A EXAME já mostrou como o avanço dos data centers entrou na disputa eleitoral americana. Não. As medidas acompanhadas pela Ballotpedia tratam de regras e decisões locais. A moratória suspende temporariamente uma atividade ou a concessão de licenças. Uma proibição impede os usos definidos em seu texto, sem necessariamente estabelecer o mesmo prazo.

artigo.texto: Eco Wave Power's wholly-owned U.S. subsidiary has entered into a three-year memorandum of understanding (MoU) with quantum cybersecurity and space IoT company WISeQey Corp., together with its subsidiaries SEALSQ and SEALCOIN AG, to evaluate connecting renewable energy producers with AI data centers, industrial facilities, energy aggregators and utilities. The collaboration combines wave energy production, secure digital identities and automated transactions, with potential applications for AI data centers and industrial energy buyers. According to Eco Wave Power, the collaboration combines its renewable energy technology, SEALSQ’s secure semiconductors, WISeQey’s digital identity expertise and SEALCOIN’s machine communication and transaction infrastructure to explore how renewable energy assets can securely interact with digital services and potential energy buyers. Using Eco Wave Power’s wave energy installation in Jaffa Port in Israel, the companies have demonstrated connecting physical energy production to an authenticated digital representation, allowing the origin and integrity of production data to be verified, as well as the usage of trusted production data to initiate a secure, authorized and auditable transaction between known counterparties under predefined commercial conditions. The demonstration is said to connect physical energy production with digital identity, secure communications and automated transactions, establishing a foundation for future machine-to-machine commercial interactions. Jonathan Llamas, Chief Product & Strategy Officer of SEALCOIN, said: “Until now, machines have primarily been designed to exchange information. We are taking this a step further by enabling them to turn trusted physical-world data into autonomous economic actions. With Eco Wave Power, we have demonstrated how authenticated energy production can feed a digital twin and trigger a secure, auditable transaction between authorized parties.” Under the MoU, the parties plan to further develop and evaluate these capabilities for potential commercial applications, particularly connecting renewable energy producers with AI data centers, industrial facilities, energy aggregators and utilities. Eco Wave Power further announced that it had initiated discussions with data center developers and infrastructure partners to explore potential future electricity supply opportunities. The companies also intend to explore future integration of SEALSQ’s QS7001 post-quantum secure element and quantum-resistant cryptographic technologies, supporting the long-term security requirements of critical infrastructure. “Building the energy infrastructure for AI requires both new sources of electricity and trusted systems capable of connecting those sources with customers. Our ambition is to bring wave energy into that ecosystem," said Inna Braverman, Founder and CEO of Eco Wave Power. "Together with SEALCOIN, SEALSQ and WISeQey, we have demonstrated how physical wave energy production can become trusted digital information and initiate a secure, auditable transaction. We believe this creates an important foundation for a future in which wave energy producers can securely connect with AI data centers and other energy buyers, transact under agreed commercial terms and ultimately participate directly in the digital energy economy.” To remind, Eco Wave Power, together with partner Germany-based AI engineering, recently completed the first phase of the AI-powered digital twin development program for its wave energy technology, which saw the creation of a physics-based digital model of how ocean waves interact with the company's proprietary floaters.

artigo.texto: The CEO of one of the world’s biggest suppliers of electrical equipment sees the AI-driven global construction boom continuing for years — and driving a shift from traditional low-voltage systems to 800-volt direct-current architecture for data centers. In August 2025, Eaton Corp. paid $86 million for Resilient Power Systems, a solid-state transformer developer. Using magnets and semiconductors rather than specialized steel alloys and vast amounts of copper wiring, solid-state transformers, or SSTs, are more compact and efficient than traditional low- and medium-voltage transformers. Data centers built on the 800-volt direct-current architecture that Eaton expects will soon become the industry standard could reduce non-IT capital expenditures by up to 18%, according to a recent McKinsey analysis. Earlier this year, the Electric Power Research Institute, New York Power Authority and North Carolina State University tested a 1-MW SST under “real-world” conditions and cut power losses in half compared to a traditional transformer configuration. Paulo Ruiz, CEO of Eaton, told investors on Tuesday that the company’s 15-kV, 2-MW SST became, “to our knowledge,” the first multi-megawatt unit to pass all tests under a new UL Solutions standard for the technology. However, it may be some time before Eaton SSTs are widely deployed, he cautioned. “The good thing for us to keep in mind is that this direction of travel, in terms of migrating from AC to DC, is real because of the large power savings that the customers see in this new technology,” he said. “But the timing of that transition is not under our control.” He added that SSTs are only one of several “key building blocks” needed, along with DC breaker, power quality and advanced cooling technologies. “The AC architectures are not bad, and we are fine either way,” Ruiz said. “We win in either path.” Ruiz said he sees no letup in the global demand for power equipment from data centers and utilities. Eaton, which is headquartered in Ireland but is one of the largest suppliers in the U.S. market, makes and markets low- and medium-voltage electrical products such as single- and three-phase power quality systems, utility-grade power distribution equipment, circuit protection and power reliability equipment. It reported a record $8.9 billion in third-quarter sales, up 28% year over year. “We track the [worldwide] projects that are announced, and now they amount to 366 GW,” Ruiz said, of data centers. “Contrast that with the installed capacity of 50 GW. It's an enormous build-out. In my opinion, this will last for many years to come.” Eaton predicts end market growth of about 11% in 2027. In 2025, data centers and distributed IT accounted for 21% of sales, while utilities accounted for 11%. A little less than half the total of third-quarter sales came from Eaton’s Electrical Americas segment. That unit benefits from broad-based demand from data centers and other electrification “mega-projects,” helping to widen profit margins, Ruiz said. The Electrical Americas segment saw its backlog rise to $16 billion – up 33% year over year – while orders increased 39% on a rolling 12-month basis. Ruiz emphasized that data centers were not Eaton’s only high-growth customer segment. Utility investment and other large-load industrial customers are propelling business, too, he said. “Demand continues to run ahead of what we can convert,” Ruiz said. “This is a business that continues to benefit from powerful secular trends, utility investment, grid modernization, industrial reshoring, AI-driven data center expansion and broader electrification.” Doubling down on data centers In the past two years, Eaton has acquired multiple companies with data center exposure. The most recent was a roughly $920 million deal for COL Group, an Italian manufacturer of medium-voltage electrical distribution equipment, grid automation technologies and modular power systems that Eaton said would boost its sales to data center and utility customers in Europe. In March, Eaton paid about $9.6 billion to acquire Boyd Thermal, “a U.S.-based global leader in thermal components, systems, and ruggedized solutions for data center, aerospace and other end-markets,” the company said in a securities filing this week. The Boyd pickup will help Eaton develop integrated power and cooling architectures for data center customers and “deliver differentiated grid-to-chip solutions while increasing our exposure to some of the fastest-growing segments of the data center market,” Ruiz said.

artigo.texto: 247 – A expansão acelerada da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial nos Estados Unidos enfrenta um novo obstáculo político após a vitória de candidatos democratas que prometeram restringir a construção de data centers. As eleições de terça-feira (3) colocaram em risco projetos bilionários de grandes empresas de tecnologia e evidenciaram a crescente resistência da população aos impactos ambientais e econômicos dessas instalações. Segundo reportagem do Financial Times, reproduzida pela Folha de S.Paulo, os resultados no Texas, na Geórgia e em Ohio representam um revés para o presidente Donald Trump, defensor da ampliação da infraestrutura de IA. Os três estados concentram investimentos estratégicos do setor e elegeram governadores democratas favoráveis à suspensão ou à imposição de condições mais rigorosas para novos empreendimentos. No Texas, a democrata Gina Hinojosa derrotou o governador republicano Greg Abbott e prometeu interromper imediatamente a construção de novos data centers até a criação de mecanismos legais de proteção. O estado tornou-se um dos principais destinos de investimentos de empresas como OpenAI, Anthropic, Oracle, Microsoft, Google, Meta e Amazon, atraídas por incentivos fiscais e pela disponibilidade de energia e terrenos. Vitórias democratas atingem principais polos de inteligência artificial Na Geórgia, a ex-prefeita de Atlanta Keisha Lance Bottoms venceu a disputa pelo governo estadual com a promessa de suspender temporariamente novos projetos. A região metropolitana de Atlanta concentra quase 2,9 gigawatts de capacidade de data centers em construção, segundo a consultoria imobiliária CBRE, superando o norte da Virgínia como principal polo de expansão dessas instalações no país. Em Ohio, Amy Acton derrotou o republicano Vivek Ramaswamy e defendeu o congelamento de autorizações para empreendimentos que não cumpram exigências rigorosas relacionadas ao consumo de energia e água. A resistência também apareceu nas consultas populares realizadas simultaneamente às eleições. Em Edgewater, na Flórida, 77% dos eleitores aprovaram uma proposta para proibir a construção de data centers no município. Em Trenton, Ohio, uma votação favorável a restrições deve dificultar os planos da Amazon de instalar um complexo na cidade. Consumo de energia e aumento das contas mobilizam eleitores A oposição aos data centers ganhou força diante das preocupações com o elevado consumo de eletricidade e água, a poluição sonora e atmosférica e os possíveis aumentos nas tarifas pagas pelos consumidores. Pesquisa de boca de urna da NBC apontou que 56% dos entrevistados consideraram a inteligência artificial e os data centers fatores cruciais ou importantes para decidir o voto nas eleições para o Congresso. Antes da votação, 26 candidatos ao governo de 21 estados já defendiam alguma modalidade de suspensão de novos empreendimentos. Somente em Ohio, os eleitores analisaram 21 propostas relacionadas ao setor. A pressão eleitoral levou inclusive republicanos a rever suas posições. Em setembro, Abbott determinou a suspensão temporária de licenças ambientais para novos data centers conectados à rede elétrica do Texas, enquanto uma auditoria fosse realizada. A decisão ocorreu após Hinojosa transformar a oposição aos projetos em uma das principais bandeiras de sua campanha. Trump sofre revés em estratégia apoiada por gigantes da tecnologia A resistência eleitoral contraria a estratégia de Trump de acelerar os investimentos em inteligência artificial. Em setembro, o presidente classificou como “farsa” as críticas aos data centers e as preocupações relacionadas à segurança da tecnologia. O avanço dessas instalações tornou-se um componente importante da valorização das grandes empresas de tecnologia no mercado financeiro. Amazon, Meta, Microsoft e Alphabet, controladora do Google, devem investir conjuntamente até US$ 740 bilhões, aproximadamente R$ 4,04 trilhões, em despesas de capital em 2026. A Nvidia, fabricante de semicondutores utilizados no desenvolvimento de sistemas de IA, estima que os investimentos mundiais em infraestrutura do setor poderão alcançar entre US$ 3 trilhões e US$ 4 trilhões até 2030. Os resultados eleitorais também provocaram uma reação de Elon Musk, aliado de Trump e investidor em grandes complexos de processamento de dados. “Data centers no espaço parecem bastante atraentes agora”, publicou o empresário na noite de terça-feira. Investidores temem restrições e impacto sobre empresas de tecnologia Antes das eleições, analistas do BMO Capital Markets já alertavam para os riscos de uma reação política contra a expansão da infraestrutura de IA. Segundo eles, os resultados no Texas e das consultas populares em Ohio poderiam revelar a intensidade da resistência dos eleitores. “Estamos preocupados com as avaliações das empresas do setor de tecnologia caso esse resultado se concretize”, escreveram os analistas. As novas administrações estaduais, entretanto, poderão enfrentar obstáculos para implementar as suspensões prometidas. O alcance das medidas depende da legislação de cada estado, e mudanças mais amplas poderão exigir negociações com os parlamentos locais. As propostas seguem uma tendência iniciada em Nova York, onde a governadora Kathy Hochul determinou, em julho, uma suspensão de um ano para o desenvolvimento de data centers com capacidade igual ou superior a 50 megawatts. Trump criticou a iniciativa, classificando-a como uma “decisão terrível”. Com a vitória democrata em estados estratégicos, a expansão da inteligência artificial passa a enfrentar um cenário de maior incerteza regulatória nos Estados Unidos, justamente quando as grandes empresas de tecnologia planejam investimentos sem precedentes em infraestrutura computacional.

artigo.texto: Masdar and Endesa Begin Construction on Three Battery Storage Projects in Spain Masdar, the Abu Dhabi-based clean energy company, and Endesa, a Spanish utility, have broken ground on three battery energy storage facilities in Spain. The projects are designed to help the European country bring more clean electricity onto its grid. According to a Thursday statement from Masdar, the three sites — Ardila, La Vega I and La Vega II — represent a combined investment of EUR25.2 million, or $28.3 million. Once built, they will attach 60.16 megawatts of battery storage capacity and 120.34 megawatt-hours of storage to solar plants located in Extremadura and Andalusia. Operations are scheduled to begin by the close of next year, and the facilities are expected to generate 50 jobs. Such storage installations give the grid flexibility by retaining electricity when demand is low and discharging it during peak periods. This approach helps smooth out and steady the variable output of renewable sources while increasing the flow of clean power to the grid. Ibraheem Almansouri, Masdar's acting chief operating officer, described Spain as one of Europe's fastest-expanding major economies and said that growth demands dependable, robust power. He noted that the projects would assist in bringing more clean electricity onto the grid and improving the electricity system's stability, and he added that Masdar intends to keep investing in Spain in support of its economic goals. Spain, in common with other European countries, is pursuing net zero emissions by 2050 and is hastening the rollout of new renewable energy capacity. By 2030, it aims to generate 81 per cent of its electricity from renewable sources, including 62 gigawatts of wind capacity and 76 gigawatts of solar. Thursday's announcement comes after Masdar bought a stake in a portfolio of Endesa's solar assets in Spain during 2024. Masdar presently operates 4.1 gigawatts of capacity throughout the Iberian Peninsula, with roughly 1 gigawatt still in development. Masdar, which is jointly held by Abu Dhabi's Taqa, Adnoc and Mubadala, is pursuing a 100-gigawatt portfolio by 2030 as it keeps building renewable projects around the world. Last month, the company began work on its inaugural Malaysian project, which is expected to rank among South-East Asia's biggest floating solar installations. The 200MW Chereh Dam solar photovoltaic scheme in Parang state is being constructed by a consortium that includes Citaglobal, a Malaysian construction company, and Tiza Global, an investment firm. In August, Masdar started its second battery energy storage system project in Rochdale, close to Manchester in the UK, after launching a separate project near Stockport in December. - 1. artigo.texto: O Grupo Greenvolt assinalou a entrada em funcionamento dos seus dois primeiros sistemas autónomos de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês) no Japão. A operação, concretizada através da Greenvolt Power — braço do grupo dedicado às renováveis de grande escala —, marca uma nova etapa na estratégia de consolidação da empresa portuguesa no continente asiático. Localizados na região de Kyushu, no sudoeste do arquipélago nipónico, os dois novos ativos somam uma capacidade de potência de quatro megawatt (MW) e uma capacidade de armazenamento de oito megawatt-hora (MWh). As instalações funcionam sob o modelo de mercado livre (merchant), obtendo rentabilidade a partir da negociação direta nos mercados de eletricidade, ao mesmo tempo que apoiam a estabilização e a flexibilidade da rede elétrica local. A concretização destes projetos reforça a pegada internacional da tecnológica energética, que soma já um conjunto de ativos de armazenamento (pipeline) de cerca de 4,6 gigawatt (GW) repartidos pela Europa, América do Norte e Ásia. Do total da carteira global, a empresa contabiliza mais de 1 GW em fase de construção ou em operação efectiva, além de ter alienado mais de 800 MW ao abrigo da sua política de rotação de ativos. O investimento no mercado japonês junta-se a várias empreitadas de grande dimensão concluídas recentemente pela Greenvolt no continente europeu. Na Polónia, a empresa finalizou a infraestrutura dos projetos de Ełk e Turośń Kościelna (400 MW / 1,6 GWh de capacidade conjunta) e deu início à empreitada de Siedlce — um dos maiores parques de baterias do continente, com 600 MW / 2,4 GWh. Na Hungria, entrou também em exploração a central de armazenamento de Buj, dotada de 99,8 MW / 288,6 MWh. Para João Manso Neto, presidente executivo (CEO) do Grupo Greenvolt, o arranque das operações no Japão traduz "um passo importante no reforço da presença da Greenvolt na Ásia e na consolidação da presença global em três continentes", destacando a posição da empresa com "um dos maiores pipelines de projetos BESS da Europa". Por sua vez, Spiros Martinis, líder da Greenvolt International Power, sublinha o interesse em aprofundar posições em geografias como a Coreia do Sul, Indonésia e no próprio mercado nipónico. Segundo o responsável, "o crescimento das necessidades de eletricidade cria oportunidades para aproveitar a experiência que temos vindo a desenvolver em diferentes mercados e contextos de negócio".

artigo.texto: AI, energy storage, and more: ISO-NE staff share expertise at October events Collaboration, expertise, and innovation are three of ISO New England’s core values. Staff embody these values by presenting their work at electricity industry conferences and events around the region, the country, and the world. Here’s a selection of their October speaking engagements. Chris Geissler, director of Economic Analysis, Market Development, discussed the Capacity Auction Reforms key project at the Northeast Energy and Commerce Association Fuels Conference in Boston on Oct. 1. He highlighted efforts to modernize the capacity market through seasonal resource accreditation and incentives that support resource performance and winter reliability. Xiaochuan Luo, director of Power System Technology, Advanced Technology Solutions, took part in the Integration of Artificial Intelligence in the Electricity System workshop hosted by the National Academies in Washington on Oct. 26. He was part of a panel titled “AI in Markets, Operations and Data Centers through a Cyber-Physical Security Lens.” Parviz Alivand, principal economist and manager of Market Design, Market Development, took part in the Nodal Trader Conference in Washington on Oct. 22. He was part of a panel titled “Changing Market Dynamics and New Nodal Models,” where he discussed Capacity Auction Reforms, the Day-Ahead Ancillary Services market, and strategies for relieving congestion on the transmission system. Steven Judd, manager of Long-Term Planning, System Planning, and Melissa Winne, lead state policy advisor, External Affairs, led a webinar on Oct. 1 to provide an overview of ISO New England’s longer-term transmission planning (LTTP) process and 2025 LTTP request for proposals. Winne also presented on LTTP topics at the E2Tech Forum in South Portland, Maine, on Oct. 13. Matt Kakley, manager of Media Relations and Strategic Communications, Corporate Communications, spoke at the Connecticut Power and Energy Society’s Future of Energy conference on Oct. 29 in Fairfield. He was part of a panel titled “The Business of Communicating Energy in 2026.” Kakley discussed the ISO’s unique role in New England and how it communicates technical information to help the public understand the challenges facing our future energy landscape. Steven Otto, manager of Economic Analysis, Market Development, spoke on Oct. 26 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, at an event titled “Launching Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES) in Massachusetts: Storing Energy Today for a More Resilient Tomorrow.” He was part of a panel focused on the role of LDES in advancing the affordability and reliability of electricity. Two members of the External Affairs team, Kerry Schlichting, manager of State Policy, and Sarah Adams, senior state policy advisor, External Affairs, hosted virtual office hours on Oct. 23. The event was designed for a non-technical audience to learn about ISO New England. Adams presented on the region’s transition to a new generator interconnection framework at the REV Conference in South Burlington, Vermont, on Oct. 14. She discussed reforms that streamline the interconnection process, improve project readiness requirements, and support the efficient integration of new energy resources onto the grid. On Oct. 28, Adams provided a regional update at the Vermont System Planning Committee quarterly meeting in Killington. She covered market conditions, the ISO’s 2027 priorities, transmission planning initiatives, large load integration, and generator interconnection reforms. Adams and Ruben Flores-Marzan, policy advisor for environmental and community affairs, External Affairs, presented at the Southern New England American Planning Association Conference in Mashantucket, Connecticut, on Oct. 8. They discussed how local land-use decisions shape the region’s electricity future, highlighting the connection between community planning decisions, electricity demand growth, and the region’s evolving grid and transmission needs. Graham Jesmer, senior regulatory counsel, Legal and Compliance, presented on ISO-NE’s approach to dispatching distributed energy resource aggregations during the “Curtailment Problems and Solutions” panel at the Special Institute on Meeting the Demand conference in Denver, Colorado, on Oct. 8. - Categories - Events - Tags - ISO leadership

artigo.texto: Alhambra’s Measure DB, a city-wide data center ban by public vote, is leading with 81.8% voting yes, and 18.8% voting no. Results from the Los Angeles County Registrar’s Office included vote-by-mail ballots received before election day, vote center ballots cast before election day and election day ballots transported and counted after vote centers closed. Should voters approve Measure DB with the simple majority needed to win, Alhambra would become the second California city – following in the footsteps of Monterey Park earlier this June – to pass a city-wide data center ban by public vote. The ballot title reads: “Data Centers Prohibited. Shall an ordinance be adopted affirming the Council adopted ban on “Data Centers” by amending the Alhambra Municipal Code to again define ‘Data Centers’ and prohibit them in all zones of the City?” “Measure DB is at 82% support, showing that Alhambra, like Monterey Park and many communities across the SGV, is united against data centers,” SGV Progressive Action co-founder Andrew Yip said. “Even with little to no campaigning, Measure DB has received overwhelming support from voters.” Throughout Los Angeles County, specifically across the San Gabriel Valley, officials have considered various actions to protect residents’ health and utilities amid the data center sprawl. According to the Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning, “developers have expressed preferences for jurisdictions with municipal power utilities, such as the City of Vernon, instead of the County’s unincorporated communities.” Yip and other organizers based in the region under the coalition No Data Center San Gabriel Valley have campaigned for stronger protections like a public vote banning the technology, with Baldwin Park, Montebello and El Monte on their watchlist. Monterey Park voters in June banned the technology outright, passing Measure NDC with 88% of the vote, after a monthslong campaign by community members to prevent data center developer HMC StratCap from building a hyperscale data center at Saturn Park, a site in Monterey Park. Speaking about council’s unanimous approval to place Measure DB on the November ballot, then-Mayor Jeff Maloney said the city had “other pressing land use needs.” “The demand on the space we do have is not going down,” Maloney said in July. “Housing, recreational opportunities, business opportunities – and when you dedicate a big area of land to something, that is essentially low intensity, low economic growth.” Speaking about the poll results, Council member Maloney said he’s “not surprised.” “There was a big push against these types of projects in our community, and I think that the community was really anxious and yearning for an opportunity to have a say on it,” Maloney said. “I’m really pleased that we went through and put this on the ballot, and I’m really pleased with the results so far … these types of passive projects could have a negative impact on our environments.” Results from the Los Angeles County Registrar’s Office are still being tallied.

artigo.texto: BYD confirma novo SUV Ti7 híbrido para o Brasil em 2027 SUV plug-in, antecipado pela CNN, é do tamanho do Denza B5, tem tração integral e bateria de 35,6 kWh A BYD confirmou em Mendonza, Argentina, na convenção dos concessionários, a chegada do novo Ti7, que é vendido na China como Fang Cheng Bao. O híbrido plug-in de 408 cv tem porte do Denza B5, bateria de 35,6 kWh e estilo boxy, quadrado. O Ti7 reforçará a atuação da marca entre os SUVs que já circulam no mercado brasileiro e que estão tomando conta do segmento mais lucrativo da indústria, entre R$ 250 mil e R$ 500 mil. Leia-se: Jetour T2, Tank 400, GWM H7, G700 e Denza B5. O chinês combina desenho quadrado, opção de sete lugares e motorização híbrida plug-in. É um carro que troca as linhas arredondadas por uma carroceria de frente alta e traseira vertical que estampa uma caixa suporte que serve como compartimento de bagagem. O SUV mede 5,146 metros de comprimento, 1,995 metro de largura e 1,865 metro de altura. As três fileiras ampliam a versatilidade para as famílias e diferenciam a configuração europeia do modelo da China, visto pela CNN Brasil aqui em Dubai, com cinco lugares, 4,9 metros de comprimento e praticamente o mesmo entre-eixos de 2,9 metros. Na versão Excellence AWD, anunciada para a Europa por Stella Li, vice-presidente do grupo e CEO das Américas, o sistema DM-p combina motor 1.5 turbo a gasolina e propulsão elétrica, com tração integral e 408 cv. Carro que está em exposição nos representantes da marca. A bateria Blade tem 35,6 kWh, e a BYD anuncia aproximadamente 119 quilômetros de autonomia elétrica e aceleração de zero a 100 km/h em 4,8 segundos. Luxo de Denza? O carro internamente tem central de 15,6 polegadas, dois carregadores de celular de 50 W e refrigerador no console central, além dos mimos de segurança: ADAS, bolsas infláveis e um bom sistema de acesso à terceira fila de bancos. O Ti7 que deve ser vendido no Brasil será o de cinco lugares e promete acompanhar a entrega mais refinada já vista no Atto 8 de sete assentos e no Denza B5. *Colunista viajou a Dubai a convite da BYD

artigo.texto: Lyten Deploys Energy Storage System in Fiji to Deliver Reliable Power to Remote Islands Press Release Date 11-06-2026 SAN JOSE, CA, UNITED STATES, November 5, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Lyten, a globally leading critical energy infrastructure company, today announced the installation of its battery energy storage system, the Voltpack Mobile System (VMS), on Yasawa Island, Fiji, providing reliable electricity for the remote village of Yasawa i Rara. Lyten’s VMS product was purchased and brought to Fiji by Energy Solutions Pacific Ltd., in collaboration with Investment Fiji. The system was officially energized on October 28 by Marshall Islands Ambassador to Fiji Junior Aini, before village elders and community members gathered at dusk. “It’s been wonderful to see the impact reliable power can have on the families of Yasawa i Rara,” said Dan Cook, Co-Founder and CEO, Lyten. “Projects like this show what flexible energy storage can do for rural and off-grid communities by reducing diesel consumption and increasing the value of solar energy. We are seeing growing demand for our VMS product across Island Nations and in any region where the rapid growth in demand for reliable power exceeds grid availability.” “It is something that is going to be very useful,” Anwa Khan, Director, Energy Solutions Pacific, announced during the celebration. “This will help you and your children and everybody else.” This first deployment will improve the reliability of electricity access for up to 64 households, a cold storage facility that lets the community preserve its fish catch for longer, and essential community services, including a maternity unit and a mortuary. Without access to Fiji’s national grid, the village had depended on diesel generators, and supplemented in places by solar panels, leaving families without truly reliable power, particularly at night. Lyten’s VMS changes that: solar panels and generators now charge the batteries, and the village draws its electricity from stored power, giving residents quiet, steady electricity day and night while the generators run only when the batteries need topping up. Lyten’s VMS is a stand-alone, modular, plug-and-play energy storage system, scalable from 290 kWh to hundreds of megawatt-hours (MWh). It is built at Lyten’s energy storage manufacturing facility in Gdańsk, Poland, supplied by predominantly European supply chains. Shipped as modular units that can be easily moved by forklift, the system can be installed in a day without major construction or integration, and its weatherproof enclosures are built to withstand humidity and salt air. At Yasawa i Rara, the VMS stores energy from both solar panels and diesel generators and delivers it to the village on demand. “For too long, the growth of our rural communities, our health services, our schools and our hardworking local entrepreneurs has been capped by a single, fragile constraint: reliable energy,” said Lisala Dyer, Head of Regional and Trade Development, Investment Fiji. “When power flickers or fails or when it is absent altogether, our progress stalls.” Yasawa i Rara reflects a challenge shared across many hundreds of islands in the Pacific, where more than 3.7 million people — concentrated in Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu, and the Solomon Islands — still lack reliable electricity access. Many of these communities will likely never be reached by a national grid. For them, modular, stand-alone storage systems like the VMS offer a practical, rapidly deployable path to dependable power by maximizing the value of solar and reducing dependency on diesel. As Fiji works toward its national goal of 90% renewable electricity by 2035, installations like this one show how remote island communities can share in that energy transition, gaining reliable power for homes, health care and livelihoods by storing and making the most of the energy they already generate. Lyten, in partnership with Energy Solutions Pacific Ltd, is now ready to deploy the VMS product widely across the Pacific Islands. Go to https://lyten.com/products/energy-storage-system/ to learn more. About Lyten Founded in 2015, Lyten is a leading critical energy infrastructure company and a leader in lithium-sulfur batteries and advanced 3D Graphene™ supermaterials. Lyten holds more than 1,100 granted or pending patents and has developed products across energy storage, lithium-sulfur batteries, advanced composites, sensors, adhesives, concrete, and additive manufacturing materials. Headquartered in San Jose, Calif., Lyten is privately held, with more than $625 million in equity investment. Investors include Stellantis, FedEx, Honeywell, Prime Movers Lab, and the European Investment Fund. Lyten has been recognized as Fast Company’s #8 Most Innovative Energy Company and named one of America’s Top Green Technology Companies by TIME in 2024, 2025, and 2026. artigo.texto: Startup EDENenergy: Used E-Scooter Batteries Become Industrial Energy Storage System In Germany alone, about one million high-performance batteries from e-bikes and scooters end up in the trash prematurely every year, even though they often still retain a large portion of their capacity. At the same time, stationary energy storage systems are expensive and resource-intensive to manufacture. The Freiburg-based startup EDENenergy solves both prob-lems: It develops modular industrial storage systems from second-life batteries that are high-performance, cost-effective, and sustainable. Former researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE have developed a system featuring interchangeable battery modules and flexible power electronics that efficiently and safely combine heterogeneous batteries into stationary storage systems. In the field of car batteries, “second-life” concepts have already demonstrated just how valuable used energy storage devices can be. The potential of micromobility—that is, the millions of e-bikes and e-scooters, an increasing number of which are being returned—has not yet been tapped. This is due to the enormous variety of batteries—designs, cell types, energy management systems—which make standardized reuse difficult. This is where the startup EDENenergy comes in with power electronics developed at Fraunhofer ISE: Florian Bierwirth, who, like his co-founders Daniel Seeger and Hannes Kurzmann, previously worked in the Power Electronics Department at Fraunhofer ISE, explains : It allows different storage units to be connected and enables communication with various modules without having to disassemble the batteries, From E-Bikes to Industrial Applications To enter the market, the startup is focusing on industrial storage systems with a capacity of 70 kilowatt-hours. “In mid-October, we delivered the first storage system to a customer, which was an important milestone for our young company. With this storage size, we initially aim to target medium-sized companies in the region that have a photovoltaic system but do not yet have a storage solution.” The storage systems could also be of interest to municipal utilities, which can use them to optimize self-consumption, smooth out peak loads, or for electricity trading. For the first industrial storage system, 112 second-life e-scooter batteries—after being thoroughly tested during an initial screening—will be interconnected. Currently, EDENenergy relies on large suppliers (such as e-bike and e-scooter fleet operators), which ensures that enough batteries of the same type are available to start with. In the future, thanks to innovative power electronics, different types of batteries will also be interconnected. Florian Bierwirth, outlining the challenge, says : To do this, the connector interfaces, battery management system, and communication protocols must be adapted for each new battery. There’s a particularly wide range of options when it comes to e-bikes, In the long term, he notes, standardized communication protocols for battery storage systems and “second-life” legislation governing the use of mobile batteries in stationary applications will be necessary. The first 350 batteries tested held a pleasant surprise for the three young entrepreneurs: they were in significantly better condition than expected. While EDEN-energy had estimated a remaining capacity (“State of Health”) of 80 percent for second-life batteries, the used batteries actually had an average remaining capacity that, in some cases, was well over 90 percent. In stationary storage systems, where—unlike in their first life—they are exposed to fewer vibrations or temperature fluctuations, these batteries can continue to perform well for several more years. EDEN-energy remotely monitors the battery modules via a monitoring system. When they reach the end of their service life, the battery modules are replaced individually, which can be done even while the battery system is in operation. The batteries that are finally at the end of their useful life are then sent for recycling by partner companies. Compared to standard energy storage systems on the market, this turns an apparent disadvantage into a technical advantage: replacing individual modules makes it possible to maintain the storage system’s capacity at a constant 70 kWh even after 10 years. Due to battery degradation, conventional manufacturers typically guarantee only 80 percent of the original capacity after 10 years. In the next steps, the young company—which now employs three part-time staff members in addition to its three founders—plans to expand the storage capacity to up to 300 kWh. They are also looking for additional pilot customers among regional businesses that can receive 50 percent funding for the storage system through the state grant program “Mittelstand trifft Start-ups,” which has already been approved. EDENenergy also receives funding from the Center of Excellence for Sustainability and through the state grant program for innovative startups “BW Pre-Seed,” under which JobRad founder Ulrich Prediger is the company’s first investor. artigo.texto: Anatel fica sem dinheiro para arcar com o próprio data center Agência precisa de R$ 31 milhões para a estrutura Kleber Pizão - 03/11/2026 22h19 A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) informou ao Governo Federal a possibilidade de suspensão do pagamento de despesas básicas. A instituição acumula R$ 30,7 milhões em faturas pendentes relativas à implantação do seu próprio Data Center localizado no Distrito Federal. A infraestrutura dá suporte para o funcionamento de plataformas digitais voltadas ao público e às operadoras de telecomunicações. O espaço também é responsável pela manutenção dos sistemas internos que viabilizam fiscalizações e rotinas administrativas do órgão. Diante do cenário, o presidente da agência, Carlos Baigorri, solicitou ao Ministério do Planejamento o desbloqueio de R$ 30 milhões. O pedido não é novo e já havia sido negado pelo Ministério da Fazenda, de acordo com a apuração da Folha de S. Paulo. — As projeções apontam risco de insuficiência de limite financeiro para o pagamento integral dos compromissos previstos, especialmente no último trimestre de 2026 — afirmou o presidente da agência. A agência atribui o quadro ao bloqueio governamental de R$ 51,8 milhões determinado em maio, que reduziu sua verba discricionária de R$ 275,3 milhões para R$ 223,5 milhões, um corte de 19%. No final do ano passado a Anatel firmou um contrato de R$ 44,9 milhões com empresas de tecnologia para realizar serviços e fornecer equipamentos. A vigência do acordo vai até dezembro de 2030. Para conter os efeitos do contingenciamento, a agência reguladora adequou contratos, projetos e despesas operacionais no intuito de evitar multas e juros. O órgão relata contenções orçamentárias desde agosto, quando pediu a antecipação de R$ 23,3 milhões previstos para dezembro. — Até o momento, as medidas adotadas têm buscado mitigar os impactos decorrentes da restrição orçamentária imposta à agência. Contudo, a persistência das restrições orçamentárias e financeiras poderá exigir novas medidas de reprogramação de despesas — declarou a agência. O Ministério da Fazenda justificou que as limitações decorrem da necessidade de contingenciamento reavaliada a cada dois meses pela Junta de Execução Orçamentária, com revisão em 24 de novembro. O Tesouro analisa os pedidos para preservar a capacidade mensal de pagamento. Em reação aos cortes, cerca de 40 entidades empresariais divulgaram na terça-feira (27) um documento intitulado “Regulação não é gasto, é investimento”. A iniciativa defende a autonomia orçamentária das agências para assegurar o funcionamento pleno no Orçamento de 2027.

artigo.texto: Google planeja data center de US$ 17 bilhões em Wyoming, nos EUA O Google investirá US$ 17 bilhões na construção de seu primeiro data center no estado norte-americano de Wyoming, anunciou hoje a empresa. O projeto será abastecido, em parte, por um empreendimento de células de combustível de 702 megawatts, equipado com tecnologia de captura e armazenamento de carbono. As células de combustível serão fornecidas pela Bloom Energy. O Wyoming é um reduto republicano, onde Donald Trump obteve mais de 70% dos votos na eleição presidencial de 2024. O anúncio ocorre em um momento em que os investidores reavaliam o ritmo da construção de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial. As vitórias de candidatos democratas contrários à expansão de data centers em disputas importantes durante as eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA aumentaram preocupações de que a resistência política possa complicar a rápida expansão do setor. artigo.texto: This story was originally published by Capital B and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. Silicon Valley wants communities across the country to make room for its data centers. On Tuesday, those communities had their say. Voters considered nearly 40 data center-related ballot measures across 10 states, turning the midterms into a sprawling referendum shifting the technology industry’s demand for power into a test of political power. Of the ballot measures, just one—in Harwood, North Dakota—counted as a victory for the tech industry. In the other measures, which were voted on in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey, Ohio, and Wisconsin, voters either banned data center construction or halted the development of all planned facilities in their municipalities. When Jamil Davis, an organizer with Black Voters Matter in northern Florida, knocked on doors this fall, he saw this growing outrage against data centers. Before asking people to vote, he said, organizers have to listen to the problems shaping their lives. “And almost every time, utility bills, data centers, [are] the key things that people bring up,” he said. The fight over data centers belongs to a much older struggle against environmental racism: Who gets the benefits of industrial development, and who is left to live with its burdens? Data centers, which are connected to a slew of environmental issues like water depletion and air pollution, are more likely to be located in communities of color. Largely, the current struggle against data centers has roots in Memphis, Tennessee, where Black-led groups such as Memphis Community Against Pollution and Young, Gifted & Green challenged the pollution and lack of public oversight surrounding Elon Musk’s xAI facility. The national opposition, made clear on November 3, could advance a demand Black environmental activists have pressed for generations: not simply protection from pollution, but a meaningful say in whether the facilities producing it get built in their communities at all. “They’re choosing marginalized and predominantly Black communities to build data centers, and it is an environmental justice issue,” David explained. The growth of data centers, which are needed for virtually every internet service from scrolling social media to streaming TV and using ChatGPT, has also contributed to skyrocketing utility prices nationwide. More than half of the ballot initiatives were first introduced by citizen initiatives rather than elected officials. In all, 77 percent of voters rejected data center development. In Joliet, Illinois, where Black and Latino residents have long fought against pollution from the warehouse and trucking industry, nearly 80 percent of voters moved to restrict data centers. A nationwide poll Wednesday found that more than half of midterm voters considered AI and data centers to be a major or crucial factor in their vote. The results of the measures were also a rebuke of President Donald Trump, some political analysts said. Trump has vowed to make America the “AI capital of the world.” Even a majority of Republicans oppose new data center construction in their communities. Elizabeth Bast, executive director at Oil Change Action, said voters sent a “clear message.” “They’re fed up with Trump’s agenda of fossil fuel giveaways, illegal and immoral wars, and unchecked data center expansion that makes their lives more expensive while lining the pockets of Big Oil and Big Tech,” she said. “This incoming Congress must listen to the people who elected it.” Tech corporations and their allies outspent the local citizen campaigns by approximately 100 to 1 nationwide in an attempt to block these measures, according to the group Data Center Resistance. Elon Musk alone spent $474 million backing Republicans, conservative groups, and pro-AI candidates during the 2026 US midterm elections, the largest amount ever contributed by an individual donor in a single election cycle. In California, Google, Meta, and other Big Tech interests account for at least 20 percent of all the contributions on the state’s legislative races, according to a CalMatters analysis of campaign finance disclosures. “This is nothing short of a political earthquake,” said Ed FitzGerald, director of Data Center Resistance. “They had the money, but we had the people.” Across the South, tech companies have attempted to operate in secrecy by entering non-disclosure agreements with elected officials, shielding citizens from learning important details about these facilities. In Alabama, the League of Conservation Voters invested $300,000 in digital ads targeting Rhett Marques, a Republican supporter of data centers, focusing on how the data center boom has directly increased utility bills for Alabamians. Marques went on to lose to US Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black politician whose position was under threat because of the weakening of the Voting Rights Act. “This win is a huge victory, especially for Black communities in Alabama whose voice was attempted to be silenced by the racial gerrymandering efforts of the state legislature and Supreme Court earlier this year,” LCV President Pete Maysmith said.

artigo.texto: AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company’s gaming segment cratered. AMD CFO Jean Hu said, “We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. The middle point of our guidance represents approximately 66% year-over-year revenue growth, primarily driven by the acceleration of our Data Center segment.” AMD says its Q4 revenue projections are up another 27 percent from this quarter’s results. As reported by Tom’s Hardware, Intel’s Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion. That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history. The data center segment of AMD’s business was up 97 percent year over year, with a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs. Sales of AMD Ryzen mobile chips led growth in the Client business, which includes desktop Ryzen processors and posted $2.95 billion in revenue, up 7 percent year over year. Gaming revenue fell sharply for the company, posting a 40 percent drop in revenue at $773 million, which AMD attributes to “lower semi-custom and graphics revenue.” Operating margins in AMD’s data center business expanded from 25 percent to 34 percent, with operating income surging 168 percent to $2.88 billion. Embedded segment revenue, or all the SoCs, FPGAs, and boards under AMD’s umbrella that go into other hardware, was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent. AMD attributed this growth to gains made in the “aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial end markets.”

artigo.texto: Waaree maps Rs 18,000-20,000 crore BESS revenue potential Key highlights - Waaree estimates Rs 18,000 crore to Rs 20,000 crore of BESS revenue potential at 20 GWh of capacity. - Phase 1 could generate Rs 4,000 crore to Rs 5,000 crore from 5 GWh under management's container-sales illustration. - Phase 1 includes 5.1 GW each of container and pack manufacturing, plus 3.5 GWh of cell manufacturing. - Waaree said BESS orders are small while it pursues long-term offtake agreements in India and overseas. powered by IRIS During the earnings call, Waaree Energies Limited said its planned 20 gigawatt-hour battery energy storage system business could generate Rs 18,000 crore to Rs 20,000 crore of revenue at capacity. Waaree based the framework on utility pricing of about US$100 per kilowatt-hour, while saying current battery-storage orders are small and larger offtake talks continue. Know Waaree Energies inside out Results, valuation, peers and who's buying, in one view. What is Waaree's BESS revenue potential at 20 GWh? Waaree estimates that 20 gigawatt-hours, or GWh, of battery energy storage system capacity could support Rs 18,000 crore to Rs 20,000 crore of revenue. Management split this framework between a Phase 1 estimate of Rs 4,000 crore to Rs 5,000 crore and a Phase 2 estimate of Rs 14,000 crore to Rs 15,000 crore. The estimate is a capacity-based illustration rather than reported BESS revenue, a contracted order book or formal financial guidance. Management said a broad utility-market price of around US$100 per kilowatt-hour could be used for calculation purposes, and that 5 GWh of Phase 1 capacity could yield about Rs 4,000 crore to Rs 5,000 crore at peak if Waaree sells containers. The Rs 18,000 crore to Rs 20,000 crore range therefore depends on sales from both phases at the indicated capacity. The call did not disclose a timetable for achieving that revenue level, assumed utilisation, BESS margins, contracted pricing, or the mix between container, pack and cell sales. How is Waaree commissioning its Phase 1 BESS line? Waaree is building Phase 1 with 5.1 gigawatts, or GW, of container manufacturing, 5.1 GW of pack manufacturing and 3.5 GWh of cell manufacturing. Management said the container line was commissioned in the previous quarter, the pack line was expected to go live in the current quarter, and the cell line was expected to begin pilot production in the next quarter. Management expects the fully integrated Phase 1 line to start in the current financial year. The sequence combines containers, battery packs and cells, but Waaree did not disclose production volume, commercial sales, capital expenditure, manufacturing yield or utilisation for the container line already commissioned. Waaree also described a route to revenue beyond sales of complete containers. Management said it could sell cells separately while using imported cells in locally made containers, potentially adding direct sales, supplies and exports to the Rs 4,000 crore to Rs 5,000 crore container-sales illustration. The BESS plan forms part of a broader effort to diversify beyond modules. Management said modules currently account for more than 92% of retail revenue, with inverters and other products making up the balance, and said increasing battery-storage and inverter contributions should move the mix toward non-module components in coming quarters. Got a follow-up? Ask IRIS Does Waaree have enough BESS orders to support expansion? Waaree said it has started receiving BESS orders, but described their sizes as small. Management did not disclose the number of orders, their capacity, value, delivery schedule, customer geography or whether any order is included in the 20 GWh revenue framework. Waaree said it is building the BESS order book and discussing long-term offtake agreements with multiple large clients in India and overseas. These discussions matter because management made additional overseas orders one of the conditions for investing in the battery portion of Phase 2, while no signed long-term BESS offtake agreement was identified on the call. Customer advances elsewhere in the business should not be treated as BESS order evidence. Management said higher other current liabilities reflected customer advances after orders received during the quarter, with utility customers in India and overseas providing the bigger portion and retail advances representing around 10% to 15%. Management also referred to a single 2 GW order while explaining advances, but did not identify it as a battery-storage contract. The disclosed BESS demand position is therefore limited to small received orders and ongoing discussions, rather than a quantified BESS backlog supporting the full Rs 18,000 crore to Rs 20,000 crore capacity scenario. What must happen before Waaree starts Phase 2 investment? Waaree has finalised a Phase 2 location, but management said it will invest in the battery portion only after receiving more policy clarity and/or more overseas customer orders. This means the location and broad capacity plan are identified, while the capital commitment for Phase 2 battery operations remains conditional. Management described Phase 2 as comprising 16.5 GW of cell capacity and 15 GWh of container capacity. Its Rs 14,000 crore to Rs 15,000 crore revenue illustration is larger than the Rs 4,000 crore to Rs 5,000 crore Phase 1 illustration, making a Phase 2 decision necessary to reach the combined 20 GWh framework. Policy considerations extend across Waaree's manufacturing strategy. Management said the government was pushing localisation across the solar value chain, described batteries as the next priority after modules and cells, and said cell localisation would happen over the next 12 months; it did not specify a battery policy, incentive or approval required for Phase 2. artigo.texto: Sungrow Commissions 350 MW / 1,243 MWh Hams Hall Battery Storage Project in 20 Days Sungrow has announced the commissioning of a battery energy storage system at Hams Hall in the West Midlands, UK, in partnership with energy storage owner-operator BW ESS, according to a Sungrow press release. The company said the 350 MW / 1,243 MWh project, powered by its PowerTitan 2.0 technology, moved from grid connection to commercial operation in 20 days. The project is expected to be Europe's largest operational BESS by storage capacity, measured in MWh. Located next to National Grid's Hams Hall substation, it is intended to help balance electricity supply and demand, support the integration of renewable energy into the UK's electricity system and strengthen grid resilience as the country expands its renewable energy capacity. Delivery Approach Sungrow attributed the speed of the first phase's delivery to several measures. The company deployed dedicated BESS engineers directly to the site so technical challenges could be investigated and resolved with input from the teams responsible for the technology, reducing reliance on remote escalation. During the initial warm commissioning phase, the team prioritised fault identification and chiller operation to address potential issues before hot commissioning began, with dedicated operational technology engineers present throughout hot commissioning to support system integration and troubleshooting. Customer representatives were on site almost daily and established escalation channels to Sungrow's headquarters, which the company said helped both teams address outstanding issues quickly and minimise delays between commissioning activities. James Li, Vice President, Europe at Sungrow, said that delivering a battery storage project of this scale depends on bringing together engineering expertise, careful preparation and close collaboration at every stage, and that the teams worked alongside BW ESS to resolve challenges quickly. Nan Jia, Chief Technology Officer at BW ESS, described moving the 1,243 MWh system from grid connection to commercial operation in 20 days as a remarkable result that was possible because both companies treated it as a shared engineering challenge, adding that the project follows their earlier work together at Bramley. Capacity and UK Context The project is expected to expand in a second phase, raising total capacity to 400 MW / 1,424 MWh. At full capacity, BW ESS estimates it will be capable of supporting the electricity needs of approximately 1.3 million homes for up to 3.5 hours. Hams Hall adds to the UK's growing battery storage infrastructure. As more renewable energy comes onto the electricity grid, large-scale storage projects are described as increasingly essential to managing fluctuations in generation and demand and maintaining a reliable electricity system. The project also builds on Sungrow's ongoing collaboration with BW ESS in the UK, including the Bramley BESS project in Hampshire. Sungrow describes itself as a global leader in renewable energy technology that has pioneered sustainable power solutions for over 29 years. artigo.texto: Canberra launches largest energy storage system — ABC News Australia Australia’s Canberra has launched the largest energy storage system in the Australian Capital Territory. The complex in Williamsdale, south of the Tuggeranong district, can, if needed, cover up to one-third of Canberra’s electricity demand for two hours during periods of peak demand, ABC News reports. The facility consists of 136 Tesla Megapack 2 battery modules combined into 12 collector groups. The system has a capacity of 250 MW and can rapidly store up to 500 MWh of electricity before supplying it to the grid. How the complex will operate The batteries are connected to the infrastructure of operator Evoenergy. During periods of low demand, they store surplus electricity, including power generated by wind and solar sources. When demand rises—for example, on hot evenings or during intensive industrial activity—the system feeds stored energy into the grid, reducing the load on it. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Eku Energy policy director Rachel Rundle said that the system can store and supply up to 500 MWh of energy every day. At the same time, the company’s chief operating officer, Tom Best, stressed that the complex does not guarantee lower household electricity bills because it operates on the open market. Terms of the agreement with the authorities The project is a partnership between the Australian Capital Territory government and private company Eku Energy. The company designed, built and owns the battery system. Under the operating agreement, the government is to pay Eku Energy $368 million in installments over 15 years. In return, the territory is entitled to 50% of the battery complex’s net revenue from electricity sales to the grid. Australian Capital Territory Chief Minister Andrew Barr said he expects the project to deliver a positive financial outcome for the territory. Construction was initially planned for completion in 2025, later postponed to early 2026, but the facility was commissioned later.

artigo.texto: O desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial (IA) e a construção de infraestrutura para esta tecnologia funcionar (leia-se: data centers) andavam num ritmo desenfreado nos Estados Unidos. E as eleições de meio de mandato podem jogar água na fervura. Com o Partido Democrata conquistando não apenas a Câmara e o Senado americanos, mas também governos de estados como Texas, Ohio e Geórgia, investidores esperam o surgimento de mais obstáculos para a construção de data centers. Ou seja: a “onda azul” pode levar a uma desaceleração nacional na expansão da capacidade computacional voltada para a IA. Paradoxalmente, isso poderia favorecer muitos agentes do setor. Entre eles, empresas gigantes de tecnologia. Também seria bom para o Brasil. Entenda possíveis impactos das eleições de meio de mandato dos EUA no mercado de tecnologia Até então, investidores tinham receio do custo astronômico para erguer tanta infraestrutura acabar esmagando a lucratividade de empresas de IA. Só que o movimento recente de resistência de comunidades e governos contra a expansão desenfreada da infraestrutura de IA ameaça desacelerar o crescimento de empresas menores, que dependem de novas instalações para ampliar suas capacidades de computação. Com o ritmo de novas obras reduzido, custos com crédito, materiais e mão de obra tenderiam a cair. Em paralelo, os data centers que já operam ganhariam “valor de escassez”. É aí que gigantes como Meta, Amazon e Microsoft levariam vantagem, segundo o Wall Street Journal. Big techs já controlam complexos de data centers. Além disso, têm caixa e poderio financeiro o suficiente para absorver regulamentações ou negociar compensações locais. Na prática, o mercado ficaria mais restrito e menos competitivo. E empresas gigantes se beneficiariam disso ao se distanciarem de concorrentes menores que sofrem com crédito mais apertado. Presidente da Meta diz que resultados das midterms dificultam construção de data centers A presidente da Meta, Dina Powell McCormick, disse que construir novos data centers nos EUA ficou mais difícil após os resultados das eleições de meio de mandato (midterms, em inglês). Data centers são estruturas enormes recheadas de computadores potentes. Eles são essenciais para treinar e rodar sistemas de IA. E devoram energia e água, o que costuma preocupar quem mora perto dessas instalações. Por causa disso, governadores democratas eleitos em estados-chave, como Ohio e Texas, manifestaram resistência a data centers. E pediram o congelamento temporário de novas construções. No entanto, a executiva compartilhou uma anedota, durante evento do Wall Street Journal, que sugere margem para negociação. “Tivemos um governador eleito ontem à noite que, inclusive, colocou os data centers como um ponto central de sua plataforma; ele disse: ‘Assim que passarmos pela cerimônia de posse, vamos nos reunir, pois não queremos perder esse investimento em nossa cidade. Não queremos que esses empregos vão para outro lugar’”, contou McCormick, na quarta-feira (04). A empresa está construindo um enorme data center na Louisiana, chamado Hyperion; outro em Ohio, chamado Prometheus; e um terceiro no Texas, como parte de um empreendimento com a BlackRock. A executiva também disse que empresas como a Meta teriam mais facilidade para expandir projetos de data centers já existentes “porque elas possuem um histórico consolidado de alguns anos, e a comunidade tem sentido esses benefícios”. “Elas não sentiram os custos; na verdade, sentiram os benefícios”, disse a presidente da Meta no evento. Além disso, McCormick disse que a Meta também está de olho em outros países, onde talvez consiga construir data centers num ambiente mais favorável. Midterms nos EUA jogam data centers no colo do Brasil Resultados das eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA mostram uma “mudança de clima”, analisa o doutor Alvaro Machado Dias, professor da Unifesp, neurocientista e futurista, em entrevista ao Olhar Digital News. “Certamente as licenças vão pingar de maneira mais devagar, os custos consequentemente para as empresas vão ser maiores e, definitivamente, os interesses e as preocupações das populações locais espalhadas pelos Estados Unidos vão ser mais escutados”, diz o especialista. O doutor Alvaro duvida que a maioria democrata no Congresso americano signifique uma pausa na expansão dos data centers. “O que muda é muito mais o custo dessa expansão”, afirma o futurista. Para o especialista, esse novo cenário nos EUA é muito bom para o Brasil. O doutor Alvaro explica: “Se já havia um bom argumento para a instalação de data centers no Brasil, que era o Redata, agora o argumento é melhor ainda. Isso porque está mais caro e mais difícil instalar data centers nos Estados Unidos.” O Brasil “tem política nacional, interesses empresariais – a gente tem tudo orientado a trazer data centers para cá”, observa o especialista. O professor acrescenta que essa intenção constava nos planos de governo de ambos os candidatos à presidência do Brasil em 2026. Outro ponto importante para o doutor Alvaro é como “a nossa maneira de pensar a política pública já começou superior à americana”. “A discussão americana gira muito em torno do quanto as populações locais estão sendo prejudicadas pela instalação dos data centers porque essa instalação não está ponderando os impactos locais e, por exemplo, não está ponderando esses impactos do ponto de vista do consumo da água”, começa o especialista. O doutor Alvaro continua: “O Redata exige que o data center contrate ou produza energia suficiente para toda a própria demanda e coloca limite no consumo de água. A gente pode falar mal dos nossos parlamentares, mas, de fato, esse foi um projeto que pensou nesse detalhe que agora está dando tanta dor de cabeça lá fora.” Já sobre o que o Brasil poderia aprender com o que está acontecendo nos EUA, o especialista disse o seguinte: “O que a gente teria para aprender já está aprendido.
