artigo.texto: Voters in Urbana and Piqua reject data center projects, leaving next steps unclear PIQUA AND URBANA, Ohio (WKEF) -- Voters in Urbana and Piqua delivered a clear message at the ballot box, backing measures intended to block data center construction in both cities. The votes leave major questions about what happens next for the projects, including how the results could affect ongoing legal and contractual issues. Data centers have drawn national attention and debate over potential environmental impacts, rising utility costs and water consumption. In the Miami Valley, two proposed developments became the focus of local ballot measures. In Piqua, residents voted to support amending the city’s charter to stop construction, with 66 percent voting in favor. The vote followed months of controversy, including what some residents described as an extended period without transparency from city leaders. Residents said city leaders pushed the data center deal forward without consulting the city first, prompting protests and petition efforts to get the issue on the ballot. With unofficial results showing support for blocking development, the city provided the following statement: Based on the unofficial results of the Piqua Special Election on Tuesday, November 3, voters approved a measure that adds Section 138 to the Piqua City Charter. The amendment prohibits the construction of data center facilities that meet specific criteria. .City officials are currently reviewing the Charter amendment language and will work with the City Commission regarding implementation. It is unclear at this time if and how this Charter amendment may affect the Meta data center project currently underway within the Piqua I-75 Business & Industrial Park on the east side of Washington Road, north of Farrington Road. RELATED COVERAGE: Meta pledges $8M for Piqua emergency services, cites potential $1B data center investment RELATED COVERAGE: Piqua residents rally at City Hall, demand more details on proposed data center RELATED COVERAGE: Four candidates vie for three Piqua commission seats in Nov. 3 special election Piqua 2nd Ward Commissioner Paul Simmons also raised concerns about uncertainty surrounding the situation, pointing to existing agreements and possible legal issues. “There's a contract that's already been made,” Simmons said. “There are other legal things that people are talking about. I have no idea. I'm not involved with that. I don't know if they're trying to stop it or not.” In Urbana, voters approved a ban on data center construction by an even wider margin, with 77 percent voting yes. The city is also weighing whether to settle with data center developer Thor Equities or continue fighting in court. An emergency moratorium was issued in March. City commissioners were contacted for comment about next steps in the legal fight. One commissioner said they would not be available for comment, saying it would be in their best interest not to comment while the lawsuit is ongoing. Requests for comment were also sent to the data center companies. The following are some of the questions asked: - How is the company responding to the election results - What do the results mean for the project? - Would another site be considered if the votes interfere with plans? - Is Meta considering legal action if plans cannot move forward due to the election results? - Would Thor Equities consider another resolution if the results interfere with prior plans for data center development? We are waiting for a response. Questions remain about the future of both projects as the cities sort through the legal and practical implications of the votes.

artigo.texto: Carbon Market Watch - Carbon prices climb as policy reforms take shape Carbon prices have risen towards 90 EUR/tCO2, supported by tighter allowance supply and gas market pressures. EU ETS reform will shape longer-term market conditions, while we retain our Q4 average forecast of 86 EUR/tCO2. - CBAM is becoming a financial obligation for importers, with proposed broader coverage increasing the importance of reliable emissions data - EU-UK ETS linkage could support UK carbon prices and narrow the price gap, although implementation timing remains uncertain European carbon prices have been trending upwards. The benchmark December-2026 EUA contract rose from roughly 76 EUR/tCO2 in early July to about 86.6 EUR/tCO2 in late July. Prices then stabilised at around 82–84 EUR/tCO2 in August before climbing towards 88 EUR/tCO2 in September and October. At the time of writing, the price is hovering around 90 EUR/tCO2. Several factors have supported this rally. On the supply side, lower auction volumes and the planned withdrawal of around 190 million allowances into the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) have reinforced expectations of tighter supply in the short term. The end-September deadline for surrendering allowances also supported prices. Weather conditions have become an important driver of demand: colder temperatures and weaker winds increase reliance on conventional power generation, while high gas prices encourage a switch from gas to more carbon-intensive coal. Both developments increase demand for carbon allowances. Higher trading volumes and renewed buying interest have provided further support following August’s period of stable prices. Finally, discussions about reforms to the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and a potential link between the EU and UK carbon markets have reformed expectations about long term prices. In this note, we review the latest developments that are expected to reshape the carbon market in the coming years. CBAM: Rising import costs and broader coverage ahead CBAM is moving from a reporting requirement to a real cost for companies importing carbon-intensive goods into the EU. The financial reporting phase started in January 2026, CBAM certificates will go on sale in February 2027, and the first compliance deadline is September 2027 for 2026 imported emissions. The impact will vary significantly depending on the carbon footprint of imported products. Companies that can provide reliable, verified emissions data can pay substantially less than those relying on standard EU default values, making emissions data and supplier transparency increasingly important. Looking ahead, CBAM is expected to have broader coverage and become more impactful from 2028 onwards. The EU is considering adding around 180 downstream products from January 2028, which could roughly triple the value of imports initially covered by CBAM and extend the impact particularly to machinery, automotive and electrical equipment. During 2027, further decisions are also expected on this expansion and on how carbon prices already paid outside the EU will be recognized. Overall, CBAM is likely to increasingly affect import costs, competitiveness, sourcing decisions and supply chains, while giving an advantage to companies and suppliers with lower emissions and good-quality emissions data. UK linkages: progress towards a connected market EU–UK ETS linkage is at an advanced stage: negotiations are reportedly complete to a large extent, although the agreement has not yet been formally published or brought into force. The next key milestone is the UK-EU Summit on 20 November 2026, when further progress is expected. We expect 2027 likely to be a transition year, rather than the start of full linkage. Meanwhile, the UK CBAM is currently due to begin on 1 January 2027. We expect the two systems and carbon prices to move closer during 2027-28, with full linkage potentially around 2029, but this is more like a prediction, rather than an agreed timeline. Moving forward, the main impact is likely to be higher UK carbon prices, as UK allowances move closer to the generally more expensive EU allowances. This price gap could narrow during 2027-28, although prices may remain volatile until the legal timing is clear. For the EU market, the effect should be smaller and could slightly reduce prices because the combined market would have more allowances and trading activity. Linking the systems should also improve liquidity, make carbon prices more consistent across Europe, and reduce CBAM-related costs and paperwork for trade between the UK and EU. Overall, the market is likely to react positively to a confirmed deal, especially UK allowances, but any delay or uncertainty could cause price movements. More on CBAM impacts and other price projection in our earlier publication here. EU ETS review: Key decisions ahead Since the European Commission published its EU ETS review on 17 July 2026, the proposal has moved into the legislative scrutiny and negotiation phase. The most recent publicly documented positions indicate that Member States are now testing the balance between industrial competitiveness/cost containment and environmental integrity. The next major milestone is the Council position, currently targeted for 11 December 2026, while the European Parliament is developing its own position; only after both co-legislators establish mandates can trilogue negotiations with the Commission begin, with an indicative ambition to reach a compromise by end-Q1 2027, although that timetable remains politically dependent. For November and early December, the key development to watch is the emergence of Council compromises and parliamentary amendments. artigo.texto: Some voters went to the polls looking to elect people to help in their fight to keep data centers out of their communities. One newly elected commissioner on a public utilities board is already calling for a moratorium on new data centers. [DOWNLOAD: Free WSB-TV News app for alerts as news breaks] People who live along Cole Lake Road in Dallas are happy they have someone on the Georgia Public Service Commission who wants to stop data centers from being built for now. “What is true is they don’t belong in the residential areas,” Todd Pownall told Channel 2’s Tom Jones. He is emphatic data centers don’t belong in residential areas. “If they were put somewhere where they wouldn’t bother the neighborhood,” then, he said, they wouldn’t concern him as much. But he says a large proposed data center has been approved to be built on property that butts up to his. “It’s right behind my house,” Pownall said. RELATED STORIES: - Georgia Election 2026: Democrats take control of State House - Georgia’s newly elected leaders say affordability will be a Day 1 priority - Georgia Election 2026: Black women now hold nearly all state executive offices Communities all over are fighting to keep data centers from being built in their communities. The midterm election could bring more elected officials who will fight with them. Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms has called for a moratorium on data centers. “I think it should be longer than a year,” Public Service Commissioner-elect Shelia Edwards said. “We have to make sure that they have a guardrail. That they’re doing things within that guardrail. That’s not encroaching on people,” she said. Edwards is concerned about data centers using excessive amounts of water and electricity. She’s also concerned about the centers making billions but getting tax breaks. “Pay your fair share,” Edwards said. “We don’t want them here,” Pownall reiterated. He wants more research before the centers are built. “You need to have buffers in place. You need to have guardrails in place,” Pownall said. Edwards says everyone throughout the state should have a voice in where data centers can be built and how they should operate. [SIGN UP: WSB-TV Daily Headlines Newsletter] ©2026 Cox Media Group

Realizar o leilão de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em dezembro, no meio de uma discussão no Congresso sobre o rateio dos custos de contratação das baterias, é uma “irresponsabilidade regulatória”, afirmou a sócia do Fernanda De Paula Advocacia e Consultoria Jurídica, Fernanda De Paula. Em entrevista ao estúdio eixos, durante a EVEx Lisboa 2026, a advogada defendeu que a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) suspenda o cronograma da licitação para um diálogo transinstitucional, diante das perspectivas de mudança nas regras. Confira na íntegra. “Hoje, com a atual situação do país, é uma irresponsabilidade regulatória a gente fazer um leilão de baterias sem que a gente conheça todos os preços e todos os custos envolvidos. E por que eu estou dizendo isso? A gente tem hoje um cenário de modificação, de tentativa de modificação legislativa, que é importante”. Fernanda De Paula faz referência à aprovação, na Câmara dos Deputados, em outubro, do requerimento de urgência para o projeto de lei 3716/2026, que altera o rateio dos custos da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento (BESS). O PL, de autoria de Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), altera a lei nº 15.269/2025, que estabelece que o custo do armazenamento é arcado pelas geradoras de energia. A nova proposta estabelece a divisão dos valores com os consumidores. A advogada cita o risco de que, uma vez aprovado o PL, que o leilão seja judicializado. “Se o projeto de lei passar, a gente teria que cancelar o leilão, refazer as fases de precificação. Porque já que isso vai para o consumidor final, isso vai ter um custo diferenciado. Até acho que na matemática isso não vai ter um impacto tão grande – a gente só está trocando quem paga os custos… Mas fato é que muda a matemática de pra onde a conta vai”, completou. Principais assuntos tratados: - Leilão de baterias de dezembro pode ser cancelado se o Congresso mudar o rateio, pois empresas já precificaram com a regra atual. - Lei 15.269 manda que o custo seja pago por quem gera, enquanto PL de Arnaldo Jardim e Danilo Forte defende dividir com os consumidores. - Cobrança de TUSD na entrada e na saída é criticada, pois outros países não cobram nada, e Aneel seguiu solução intermediária. - Advogada defende diálogo transinstitucional entre Aneel, Congresso, MME e TCU para suspender o leilão por 45 dias. - Adiamento gera menos insegurança que manter o certame com regra que pode mudar, pois insegurança jurídica eleva custo de capital. - Histórico de judicialização do LRCAP preocupa, e advogada defende fortalecimento de órgãos de controle. artigo.texto: A energia solar gera a maior parte da sua produção durante o dia, enquanto a demanda de eletricidade de muitas residências aumenta à noite. Os Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias (BESS) ajudam a armazenar o excedente de eletricidade para uso quando necessário, aumentando a capacidade de gerenciar proativamente as fontes de energia locais. Com base nessa necessidade, a GG Power desenvolveu o ENERGY HUB S16 NEW, projetado para famílias que utilizam energia solar, com um design adequado para atender às necessidades de longo prazo. A GG Power desenvolve baterias de armazenamento de energia para uso doméstico, visando aumentar o índice de nacionalização da produção. Com a crescente popularidade da energia solar, o desafio para as famílias vai além da simples geração de eletricidade limpa; também envolve o armazenamento e a utilização dessa energia no momento certo. Com o ENERGY HUB S16 NEW, a GG Power visa criar uma linha de baterias de armazenamento de energia "nacional", desenvolvida com base nas necessidades reais e na capacidade de produção das empresas vietnamitas. Este produto utiliza células de bateria Cornex de Grau A – um dos principais fabricantes mundiais de células de bateria – com características térmicas estáveis e uma vida útil projetada de até 8.000 ciclos de carga/descarga. A compatibilidade com muitos modelos populares de inversores híbridos o torna adequado tanto para novos sistemas quanto para atualizações de sistemas existentes. O produto possui classificação de proteção IP21, sendo adequado para instalação em ambientes internos ou protegidos. Seu design compacto e elegante, com conexões traseiras discretas, garante que o dispositivo se integre perfeitamente a qualquer ambiente. Uma característica notável do ENERGY HUB S16 NEW é seu foco na localização, desde a pesquisa até a produção. O produto é desenvolvido por uma equipe de engenheiros vietnamitas e fabricado em uma fábrica em Hung Yen , que ocupa aproximadamente 1,2 hectares, com um sistema de armazenamento de energia (BESS) dedicado com capacidade de até 5 GWh/ano. Simultaneamente, a GG Power está gradualmente construindo uma cadeia de valor nacional, conectando sua capacidade de produção com fornecedores vietnamitas. Atualmente, mais de 20 unidades nacionais participam da cadeia de suprimentos da empresa, com o objetivo de atingir um índice de nacionalização superior a 52% até 2027. Essa direção também se reflete no processo de aprimoramento da linha de produtos ENERGY HUB S16 PRE. Em colaboração com a An Vinh, a GG Power modernizou o revestimento com linhas mais refinadas, aplicando soldagem robótica, jateamento abrasivo e pintura eletrostática a pó. A NCI Vietnam (fornecedora de componentes de longa data e parceira da Honda Vietnam ) é responsável pela produção das etiquetas em relevo 3D para o logotipo e o nome do produto, substituindo o método anterior de serigrafia. A participação de parceiros nacionais contribui para aprimorar tanto a qualidade quanto a aparência dos produtos de armazenamento de energia "Made in Vietnam". Além da capacidade de produção, a GG Power concentra-se na capacidade de fornecer componentes e suporte pós-venda. A empresa construiu um sistema de escritórios de representação e armazéns de componentes nas três regiões do Vietnã, conectando fabricantes com distribuidores, instaladores e usuários. A bateria de armazenamento ENERGY HUB S16 NEW, popular em todo o país, vem com garantia de fábrica de 5 anos e suporte no local; o processo de recebimento de relatórios e fornecimento de suporte técnico no local é organizado para reduzir o tempo de processamento e minimizar o tempo de inatividade. Com a GG Power, o armazenamento de energia em baterias "nacional" atende às necessidades de muitas famílias, com o suporte da capacidade de produção nacional e do ecossistema da cadeia de suprimentos. De uma equipe de engenheiros vietnamitas, uma fábrica em Hung Yen, a uma rede de parceiros e serviços pós-venda em todo o país, a empresa está gradualmente aproximando o ENERGY HUB S16 NEW de 14 milhões de famílias vietnamitas, contribuindo para ampliar sua capacidade de usar energia limpa de forma proativa.

artigo.texto: ROME — The debate continues over whether or not Demeter Land Holdings can build its proposed battery energy storage system (BESS) on Canal Street following the monthly meeting of the Rome Planning Board Tuesday evening. BESS are large battery facilities — most often using lithium-ion batteries — that plug into the power grid and withdraw power during the night to then give back to the grid during peak hours in the daytime. In October, the board decided that Demeter can present its site plan for its BESS proposal even though the Rome Common Council has issued a ban on future BESS proposals. It was ruled that Demeter was grandfathered in ahead of the ban. The site plan was met with more questions by the board at its meeting on Tuesday. Board members said they wanted to know more about proposed walls, fire safety and decommission plans, among other issues — while noting that the council's ban replaced a proposed 6-month moratorium that would have led to additional research on such projects. The Planning Board proposed hiring a third party to review the plan to provide that research. "I think there's still a lot of outstanding questions. There's a lot of uncertainties, maybes. I think a third party review would be beneficial to give us some additional insight," said board member Brittany Fumarola. "I think we as a board have to be able to make an educated decision, and I don't think we have the resources available to us at this time to do that." Demeter representative Mike Atkinson said the company is open to a third party review, but would like that to be part of a conditional approval on the project "that allows us comfort to continue investing in engineers" and other expenses. He said the company would like some indication that the project itself would be approved before investing further. Fumarola said a conditional approval "would defeat the purpose" of requiring the third party review. The proposed site plan was tabled again to bring in a third party review, and Atkinson said he would need to speak with his colleagues to see if they wanted to bother. Other projects: • A request from Friendly Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram at 5827 Rome-Taberg Road for an expansion project was approved. The car dealership is looking to do a “facelift of the existing building,” according to Marks Engineering, which will involve adding a service bay entrance, removing an old office building and reworking parts of the parking lot, among other additions. • An 84-lot subdivision of the proposed housing project at 7900 Turin Road in the Nascentia Neighborhood was approved. • The site plan for 12 proposed cottages at Beeches Manor was approved. The cottages, which will count as a campground, are expected to be used as rentals for weddings and other major events at the manor house, not as full residences. • Jerrit Williams, owner of Ret's Card Utopia, is looking to move into the former Dream City Mattress at 1239 Erie Blvd. West. A request to add a few more parking spaces to the rear of the building was approved. • Several requests from MetLife for the new building on Hangar Road — an expanded patio area, a service door and switching one generator to two — were approved by the board.

artigo.texto: New Delhi: Germany is keen to collaborate with Indian companies to manufacture solar panels and batteries in India as the two countries seek to strengthen energy security, expand clean energy capacity and reduce dependence on global supply chains, German Ambassador to India Jasper Wieck has said. Speaking to PTI on Tuesday on the sidelines of the 20th anniversary of the Indo-German Energy Forum (IGEF), Wieck said recent disruptions to global energy supplies had underscored the importance of developing domestic renewable energy resources. "Renewable energies are a very important part of the answer to the question of disruptions on energy supply worldwide," he said. The ambassador pointed to supply disruptions affecting Europe and Asia, including shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil shipments. The ongoing conflict involving Iran has heightened concerns over energy security and dependence on imported fuels. Wieck said expanding domestic renewable energy production would make India more resilient to external shocks while supporting its long-term energy independence. Highlighting opportunities for industrial cooperation, Wieck said German companies were ready to work with Indian manufacturers to establish domestic production capabilities in solar panels, batteries and other clean energy technologies. "Where do the solar panels come from? Where do all the batteries come from? In the future, they should be produced in India, and German companies stand ready to cooperate with Indian companies in order to make that happen," he said. He cautioned that India must avoid replacing dependence on imported fossil fuels with dependence on imported renewable energy equipment. The concern is significant given China's dominance in global solar manufacturing. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), China accounts for more than 80 percent of manufacturing capacity across the major stages of solar panel production. Wieck said stronger domestic manufacturing would complement India's Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative. "That means more self-reliance, more resilience, more independence, and that is very much in the philosophy of Atmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India)," he said. The ambassador described the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit 2026, inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday, as an important platform for strengthening business partnerships between the two countries. "I'm very proud that we have a very strong business delegation which came from Germany," he said. The summit offers Indian and German companies opportunities to explore joint manufacturing, technology partnerships and investments across the renewable energy value chain. Wieck also highlighted the role of the Indo-German Energy Forum, established in 2006, in advancing bilateral cooperation in renewable energy integration, energy efficiency, battery storage and green hydrogen. "The Indo-German Energy Forum has become a true success story," he said. The two countries launched the Indo-German Green Hydrogen Roadmap in October 2024 to deepen cooperation in hydrogen production, infrastructure, industrial applications and sustainable energy trade. Looking ahead, Wieck said the partnership would increasingly focus on building industrial capabilities and developing future clean energy supply chains. "I believe the most exciting chapters of our energy partnership are still ahead of us. Our ambition is to work with our Indian partners not only to expand renewable energy, but also to build the industries and value chains of the future," he said. The proposed expansion of manufacturing cooperation comes as India seeks to scale up renewable energy deployment while strengthening domestic supply chains for solar equipment, energy storage systems and green hydrogen technologies. artigo.texto: Octopus explores home battery storage tech with CATL and Amperex The MoU sees Ampace and Octopus explore combining their hardware and software, respectively, in next-generation smart home energy storage solutions. Octopus Energy has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Xiamen Ampace Technology Limited (Ampace) for domestic energy storage systems. Ampace is a lithium-ion battery technology company formed as a joint venture (JV) in 2021 between Chinese OEM CATL and Hong Kong-headquartered battery manufacturer Amperex Technology Limited (ATL). The MoU sees Ampace and Octopus explore combining their hardware and software, respectively, in next-generation smart home energy storage solutions. Octopus said that the agreement brings together “industry heavyweights”, combining CATL and Ampace’s battery chemistry and manufacturing with the UK company’s software platform, smart tariffs and virtual power plant (VPP) capabilities. The MoU will see the companies collaborate to produce “safer, greener and far more affordable home batteries”. Octopus currently offers a heat pump range and an EV charger range and has announced it will begin offering a home battery range called Octopus Nook. Octopus Nook will be available as a 2kWh plug-in system and a wall-mounted system at 5kWh or 10kWh, both of which will be stackable. No further information, such as the cell technology it will use, is available. According to Raymond Ye, president of residential energy storage systems at Ampace: “By bringing together CATL’s leadership in battery innovation, Ampace’s expertise in energy storage technology and manufacturing, and Octopus Energy’s strengths in digital energy management and services, we see great potential to accelerate innovation and deliver greater value to the market.” It could see Octopus offer European customers home energy storage systems using next-generation battery chemistries, building on Ampace’s research into sodium-ion technology, high-density cell designs, and ultra-long lifecycle systems. The partnership will initially look at opportunities in European markets where Octopus has retail energy offices. Octopus and CATL have previously collaborated in a JV for battery swapping for electric heavy-duty vehicles in Europe, covered on our sister site EV Infrastructure News. CATL actually originated from ATL, which was founded by CATL's chairman and founder, Robin Zeng, in 1999 as a manufacturer of rechargeable lithium batteries. artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Commercial energy intelligence company GridPoint is expanding its platform with on-site battery storage as U.S. electricity demand and costs, decarbonization commitments and grid risks drive facilities to implement battery energy storage systems at scale, the company said Wednesday. - The company is targeting 2 gigawatts of distributed storage capacity across its footprint, which includes more than 20,000 buildings. GridPoint’s platform manages HVAC, refrigeration, lighting and other controllable loads for multi-site operators. - The move comes as building owners turn to battery energy storage systems for resilience against grid disruptions, support for decarbonization commitments and as a way to reduce energy costs, says a joint report by the Urban Land Institute and UL Standards & Engagement. Dive Insight: Commercial electricity rates rose 42% across GridPoint sites over the past five years, the company said in a release. National battery storage capacity reached nearly 58 gigawatt-hours in 2025, the largest year of new capacity on record, and the market is expected to install an additional 500GWh of storage between 2026 and 2031, a 250% increase over the previous five-year period, according to the American Clean Power Association. Although battery investment has accelerated across utility-scale, large industrial and data center applications, commercial buildings remain “largely untapped,” creating opportunity, GridPoint said. “Despite this momentum, market adoption of BESS is still in its early stages,” ULI and ULSE say in their report, released Oct. 27. “Many property owners remain uncertain about where to start, which technologies fit their building type, and how local utility conditions affect financial returns. Community resistance in some jurisdictions, driven by fire safety concerns over large battery installations, has led to development slowdowns in select markets.” Even with these impediments, factors including grid stress, corporate decarbonization mandates and the growing premium for energy-secure assets suggest that on-site storage will be an increasingly standard component of real estate underwriting and development strategy in the years ahead, the report says. “GridPoint was founded on the belief that commercial buildings could play a much more active role in the energy system,” GridPoint co-founder and CEO Adrian De Luca said in a statement. “Over two decades later, the need for that is becoming much more urgent. We have the customers, the performance data, the building controls and the field infrastructure already in place to integrate storage as the next layer to transform our installed base into a much larger distributed energy resource.” GridPoint says adding battery storage to its platform allows operators to lower energy costs and add grid revenue. BESS reduces peak demand and charges by shifting when a facility draws power from the grid, while stored energy and flexible capacity can also be used to earn payments through utility and capacity programs so commercial facilities capture value when the power system needs capacity, the company says. Demand charges — utility fees based on a building’s peak electricity consumption — often represent 30% to 50% of a commercial electricity bill, according to research from the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The analysis estimates there are roughly 5 million commercial customers in the U.S. who can subscribe to retail electricity tariffs that have demand charges in excess of $15 per kilowatt, or over a quarter of the 18 million commercial customers nationwide. ULI and ULSE say that these charges are a particularly powerful driver of market adoption as they allow operators to shave peaks by discharging cheap stored energy during high-demand windows. Federal incentives are also still favorable for BESS, especially when considering energy community and domestic content incentives, while 13 states have also established procurement mandates aimed at boosting behind-the-meter storage. “Together these benefits can cut bills by up to an additional 15% at qualifying sites, on top of the 20% GridPoint customers typically save today,” GridPoint said. “As the grid becomes more strained, batteries can also provide resilience: in the past year alone, GridPoint customer sites in 26 states experienced 1,699 weather-driven outages.”

artigo.texto: Leilões de baterias impulsionam energia no Brasil Leilões de baterias previstos para dezembro colocam os sistemas de armazenamento no centro do planejamento elétrico e ampliam o debate sobre segurança energética, flexibilidade da rede e integração de fontes renováveis. O setor elétrico brasileiro se prepara para uma nova etapa de desenvolvimento com os primeiros Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade destinados à contratação de potência de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês). A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou os editais dos certames, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. A iniciativa busca ampliar a disponibilidade de potência no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), contribuindo para a segurança do fornecimento de eletricidade. Os leilões contemplam duas modalidades: uma com exigência de nacionalização dos equipamentos e outra sem esse requisito específico. Os contratos preveem o início do suprimento em agosto de 2028, com duração de 15 anos. A iniciativa também coloca em evidência as condições necessárias para desenvolver uma cadeia de fornecedores e serviços especializados em armazenamento de energia no país. A expansão das fontes renováveis e as mudanças no perfil de consumo de eletricidade aumentam a necessidade de recursos capazes de proporcionar maior flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico. Projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), reunidas no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE), subsidiam o planejamento da oferta e da demanda de energia no país. Nesse contexto, os sistemas de armazenamento podem absorver eletricidade e disponibilizá-la posteriormente, contribuindo para o atendimento da demanda em horários de maior consumo e para a integração de fontes cuja geração varia conforme as condições climáticas. Dados e análises da BloombergNEF (BNEF) também acompanham a evolução das tecnologias de armazenamento e seu papel nos sistemas elétricos. Entre as características das baterias está a capacidade de responder rapidamente a comandos operacionais, permitindo absorver ou fornecer energia conforme as necessidades da rede. A contribuição efetiva desses sistemas depende, entre outros fatores, do dimensionamento dos projetos, das condições de conexão e dos requisitos operacionais estabelecidos. A implantação de empreendimentos BESS envolve mais do que os módulos de bateria. Os projetos também dependem de conversores de potência, sistemas de controle e gerenciamento, proteções elétricas, monitoramento e infraestrutura de conexão. A compatibilidade entre esses componentes e o atendimento aos requisitos técnicos são aspectos importantes para a integração dos sistemas à rede. Nesse processo, as etapas de testes e comissionamento permitem verificar o funcionamento dos equipamentos e das interfaces antes da entrada em operação. Conforme as características de cada empreendimento, os procedimentos podem incluir ensaios de carga e descarga, verificações de desempenho, avaliação dos sistemas de proteção e validação da comunicação entre os diferentes componentes. A infraestrutura elétrica de suporte também pode ser necessária para a realização de ensaios e a verificação das condições operacionais previstas no projeto. A exigência de conteúdo nacional em uma das modalidades dos leilões reforça a discussão sobre o desenvolvimento da cadeia produtiva brasileira. Além da fabricação de equipamentos, a estruturação desse mercado envolve competências em engenharia, integração de sistemas, instalação, testes e suporte técnico, com a participação de diferentes fornecedores e prestadores de serviços. Para Jorge Moreno, diretor de Novos Negócios da Tecnogera, a integração dos componentes é um dos pontos de atenção na implantação dos sistemas de armazenamento. "Os projetos de armazenamento exigem uma visão integrada de engenharia. Além das baterias, é necessário considerar os inversores, os sistemas de controle, as proteções e a infraestrutura elétrica, garantindo que os diferentes componentes funcionem de forma coordenada. Os testes e a validação técnica são etapas importantes para verificar o atendimento aos requisitos de cada projeto", afirma o executivo. Com os primeiros leilões, o armazenamento em baterias passa a ocupar um espaço mais definido no planejamento da capacidade elétrica brasileira. A implantação dos empreendimentos dependerá dos aspectos contratuais, dos requisitos técnicos e das condições de conexão à rede, além da capacidade de fornecedores e integradores de atenderem às necessidades de cada projeto.

artigo.texto: Seminário promovido pelo Crea-PE analisa desafios da expansão dos data centers e o papel das energias eólicas e solares no Nordeste por Redação Jamildo.com Publicado em 04/11/2026, às 13h23 - Atualizado às 13h43 O Conselho Regional de Engenharia e Agronomia de Pernambuco (Crea-PE) promove, na próxima terça-feira (10), o seminário “Perspectivas da Energia Elétrica para o Nordeste e o Brasil”. O evento, aberto ao público, ocorre das 14h30 às 18h no auditório da Federação das Indústrias do Estado de Pernambuco (Fiepe), no Recife, com o objetivo de discutir a capacidade de atendimento da infraestrutura elétrica frente aos novos hábitos de consumo tecnológico. A discussão ganha relevância com a consolidação da região Nordeste como polos produtores de energia solar e eólica, associada ao avanço da Inteligência Artificial (IA) e à implantação de infraestruturas de alto consumo energético. Segundo projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), a demanda por energia voltada para data centers no Brasil deve registrar um crescimento médio de 13,7% ao ano até o ano de 2036. O presidente do Crea-PE, Adriano Lucena, destacou que o debate busca apresentar diagnósticos sobre a capacidade técnica e operacional do setor elétrico para absorver essa carga. De acordo com a organização do evento, o principal ponto crítico do sistema não reside na capacidade bruta de geração, mas nos desafios de transmissão, subestações e armazenamento para garantir a estabilidade do fornecimento frente às oscilações das fontes renováveis. A programação conta com palestras de especialistas do setor energético e ambiental, abordando temas como a evolução da matriz elétrica regional e nacional, os gargalos socioambientais e os riscos associados aos novos grandes consumidores. Entre os exemplos de expansão da infraestrutura digital na região está o projeto anunciado no Ceará para a instalação de um complexo de data centers orçado em R$ 200 bilhões, com demanda prevista de 200 MW. A mediação será realizada pelo coordenador técnico do seminário, José Carlos Miranda, com participação dos debatedores Emmanoelle Lira e João Bosco de Almeida, integrantes do Comitê Tecnológico Permanente do conselho. As inscrições para o evento são gratuitas e podem ser efetuadas previamente de forma online. O encontro busca reunir dados técnicos sobre a infraestrutura elétrica nordestina em um momento de transição da matriz energética nacional. A definição de diretrizes para o armazenamento e a transmissão de eletricidade é apontada por especialistas como fator crucial para viabilizar novos investimentos tecnológicos sem comprometer a estabilidade do abastecimento na região.

artigo.texto: The Trump administration is considering… Africa has officially established the… India plans to soon mandate state-owned utilities to add energy storage capacity to take advantage of the clean energy boom with reduced waste of generated power amid lagging storage capacity, a senior official said on Thursday. India’s federal authorities will require the state utilities to add storage capacity, Pankaj Agarwal, secretary of the Indian Power Ministry, said at the ongoing Bharat Renewable Energy Summit. India is working to launch additional clean energy tenders for energy storage, the official added. Grid, flexibility, and transmission constraints amid limited battery storage forced India to curtail as much as 118.6 gigawatts (GW) of solar and wind power capacity in September, data by India’s JMK Research & Analytics showed last month. “Key reasons for RE curtailment include demand-generation mismatches, transmission constraints, limited storage and grid flexibility, and seasonal overlaps between high renewable output and moderate demand,” JMK Research & Analytics said. India’s record renewable power generation and solar output were overshadowed by curtailments in July and August when India experienced power availability shortages. To address curtailments and a lack of flexibility in renewable energy sources, India plans to introduce, from July 2027, a regulation requiring developers of solar and wind energy projects to have battery storage installed at the sites. Earlier this week, India’s federal government approved a $1.54 billion (145 billion Indian rupees) program to fund the development of 92 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of grid-scale energy storage systems. The so-called Viability Gap Funding (VGF) Scheme aims to support the development of 92 GWh of yet-to-be-commissioned energy storage capacity, including 30 GWh battery energy storage systems, 60 GWh pumped storage projects, and 2 GWh emerging storage technologies. The support “will help improve the financial viability of these projects and accelerate the deployment of large-scale energy storage infrastructure in the country,” the government said. artigo.texto: Leilões de baterias impulsionam energia no Brasil AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 4 de novembro de 2026 O setor elétrico brasileiro se prepara para uma nova etapa de desenvolvimento com os primeiros Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade destinados à contratação de potência de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês). A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou os editais dos certames, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. A iniciativa busca ampliar a disponibilidade de potência no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), contribuindo para a segurança do fornecimento de eletricidade. Os leilões contemplam duas modalidades: uma com exigência de nacionalização dos equipamentos e outra sem esse requisito específico. Os contratos preveem o início do suprimento em agosto de 2028, com duração de 15 anos. A iniciativa também coloca em evidência as condições necessárias para desenvolver uma cadeia de fornecedores e serviços especializados em armazenamento de energia no país. A expansão das fontes renováveis e as mudanças no perfil de consumo de eletricidade aumentam a necessidade de recursos capazes de proporcionar maior flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico. Projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), reunidas no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE), subsidiam o planejamento da oferta e da demanda de energia no país. Nesse contexto, os sistemas de armazenamento podem absorver eletricidade e disponibilizá-la posteriormente, contribuindo para o atendimento da demanda em horários de maior consumo e para a integração de fontes cuja geração varia conforme as condições climáticas. Dados e análises da BloombergNEF (BNEF) também acompanham a evolução das tecnologias de armazenamento e seu papel nos sistemas elétricos. Entre as características das baterias está a capacidade de responder rapidamente a comandos operacionais, permitindo absorver ou fornecer energia conforme as necessidades da rede. A contribuição efetiva desses sistemas depende, entre outros fatores, do dimensionamento dos projetos, das condições de conexão e dos requisitos operacionais estabelecidos. A implantação de empreendimentos BESS envolve mais do que os módulos de bateria. Os projetos também dependem de conversores de potência, sistemas de controle e gerenciamento, proteções elétricas, monitoramento e infraestrutura de conexão. A compatibilidade entre esses componentes e o atendimento aos requisitos técnicos são aspectos importantes para a integração dos sistemas à rede. Nesse processo, as etapas de testes e comissionamento permitem verificar o funcionamento dos equipamentos e das interfaces antes da entrada em operação. Conforme as características de cada empreendimento, os procedimentos podem incluir ensaios de carga e descarga, verificações de desempenho, avaliação dos sistemas de proteção e validação da comunicação entre os diferentes componentes. A infraestrutura elétrica de suporte também pode ser necessária para a realização de ensaios e a verificação das condições operacionais previstas no projeto. A exigência de conteúdo nacional em uma das modalidades dos leilões reforça a discussão sobre o desenvolvimento da cadeia produtiva brasileira. Além da fabricação de equipamentos, a estruturação desse mercado envolve competências em engenharia, integração de sistemas, instalação, testes e suporte técnico, com a participação de diferentes fornecedores e prestadores de serviços. Para Jorge Moreno, diretor de Novos Negócios da Tecnogera, a integração dos componentes é um dos pontos de atenção na implantação dos sistemas de armazenamento. “Os projetos de armazenamento exigem uma visão integrada de engenharia. Além das baterias, é necessário considerar os inversores, os sistemas de controle, as proteções e a infraestrutura elétrica, garantindo que os diferentes componentes funcionem de forma coordenada. Os testes e a validação técnica são etapas importantes para verificar o atendimento aos requisitos de cada projeto”, afirma o executivo. Com os primeiros leilões, o armazenamento em baterias passa a ocupar um espaço mais definido no planejamento da capacidade elétrica brasileira. A implantação dos empreendimentos dependerá dos aspectos contratuais, dos requisitos técnicos e das condições de conexão à rede, além da capacidade de fornecedores e integradores de atenderem às necessidades de cada projeto. artigo.texto: AMD beats expectations as agentic AI sparks its data center revenue growth engines Shares of the chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc. rose more than 5% in late trading today after it delivered solid third-quarter earnings and revenue today, with data center sales almost doubling from a year ago. The company reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.09 per share, easily beating Wall Street’s forecast of $1.95 per share. Revenue for the period jumped 45% from a year earlier, to $13.38 billion, ahead of the $13.09 billion analyst consensus estimate. All told, the company’s net income for the quarter came to $3.47 billion, up 77% from the previous year when it posted a profit of just $1.96 billion. The star performer in the quarter was AMD’s data center business unit, which accounted for 64% of its overall revenue, up from just 47% one year ago. After spending years trying to compete with Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units for artificial intelligence market share, the company’s traditional central processing units or CPUs are suddenly back in vogue thanks to the emergence of agentic AI applications such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse. Autonomous AI agents can run much more efficiently on CPUs than they can on GPUs, boosting demand for the chips. Looking ahead, AMD expects its server revenue to double year-over-year in fiscal 2027, with AI growth likely to accelerate even faster than the company projected just three months ago. “Adoption is just starting and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work,” AMD Chief Executive Lisa Su (pictured) said on a conference call with analysts. AMD’s data center story isn’t all about CPUs, though. The company also sells GPUs, including bundles of them shipped inside data center-ready rack-scale systems called Helios, and that system’s popularity is growing fast. Su said Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC, Microsoft Corp., Oracle Corp. and Meta are all using AMD Helios systems in their data centers. Last week, Meta said its first Helion racks are already up and running as it revealed that AMD invested $1 billion in its latest equity offering. The chipmaker has also committed to a $5 billion investment in Anthropic, which last week revealed the long-awaited prospectus for its upcoming initial public offering. AMD delivered its latest earnings report just days after its rival Intel Corp. did the same. Intel also posted strong data center revenue growth, but its stock fell more than 30% on Friday on weak guidance and concerns about its ability to meet demand for its products. But Su said AMD had no such problems. Last month she made a high-profile visit to Taiwan, where she held meetings with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and a number of supply chain partners, and said after the trip that the company plans to substantially increase its supply in the coming year. “We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year,” Su added. AMD’s results will go some way toward reassuring investors who have become increasingly nervous about the direction of the AI industry and whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on it each year is actually going to generate a return on their investments, said eMarketer analyst Jacob Bourne. “The results are a test of AMD’s own performance and the broader AI trade, and its data center and revenue beats will encourage investors after the recent semiconductor selloff,” he added. Though AMD is far from immune to the recent volatility that has afflicted AI-related stocks, its future still looks increasingly rosy for now. “Demand for AI computing is not going to fall off a cliff, and AMD has the competitive products and major customer relationships to capitalize on that demand,” Bourne said. Strength in the data center unit is helping AMD to ride out difficulties in its traditional market for personal computers, which is the reason for Intel’s poor outlook. During the second quarter, global PC shipments fell 4% from a year earlier, with buyers dissuaded by the rising cost of components such as memory chips, according to data from Counterpoint Research. Along with Intel, AMD is a leading manufacturer of the x86 CPUs that power most of the world’s computers and laptops. The company reports PC chip revenue within a segment that also includes its chips for games consoles, and that unit saw its revenue decline 8% from a year earlier, to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue fell 40% from the previous year. For the current quarter, AMD is targeting revenue of abouot $17 billion at the midpoint of its guidance range, ahead of the Street’s $16.2 billion consensus estimate. The company also sees its gross margins coming in at 55%, just below the Street’s forecast of 55.3%. AMD was busy on the acquisition front during the quarter. In September it revealed it’s going to buy World Labs Inc. for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by the AI industry luminary Fei-Fei Li, has developed world models that can simulate 3D environments to support the training of intelligent robots and other physical AI applications. The company also acquired a startup called Taalas Inc. that makes specialized model-specific integrated circuits, which are essentially chips that can be customized to run a specific AI model more efficiently. That acquisition should help to boost AMD’s position in AI inference. AMD also invested in the AI image generation model maker Stability AI Ltd., which raised $76 million in funding in August. artigo.texto: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved Rs. 14,500 crore financial support for developing grid-scale energy storage systems (ESS) over FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31. The government has approved a Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme to support the development of around 30 GWh of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), 60 GWh of Pumped Storage Projects (PSPs) and 2 GWh of capacity through emerging energy storage technologies. Through this decision, the Cabinet aims to accelerate renewable energy integration, strengthen grid stability and ensure a reliable and affordable round-the-clock power supply. The introduction of a mandatory Domestic Content Requirement (DCR) for BESS projects is also expected to promote indigenous manufacturing and reduce import dependence. Scheme to Support 92 GWh of Energy Storage Projects Through the scheme, the Cabinet aims to support the development of 92 GWh of energy storage capacity across the country that is yet to be commissioned. The scheme will support the creation of new capacity equivalent to 170% of the country's present grid-scale energy storage capacity and help meet the estimated requirement of 411 GWh of grid-scale ESS capacity by 2031-32. The scheme aims to strengthen India's power sector infrastructure, facilitate large-scale integration of renewable energy and ensure round-the-clock power supply. It will also provide an impetus to domestic manufacturing of battery energy storage systems, reduce import dependence and enhance the country's long-term energy security. Scheme Targets 60 GWh of PSP, 30 GWh of BESS and 2 GWh of Alternative Storage Technologies The scheme envisages the development of 60 GWh of Hydro Pumped Storage Plant (PSP) capacity, 30 GWh of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity and 2 GWh through alternative energy storage technologies. The total estimated investment for these projects is ₹97,600 crore. The VGF support is expected to improve the financial viability of these projects and accelerate the deployment of large-scale energy storage infrastructure in the country. Energy storage capacity will be allocated through a tariff-based competitive bidding process. Public and private sector electricity distribution companies will be eligible for VGF support for BESS and Hydro PSP projects, while projects based on alternative energy storage technologies will be implemented by public and private sector entities. The scheme also aims to strengthen India's domestic energy storage manufacturing ecosystem through demand-side financial support and reduce dependence on imported components. BESS projects will be required to meet a minimum Domestic Content Requirement (DCR) of 40% to encourage domestic manufacturing, and create opportunities for Indian industry and complement existing supply-side incentives for battery manufacturing. By accelerating the deployment of grid-scale energy storage, it will facilitate greater utilisation of renewable energy, address the variability of renewable energy generation and reduce dependence on conventional generation to balance the grid and ensure round-the-clock power supply.

artigo.texto: Denza Z9GT: conheça a perua elétrica de luxo de 1.156 cv em impressões ao volante Denza Z9GT combina três motores elétricos, 1.156 cv e tecnologia de luxo em uma perua que acelera de 0 a 100 km/h em 2,7 segundos. Crédito: Estadão Ah, a busca por recordes... Elas costumam render fotografias de executivos sorridentes ao lado de números superlativos. Só que o que acontece antes nem sempre é emoldurado. No caso da BYD, a fabricante resolveu mostrar um capítulo menos glorioso do desenvolvimento do Yangwang U9 Xtreme. Um acidente que deixou o hipercarro elétrico destruído durante um teste de alta velocidade. O piloto passou por avaliação médica e não sofreu ferimentos graves, segundo a fabricante. Divulgadas pela companhia, as imagens mostram o modelo atingindo uma barreira de proteção e rodando pela pista, enquanto peças se espalham pelo caminho. Segundo relato publicado pelo site especializado Electrek, a equipe havia realizado passagens acima de 350 km/h e de 420 km/h. Na tentativa seguinte, a derradeira, o objetivo era superar os 450 km/h. Foi quando o ensaio terminou em uma sequência de impactos. Carro ficou destruído; piloto não sofreu ferimentos graves Embora as extremidades do U9 Xtreme tenham sofrido danos severos, a célula do habitáculo, construída em fibra de carbono, preservou o espaço ocupado pelo motorista. Segundo a BYD, exames médicos não identificaram lesões graves. O prejuízo material, de fato, impressiona, mas o desfecho para quem estava ao volante é a informação que realmente importa. A divulgação das imagens também não deve ser confundida com a data do acidente. De acordo com reportagem da imprensa australiana, a batida aconteceu durante a preparação para a tentativa que levaria o modelo à marca de 496,22 km/h, na Alemanha, em setembro de 2025. Mais de 3.000 cv O U9 Xtreme tem quatro motores elétricos, capazes de entregar potência combinada superior a 3.000 cv. A arquitetura elétrica trabalha com 1.200 volts, enquanto pneus semi-slick e suspensão recalibrada completam o pacote. A produção será limitada a 30 unidades. Em setembro de 2025, conforme mencionamos anteriormente, o alemão Marc Basseng levou o modelo aos 496,22 km/h no centro de testes de Papenburg. A próxima ambição é ultrapassar os 500 km/h em uma tentativa nos Emirados Árabes Unidos. Carregando ofertas...

artigo.texto: O governo e representantes dos setores de mineração, energia e transporte debateram, na quinta-feira (5 de novembro), como o mercado regulado de carbono pode abrir negócios para as três áreas, durante o primeiro painel da série CNN Talks (A Economia da Transição). A secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, Cristina Reis, afirmou que o governo pretende concluir até dezembro a primeira fase de implementação do sistema. Estamos implementando a lei. Essa implementação se dá em fases. A primeira, que termina agora em dezembro, é referente à publicação das principais normas, que são a base desse mercado. O modelo prevê limites de emissão para empresas de setores regulados, a partir de um Plano Nacional de Alocação. Quem emitir mais de 25 mil toneladas de CO2 equivalente por ano precisará negociar cotas conforme seu desempenho. Quem reduzir emissões além do exigido poderá vender cotas excedentes. Quem ultrapassar os limites vai precisar comprar ativos para compensar a diferença, a partir de 2030. Os números mostram o tamanho da aposta: é um mercado ainda em formação, mas que já movimenta somas bilionárias e tem prazo definido para funcionar em escala plena. O que cada setor diz sobre a transição Na mineração, a aposta é no chamado minério verde. "Essa indústria promete diminuir 95% sua emissão de carbono. Para que ela faça isso, precisa do minério verde", afirmou Rodrigo Uchoa, diretor de Comunicação Corporativa da Cedro Mineração. Publicidade A indústria brasileira já capta recursos para isso: em junho, Brasil e México receberam investimento de US$ 500 milhões para descarbonização industrial. Na energia, a Ultragaz aposta na diversificação. "O produto que vai ser utilizado é aquele que vai mais se adaptar àquela necessidade", disse a diretora jurídica e de Relações Institucionais da empresa, Fabiana Molina, que citou a expansão em biometano e energia elétrica. No transporte, a CNT rebateu a ideia de que descarbonizar prejudica a competitividade do setor. Vinicius Ladeira, representante da confederação, citou os caminhões movidos a biometano como alternativa já viável. O que acontece agora A primeira fase do mercado regulado deve ser concluída em dezembro, com a publicação das normas que vão orientar seu funcionamento. Enquanto o mercado interno avança, o Brasil negocia com a China a venda de créditos de carbono até a COP31, movimento que amplia o mercado externo desses ativos. O Eco Invest Brasil, citado por Cristina Reis, já fez cinco leilões. O quinto liberou R$ 13,2 bilhões para projetos sustentáveis.

artigo.texto: PRESS RELEASE: Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to EIA by operators. Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028. When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment. We publish unit-level generator inventory data based on our annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies. Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report Principal contributors: Glenn McGrath, Alex Mey

artigo.texto: Responsible data center rules can protect communities, create union careers Data centers have moved to the center of Illinois’ public debate, which is understandable given the role they play in today’s economy. Send an email, join a video call, check a medical record, or use an AI tool, and a data center somewhere is processing that information. The economy increasingly relies on these facilities, but their rapid growth also raises fair questions about electricity, water, land use and who pays for new infrastructure. Gov. JB Pritzker has called for responsible growth of data centers. For suburban communities, that should mean protecting ratepayers and natural resources while requiring projects to create good jobs, expand the tax base and make meaningful local investments. Labor organizations including IBEW Local 134, the Chicago Laborers’ District Council (LIUNA), International Union of Operating Engineers Local 150, and the Illinois Pipe Trades Association came together to form the Coalition for Responsible Data Centers because we believe data centers are a net benefit to Illinois. Nowhere is that more apparent than in the thousands of union jobs they create. Data centers employ electricians, operating engineers, laborers, pipefitters and other skilled tradespeople for years during construction and expansion. These are family-sustaining union careers with health coverage, retirement security and apprenticeship training. A multi-year construction job is not temporary to a tradesperson who moves from one major project to the next. It is a career and, for many young people, a path to the middle class without four-year college debt. Meta reports that its DeKalb project averaged 1,200 skilled trade workers on site at peak construction. Elk Grove Village estimates that, over the next five years, more than 1,000 people will work on data center construction in the village on an average day, supporting local businesses by purchasing fuel, eating at local restaurants, and spending money in the community. Beyond jobs, data centers create much-needed tax revenue for Illinois communities and provide relief for residents. Elk Grove Village reports that data centers generated approximately $60 million in property taxes for the 2025 tax year. In DeKalb, tax revenue from the Meta data center recently funded a new school downtown, while the city reports residents’ property taxes are less than half of what they would be without it. Those results should inform the statewide debate, but they should not end it. Responsible development means developers covering the infrastructure costs associated with their projects, supporting the additional power needed to serve them, using water efficiently, and meeting strong environmental standards. Above all, host communities deserve a voice early in the process and commitments that deliver tangible community benefits tailored to local needs, from workforce training and school funding to infrastructure improvements. Labor standards must be part of the framework. Illinois' Data Center Investment Program required qualifying projects to use a state-approved project labor agreement, meet investment and job commitments and comply with environmental or green-building requirements. The state stopped processing new applications in July, leaving new Illinois projects without the program’s enforceable labor standards. Pausing incentives or placing blanket moratoriums on development does not eliminate demand for digital infrastructure. It redirects projects, paychecks and local revenue to states that remain open to responsible development. Illinois is competing with neighboring states for these projects, while the United States competes with China for AI leadership. China is investing heavily in the infrastructure required to lead. Illinois should seize this opportunity to build on our terms, strengthen America’s competitive edge, and ensure our workers and communities share in the benefits. Policymakers have a better option. Responsible growth means protecting ratepayers and natural resources, supporting union jobs, and delivering community benefits. Developers that meet those expectations should have a clear path to build. Data centers are going to be built because the economy depends on them. Illinois has an opportunity to lead by pairing responsible development with lasting benefits for workers and host communities. That is what responsible growth should mean. • Neil Parish is director of the Coalition for Responsible Data Centers, a labor-led coalition promoting responsible infrastructure growth that supports local economies, protects ratepayers and natural resources, strengthens communities and creates meaningful career opportunities for working men and women through Illinois.

artigo.texto: The IRS may be the one government agency that can help guarantee local communities reap some financial benefit from the data centers landing in their neighborhoods. Yet this high-stakes responsibility arrives at the IRSâs door in the wake of historic budget and workforce reductions. The public debate on data centers has reached a boiling point. Community opposition to data centers is rising, while industry leaders and some public officials are responding with promises of economic windfall. President Donald Trump even wrote âlet Data Reignâ if communities want lower taxes and jobs. Much of this rhetoric is little more than predictions and aspirations. But there is a legally enforceable bargain between data center investors and local communities buried within the complexity of our tax laws: The private sector agrees to deliver good-paying jobs and apprenticeship opportunities if taxpayers agree to defray the cost of construction through federal tax breaks. Letâs unpack the tax break side of the bargain, which is so large it can turn a proposed data center from a âmaybeâ to âfull steam ahead.â The Clean Electricity Investment Credit provides a federal tax credit that starts at 6%. But if the investment meets prevailing-wage and apprenticeship requirements â Washington-speak for making sure construction workers receive good wages and training opportunities â the tax credit jumps to 30%. This means that for a qualifying $1 billion investment in clean-electricity generation or energy-storage technology, a $60 million tax break jumps to $300 million if the good-paying-jobs promise is made and kept. Thatâs a $240 million puzzle piece that makes the economic picture considerably more attractive for investors. On the community side of the bargain, taxpayers are promised good-paying, temporary construction jobs. That may seem like table scraps compared with the size of the tax break and the specter of a large, obtrusive data center that will remain in their neighborhood for decades, but itâs worth fighting for. A temporary job can put thousands of additional dollars into a familyâs pocket. Across thousands of workers and millions of labor hours, those wages represent real economic value. Regardless, a community that ends up with a data center â even over its objections â should at least be able to count on the other side of the bargain being honored. And itâs the IRS thatâs charged with holding companies to this promise. However, this same IRS has lost a quarter of its workforce â including 26% of its revenue agents, the auditors responsible for determining whether taxpayers have complied with the law. And just as itâs confronting this depleted capacity, the enforcement challenge is only beginning. A recent Government Accountability Office report found that the IRS expects to begin examining compliance with these wage and apprenticeship requirements as it audits 2024 tax returns. So itâs less than ideal timing that the IRS assumes the responsibility of scrutinizing a tax benefit of this size and importance. Compounding the challenge of a smaller team tackling the task, the requirements at issue arenât simple to police. Prevailing wages vary by geography and worker classification. Requirements can extend through contractors to include subcontractors. Apprenticeship rules govern labor hours and participation. And records must be kept that demonstrate the requirements were ultimately achieved. All hope isnât lost. First, companies financing these projects have a huge incentive to play by the rules. If they assumed a $300 million tax benefit into the economics of an investment, they had better be sure they qualified for it. Discovering later that they didnât appropriately comply with these complex requirements could produce an awfully large tax bill for them down the road. Second, Iâve learned over a long career in government, including as a former IRS commissioner, never to bet against the resiliency of IRS civil servants. I caution against doing so. But resilience is no substitute for resources. Communities hoping this bargain comes through would be better served by an IRS with the right tools to navigate the complexity, with knowledge of where to find the biggest dollars and risks, and with the training to deftly adjudicate whether taxpayers are eligible for the significant benefits theyâre claiming. As a result, the importance of the IRS work here could encourage political alignment on both sides of the aisle for increased resources in the next budget cycle. As IRS commissioner, I looked for stress points in our enormously complicated tax system. These were places where the dollars at stake and the consequences of non-compliance were significant enough to merit greater focus. When satisfying a complicated set of labor requirements can mean the difference between a $60 million tax benefit and a $300 million one, youâve found a stress point. Today, as a private citizen watching our nation and the world live in the AI era, I see a different type of stress point. Public officials and industry leaders will continue making big promises about the public benefits of AI and the infrastructure needed to support it. Many of those promises may never be legally enforceable. But this one is. What message are we sending about broader accountability and expectations for the AI industry if we fail to enforce a promise that actually has the force of law? Thatâs a stress point worth our collective focus. And in this case, defending it requires an IRS with the people and expertise to do the job. Danny Werfel has twice served as IRS commissioner, most recently from 2023 to 2025. He is now a senior fellow at the Johns Hopkins School of Government and Policy and a distinguished fellow at the Polis Center for Politics at Duke University, writing about the intersection of tax and policy. artigo.texto: On Nov. 3, voters in 10 states will vote on 41 ballot measures affecting local data center policy. A “yes” vote on 28 of these measures would limit data center development through policies such as bans or moratoriums. A “yes” vote on the remaining 13 measures would facilitate data center development through policies like zoning. Voters have already decided six measures this year and, in each case, a majority of voters favored greater limits on data center development, either by approving new restrictions or requirements or by rejecting a measure that would have facilitated or supported development. Including these measures, and three that voters will decide after Nov. 3, Ballotpedia is covering 50 local ballot measures in 13 states related to data centers this year. Ohio voters will decide on 21 measures, more than any other state. Illinois follows with seven measures. Maine voters will decide four, and Kansas voters will decide three. Voters in California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, and Wisconsin will decide one each. State policies on data centers State and local governments can affect data center construction through policy actions like permitting, zoning, and tax incentives. As of April 2026, 38 states had created tax incentives to encourage data center construction. State and local governments can also use some of these policy actions to prevent or limit data center construction, for example through moratoriums (temporary halts) on issuing permits for new projects. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) issued an executive order for the first state-level moratorium on data center construction. This one-year moratorium barred state regulators from issuing permits for new data centers expected to use 50 megawatts or more of electricity. Other states have also issued moratoriums on administrative measures like tax breaks and environmental permits for data center construction. What the Nov. 3 ballot measures would do Twenty-eight measures, if approved, would limit data center development: - Seventeen would ban data centers. Twelve of these would ban data centers above a certain size threshold. For example, one measure in Kansas would ban data centers using more than 25 megawatts of electricity. Five would ban all data centers. - Three would issue six-month moratoriums on data center development. One measure for a moratorium in Wells, Maine, would also retroactively "nullify any final permit, license, or other approval of a new or expanded Data Center issued by a municipal reviewing authority within 45 days of the effective date." - Two measures in Ohio would establish zoning regulations for unincorporated areas of the local jurisdictions. If the measures are successful and the areas are covered by zoning regulations, they would have to be zoned for a use consistent with data center construction (such as industrial) for a project to be built there. - One measure in Ohio would require voter approval for data center projects above land, water, and power use thresholds, while another measure in Wisconsin would require voter approval for a specific data center project if it costs more than $450 million. - A measure in North Dakota would require independent professional review and a public hearing for projects exceeding various land area, power, and water use thresholds, as well as projects requiring a major air quality permit. - A measure in Ohio would require data center developers receiving tax incentives to provide financial guarantees to the community. - Two non-binding measures in Illinois would express voter disapproval of data center projects. Thirteen measures, if approved, would facilitate data center development: - One measure in Nevada would add data centers as an approved use for a particular area of land. - One measure in Ohio would uphold a town agreement with a specific data center company. - Four measures in Wilmington, Ohio would rezone specific areas of land from residential to industrial uses, allowing data center construction at these sites. According to WCPO News, a specific data center company may build on this land if it is rezoned. - Seven non-binding measures in Illinois, New Jersey, and Ohio would express voter approval of data center projects. Voters in four states have already voted on six data center-related measures. - On March 10, voters in Canterbury, New Hampshire, approved a ban on data centers 83.6% to 16.4%. - On April 7, voters in Port Washington, Wisconsin, approved an initiative 66.4% to 33.6% requiring voter approval for the city to create a Tax Incremental District if projects in the district cost $10 million or more. - On June 2, voters in Monterey Park, California, approved a ban 88.3% to 11.7%. - On Aug. 4, voters in Augusta Township, Michigan, defeated a measure 89.6% to 10.4% that would have rezoned specific areas of land for a proposed data center. - On Aug. 11, voters in the village of Wrightstown, Wisconsin, defeated a nonbinding measure 87.3% to 12.8% that would have recommended village actions to support data centers. - On Sept. 8, voters in Nottingham, New Hampshire, approved a one-year moratorium on data center permitting 90.3% to 9.7%. On Dec. 1, voters in Clarksville, Arkansas will decide whether to uphold two different city bond issue ordinances intended to support a data center project. On Dec. 15, voters in Mandan, North Dakota will vote whether to ban data centers using 25 megawatts or more. Click here to learn more about data center-related ballot measures in 2026.
