artigo.texto: EDENenergy, a Germany-based startup that develops industrial BESS from second-life batteries, has delivered its first 70 kWh storage system to a customer. The system has been assembled from 112 used e-scooter batteries, each of which had been tested in a screening before it was connected. Power electronics that the founders had developed at Fraunhofer ISE make that possible without the batteries being taken apart. EDENenergy had assumed a remaining capacity of 80%, but some of the first 350 batteries that were tested retained well over 90%. Because worn modules can be replaced while the system is running, the company expects it to hold 70 kWh after 10 years. The first customers are to be medium-sized companies that already have a photovoltaic system, and systems of up to 300 kWh are planned next. EDENenergy delivers 70 kWh BESS built from used e-scooter batteries In Freiburg, Germany, the startup EDENenergy has handed its first industrial BESS to a customer after it had assembled the 70 kWh system from used e-scooter batteries. artigo.texto: Lithium-ion batteries and lithium-ion capacitors are no longer competing technologies but complementary ones, according to a comprehensive new review that maps how electrode materials, electrolyte chemistry, and the fragile interfaces between them jointly determine the performance, safety, and sustainability of modern energy storage. The review, published in Discover Electrochemistry, argues that the choice between a battery and a capacitor should follow the application: batteries for energy-dense electric vehicles and grid storage, capacitors for regenerative braking, rail transport, and industrial peak-power leveling where fast charge and discharge cycles matter more than total energy. The two devices differ fundamentally in how they store charge. A lithium-ion battery relies on reversible intercalation of lithium ions into both electrodes, with layered transition-metal oxide cathodes such as NMC and NCA delivering high specific energy but suffering from limited thermal stability and constrained resource availability. Phosphate cathodes like LiFePO4 trade some energy density for superior thermal and chemical stability, making them a preferred option for grid storage and safety-critical deployments. Lithium-ion capacitors instead pair a lithium-intercalating anode that stores charge through faradaic reactions with a porous carbon cathode that stores charge electrostatically through ion adsorption at the electrode-electrolyte boundary. Because the capacitor cathode does not change structure during operation, these devices achieve extremely high cycling stability and power density, though at lower energy density than batteries. Carbon remains the backbone of both technologies. Graphite still dominates commercial anodes thanks to its well-understood lithium intercalation chemistry and excellent cycling stability, but its limited capacity constrains further gains in energy density. The review documents how modified carbon architectures address this ceiling. Graphene added to activated carbon raised cathode capacity to 85.9 mAh g−1, while incorporating graphene into soft carbon lifted anode capacity from 247.9 to 286.6 mAh g−1; an LIC built with 10 percent modified graphene in both electrodes reached a peak energy density of 106.3 Wh kg−1 at a high-power operation of 4.4 kW kg−1. A pouch-type LIC with 1100 F capacitance and 30.8 Wh kg−1 energy density has also been demonstrated, suggesting a path toward practical application. Hybrid carbon scaffolds appear to hold a distinct advantage in long-cycling stability. Across nine systems cycled between 50 and 35,000 cycles, carbon-scaffolded architectures—including CNT/rGOR composites, hollow-carbon-sphere paired with activated-carbon dual-carbon cells, and graphene-modified soft-carbon pouch cells—retained more than 87 percent capacity at their maximum cycle counts. By contrast, a NiO-rGO composite paired with activated carbon retained only 72.1 percent after 10,000 cycles. A dual-carbon design using a hollow carbon sphere anode and superactivated carbon cathode at a 2:1 mass ratio achieved 68 Wh kg−1 at 30 kW kg−1 with greater than 92 percent capacity retention after 35,000 cycles. Metal-oxide-containing electrodes still hold an edge in specific capacity at a given cycle number, but the review concludes that carbon scaffolds currently lead in durability. Beyond carbon, transition-metal oxides, phosphates, and layered chalcogenides extend the achievable capacity range. TiO2, MnO2, Fe3O4, and V2O5 all undergo lithium insertion or conversion reactions that deliver higher capacities than carbon, though low electronic conductivity and sluggish ion diffusion limit practical performance unless the materials are nanostructured or hybridized with conductive carbon. Conversion-type oxides such as Fe3O4 and Co3O4 offer very high theoretical capacities but swell significantly during cycling; dispersing their nanoparticles in a conductive carbon matrix accommodates the volume change and preserves electrical connections. Layered sulfides like MoS2 and WS2 provide two-dimensional channels for lithium diffusion, and a MoS2/expanded graphite composite anode reported roughly 796 mAh g−1 at 0.5 A g−1 with strong high-rate performance. Silicon and lithium metal represent the most aggressive anode frontiers. Silicon offers extremely high capacity but suffers from volume expansion, low conductivity, and unstable solid-electrolyte interphase formation; a Si/activated carbon composite containing 10 to 30 weight percent silicon delivered an initial capacity of 1634 mAh g−1 and a stable 935 mAh g−1 after 400 cycles at C/10. Lithium metal carries an ultrahigh theoretical capacity of 3860 mAh g−1 and a low electrochemical potential of −3.04 V versus SHE, but repeated plating and stripping cause effectively infinite volume change, cracking the SEI and promoting dendrite growth that can pierce the separator and trigger internal short circuits. Surface modification of the separator through alloying with silver and silicon, forming Li-Ag and Li-Si alloys at the separator surface, has been proposed as a route to a new lithium metal-lithium alloy anode that mitigates these failure modes. Electrolyte chemistry emerges as the decisive factor for cycle life and safety. Aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety, nonflammability, low cost, and ionic conductivity of 10 to 100 mS cm−1, far exceeding the 1 to 10 mS cm−1 typical of organic carbonate systems, but their electrochemical stability window is constrained to roughly 1.23 V by water splitting. Water-in-salt electrolytes based on highly concentrated LiTFSI push that window to nearly 3 V by binding almost all water molecules into coordination shells around lithium ions, enabling a 2.3 V aqueous lithium-ion battery with stable cycling and high coulombic efficiency. artigo.texto: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput. Some of the largest AI infrastructure projects in the world are underway in Texas. A dramatic political shift could slow their construction—and deepen concerns about the economics of the AI boom. Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry's DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That's when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself. Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether. The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana. The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects. Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it. A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere. It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red. This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices. Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it. artigo.texto: Sungrow, a globally leading PV inverter and energy storage system provider, announced the Australian debut of its all-in-one residential energy storage system, PowerHarbour, at All-Energy Australia 2026. The platform responds to Australia’s booming home battery market, with accelerating uptake driven by the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries Program. Built around Sungrow’s “Triple W” value proposition — Win More, Waste Less, Work Faster — PowerHarbour combines intelligent energy management, flexible storage and simplified installation in an integrated solution. It aims to simplify energy management for Australian households, whether installing a new solar-plus-storage system or upgrading an existing setup. Integrated EV Charging: Empowering the EV and V2X Era Australia’s growing EV market is also reshaping household energy needs. According to the Electric Vehicle Council, battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles accounted for 34.5% of new vehicle sales in September 2026, highlighting the increasing relevance of home charging. Responding to this shift, the PowerHarbour Pro range introduces integrated EV charging in selected configurations*, bringing the inverter, energy management system and charging hardware together within a compact power core. Designed with future V2X applications in mind, it reflects Sungrow’s approach to connecting home energy management with electric mobility. High Flexibility & Scalability: Tailored for Australia’s Large Residential Loads For many Australian households, solar generation peaks during the day, with Solar Sharer offering free midday electricity in some regions; Household electricity demand often surges in the evening. To address this mismatch, PowerHarbour incorporates AI-driven energy management that analyses weather forecasts, solar predictions, consumption patterns, and electricity pricing to optimize energy scheduling—helping homeowners, especially those in larger properties with higher electricity demands, make the most of the energy they generate. Maximized PV Yields & Scalable Storage: Supporting up to 200% PV oversizing in applicable configurations and flexible battery expansion up to 120 kWh**. Seamless System Retrofits: For homes with existing PV systems, new-generation SMD battery modules can pair with compatible Sungrow storage inverters, including selected SHT and SHRS models. Calibration-Free Battery Expansion: The modular battery design supports expansion using compatible new and existing battery modules without requiring state-of-charge (SOC) calibration or pre-charging, helping simplify future capacity upgrades. Heavy-Duty Protection: Built for Extreme Australian Climates From coastal salt mist to harsh inland conditions, PowerHarbour is engineered for high durability across Australia’s environmental extremes: Rugged Enclosure: Features IP66 protection and C5 corrosion resistance to ensure reliable long-term outdoor operation. Compact Safety: Utilizes high-energy-density 314+ Ah battery cells, stackable modules up to 10 kWh with built-in battery optimizers, and a slim profile as narrow as 255 mm***. Optimized Installation: Streamlined for Local Clean Energy Contractors For Australian installers, PowerHarbour’s integrated architecture streamlines new installations and existing system upgrades. Its stackable battery modules and plug-and-play design help reduce installation complexity and additional wiring requirements. Stackable & Plug-and-Play Design: Stackable battery modules reduce installation complexity and additional wiring requirements. Integrated EnergyBridge: Applicable configurations include Sungrow’s compact EnergyBridge backup as standard, consolidating 5 key electrical functions into a single device to reduce separate wiring. Rapid Commissioning: Pairs with the plug-in iHomeManager Mini and upgraded iSolarCloud monitoring platform to simplify commissioning while offering homeowners real-time visibility into generation, storage, and consumption. Whisper-Quiet Performance: Featuring a high-thermal-conductivity substrate and optimized cooling design, it operates at noise levels below 30 dB(A), helping maintain a peaceful home environment. “Australia’s transition towards more connected home energy systems presents a significant opportunity for the industry. We believe the next step is not simply adding more features, but making solar, storage and energy management work together more effectively. With PowerHarbour, our focus is on bringing these technologies together in a practical, flexible solution that can support different household needs as the market evolves.” Said Scott Su, Technical Service Director, Sungrow Australia. As Australia’s residential energy landscape evolves, Sungrow aims to support smarter home energy systems through PowerHarbour and close collaboration with local distributors and installers, helping households meet changing energy needs and move toward a more sustainable energy future. * Built-in EV charging is available in selected PowerHarbour configurations. The SHSA-Pro model is marked as coming soon in the Australian product presentation. Product availability and V2X functionality are subject to local market release and compatibility requirements. **Up to 120 kWh storage capacity is achievable through supported combinations of the integrated unit and additional battery clusters. Battery stacking and expansion configurations are subject to the applicable product datasheet. ***The 255 mm depth applies to specific configurations. Dimensions may vary by model. artigo.texto: Modaso Energy, a company under MISA Group, has partnered with Zimbabwean renewable energy developer Tatanga Energy to develop the 278 MW Guruve-Mazowe (Chikonyora) Hybrid Renewable Energy Project in Mashonaland Central, Zimbabwe. The project is expected to become the country’s first utility-scale wind farm and the first utility-scale facility outside South Africa in sub-Saharan Africa to integrate wind, solar power and battery storage at a single location. The proposed project will comprise 128 MW of wind power capacity, 100 MWac of solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity and a 50 MW/100 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS). All three components will operate through a single 100 MW connection to the national electricity grid. The facility is expected to generate approximately 550 GWh of clean electricity annually, equivalent to around 5% of Zimbabwe’s total national power generation. Tatanga Energy initiated the development in 2021 and is responsible for local project operations, including land acquisition, community engagement, permitting and coordination with government authorities. Modaso Energy is leading the technical development and financial structuring. The company has redesigned the original wind-only proposal into an integrated renewable energy project combining three technologies. It is also overseeing electricity offtake arrangements, contracting and debt financing. MISA Group, headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, is providing financial backing and facilitating connections with international lenders and investors. Zimbabwe’s state-owned power utility, ZESA, is expected to serve as the primary electricity buyer. Negotiations are underway for the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) and Use of System Agreement. Meanwhile, Africa GreenCo, through its subsidiary ZimGreenCo, has signed Heads of Terms to purchase a portion of the project’s electricity under a long-term arrangement. Additional power could be traded through the Southern African Power Pool, providing access to regional electricity markets. Standard Bank has agreed to a debt term sheet and will act as the appointed lead arranger for the project’s debt financing. The development represents an estimated foreign direct investment of approximately USD 300 million. Financial close is expected in mid-2027, with construction scheduled to follow. The project is targeting commercial operations in 2029. The integration of wind, solar and battery storage is expected to improve electricity generation throughout the day by balancing the different production profiles of the technologies. The facility is designed to achieve an average grid capacity factor of more than 60%. According to the project details, this hybrid configuration could deliver approximately 40% more energy through a single grid connection compared with standalone renewable energy systems. The project is also expected to strengthen Zimbabwe’s electricity supply by reducing dependence on rainfall, Kariba Dam water levels and imported fossil fuels. Its battery storage system will provide fast-response grid support, helping improve power system reliability and flexibility. The development is expected to create around 1,000 construction jobs, with priority given to local workers, while introducing specialised skills in wind energy and hybrid power plant management. It is projected to avoid approximately 0.5 million tonnes of carbon emissions annually, contributing around 11% towards Zimbabwe’s National Renewable Energy Policy target of 2,100 MW by 2030. The project will also finance permanent road improvements along the turbine transportation route and requires no community resettlement. artigo.texto: The Union Cabinet on November 4 approved a Rs 14,500-crore viability gap funding (VGF) scheme to support the development of 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage capacity by FY31, as India looks to expand storage infrastructure to integrate a larger share of renewable energy into its electricity grid. The scheme will support the development of 60 GWh of pumped hydro storage capacity, 30 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 2 GWh of alternative storage technologies. The projects are expected to entail a total investment of Rs 97,600 crore, with the government providing financial support over FY27 to FY31. The scheme is aimed at improving the financial viability of large-scale storage projects, which are critical to managing the intermittent generation of solar and wind power and ensuring round-the-clock electricity supply. The proposed capacity addition is equivalent to 170% of India’s existing grid-scale energy storage capacity and will contribute towards meeting the country’s projected requirement of 411 GWh by FY32. According to the Central Electricity Authority's (CEA) National Electricity Plan, India will require 411.4 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2031-32, comprising 236.22 GWh of battery energy storage systems and 175.18 GWh of pumped hydro storage. The requirement is projected to reach 336.4 GWh by 2029-30. The 92 GWh capacity supported under the newly approved VGF scheme would meet around 22% of the projected storage requirement by FY32. Under the scheme, energy storage capacity will be allocated through a tariff-based competitive bidding process. Public and private sector electricity distribution companies will be eligible for viability gap funding for battery storage and pumped hydro projects, while alternative storage technology projects can be implemented by public and private sector entities. In a move to promote domestic manufacturing, battery storage projects supported under the scheme will be subject to a minimum domestic content requirement of 40%. The government said the provision is intended to encourage indigenous manufacturing, create opportunities for domestic industry and reduce dependence on imported components. The scheme is also expected to complement existing supply-side incentives for battery manufacturing and strengthen India’s energy storage supply chain. The government’s push for large-scale energy storage comes amid rising renewable energy capacity and the need for greater flexibility in the power grid. Storage systems can help absorb surplus renewable electricity during periods of high generation and release it when generation falls or demand rises, reducing the need for conventional power generation to balance the grid. The Cabinet said the scheme would strengthen grid stability, improve renewable energy integration and support the availability of reliable and affordable round-the-clock power. The latest approval builds on the government's earlier efforts to make battery storage projects financially viable through viability gap funding. In September 2023, the Cabinet approved a Rs 3,760-crore budgetary support scheme to develop 4 GWh of battery storage capacity, which was subsequently expanded to around 13.85 GWh as battery prices declined. In June 2025, the Power Ministry also extended VGF support for another 30 GWh of battery storage capacity, with Rs 5,400 crore in financial support from the Power System Development Fund. The latest scheme expands the government's support to include pumped hydro and alternative storage technologies.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 4 de novembro de 2026, às 16:20 Por Aramis Merki II* São Paulo, 04/11/2026 – A vitória democrata nas eleições de meio de mandato dos Estados Unidos abre uma nova frente de incerteza para os investimentos em inteligência artificial (IA), com perspectiva de maior regulação sobre o setor e restrições à construção de data centers. Embora a pressão possa desacelerar a expansão da infraestrutura tecnológica no país, empresas já estabelecidas, como Amazon, Microsoft e Alphabet, podem sair relativamente fortalecidas diante de barreiras maiores para novos concorrentes. As três empresas já têm grandes operações de computação em nuvem, capacidade financeira para investir e uma base de clientes estabelecida. Para a analista do setor de tecnologia do banco de investimento Needham & Companhia Laura Martin, novos entrantes no setor podem ter mais dificuldade de se estabelecer diante de uma nova realidade com regras mais restritivas. As ações das três grandes provedoras de computação em nuvem avançavam por volta das 15h28 (horário de Brasília). A Amazon, que oferece serviços de nuvem por meio da Amazon Web Services (AWS), subia 7,41%, enquanto a Microsoft, dona da plataforma Azure, registrava alta de 6,63%. A Alphabet, controladora do Google e provedora do Google Cloud, avançava 4,09%. Na contramão das gigantes, empresas menores ligadas à operação de data centers registravam perdas. Caso de destaque é a CoreWeave, com queda de mais de 8%. Entre as fornecedoras de componentes para essa infraestrutura, a Marvell caía 8,26%, enquanto a Micron perdia 5,46%. A Nvidia, principal fornecedora de chips para aplicações de inteligência artificial, recuava 1,25%. O novo cenário político traz perspectiva de maior fiscalização, audiências e questionamentos de congressistas sobre as práticas das grandes empresas de tecnologia. Para o gestor da Jupiter Asset Management, Amadeo Aletorn, o avanço democrata deve ampliar o escrutínio sobre as ações do governo e aumentar a pressão política por medidas regulatórias. O resultado também pode dificultar a execução da agenda do Executivo, mas não representa, por si só, uma mudança estrutural no ambiente de negócios, segundo a avaliação do gestor. Na avaliação da economista política da Aberdeen Lizzy Galbraith, o resultado eleitoral aumenta a possibilidade de iniciativas federais para regular a inteligência artificial e a construção de data centers. Entre as alternativas em discussão estão mudanças nos incentivos fiscais e regras mais rigorosas para licenciamento e planejamento de novos empreendimentos. O UBS aponta em relatório que, embora o terreno regulatório fique mais hostil para as big techs, com potencial volatilidade nas ações do setor, o resultado não altera de forma significativa os fundamentos das companhias no médio prazo. Para o banco, as incertezas políticas não são suficientes, neste momento, para justificar mudanças nas carteiras de investimento. O UBS também pondera que, no caso dos data centers, decisões de governos estaduais, como o do Texas, podem ter impacto mais direto sobre a expansão dos projetos do que eventuais medidas do Congresso americano. Pressão sobre data centers e Musk O analista de Wedbush Dan Ives avalia que a vitória democrata criará obstáculos à expansão da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) nos próximos dois anos, especialmente no Texas, que concentra parcela relevante dos projetos planejados. O Estado ganhou importância na discussão após a eleição da governadora democrata Gina Hinojosa, que defendeu uma moratória para novos projetos de data centers até que sejam aprovadas regras que ampliem as proteções às comunidades locais, além do fim de incentivos fiscais ao setor. O senador eleito James Talarico, também democrata, defendeu maior regulação sobre a atividade. A mudança política coloca sob pressão os planos de Elon Musk, que transferiu para o Texas as sedes da Tesla e da SpaceX. A companhia que fabrica foguetes anunciou em agosto um investimento de mais de US$ 16,8 bilhões na primeira fase da Terafab, uma fábrica de semicondutores no condado de Grimes, no Texas, planejada para atender à demanda por chips de IA e aplicações espaciais. O empreendimento recebeu a promessa de US$ 30 milhões em incentivos estaduais. Embora não seja um data center, o projeto integra a estratégia de expansão da infraestrutura de IA do empresário e pode enfrentar maior resistência política. A eleição também representou um revés político para Musk, que destinou recursos em apoio a candidatos republicanos. No mercado, as ações da SpaceX recuavam 4,03%, enquanto os papéis da Tesla caíam 2,50%. Contato: Merki@broadcast.com.br *Com informações da Dow Jones Newswires Veja também

artigo.texto: IOI Corporation Berhad has entered into a strategic renewable energy partnership with Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) and a consortium of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to jointly develop a 500 MWac large-scale solar photovoltaic project integrated with a 250 MW/1,000 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Malaysia. The project marks IOI’s first participation in a large-scale renewable energy development under the Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS). The agreement was signed on 3 November 2026 through IOI’s wholly owned subsidiary, Luminous Aspect Sdn Bhd, which entered into a joint venture and shareholders’ agreement with TNB Renewables Sdn Bhd (TRe) and CSP 500MW Sdn Bhd, representing a consortium of SMEs. The partnership aims to develop the solar and energy storage project through Bahau Energy Ventures Sdn Bhd, an established renewable energy development company. Under the agreed ownership structure, TRe, a wholly owned subsidiary of TNB, will hold a 70% stake in the project development company. Luminous Aspect will own 25%, while the consortium of SMEs will hold the remaining 5% shareholding. The agreement also includes a long-term land lease arrangement between the development company and IOI for approximately 1,300 acres of land located in Bahau, Negeri Sembilan. The project will be supported by a long-term renewable energy offtake agreement between TNB and DayOne Data Centres Limited, a Singapore-headquartered global digital infrastructure platform. Under the agreement announced on 11 June 2025, DayOne is expected to procure up to 500 MWac of renewable energy over a 21-year period to meet the electricity requirements of its data centre operations in Malaysia. The integration of a large-scale battery energy storage system is expected to support renewable energy supply by providing storage capacity and improving the availability of solar power. The project will also contribute to meeting the growing electricity demand from Malaysia’s expanding digital infrastructure and data centre industry. IOI Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Dato’ Lee Yeow Chor said the partnership provides an opportunity to participate in one of Malaysia’s largest solar and energy storage developments under the CRESS framework. He highlighted that the long-term offtake arrangement with an established data centre operator is expected to generate stable recurring income for IOI through its shareholding in the development company and its role as the project land lessor. The investment aligns with IOI’s Five-Year Strategic Roadmap for 2025–2029, which focuses on expanding its renewable energy portfolio and supporting Malaysia’s transition towards a low-carbon energy future. artigo.texto: The Lone Star State of Data Centers After Historic Texas Midterms The state’s vast supply of habitable and usable land combined with abundant rural and suburban real estate made it ideal for new projects. Sign up for smart news, insights, and analysis on the biggest financial stories of the day. As Jeopardy host Ken Jennings said after Tuesday’s midterm elections: “All my exes now live in Blexas.” Democrats won or led in every statewide race in Texas as of yesterday, turning the Lone Star State blue (hence Blexas) for the first time in three decades. The upset victory in the gubernatorial vote by Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who has pledged to hit the brakes on new data center approvals, could alter the trajectory of the state’s nation-leading buildout. But Texas’ AI infrastructure buildout isn’t buzzard bait just yet. Rodeo Circuit Breaker Until earlier this year, data center development in Texas was as hot as a two-dollar pistol. The state’s vast supply of habitable and usable land combined with abundant rural and suburban real estate made it ideal for new projects. A deregulated electricity market, its own independent power grid, and direct access to liquified natural gas allowed developers to negotiate large-scale power deals and build on-site energy sources. Throw in a pro-business regulatory climate along with no traditional state taxes, and you’re fine as cream gravy. With all those favorable factors, analysts at global real estate firm JLL earlier this year tipped Texas to leapfrog Virginia as the world’s largest data center market by 2030. Among those developing major campuses are Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Vantage. Recent months, however, saw momentum stall. Texans voiced increasing concerns about air quality, noise pollution, electricity and water bills. Polls showed a majority of them oppose having data centers in their communities. Politicians on both sides of the aisle responded. In September, outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott ordered a moratorium on new data center permits until the state grid operator completed an audit of existing applications. This put almost one fifth of the 253-GW data center development pipeline in all the United States at risk of delay. Hinojosa, set to be inaugurated on January 19, pledged to go one two-step further. She campaigned on a statewide moratorium on new data center approvals until the Texas Legislature passes a slate of new regulations: - Analysts at Jefferies wrote that a Hinojosa victory would mean greater political risk for data centers as it could translate to “tighter rules around who pays for grid infrastructure, water use and data center tax incentives.” However, they added it’s “more likely to increase development costs and requirements than materially restrict the Texas pipeline.” - At the federal level, Yorkville Ives Managing Director Dan Ives wrote Wednesday that “there is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation.” He forecasts the 800 to 1,000 data centers currently planned across the US will face delays and that 10% of them “will not happen now.” Portfolio Swings: The election results slammed cloud providers CoreWeave and IREN, which closed down 9.9% and 11.2%, respectively, on Wednesday. Data center cooling and temperature systems makers Vertiv and Modine fell 12.9% and 21.4%, respectively. But post-election certainty gave the more diversified Big Tech hyperscalers, which are financing the AI buildout, a boost: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft rose 3.3%, 6.1%, 1.4% and 6.7%, respectively.

artigo.texto: European quantum hardware manufacturer IQM Quantum Computers (Nasdaq: IQMX) and Volkswagen Group Innovation have demonstrated algorithmic and experimental advances in Quantum-Classical Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo (QC-AFQMC), reducing the classical post-processing runtime scaling of the hybrid electronic structure algorithm by an order of magnitude. Detailed in a technical study titled Quantum-Classical Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo at the Edge of Practicability, the collaboration achieved up to a 124× reduction in classical execution time for a 50-orbital benchmark and validated the workflow on IQM’s commercial Emerald superconducting processor. Simulating complex chemical reactions—such as the intermediate stages of lithium-air battery cycles—presents severe challenges for classical electronic structure methods due to the exponential growth of Slater determinants needed to capture strong electron correlation. Standard classical phaseless AFQMC (ph-AFQMC) mitigates sign problems by projecting random walks against a trial wavefunction; however, the method incurs systematic bias if that trial state cannot accurately represent multi-reference character. While QC-AFQMC leverages a quantum computer to prepare high-fidelity multi-determinant trial states, calculating the overlaps between the quantum trial state and classical Monte Carlo walkers has historically created a prohibitive computational bottleneck. Rather than using deep modified Hadamard test circuits (which the authors estimate would require millenia of execution time for even modest systems), the team utilized matchgate shadow tomography to reconstruct state overlaps via classical post-processing. By applying Aitken’s block transformation to resolve the singular Pfaffians that naturally arise in matchgate shadow kernels, the researchers reduced per-snapshot overlap evaluation from O(N4) to O(N3). Combined with algorithmic differentiation for Jacobian-vector products in the force bias calculations, the overall per-step classical post-processing dropped from Õ(N5.5) to Õ(N4.5). To validate the workflow against physical hardware noise, the team calculated the ground-state energy of an H8 hydrogen chain on the 54-qubit IQM Emerald processor, applying matrix product state (MPS) filtering to discard noisy measurements. The researchers then scaled the methodology in classical simulation to model the rearrangement pathway of a lithium superoxide dimer (Li2O4) across a 40-qubit active space, accurately capturing the activation barrier and transition-state geometry governing battery charge/discharge mechanisms. Technical whitepaper summaries are accessible on the IQM Case Study Portal here and the Direct Whitepaper Document here, with the full peer-reviewed preprint available on arXiv here.

artigo.texto: OS DATA CENTERS PODEM PREJUDICAR O PARTIDO DE TRUMP NAS ELEIÇÕES DOS EUA? O repórter do Estadão, Daniel Gateno, fala sobre o documentário “Estadão na América”, que estreia nesta semana, e o medo dos americanos com o futuro dos Estados. A OpenAI propôs renomear os data centers para “centros de computação de IA”, como parte de uma campanha de relações públicas para se alinhar ao possível novo cenário político dos Estados Unidos após as eleições de meio mandato, conforme noticiou a Axios na segunda-feira (2). A startup já até estreou a nova terminologia ao anunciar seu “Programa de Proteção da Rede Elétrica”. Um dos objetivos da mudança de nome é tentar melhorar a reputação das instalações em que funcionam a infraestrutura por trás das soluções de inteligência artificial. Além disso, a empresa estaria se preparando para lidar com um cenário regulatório mais hostil caso o Partido Democrata conquiste a maioria da Câmara e do Senado, como destaca a reportagem. Estratégia inclui mais mudanças Responsável por liderar a campanha, Chris Lehane, diretor de assuntos globais da OpenAI, disse que as eleições realizadas neste início de novembro funcionam como uma espécie de “trailer” para o que acontecerá daqui a dois anos. Para ele, a IA será um dos temas centrais da eleição presidencial de 2028 nos EUA. - Dessa forma, a dona do ChatGPT planeja influenciar o debate em torno da tecnologia, começando pela troca de nome dos data centers; - A inciativa liderada pela empresa inclui várias outras propostas, como a definição de “limites de velocidade para a IA”, com salvaguardas obrigatórias para frear modelos poderosos; - Fazer as pessoas enxergarem a IA como algo positivo para a sua carreira profissional e as tarefas do dia a dia também está nos planos; - Outra ideia é pressionar a Casa Branca para que os EUA desenvolvam padrões globais da tecnologia baseados em valores democráticos. Quanto ao uso do termo “campos de computação de IA”, a empresa acredita que ele descreve melhor o papel dos centros de dados. “São investimentos de longo prazo em computação, infraestrutura de energia e mão de obra qualificada”, disse um porta-voz da startup ao Business Insider. Porém, os esforços para tentar melhorar a imagem dos data centers junto à população não têm obtido bons resultados. Como lembra a publicação, uma pesquisa recente do Pew Research Center mostrou que 54% dos americanos consideram essas instalações prejudiciais ao meio ambiente. Críticas à proposta A ideia de chamar os data centers de campos de computação de IA não foi bem recebida por grupos ativistas como o PauseAI US. A fundadora da entidade, Holly Elmore, disse ao The Verge que a preocupação não é a nomenclatura e sim “os gigantescos e poluentes projetos de construção” associados às empresas de IA. Pensando de maneira semelhante, a diretora do Centro para Justiça Ambiental e Climática da NAACP, Abre’ Conner, tratou a mudança como uma solução ineficaz. “Mudar o nome não resolve o problema e dá a impressão de que a saúde das pessoas e o nosso meio ambiente são problemas de relações públicas, e não preocupações ambientais e climáticas”, disse ela à reportagem. Recentemente, Donald Trump mudou oficialmente o nome da IA no país e chamou de inimigo quem se recusar a adotar o termo superinteligência. Saiba mais nesta matéria. Com informações de Axios, Business Insider e The Verge.

artigo.texto: A rooftop solar system can generate electricity throughout the day, but maintaining access to that energy beyond daylight hours requires an effective storage solution. With energy storage becoming an increasingly important component of distributed solar systems, battery performance, scalability and intelligent management are key considerations for system owners. Polycab India’s PHLVB-5K-AG3 low-voltage battery is designed to address these requirements through lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology, offering a combination of energy storage capacity, operational flexibility and integration with hybrid inverter systems. Compact Storage with Practical Energy Capacity The PHLVB-5K-AG3 battery provides 5.12 kWh of nominal energy capacity and 5 kWh of usable energy under specified test conditions. Built using LFP battery cell technology, the unit is designed for applications prioritising solar self-consumption and backup power availability. Each battery operates as a standalone unit with a dedicated Battery Management System (BMS), supporting individual battery monitoring and management. Key Technical Highlights - Battery technology: Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) - Usable capacity: 5 kWh per unit - Maximum continuous discharge: 150A, up to 7.2 kW - Round-trip efficiency: ≥96% under specified test conditions - Cycle life: More than 6,000 cycles (70% end-of-life capacity) - C-Rate & Maximum continuous discharge: High Unique C-rate capability 1.5C , Suitable for EV Grade applications , supporting 150A continuous discharge , yielding up to 7.2 kW of power delivery per unit. Scalability for Evolving Energy Needs One of the battery’s notable characteristics is its modular expansion capability. The system supports parallel connection of up to 30 battery units, enabling a total storage configuration of up to 150 kWh. This flexibility allows users to begin with a smaller storage installation and expand capacity as their energy requirements increase. The battery supports multiple parallel connection arrangements, including direct connections, combiner boxes and busbars. The product is specified for on-grid, on-grid with backup, and off-grid applications, providing flexibility across different solar power system configurations. Intelligent Battery Management and Operational Reliability Beyond storage capacity, the battery incorporates features intended to simplify monitoring and system operation. CAN communication supports interaction with compatible inverter systems, while remote diagnosis and updates can be performed through the inverter. An automatic reboot function following undervoltage conditions adds another layer of operational convenience. The battery supports continuous discharge currents of up to 150A and a maximum continuous charging current of 90A. Actual operating performance depends on factors including temperature, battery state of charge and the connected inverter model. With a specified cycle life exceeding 6,000 cycles at 70% end-of-life capacity, the LFP-based system is positioned for applications requiring repeated charging and discharging over extended operating periods. Installation Flexibility and Warranty Support The battery weighs approximately 44 kg and supports wall-mounted installation, with floor-mounted and standard 19-inch rack configurations available through optional accessories. It carries an IP20 ingress protection rating, making appropriate installation conditions an important consideration. The product literature also lists IEC 62619 and IEC 63056 among its safety standards. Polycab specifies a 10-year warranty when the battery is paired with its single-phase hybrid inverters and an eight-year warranty when combined with its three-phase hybrid inverter range, subject to applicable terms. With its modular architecture, integrated battery management and flexible installation options, the PHLVB-5K-AG3 provides a storage solution for solar applications seeking to improve energy utilisation and backup power availability. artigo.texto: Data centers do Texas têm futuro incerto após vitória democrata nos EUA O setor de centrais de processamento de dados do estado norte-americano do Texas foi mergulhado na incerteza pela promessa da governadora eleita, a democrata Gina Hinojosa, de reprimir seu crescimento acelerado. Hinojosa, que derrotou o republicano Greg Abbott em uma virada dramática ontem, reforçou essa mensagem nas últimas semanas de sua campanha, pedindo uma moratória em todo o estado e prometendo, dias antes da votação, "impedir a invasão dos data centers". Com abundante oferta de energia, terrenos relativamente baratos e uma política favorável aos negócios, o Texas se tornou uma das regiões mais promissoras para o desenvolvimento de centrais de processamento de dados nos EUA nos últimos anos. Grandes empresas de tecnologia, incluindo Meta, Google e Microsoft, anunciaram importantes projetos no estado nos últimos dois anos. Mas a crescente oposição das comunidades rurais e um aumento repentino nos pedidos de conexão à rede elétrica estadual levaram até mesmo o governador republicano, Abbott, a ordenar uma pausa nas licenças para data centers no início deste ano. Antes da eleição, Hinojosa afirmou que levaria a repressão às centrais de processamento de dados um passo adiante, proibindo todas as aprovações até que a assembleia legislativa aprovasse leis "para proteger os texanos, de modo que eles tenham voz ativa na decisão de se e como essas instalações serão feitas em nossa comunidade". O setor já vinha sofrendo pressão antes das eleições de ontem. Em 3 de agosto, Abbott tornou-se um dos primeiros governadores republicanos dos EUA a suspender a conexão de novos data centers à rede elétrica do estado. Ele também ordenou uma auditoria abrangente dos projetos, com foco na demanda de energia, nos impactos ambientais e nos incentivos fiscais concedidos aos desenvolvedores. A postura representou uma mudança drástica na abordagem de Abbott em relação aos centros de dados, que ele havia apoiado apenas alguns meses antes. Na época em que o Texas suspendeu a conexão de novos data centers à rede elétrica, a ERCOT, operadora estadual da eletricidade, informou que estava monitorando pedidos de conexão de mais de 400 gigawatts de projetos de centrais de processamento de dados, o que equivale à energia necessária para abastecer todo o sul dos EUA. A reviravolta de Abbott também colocou em risco dezenas de bilhões de dólares em projetos planejados no Texas e levantou dúvidas sobre se centenas de milhões em depósitos de garantia pagos pelos centros de dados que buscavam se conectar à rede no estado serão devolvidos. Desde que ordenou a auditoria, Abbott também tomou medidas para penalizar retroativamente as violações relacionadas ao uso de água pelos data centers e proibiu temporariamente o estado de emitir licenças ambientais para os projetos. Abbott, no entanto, não decretou uma moratória formal sobre os data centers, o que Hinojosa prometeu fazer. Certas medidas de Abbott também tinham prazo de validade curto, como a proibição das licenças ambientais e a auditoria, que deveria ser concluída no final de 2026. Cerca de 42% dos eleitores registrados em uma pesquisa da Reuters/Ipsos publicada nesta semana afirmaram que limitar a construção de centros de dados para inteligência artificial era uma questão muito importante ou a mais importante para eles. Cerca de 76% dos eleitores em todo os EUA afirmaram se opor à construção de um novo data center em sua comunidade, de acordo com uma pesquisa de boca de urna da NBC e da SSRS. Antes da votação, uma pesquisa da Universidade de Houston realizada em outubro revelou que 79% dos prováveis eleitores do Texas apoiavam limites ao número de instalações de processamento de dados que podem ser construídos no estado.

artigo.texto: Home › Investment & Trading ›Pentagreen, Candi Solar Announce USD 50 Mn Financing Partnership for 400 MWp Solar + BESS in India Pentagreen, Candi Solar Announce USD 50 Mn Financing Partnership for 400 MWp Solar + BESS in India Pentagreen Capital and Candi Solar have signed a USD 50 million financing partnership to develop 400 MWp of solar and battery energy storage projects for SMEs across India. November 06, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey Pentagreen Capital and Candi Solar have signed a USD 50 million financing partnership to support approximately 400 MWp of solar and battery energy storage projects in India, targeting underserved small and medium enterprises (SMEs). Pentagreen Capital, manager of the Green Investments Partnership (GIP) under Singapore’s Financing Asia’s Transition Partnership (FAST-P) initiative, will provide financing to support Candi Solar’s expansion across India’s commercial and industrial (C&I) segment. The partnership will also support Candi’s objective of more than doubling its operational capacity to exceed 1 GW over the next 24 months, Candi Solar said in a statement. It further added that the facility will finance rooftop, ground-mounted and open-access solar installations paired with battery energy storage systems (BESS) across key business hubs in India. These projects are expected to generate 560 GWh of renewable energy annually, serve 227 C&I customers, of which 78 percent are SMEs, and avoid an estimated 397,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually. Commenting on the partnership, Marat Zapparov, CEO of Pentagreen Capital, said, “India’s growing energy demand and need to reduce oil imports make the transition to clean energy both a strategic and an economic priority. Together, we are unlocking finance for projects that make clean energy accessible to an underserved segment, help businesses stabilise their energy costs, and strengthen India’s energy security.” Fabio Eucalipto, Co-founder and Director of Candi Solar, said, “By combining rooftop and ground-mounted open-access solutions with flexible financing, we can deliver tailored energy solutions at scale. Our partnership with Pentagreen is an important milestone and the first building block in our next phase of growth.” The partnership is expected to expand clean energy access among SMEs, which account for 31 percent of India’s GDP and 35 percent of its manufacturing output, but remain underserved in renewable energy adoption, Candi Solar stated. The company further added that under Candi’s turnkey shared-value model, customers preserve their capital and pay only for the clean energy generated, while Candi manages engineering, construction and long-term operational performance. Its flexible, performance-linked solar and storage solutions are designed to help businesses reduce dependence on conventional energy sources, manage energy costs and limit exposure to fluctuations in diesel and grid electricity prices. Candi Solar plans to use the financing alongside additional shareholder commitments and an equity round planned for early 2027 to accelerate its expansion and bring clean energy to more businesses across India, the company stated. artigo.texto: AlphaESS é nomeada fabricante de sistemas de armazenamento de energia de nível 1 pela BloombergNEF pelo quinto trimestre consecutivo no quarto trimestre de 2026. AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 5 de novembro de 2026 NANTONG, China, 5 de novembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A AlphaESS foi mais uma vez reconhecida como fabricante global de armazenamento de energia de nível 1 pela BloombergNEF (BNEF) em sua lista do 4º trimestre de 2026, reafirmando seu histórico estabelecido em projetos de armazenamento de energia e presença crescente no mercado global de escala de serviços públicos. Neste trimestre, a BNEF introduziu critérios de viabilidade financeira mais rigorosos, exigindo que os fornecedores de equipamentos de armazenamento de energia demonstrem experiência em projetos, respaldada por financiamento sem recurso de pelo menos dois bancos comerciais, em projetos elegíveis. A inclusão contínua da AlphaESS oferece aos desenvolvedores, investidores e parceiros de EPC uma referência adicional ao avaliar potenciais fornecedores de armazenamento de energia. Expansão de projetos de grande escala para serviços públicos em toda a Europa A AlphaESS continua a desenvolver projetos de armazenamento de energia em grande escala em toda a Europa, com desenvolvimentos recentes na Lituânia, Áustria e Alemanha totalizando 200 MWh. Na Lituânia, um projeto de armazenamento de energia em baterias de 120 MWh com o sistema Aster 5000 da AlphaESS passou com sucesso pelo Teste de Aceitação de Fábrica (FAT), com o equipamento pronto para envio. Na Áustria, a AlphaESS forneceu o sistema de baterias do lado CC para um projeto de 30 MW / 60 MWh em Hörsching. Integrando geração de energia solar, armazenamento em baterias e carregamento de caminhões elétricos, o projeto também oferece suporte a serviços de rede e energia de reserva. Sua seção de serviços de rede de 40 MWh entrou em operação em setembro de 2026. Na Alemanha, a AlphaESS está fornecendo o sistema de baterias do lado CC para um projeto de 20 MWh na Baviera, projetado para balanceamento de rede e arbitragem de energia, com comissionamento planejado para 2027. Equipado com a tecnologia Aster 5000. Apoiando seu portfólio de escala de utilidade, o Aster 5000 da AlphaESS é um sistema de armazenamento de energia de bateria refrigerado a líquido alojado em um contêiner de 20 pés, oferecendo aproximadamente 5 MWh de capacidade por unidade. Com gerenciamento térmico inteligente, um sistema avançado de gerenciamento de baterias e proteção de segurança multicamadas, ele foi projetado para implantação flexível em aplicações de grande escala, incluindo estabilização da rede e integração de energia renovável. Em conjunto, esses projetos e tecnologias demonstram a crescente capacidade da AlphaESS em fornecer soluções de armazenamento de energia escaláveis para diversas necessidades de mercado. Sobre a AlphaESS Fundada em 2012 e sediada em Nantong, na China, a AlphaESS fornece soluções de armazenamento de energia para os setores residencial, comercial, industrial e de serviços públicos. Presente em mais de 130 países e regiões, com mais de 400 pontos de atendimento em todo o mundo, a AlphaESS está comprometida em apoiar uma infraestrutura de energia confiável e flexível. artigo.texto: OS DATA CENTERS PODEM PREJUDICAR O PARTIDO DE TRUMP NAS ELEIÇÕES DOS EUA? O repórter do Estadão, Daniel Gateno, fala sobre o documentário “Estadão na América”, que estreia nesta semana, e o medo dos americanos com o futuro dos Estados. A OpenAI iniciou, nesta quinta-feira (5), uma nova campanha para tentar melhorar a imagem dos data centers de inteligência artificial perante a população dos Estados Unidos. A iniciativa ganhou importância após as eleições de meio de mandato que tiveram o Partido Democrata obtendo vitórias expressivas, inclusive em estados considerados essenciais para a construção dessas instalações. O objetivo é reduzir a rejeição popular contra os planos da indústria de IA de erguer novos centros de dados em todo o país. Para tanto, as políticas atualizadas da startup preveem uma maior aproximação com as comunidades que receberão a infraestrutura, mostrando como a obra pode beneficiar os moradores. Acesso a contratos e fonte de empregos Uma das estratégias que a dona do ChatGPT passa a adotar é não usar mais acordos de confidencialidade com autoridades públicas ao negociar possíveis locais para futuras instalações. A empresa afirma que isso tornará as conversas mais transparentes, reduzindo a desconfiança em torno do negócio. - Normalmente, esses acordos restringem a divulgação de detalhes, impedindo o compartilhamento de informações essenciais; - Apesar da mudança, a OpenAI ressalta que determinados dados comerciais proprietários permanecerão em sigilo; - Os moradores também poderão conferir os planos de construção e os potenciais impactos do empreendimento para o trânsito local, a energia e os ruídos envolvidos; - Além disso, a empresa vai tratar os data centers como uma importante fonte de empregos, abrindo oportunidades para as pessoas que residem nas proximidades. Segundo Chris Lehane, diretor de assuntos globais da OpenAI, uma instalação que funcionará no estado de Ohio vai gerar cerca de 2.500 empregos de longo prazo. O salário médio anual oferecido aos contratados será de US$ 80.000, o equivalente a cerca de R$ 438.000 pela cotação atual. “Esses projetos não são o tipo de data center que as pessoas imaginavam, que eram uma espécie de caixa-preta em um pasto, que contribuíam muito pouco em termos de utilidade econômica para os comunidades onde estavam localizados”, disse o porta-voz da companhia, durante coletiva. Possíveis restrições A nova estratégia da startup também será primordial para lidar com as mudanças no cenário político do país. Candidatos que prometeram barrar novas licenças para data centers foram eleitos em estados como Texas, Ohio e Georgia, o que pode afetar os planos da indústria de IA. Um dos trunfos da OpenAI é o próprio Lehane, que afirmou ter uma “vasta experiência” com os Democratas ao ser questionado sobre como lidaria com as restrições aos data centers defendidas por alguns membros do partido. Ele trabalhou como porta-voz do governo de Bill Clinton e na campanha do vice-presidente, Al Gore. Como parte da iniciativa, a empresa decidiu renomear seus centros de dados. Saiba mais detalhes nesta matéria. Com informações de Reuters.

artigo.texto: Incentivos fiscais e transição energética impulsionam data centers no Brasil Nova lei estimula infraestrutura digital com energia limpa, enquanto especialistas alertam para a necessidade de adaptar a rede e garantir eficiência Clique aqui e escute a matéria Visando uma projeção maior no mercado de infraestrutura digital, o Brasil sancionou uma lei (nº 15.504/2026) que concede incentivos fiscais para empresas instalarem ou ampliarem centros de processamento de dados (também conhecidos como data centers) no País. A medida, que suspende por 5 anos os tributos na compra de equipamentos para empresas que usam energia renovável e estão em dia com o Fisco, interessa não apenas ao setor tecnológico, mas também ao energético. Para o engenheiro e diretor de operações da Qair Brasil Gustavo Rodrigues Silva, o crescimento dos data centers e da inteligência artificial (IA) exigirá uma grande adaptação do sistema elétrico brasileiro. "São enormes concentrações de cargas críticas, com demandas elevadas e contínuas, operando 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, e exigindo padrões excepcionais de confiabilidade", detalha. O especialista afirma que a segurança e a estabilidade do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) devem ser os principais impactados pela concentração de demanda: há a probabilidade de sobrecarregar a infraestrutura de transmissão, agravar congestionamentos, comprometer margens de segurança operativa e ampliar os efeitos de eventuais contingências, com reflexos sobre outros consumidores. "Não basta termos energia disponível. Precisamos garantir que o sistema seja capaz de entregá-la continuamente, sem colocar em risco sua própria estabilidade", alerta. Para o processo de adaptação do sistema elétrico, Gustavo elenca como necessários novos modelos de planejamento e operação, com destaque para as microgrids, integrando geração renovável, armazenamento e sistemas inteligentes de controle, capazes de proporcionar maior autonomia e resiliência aos empreendimentos e reduzir sua exposição e seus impactos sobre o SIN. Além disso, o engenheiro avalia como indispensável o desenvolvimento do ambiente regulatório, com segurança jurídica, previsibilidade e regras claras sobre responsabilidades, acesso à rede e investimentos em infraestrutura. Potencial do Nordeste e atração de investimentos Gustavo afirma que o Brasil possui condições excepcionais para se tornar um hub global de data centers sustentáveis, especialmente pelas estruturas de fontes renováveis em sua matriz elétrica. Ele destaca, ainda, o potencial do Nordeste como um protagonista estratégico por combinar a disponibilidade de energia eólica e solar com a localização geográfica privilegiada, conectividade internacional por cabos submarinos e infraestrutura em desenvolvimento. Atualmente, a região conta com uma base consolidada de empreendimentos já operacionais em diferentes capitais. Em Fortaleza, destacam-se a estrutura Tier III e ponto neutro da Angola Cables na Praia do Futuro, a unidade da Ascenty voltada para colocation, além do edge data center Big Lobster, pertencente à Tecto Data Centers/V.tal. A HostDime mantém uma das principais instalações de alta disponibilidade da região em João Pessoa, complementada por estruturas em Recife, enquanto operadoras como a Claro/Embratel operam data centers corporativos e de rede distribuídos entre Recife, Salvador e Fortaleza. Em paralelo, uma nova onda de investimentos está em desenvolvimento e promete transformar o perfil tecnológico nordestino. O principal destaque em construção é o mega data center da Omnia, localizado no Complexo do Pecém (Caucaia, no Ceará), projetado para abrigar a infraestrutura de dados da ByteDance (proprietária do TikTok) com capacidade inicial de 200 MW. No entanto, para atrair investimentos da nova economia digital, o especialista elenca a necessidade da elaboração de um planejamento energético integrado, da dedicação de investimentos em infraestrutura e da garantia de segurança jurídica e de políticas públicas capazes de conectar a expansão digital à transição energética. "Enquanto muitos países precisam ampliar o uso de combustíveis fósseis para acompanhar o crescimento da inteligência artificial, o Brasil parte de uma condição privilegiada", ressalta. O especialista também defende que o Brasil não pode se limitar a ser mero fornecedor de capacidade energética bruta para serviços digitais estrangeiros, sem agregar valor local. Para ele, o País deve assegurar investimentos que promovam inovação, empregos qualificados, o fortalecimento das cadeias produtivas locais e o desenvolvimento regional com responsabilidade socioambiental. Para Gustavo, o País deve utilizar suas relações comerciais e diplomáticas para atrair investimentos internacionais e construir parcerias que vão muito além da instalação de data centers - especialmente na região Nordeste. "Essas parcerias podem envolver financiamento verde, transferência de tecnologias de armazenamento, refrigeração eficiente, automação e gestão inteligente de energia, além de investimentos conjuntos na modernização das redes elétricas. Entretanto, não podemos atrair grandes consumidores de energia sem assegurar que a infraestrutura necessária acompanhe esse crescimento, preservando a confiabilidade do Sistema Interligado Nacional", detalha. Resfriamento dos data centers entra no debate Um tópico que tem atraído a atenção de toda a sociedade é a quantidade de água utilizada no resfriamento de data centers, que gera uma quantidade significativa de calor em espaços reduzidos. Mas, de acordo com Gustavo, o consumo elevado de água não é uma condição inevitável para o funcionamento dos data centers. O especialista afirma que já existem tecnologias comerciais avançadas, como refrigeração líquida em circuitos fechados, sistemas de dissipação de calor a seco e soluções híbridas, capazes de reduzir drasticamente a necessidade de água. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Ações de empresas de data centers caem após vitória democrata no Texas elevar risco de desaceleração Publicado 04/11/2026 • 14:32 | Atualizado há 17 horas O que os bilionários de Wall Street estão dizendo sobre a vitória esmagadora dos democratas nas eleições de meio de mandato Trump fala sobre salão de festas da Casa Branca enquanto Vance atribui derrota republicana à guerra contra o Irã Empresas hyperscalers e Apple disparam após resultados eleitorais eliminarem incerteza dos investidores Bilionários da tecnologia sofrem com a vitória esmagadora dos democratas sobre os republicanos Eleições nos EUA: primeiras urnas fecham enquanto o controle da Câmara e do Senado permanece indefinido KEY POINTS Foto: pexels Ações de empresas de centros de dados de IA ficaram sob pressão após democratas conquistarem vitórias expressivas nas midterms. As ações de empresas ligadas a centros de dados de inteligência artificial (IA) ficaram sob pressão após os democratas, favoráveis à imposição de moratórias sobre a expansão dessas estruturas, conquistarem vitórias expressivas nas eleições de meio de mandato dos Estados Unidos, inclusive em importantes polos tecnológicos, como o Texas. Os mercados já esperavam que os democratas conquistassem a Câmara dos Representantes e possivelmente assumissem o controle do Senado. No entanto, a vitória democrata na disputa pelo governo do Texas foi considerada um grande revés por analistas. A democrata Gina Hinojosa, que defende a implementação de uma moratória imediata para a construção de centros de dados no estado, derrotou o governador republicano Greg Abbott, que tentava a reeleição. Segundo o Wells Fargo, 27% da capacidade de geração de energia prevista para os centros de dados planejados nos Estados Unidos está concentrada no Texas. As eleições de meio de mandato devem desacelerar o ritmo de expansão dos centros de dados em todo o país, afirmou Dan Ives, sócio da Yorkville Ives & Co., em nota divulgada na manhã desta quarta-feira (04). “Não há como suavizar o fato de que os democratas assumirem o controle, especialmente do Senado, criará grandes obstáculos para a legislação de IA e tecnologia em Washington nos próximos dois anos”, afirmou. Ele acrescentou que o resultado da eleição no Texas foi a “maior preocupação” da noite para os investidores de tecnologia e para o mercado de inteligência artificial, já que cerca de 25% a 30% da capacidade de geração de energia destinada aos centros de dados deverá vir do estado. As ações da SpaceX, empresa de Elon Musk, recuaram 7%. A vitória democrata no Texas representa um grande revés para o bilionário, que apoiou fortemente candidatos republicanos no estado, onde também estão sediadas suas empresas Tesla e SpaceX. Musk gastou pelo menos US$ 474 milhões nas eleições de meio de mandato, um valor recorde, e destinou US$ 224 milhões apenas ao Texas. No estado, o candidato republicano ao Senado, Ken Paxton, e o governador Greg Abbott foram derrotados pelos democratas. A SpaceX está atualmente desenvolvendo projetos que somam vários gigawatts de capacidade para centros de dados, incluindo instalações no Texas. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC “Centros de dados no espaço parecem bastante atraentes agora”, publicou Musk na rede social X nas primeiras horas desta quarta-feira (4), em referência a seus planos ainda especulativos de construir infraestrutura de inteligência artificial fora do planeta. As empresas de infraestrutura de computação em nuvem CoreWeave e Iren recuaram 7% e 6%, respectivamente. A concorrente Nebius Group caiu 3%, enquanto a Oracle perdeu 4,3%. As ações da Nvidia também operavam em leve queda. Já as gigantes de tecnologia Alphabet, Meta e Microsoft contrariaram a tendência predominante e registraram alta. A vitória democrata no Texas acrescenta pressão sobre o mercado de inteligência artificial, que vinha liderando a alta das bolsas. O índice Nasdaq-100 entrou em território de correção no fim de outubro, em meio a preocupações de que o crescimento dos investimentos em centros de dados pelas grandes empresas de computação em nuvem, conhecidas como hyperscalers, e pelas gigantes privadas de IA OpenAI e Anthropic estivesse perdendo força. Leia também: Bilionários da tecnologia sofrem com a vitória esmagadora dos democratas sobre os republicanos “ Acreditamos que a reação do mercado de ações às eleições de meio de mandato depende principalmente do resultado da disputa pelo governo do Texas. Uma vitória democrata poderia representar um evento de risco extremo negativo para o mercado de IA”, alertou Ohsung Kwon, estrategista-chefe de ações do Wells Fargo, em relatório divulgado nesta semana. Os democratas também conquistaram ou mantiveram o governo de outros estados importantes para o setor de centros de dados, como Geórgia, Pensilvânia e Ohio. Segundo estimativas do Wells Fargo, a Geórgia concentra 7% de toda a capacidade de geração de energia prevista para os centros de dados planejados nos Estados Unidos. Ohio e Pensilvânia representam 5% cada. Michael Hartnett, estrategista de investimentos do Bank of America, havia alertado no início deste ano que uma vitória democrata no Senado, combinada à conquista do governo do Texas, poderia provocar uma forte queda de mais de 10% nas ações até o fim do ano. “Os centros de dados passaram de uma ferramenta popular de desenvolvimento econômico em 2024 e 2025 para uma espécie de pária quando as campanhas eleitorais de meio de mandato ganharam força”, escreveram nesta semana os analistas da equipe de políticas de Washington da Optimal Advisory. “É provável que as eleições de meio de mandato enviem uma mensagem aos governos locais e estaduais de que existe uma vantagem política em bloquear, atrasar e/ou elevar os custos dos centros de dados.” 🔷 Canal 562 ClaroTV+ | Canal 562 Sky | Canal 592 Vivo | Canal 187 Oi | Operadoras regionais 🔷 TV SINAL ABERTO: parab

artigo.texto: Babaamaajimowinan (Telling of news in different places) In at least 38 jurisdictions voters rejected or restricted data centers, delivering a major setback to the AI industry. Voters in at least 38 jurisdictions across the country passed bans or restrictions on data centers Tuesday, reflecting the widespread public revulsion to the facilities and adding to the growing pushback on the ambitions of the artificial intelligence industry. Data center construction also suffered setbacks in several states that are hot spots for the projects, as Democratic candidates promising to curb the rapid proliferation of the computing warehouses won governors' races. Many local ballot measures limiting data centers passed with overwhelming support. In Joliet Township, Illinois, nearly 80 percent of voters moved to restrict data centers. So did more than three-quarters of voters in Hubbard, Ohio, near where President Donald Trump touted his administration's embrace of America's rapid AI build-out in a rally last month.

artigo.texto: India will require 888 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2035–36 to support its expanding renewable energy base and maintain grid reliability, according to the report India’s Energy Storage by the International Solar Alliance (ISA). The report identifies project execution, financing, market development, domestic manufacturing and regulatory coordination as key factors that will determine whether the country can meet its growing storage requirements. The Central Electricity Authority’s (CEA) projections indicate that the requirement comprises 321 GWh of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and 567 GWh of Pumped Storage Projects (PSP). The report also outlines a requirement of 2,380 GWh by 2047 under its stated scenario, in line with the country’s broader Viksit Bharat 2047 ambitions. The report highlights that while India has made progress in establishing a policy framework for energy storage, the next phase will depend on converting procurement activity into commissioned projects and creating a commercially sustainable ecosystem. It calls for coordinated action across planning, regulation, investment, grid integration and manufacturing to accelerate deployment. Execution and Market Reforms Key to Scaling Storage A key concern highlighted in the report is the gap between energy storage tenders and their conversion into operational assets. Although India has pursued tenders for Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE), solar projects combined with BESS, and standalone battery storage, the conversion of awarded capacity into Power Sale Agreements has remained a challenge. The report recommends moving beyond single application procurement models focused primarily on energy arbitrage. Future tender structures, it says, should incorporate multiple revenue streams, capacity support provisions and stronger enforcement mechanisms for Power Sale Agreements. It also calls for the development of market mechanisms that allow storage assets to participate in ancillary services and other grid support functions. Revenue stacking, which enables storage projects to earn from multiple applications, is identified as an important step towards reducing dependence on government support and improving project viability. Three Scenarios Map India's Storage Deployment Path The report presents three possible deployment scenarios: Policy as Stated, Accelerated and Constrained. These account for differences in policy implementation, investment, technology adoption, manufacturing growth and project execution. Under the Policy as Stated scenario, India's storage requirement is projected at 888 GWh by 2035–36 and 2,380 GWh by 2047. The Accelerated scenario estimates that capacity could reach 1,000–1,150 GWh by 2035–36 and 3,000–3,500 GWh by 2047, supported by faster project execution, stronger investment, revenue stacking and domestic manufacturing. The report clarifies that these are scenario based estimates rather than official targets. It also notes that a definitive 2070 storage projection would require further modelling, given the uncertainty surrounding future technology costs, policy continuity and global supply chains. Report Sets Out Phased Actions Through 2070 The report's recommendations are organised across immediate, near term, medium term and long term priorities. Actions proposed by 2027 include strengthening certification and enforcement, resolving classification related ambiguity for containerised BESS, mandating grid forming inverters in new BESS tenders and completing the allocation of the second tranche of Viability Gap Funding. For 2027 to 2030, the focus shifts to enabling revenue stacking, opening ancillary services to storage, reforming Energy Storage Obligations through state specific targets and establishing a regulatory framework for behind the meter storage. The report also recommends setting up a National Energy Storage Testing Centre. Between 2030 and 2035, the proposed priorities include transitioning towards market driven procurement and achieving more than 40 per cent domestic value addition in BESS. Longer term recommendations extend to strengthening India's domestic value chain, expanding battery recycling and positioning the country as a supplier of energy storage technologies and expertise. High Dependence of PSP: A Worry Achieving the ambitious target of 888 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2035–36, including 567 GWh through Pumped Storage Projects (PSPs), may come with several challenges. Land acquisition, environmental and forest clearances, availability of suitable sites and water resources, and geological uncertainties could potentially delay project execution. PSPs involve high upfront investments, long construction periods and complex civil works, which may lead to cost overruns. Another major challenge could be ensuring the commercial viability of these projects. Uncertainty around storage tariffs, revenue models and returns on investment may make it difficult to attract private developers. Meanwhile, the remaining storage requirement will also depend on the expansion of battery energy storage systems, which face challenges related to domestic manufacturing capacity, critical mineral imports, battery costs and recycling. While India's storage ambitions are crucial for integrating higher renewable energy capacity into the grid, the real challenge will lie in translating the proposed project pipeline into financially viable and operational projects within the stipulated timeline.
